en: Preface to the Translation of the Laṅkāvatāra Assembly:
This scripture has been translated four times in total; three of these translations currently survive.
The first was translated by Guṇabhadra of the Liu Song dynasty into four fascicles, titled the *Laṅkāvatāra-ratna-sūtra*. The second was translated by Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei...
The translation by [Dharmakṣema] consists of ten fascicles and is titled the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*. The third version was translated by Śikṣānanda and Fuli et al.
during the Tang dynasty into seven fascicles and is titled the *Mahāyāna-laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*.

Since it is the subtle, supreme, and true definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) spoken by the Buddha, it is called the "Chapter on the Essence of the Buddha’s Words" (*buddha-vacana-hṛdaya-parivarta*). Bodhidharma came from the West and transmitted it to his two [disciples].
The Patriarch said, "I have the four fascicles of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* which can serve as a seal for the mind; it is the Song edition. For this reason, its transmission alone has become prominent.
However, its characters are concise and archaic, making it difficult to read. In the past, the monk Faching said to Chan Master Zhengshou:
'This is the realm of noble wisdom; it is not something that those with coarse minds can enter. If you wish to enter it, you must employ skillful means.'"

Zhengshou said, "I wish to hear the explanation of this. Nan replied, "You should try taking the seventeen fascicles of the Wei and Tang translations and place them beside the four fascicles of the Song translation.
If you verify their spiritual vision and examine their aesthetic flavor, you will be able to enter into this sutra.
Zhengshou acted according to these words; after approximately one month, his doubts and obstructions were melted away like ice. Alas! This—
The necessity of translating these assemblies cannot be overstated. Yuan Ke, a man from Mount Jing, traveled in his youth to the gate of Chan Master Yuzhi.

He profoundly investigated the essential tenets of the *Śūraṃgama-sūtra* and had already read the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*. Having extensively explored the three translations, he attained a subtle resonance with their core principles.
He then consulted with his assembly of disciples, intending to synthesize their various versions into a single work; however, he did not complete this compilation.

Later, while observing the summer retreat in the mountains together with Lu Siguang (Lu Guangzu), they discussed his original aspiration. Siguang remarked that it would be better to compile the text according to the annotated edition of Master Le, so as to avoid errors and contradictions.
The Venerable Master nodded in agreement, and thus this compilation was completed. It first publishes the Song dynasty translation, followed by those of the Wei and Tang dynasties.
Appended below is the title: *The Lankāvatāra Sūtra Assembly Translation*. This spring, the lectures were held at T'ian-ning Temple in the prefectural city.
At that time, while on leave, I was able to find an opportunity to join the assembly as a listener.
Subsequently, I solicited donations from lay believers to fund its carving into woodblocks, so that it may serve as the permanent property of T'ian-ning Temple.
Dharma said: "Five hundred years after this sutra was translated, it will degenerate into a study of names and forms.
Those who read, interpret, and translate it should directly realize their own minds; be careful not to mistake the pointing finger for the moon and fall into the foresight of the Patriarchs.
Thus, the Dharma-gift of the Superior One is truly vast!"
On the day the Buddha attained Enlightenment in the spring of the eighth year of the Wanli era, the *gengchen* year, Feng Mengzhen, having bathed in perfumed water and prostrated himself,
composed this first volume (upper part) of the *Lengqie abaduoluo bao jing* (The Precious Sutra of Laṅkāvatāra), a collaborative translation.
Originally translated by Guṇabhadra, the Tripiṭaka Master from India during the Song dynasty;
retranslated by Bodhiruci, the Tripiṭaka Master from India during the Wei dynasty;
and subsequently translated by Śikṣānanda, the Tripiṭaka Master from Khotan during the Tang dynasty.
Translated by the śramaṇa Yuánkē of Zhōngdū during the Ming Dynasty. Chapter One, Part One:
The Essence of the Mind of All Buddha-Speech.
Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was dwelling on the peak of Mount Laṅkā on the shore of the Southern Sea, adorned with various kinds of precious flowers.
To adorn [the assembly], he was accompanied by a great community of bhikṣus and a multitude of great bodhisattvas who had come from various and diverse buddha-fields.
These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possessed mastery over immeasurable samādhis and sported with supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva Mahāmati was their leader; all the Buddhas had poured water upon his head in the consecration of sovereignty.

He skillfully understands the meaning of the objective realms manifested by his own mind. He universally manifests according to the various types of beings through their diverse minds and forms, employing immeasurable gates of liberation.
He has attained ultimate penetration into the five dharmas, the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds of selflessness.
[Wei Translation] Thus have I heard. At one time the Bhagavān was staying on Mount Malaya at the edge of the great ocean, within the city of Laṅkā.
That mountain was composed of various precious substances;

the various jewels were interspersed so that its radiance blazed forth like a golden mountain illuminated by hundreds of thousands of suns. Furthermore, there were immeasurable flower gardens and fragrances.

The trees are all groves of precious incense; when a gentle breeze blows upon them, shaking the branches and moving the leaves, hundreds of thousands of wondrous fragrances are simultaneously diffused, and hundreds of thousands of exquisite sounds are simultaneously emitted.

Layered crags wind and turn in every direction, where there are countless celestial halls, numinous chambers, and grottoes, all composed of various jewels, transparent inside and out, reflecting the radiance of the sun and moon.
They could no longer appear; for these were all the places where the sages and holy ones of antiquity contemplated the Dharma as it truly is and attained the Way.
Together with a great assembly of bhikṣus and a multitude of great bodhisattvas, they had all come from various buddha-fields in other directions to gather there.
These bodhisattvas were fully endowed with immeasurable sovereign samādhis and supernormal powers.
Roaming and transforming through the world with the vigor of his powers, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati was the foremost among them.
All the Buddhas poured water upon his crown, conferring upon him the rank of a Buddha. He thoroughly understood the meaning of taking one’s own mind as the objective realm.
According to the various minds and various mental forms of sentient beings, and following their diverse thoughts and varied inclinations, he employed immeasurable gateways of liberation.

He universally manifests himself according to those who are to be delivered and according to what they ought to see. He thoroughly understands the five dharmas, the self-nature, consciousness, and the two kinds of selflessness, attaining ultimate penetration.
[Tang Translation: Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was dwelling on the summit of Mount Malaya by the shore of the great ocean.
In the city of Laṅkā, he was together with a great assembly of bhikṣus and a great assembly of bodhisattvas, all of whom had come to this gathering from various buddha-fields.
Those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas sported in immeasurable sovereign samādhis, supernormal powers, and various strengths; the bodhisattva-mahāsattva Mahāmati was their leader.
All Buddhas have poured water upon their heads. They skillfully understand the meaning that objective realms are manifestations of one's own mind;

they manifest various forms according to the minds of sentient beings to subdue them through skillful means; and they have fully mastered the five dharmas, the three natures, the various consciousnesses, and selflessness.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāmati, together with the Bodhisattva Maitreya, having traveled through all the buddha-fields,
rose from his seat by the Buddha’s spiritual power. He bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and praised the Buddha in verse.
[Wei Translation] At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva, together with all the other Mahāmati Bodhisattvas,
traveling through all the Buddha-lands, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, rose from his seat, adjusted his robes,
knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and praised the Buddha in verse.

[The Tang Translation: At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāmati, together with the Bodhisattva Mātṛceṭa, having traveled through all the buddha-fields, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, and knelt with his right knee upon the ground.
Joining his palms toward the Buddha, he bowed with reverence and spoke these verses:
"The world is free from arising and ceasing, like flowers in the sky; Since wisdom finds neither existence nor non-existence, you give rise to great compassion."
All phenomena are like illusions; they are far removed from mind and consciousness. Wisdom finds neither existence nor non-existence, yet one gives rise to great compassion.
Far removed from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism, the world is ever like a dream. Wisdom finds neither existence nor non-existence, yet one gives rise to great compassion.
[Wei Translation] The world is free from arising and ceasing, like flowers in the sky; existence and non-existence cannot be apprehended.

With the Buddha’s wisdom and great compassion, he contemplates that all phenomena are like illusions, far removed from mind, thought, and consciousness; existence and non-existence cannot be apprehended.

The Buddha’s wisdom and great compassion observe that one is far removed from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism; the world is like a dream, wherein existence and non-existence cannot be apprehended.
The Buddha’s wisdom and great compassion observe thus.
The world is free from arising and ceasing; it is like flowers in the sky. Since wisdom perceives neither existence nor non-existence, one gives rise to the mind of great compassion.
All phenomena are like illusions, transcending mind and consciousness. Since wisdom perceives neither existence nor non-existence, [one gives rise to the mind of great compassion].

They give rise to the mind of great compassion. They remain far removed from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism. The world is ever like a dream; wisdom finds neither existence nor non-existence.
Thus they give rise to the mind of great compassion.
Knowing that persons and phenomena lack selfhood, and that afflictions and their latent tendencies are eternally pure and signless, one gives rise to the mind of great compassion.
[Wei Translation: Purified by the two kinds of selflessness, the afflictive obscurations and the cognitive obscurations cannot be found as either existent or non-existent;
this is the observation of the Buddha’s wisdom and great compassion.
Knowing that persons and phenomena lack selfhood, and that afflictions and their latent tendencies are eternally pure and signless, one gives rise to the mind of great compassion.
There is no nirvana for all things; there is no Buddha who attains nirvana, nor is there nirvana within a Buddha. It is far removed from both the awakening and that which is awakened.
Whether existence or non-existence, both are entirely transcended.

[Wei Translation: The Buddha neither enters nor ceases; he likewise does not abide in nirvāṇa. Having departed from the dharmas of the perceiver and the perceived, he is free from both existence and non-existence.

The Buddha does not abide in nirvāṇa, nor does nirvāṇa abide in the Buddha. Far removed from both the awakening and that which is awakened—whether existent or non-existent—the Sage observes with tranquility;
this is the departure from birth, and it is called non-appropriation. In this life and in future lives, there is peace.
[Wei Translation] If one contemplates the Buddha in this way—as tranquil and free from arising and ceasing—that person, in this and future lives, will be free from defilement and without grasping.
[Tang Translation] The Dharma-body is like an illusion or a dream; how can it be praised? Knowing it to be without intrinsic nature and without birth, one then...
To praise the Buddha by name is not to see the Buddha, for the Buddha is devoid of the characteristics of sense bases and objects.

How could one praise or revile the Sage? If one sees the Sage as peaceful, detached, and free from birth, that person will, in this and future lives, be free from attachment and have nothing to grasp.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāmati, having praised the Buddha in verse, spoke his own name: "I am named Mahāmati;
I have attained mastery in the Mahāyāna. Now, with one hundred and eight points of meaning, I respectfully inquire of the Most Honored One."
[Wei Translation] At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, having praised the Buddha with verses in accordance with the Dharma, spoke his own name:
"My name is Mahāmati; I wish to penetrate the Mahāyāna. I now respectfully submit one hundred and eight questions to the Unsurpassed Honored One."
[The Tang Translation: At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, having praised the Buddha with verses, spoke his own name:
"I am named Mahāmati; I have attained mastery in the Mahāyāna. Now, by means of one hundred and eight points, I respectfully inquire of the Most Honored One."
The Knower of the World, having heard the verses spoken by him, surveyed the entire assembly and addressed the sons of the Buddha, saying:
"O sons of the Buddha, all of you now ask whatever you desire; I shall explain for you the realm of self-realization."
[Wei Translation] The Most Victorious Knower of the World, having heard that Great Wisdom (Mahāmati) pose his question, observed all sentient beings and addressed the sons of the Buddha, saying:
"O you sons of the Buddha, as well as Great Wisdom who has inquired, I shall now explain it for your sake."

At that time, the Knower of the World, having heard these words, surveyed the entire assembly and spoke as follows: [Tang Translation] "The realm of self-awakening. At that time, the Knower of the World, having heard these words, surveyed the entire assembly and spoke as follows.
"You sons of the Buddha, you may now all ask whatever you desire; I shall explain for you the realm of my own realization.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, having received the Buddha’s permission, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and joined his palms in reverence.
With reverence, he asked in verse: "How does one purify mindfulness? How does mindfulness increase? How does one perceive delusion? How does delusion increase?
For what reason are there lands, emanations, marks, and various non-Buddhists? And how is there the succession of no-sensation?"
Why is it called "without sensation"?

[Wei Translation: At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, having heard the Buddha grant him permission to inquire, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joined his palms in reverence, and asked in verse: "How are all perceptions purified? By what cause..."
There is cognition. For what reason is there delusion? For what reason does delusion exist?
For what reason do lands, the various externalists' manifested marks, tranquility, and the stages exist?
[The Tang Translation] At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, having received the Buddha’s permission, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and asked in verse:
“How does conceptualization arise? How is conceptualization purified? How does delusion arise? How is delusion purified?
What are the lands, transformations, characteristics, and the various non-Buddhists? And what is the shadowless?”
The sequence [of stages]. Why are they called "sons of the Buddha"? To what state does liberation lead? Who is bound, and who is liberated?

What are the realms of dhyāna? How do the three vehicles arise? We pray that you will explain these for us. From what do dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) arise? What is the agent, and what is the action?
What is the simultaneous difference in explanation? What constitutes growth? What are the formless attainments and the meditative absorption of cessation?
What is the cessation of perception? By what cause does one awaken from concentration? How do volitional formations arise? And how do they proceed, enter, and sustain the body?
What is manifest discrimination? How are the various stages produced?
[Wei Translation] What is called a Son of the Buddha? To what state does liberation lead? Who is bound, and by what cause is one liberated?

What dharma does the practitioner of meditation contemplate? By what cause are there three vehicles? By what causes and conditions do phenomena arise? By what cause is there that which acts and that which is acted upon?

What? Why are the causes differently explained? For what reason do things appear though they are non-existent? For what reason are there the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*)?

For what reason is the attainment of the extinction of perception (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodhasamāpatti*)? For what reason does one awaken from meditative absorption? How is it that a cause produces a fruit? For what reason do bodies go and stay?
For what reason does one perceive what is seen? For what reason are the various stages (*bhūmi*) produced?
[The Tang Translation: What is meant by "Son of the Buddha"? To what state does liberation lead? Who is bound, and who is able to liberate?
What is the realm of dhyāna? For what reason are there three vehicles? By what causes and conditions do they arise? What acts, and what is capable of acting?
Who says that the two are different? How do all existences arise? What is the formless absorption and the attainment of cessation?
What is the extinction of perception? How does one awaken from meditative concentration? How do karmic actions arise? How does one go, enter, and maintain the body?
How does one perceive objects? And how does one enter the various stages?
Who is it that destroys the three realms of existence? What is their body like, and where do they dwell? To what destination do they go after passing away? Who is the most excellent son?
By what cause do they attain supernatural powers, mastery, and samādhi? And what is the nature of the mind in samādhi? O Most Excellent One, please explain this to me.
[Wei Translation] Who is it that shatters the three realms of existence? By what body does one reach which destination? In what manner does one abide? What are the sons of the Buddhas?
By what cause do they attain supernormal powers, as well as mastery and samādhi? By what cause do they attain a concentrated mind?
O Most Victorious One, please explain this to me:
Who is it that can shatter the three realms of existence? Where is the body located, and of what nature is it? Where does birth and abiding occur? How is there a son of the Buddha?
How does one attain supernormal powers, mastery, and samādhi? And what are the characteristics of the mind in samādhi?
I pray that the Buddha will explain for me:
what is meant by the "storehouse" (ālaya)? What are the "mind" (manas) and "consciousness" (vijñāna)? What are birth and cessation? And how does one, having seen [the truth], return [to the source]?
What is the lineage (gotra)? What is the non-lineage and the mind-measure (cittamātra)? How are the characteristics (lakṣaṇa) established, as well as the meaning of non-self (anātman)?
Why are there no sentient beings? And how is conventional discourse (saṃvṛti-vyavahāra) explained?

[Wei Translation] For what reason is there the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna)? For what reason are there the mind (manas) and the cognitions (vijñānas)? For what reason do we perceive all phenomena (dharmas)? For what reason is that which is perceived severed?
What is the nature and what is the non-nature? Why is it that the mind has no objects? For what reason do you teach the characteristics of dharmas?
What is meant by "selflessness"? For what reason is there no sentient being? For what reason does conventional truth exist?
[Tang Translation] What is called the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*)? What is called the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)? How do various views arise? How are various views abandoned?
What is nature and what is non-nature? Why is it said that it is "mind-only"? For what reason are characteristics established?
How is non-self established? How is there no sentient being? How does one conform to worldly convention?
How do the views of annihilationism and eternalism fail to arise? And how is it that the Buddha and the non-Buddhists are not contradictory in their characteristics?
What will be in future ages? What are the various different schools? What is emptiness, and what is its cause? How do things perish in an instant? [Wei Translation:
For what reason is permanence not seen? For what reason is annihilation not seen? How is it that the Buddha and non-Buddhists do not contradict each other in their two characteristics?
For what reason will there be various different schools in future ages? What is meant by the name "emptiness"?
For what reason does mindfulness not abide?

[Tang Translation: How can one attain non-arising? Regarding the views of permanence and annihilation, how is it that the Buddha and the non-Buddhists do not contradict each other in their characteristics?
For what reason will there be various different schools in future ages? And what is meant by the emptiness of intrinsic nature?
What is momentary destruction?
What is birth from the womb? What is the immovability of the world? By what cause is it like a dream, a mirage, and a city of the Gandharvas?
The world is like a mirage in the heat, and like the moon reflected in water. For what reason are the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) and the wings of awakening (*bodhipakṣa*) taught?
Why is there turmoil in the lands? And why is there the appearance of existence?
[Wei Translation] For what reason is there the embryonic matrix? For what reason is the world immovable? How is it like an illusion or a dream?
Why is it said to be like a *gandharva* city, a mirage, or the moon in water? World-Honored One, explain this to me; how do you speak of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*)?
By what cause do the factors of enlightenment arise? By what cause does the realm become turbulent? By what cause is the view of existence produced?
[Tang Translation: How does the *garbha* (womb-matrix) arise? Why is the world not in motion?
Why are all worlds like illusions, like dreams, like cities of the Gandharvas, like mirages, and even like the moon reflected in water? By what cause do the factors of enlightenment arise?
From what do the factors of enlightenment arise? Why is the realm in disorder? For what reason are all existences perceived?
How is there neither birth nor cessation? The world is like a flower in the sky; how does one awaken to the world? Why speak of being free from words?
Who is it that is free from false conceptualization? What is the analogy of space like? How many kinds of reality are there? How many perfections are there in the mind?
By what cause does one traverse the stages? Who reaches the state of non-apprehension?
[Wei Translation] For what reason is there no arising or ceasing? For what reason is it like a flower in the sky? For what reason does one awaken to the world?
For what reason is there teaching without words? How is it that there is no conceptual discrimination? For what reason is it like empty space? How many kinds of *tathatā* (suchness) are there?
What is called "mind," and how many "shores" are there? What is the sequence based upon? True Suchness (tathatā) has no sequence.
[Tang Translation] How does one know worldly phenomena? How does one transcend words and letters? How is it like flowers in the sky—neither arising nor ceasing?
How many kinds of True Suchness are there? How many are the perfections (pāramitās) and the states of mind? How is it like empty space?
How is one free from conceptual construction? What is the sequence of the stages (*bhūmi*)? How does one attain the state of being shadowless?

What are the two kinds of selflessness (*nairātmya*)? How is the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) purified? How many types of wisdom are there? And how many are the moral precepts and the natures of sentient beings?
Who gives rise to the various natures of jewels, such as mani-gems and pearls? Who gives rise to all languages and the diverse natures of sentient beings?
[Wei Translation] By what cause are the two kinds of selflessness established? By what cause is the realm purified? How many types of wisdom and how many precepts are there?
By what cause do sentient beings arise? Who creates the various natures of jewels, such as gold and mani-gems? Who gives rise to language?
The various differences among sentient beings;
what are the two kinds of selflessness? How is the object of knowledge purified? How many types of noble wisdom are there?
The precepts for sentient beings are likewise so. From where do the mani jewels and other such treasures all emerge? Who gives rise to language?
Sentient beings and all material things, the fields of knowledge and the arts and crafts—by whom were these revealed? How many kinds of verses are there, both long stanzas and short phrases?
How many kinds of beings are there? What is called "treatise" (śāstra)? How do food and drink arise, as well as various sensual desires?
What is meant by "king"—the wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) and the minor kings? How does one protect the kingdom? And how many kinds of devas are there?
What is called "earth"? The constellations, the sun, and the moon? How many kinds of practitioners of liberation are there?
How many kinds of disciples are there? What is an ācārya? Furthermore, how many kinds of Buddhas are there? And how many kinds of births are there?
[Wei Translation] Regarding the five fields of knowledge and technical arts, who is able to speak thus? How many kinds of verses (gāthā) are there? What are the long and short meters?
Furthermore, how many kinds of dharmas are there? How many ways are there to explain their meaning? And for what reason are there various kinds of food and drink?
By what cause does desire arise? What is meant by "king"? What are the wheel-turning monarchs and minor kings? By what cause do they protect their lands?
How many kinds of devas are there? By what cause is there earth? By what cause are the stars, sun, and moon? How many kinds of liberation are there?
How many kinds of practitioners are there? How many kinds of disciples are there? How many kinds of ācāryas are there? [Tell me this], O Tathāgata.
How many kinds are there? How many kinds of Jātaka stories are there?
[Tang Translation] Regarding the fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*) and the arts (*śilpa*): by whom were they revealed?

How many kinds of verses (*gāthā*) are there, and likewise for the prose passages? How many different types of reasoning (*yukti*) are there? How many distinctions are there in the explanations? Who created food and drink?
How does sensual desire arise? What is a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin), and what are the various minor kings?
How do kings provide protection? How many distinct classes of celestial hosts are there? Regarding the earth, sun, moon, and constellations—what are these things?
How many kinds of liberation are there? How many types of teachers who practice are there? How many distinctions are there among disciples? What is an ācārya? O Tathāgata...
How many kinds are there? The same applies to the accounts of past lives (*jātaka*).

As for Māra and the various heterodox teachers (*tīrthika*), how many kinds are there of each? Furthermore, regarding intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and the mind (*citta*), how many kinds are there of each?

How are the measures of conventional designation established? I pray that the Most Victorious One will explain this. What are the void, the wind, and the clouds? What is mindfulness and what is intelligence?
What constitutes forests and trees? What constitutes creeping vines and grasses? And how are elephants, horses, and deer captured?
What constitutes being base and lowly? By what cause does one become base and lowly? How are these comprised within the six categories? What is an icchantika?
How are men, women, and those who are neither born? From what do all these arise?
[Wei Translation] How many kinds of *māra* are there? How many kinds of heterodox teachers (*tīrthika*) are there? How many kinds of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) are there?

Furthermore, how many kinds of mind (*citta*) are there? How are conventional designations (*prajñapti*) established? World-Honored One, please explain this to me. By what cause do wind and clouds arise?
By what cause is there wisdom? By what cause are there groves of trees? O World-Honored One, explain this to me. By what cause are there elephants, horses, and deer?
By what cause are they captured by men? By what cause are they short and deformed? O World-Honored One, explain this to me. By what cause are there the six seasons?
By what cause are there those who lack aspiration (icchantikas)? Tell me how males, females, and those who are neither male nor female are born.
[The Tang Translation: How many are there of the various Māras and heterodox teachers? How many different types are there of their intrinsic natures? How many distinctions are there in the mind?
How is it that they are merely provisional designations? We pray that the Buddha will explain this for us. What are wind and clouds?
By what cause do mindfulness and wisdom arise? Who is it that arranges rows of vines and trees? How are elephants, horses, and wild beasts captured?
Why are there those who are base and lowly? I pray that the Buddha will explain this to me. What constitutes the six periods of time?
What is an icchantika? How are men, women, and eunuchs born? By what means do these all come into being?
What is the regression of practice? What is the arising of practice? By what dharma does the meditation master establish what kind of person?
How do sentient beings take birth in the various realms of existence? What are their characteristics and what are their types?
[Wei Translation] For what reason does one regress from practice? For what reason does one advance in practice? To what kind of person do you teach practice?
To abide in what kind of dharma? Regarding the coming and going of all sentient beings, what are their characteristics and what are their types?
[The Tang Translation: What is the regression of practice? What is the progress of practice? How many types of yoga practitioners are there who cause others to abide therein?
What are the forms and physical characteristics of sentient beings born in the various realms of existence?
What constitutes wealth? How is wealth attained? What is the Śākya clan? By what cause does the Śākya clan exist? What is the Ikṣvāku lineage?
O Unsurpassed Honored One, please explain! What is the Sage of Long Suffering? How does he provide instruction?
How does the Tathāgata manifest at all times and in all lands in various forms and names, surrounded by the most excellent sons [of the Buddha]?
Why do you not eat meat? How did you prohibit and sever the eating of meat? For what reason do those of various kinds who eat meat consume it?
[Wei Translation] World-Honored One, please explain this to me: By what cause does one attain wealth? What constitutes the Śākya clan?
By what cause is there the Śākya clan? By what cause is there the Ikṣvāku lineage? By what cause are there the long-lived ṛṣis? And who are the kinsmen of the long-lived ṛṣis?
What is that instruction? O Bhagavān, who is like space, explain it to me in detail.
For what reason does the Buddha, the World-Honored One, manifest in all times and lands in various forms and names, surrounded by a multitude of Buddha-sons?
For what reason do you not eat meat? Why was the eating of meat prohibited? Among those species that eat meat, for what reason do they eat meat?
[Chinese Translation] Abundant and possessing great sovereignty—by what cause was this obtained? What is the Śākya clan?
What is the Ikṣvāku clan? By whom were the sages taught to perform long ascetic practices? And for what reason, O World-Honored Buddha, [did you arise]?
Manifesting in all lands in various names and forms, surrounded by a multitude of Buddha-sons: for what reason do you not eat meat?
For what reason do you cause the cessation of meat-eating? And for what reason do those sentient beings who eat meat consume it?
Some are shaped like the sun and moon, Mount Sumeru, or a lotus; some are lands with the supreme marks of lions, situated askew or inverted over the world.
Some are like Indra’s net, or composed entirely of various precious gems; others have the forms of lutes, hourglass drums, or the shapes of diverse flowers.
Or those devoid of the light of the sun and moon—such as these are immeasurable.
[Wei Translation] For what reason are there lands shaped like the sun and moon, Mount Sumeru, or lotuses; lands with the excellent marks of the lion’s form?
Tell me of these lands, those that are disordered, tilted, or inverted, like Indra’s net, and all those lands made of jewels.
For what reason do you tell me this? Like a vīṇā, a lute, or a drum, with various floral forms, how is it that there is a land devoid of the light of the sun and moon?
For what reason do you tell me this?
[The Tang Translation: For what reason do the various buddha-fields have shapes like the sun and moon, Mount Sumeru, or a lotus flower, or the form of a svastika or a lion?
For what reason do the various buddha-fields exist like Indra’s net, positioned either inverted or sideways?
Composed entirely of all kinds of jewels, why do some world-systems have the radiance of stainless suns and moons, while others take the form of flowers and fruits,
or the shape of lutes and hourglass-shaped drums?
What is the transformation Buddha? What is the retribution-born Buddha? What is the suchness Buddha? What is the wisdom Buddha?
Why does one not attain equal and perfect enlightenment in the desire realm? For what reason does one attain bodhi at the Akaniṣṭha heaven, having transcended desire?
When the Sugata has entered parinirvāṇa, who shall uphold the True Dharma? For how long will the Teacher of Gods remain, and for how long will the True Dharma abide?
How many kinds of *siddhāntas* and views are there, and how many divisions of the *vinaya* for monks? What are they, and by what causes and conditions do they arise?
For what reason do those sons of the Most Victorious Ones, the Pratyekabuddhas, and the Śrāvakas undergo a hundred transformations? How is it that they are free from a hundred sensations?

[Wei Translation] What is the transformation Buddha (nirmāṇa-buddha)? What is the recompense Buddha (vipāka-buddha)? What is the wisdom-as-such Buddha (tathatā-jñāna-buddha)? For what reason tell me this?
Why is it that one does not attain equal and perfect enlightenment in the desire realm? And why is it at the Akaniṣṭha heaven?
Attaining the Way by departing from the middle, the Tathāgata enters parinirvāṇa. Who upholds the True Dharma? For how long does the World-Honored One abide?
How long will the True Dharma remain? How many dharmas did the Tathāgata establish? What are the various types seen in each case?

Regarding the Vinaya and the bhikṣus, may the World-Honored One explain them to me. By what cause are there one hundred transformations? By what cause are there one hundred states of tranquility? [And regarding] the śrāvakas...
[The Buddha said: "Pratyekabuddhas—may the World-Honored One explain these to me.
[Tang Translation: "What is the transformation Buddha? What is the recompense Buddha? And the Tathatā-wisdom Buddha—may you explain all of these to me.
Why is it that one does not attain equal and perfect enlightenment within the desire realm? For what reason is it attained at the Akaniṣṭha heaven?"
Attaining enlightenment through the removal of defilements: after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, who shall uphold the True Dharma?
For how long will the World-Honored One remain? How long will the True Dharma endure? How many kinds of *siddhāntas* are there? And how many views are there?
For what reason was the Vinaya established, as well as the various bhikṣus, all the sons of the Buddha, the pratyekabuddhas, and the śrāvakas? How so?
How is the basis transformed? How is the signless attained?
What is mundane supernormal power? What is supramundane? And what constitutes the seven stages? We pray that you will expound upon these for us.
How many kinds of Saṃgha are there? What constitutes the breaking of the Saṃgha? What is the science of medicine?

And what are its causes and conditions? [Wei Translation: For what cause is there mundane supernormal power? For what cause is there supramundane supernormal power? For what cause is the mind of the seven stages?
O Bhagavān, explain these to me. How many kinds of Saṃgha are there? For what reason is there the schism of the Saṃgha? For what reason is there the science of medicine?
World-Honored One, please explain this for me:
How does one attain worldly penetration? How does one transcend the world? Furthermore, by what cause does the mind abide within the seven stages?
How many kinds of Saṃgha are there? How is the schism of the Saṃgha brought about? And what is meant by "for the sake of sentient beings"?
Having extensively expounded the medical treatises, for what reason did the Great Muni proclaim these words: "Kāśyapa, Krakucchanda, and Kanakamuni are I"?
Why do you speak of annihilation and permanence, as well as of self and non-self?

Why do you not at all times proclaim the true meaning, yet instead distinguish and explain for sentient beings that it is merely mind-only (*cittamātra*)? For what reason [do you mention] men, women, forests, *kharjūra* trees, and *āmalaka* fruits?
Mount Khadiraka, Cakravāḍa, Vajra, and all other mountains, adorned with immeasurable jewels and filled with sages and gandharvas.
[Wei Translation: Kāśyapa, Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, and I—why do you say that we have always been the sons of the Buddhas?
Why do you speak of a self among humans? Why do you speak of annihilation and permanence? Why do you not speak [of this] alone?
If there is only a single mind, for what reason are there forests of men and women, *harītakī* and *āmalaka* trees, Mount Kīla and the Cakravāḍa mountains,
the Vajra mountains and other such peaks, the infinite successions of mountains adorned with various jewels,
and filled with sages, musicians, and humans? O World-Honored One, please explain this to me.
[The Tang Translation: For what reason did the Great Muni proclaim these words: "Kāśyapa, Krakucchanda, and Kanakamuni are I"?
Why did he speak of annihilation and permanence, as well as of self and non-self? Why did he not always speak the truth?
"All is created by mind alone. What are the forests of men and women, the hāritaka and āmala trees, Mount Kailāsa, Cakravāḍa, and the Vajra Mountains?
Within these places, they are adorned with immeasurable jewels and filled entirely with sages and gandharvas.
By what causes and conditions do these exist? I pray that the Honored One will explain this to me."
The Unsurpassed Knower of the World, having heard those verses spoken concerning the various gateways to the perfections of the Mahāyāna—the foremost essence of the Buddhas’ minds—exclaimed:
"Excellent, excellent is your inquiry! O Mahāmati, listen well and attentively; I shall now explain to you in due order that which you have asked."
[Wei Translation] Mahādeva Buddha. Having heard those spoken verses and phrases—the various gateways to the perfections of the Mahāyāna, the foremost essence of the Buddhas’ minds—he said:
"Excellent, excellent is your question! O Mahāmati, listen well and attentively; I shall now explain to you in due order according to your inquiry."
[The Tang Translation: At that time, the World-Honored One, having heard his request for the subtle and wondrous Mahāyāna Dharma-gate of the supreme mind of all Buddhas, addressed him, saying:
"Excellent, Mahāmati! Listen attentively, listen attentively.
I shall explain to you in due order that which you have asked. He then spoke in verse:
Arising and non-arising, nirvāṇa, emptiness, and the momentary—these proceed toward the absence of intrinsic nature.
[Wei Translation] Arising and non-arising, nirvāṇa, emptiness, and the momentary—these proceed toward the absence of self-substance.
Whether arising or non-arising, nirvāṇa and the mark of emptiness;

the flow of existence lacks intrinsic nature, as do the Buddha’s various pāramitās, the sons of the Buddha, the śrāvakas, the pratyekabuddhas, the various non-Buddhists, and those who practice in the formless realms.
Regarding these various matters:
[Wei Translation] "The sons of the Buddha’s *pāramitās*, the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*, and the non-Buddhists who dwell in the formless realm.
[Tang Translation] "The sons of the Buddha’s *pāramitās*, the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*, and the non-Buddhists who practice in the formless realm."
Mount Sumeru, the great oceans, mountains, continents, islands, lands, and realms; the stars, the sun, and the moon; non-Buddhists, devas, and asuras;
liberation, mastery, and supernormal powers; the powers, dhyānas, and samādhis; cessation and the bases of psychic power; the factors of enlightenment and the path constituents.
[Sui Translation] Mount Sumeru, the oceans, and the mountains; the lands of the four continents; the sun, moon, and various constellations;
the non-Buddhists, devas, and asuras; liberation, mastery, and supernormal powers; strength, reflection, tranquility, and concentration; cessation, and the bases of psychic power.
The factors of enlightenment and the wings of the path;
[Tang translation: Mount Sumeru, the great oceans, and mountains; the continents, islands, lands, and territories; the stars and the sun and moon; the hosts of devas and asuras;
liberation, mastery, and the supernormal powers; the powers, dhyānas, and various samādhis; cessation and the bases of psychic power.
The factors of enlightenment and the path;

the meditative absorptions and the immeasurables; the aggregates, the body, and coming-and-going; the meditative attainments and the attainment of cessation; and the explanation of the mind arising from samādhi.

The mind (*citta*), its culmination, and consciousness (*vijñāna*); the five dharmas of selflessness; the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the conceptualized (*saṃjñita*), and the object of conception (*saṃjñeya*);

as well as the two views of the present. [Wei Translation: The various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and immeasurables (*apramāṇa*); the five aggregates (*skandha*) and past and future; the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) and cessation (*nirodha*).
These are spoken of by giving rise to the mind. Mind, thought, and consciousness; the five dharmas of selflessness; the intrinsic nature, the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and the object of conception.
The seen and the seer—these two; [the Chinese translation reads:
meditative concentration and the immeasurables; the aggregates and coming and going, up to the attainment of cessation;
the arising of mind and verbal expression; mind, mentation, and consciousness, and non-self; the five dharmas and the intrinsic natures; the conceptualizer and the conceptualized.
The two kinds of views—subject and object;
the vehicles and the various lineages; gold, silver, and mani-jewels; the icchantika and the great elements; turmoil and the one Buddha.
The wisdom that attains the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), the existence and non-existence of sentient beings;
[the Wei translation asks: what are the various vehicles? The nature of gold and mani-jewels, the icchantikas, the four great elements, turmoil, and the single Buddha;
the attainment of the teaching within the sphere of wisdom, and the existence and non-existence of sentient beings.
The various vehicles, the lineage, and the stage; gold, mani-jewels, and pearls; the icchantika and the great elements;
turmoil and the single Buddha; what is known by wisdom and what is attained through teaching; and the existence or non-existence of sentient beings.
How are elephants, horses, and various beasts captured? This is like the establishment of the *siddhānta* through causes, as well as the relationship between agent and action.
[Wei Translation: How are elephants, horses, and various beasts captured? It is like the correspondence of metaphors and causes;
how does the teaching of power proceed? For what reason do cause and effect exist?
[The Tang Translation: For what reason are there elephants, horses, and beasts? How are they captured? By what means of analogy are the *siddhāntas* established in accordance [with reality]?
What is the produced (*kārya*) and what is the producer (*kāraṇa*)?

The delusions of the forest-dwellers pass away; the mind-only measure does not truly exist. The various stages do not reach one another; though there be a hundred transformations, there is no experiencing of them.

Medical treatises, arts and crafts, technical skills, and all fields of knowledge—the various mountains, Mount Sumeru, the earth, the vast oceans, the sun, and the moon—all their dimensions [are likewise unreal].
Regarding the lower, middle, and superior sentient beings, how many atoms does each body contain?
[Wei Translation] To clarify the delusions as they truly are: the mind alone has no objective realm; the various stages have no fixed sequence;
there are the hundred transformations and the signless. Why do you ask me about medical treatises, the arts and crafts, technical skills, and the various fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*)?
Regarding the various mountains, Mount Sumeru, and the earth—what are their shapes and dimensions? Regarding the great oceans, the sun, the moon, and the stars—how do you ask me about these?
As for the sentient beings of the superior, middling, and inferior grades—how many atoms does each of their bodies contain?
The various forests and delusions—such is the principle of ultimate reality. It is mind-only, devoid of external objects;

there are no successive stages of the grounds. It is the basis for the transformation of signlessness. Medical science, the treatises on arts and crafts, technical skills, and all fields of knowledge.

The dimensions of Mount Sumeru, the various mountains and lands, the great oceans, and the sun and moon; the bodies of superior, middling, and inferior sentient beings—how many atoms do they each contain?
How many atoms are there in each individual world-system? How many *dhanus* are there in a *dhanus*, and how many in a *hasta*, a *krośa*, a half-*yojana*, and a full *yojana*?
[Wei Translation] A cubit-step (*hasta*) is ten *li*; twenty [cubits] and forty [cubits].
[Tang Translation] How many particles are there in one *kṣaṇa*? How many cubits (*hasta*) are there in one bow (*dhanus*)? How many bows are there in one *krośa*?
And how many are there in half a *yojana* and one *yojana*?
A rabbit-hair dust mote, a window-dust mote, and a nit; a sheep’s-fleece dust mote and a wheat-dust mote.
[Wei Translation] A rabbit-hair dust mote, a window-dust mote, and a nit; a sheep’s-fleece dust mote and a wheat-dust mote.
A rabbit hair-tip and a mote floating in a sunbeam; a nit, a wool-fiber, and a grain of barley;
a *pṛthuka* (wild rice) and several grains of barley; an *ala* (barley-measure), several grains of barley, a *droṇa*, a *khāri*, a *lakṣa*, and a *koṭi*.
Up to a *bimbara*, how many units are there in each?
[Wei Translation] How many barley grains are in one *sheng*? How many individual heads are in half a *sheng*? How many are in one *hu*, ten *hu*, one million, and ten million?
How many particles are in a *bimbara*?
[The Tang Translation: "Half a *sheng* and one *sheng*: how many grains of wild barley (*yava*) are there in each?
One *hu* and ten *hu*, one hundred thousand up to one hundred million, and even a *bimbara*: how many units are there in each?"
How many *āṭaka* are there that are called a *śarīṣapa*? How many *śarīṣapa* make one *laitya*?
How many *laitya-māṣa* make one *māṣa-dhāna*? And how many *dhāna-lava* make one *karṣa*?
How many *kāliśanas* constitute one *pala*? What is the characteristic of these accumulations? How many *palas* make up Mount Meru?
These are what should be asked; why inquire about other matters?
[Wei Translation] How many mustard seeds equal one minute particle (*paramāṇu*)? How many mustard seeds constitute one blade of grass seed? How many blade of grass seeds constitute one bean?
How many *zhu* constitute one *liang*? How many *liang* constitute one *jin*? By counting in this successive order, how many parts constitute Mount Sumeru?
Son of the Buddha, for what reason do you not now ask me this:
"How many atoms constitute a mustard seed? How many mustard seeds constitute a blade of grass? Furthermore, how many blades of grass constitute one bean?
How many beans constitute one *zhu*? How many *zhu* constitute one *liang*? And how many *liang* constitute one *jin*?"
How many *jin* (catty) make up Mount Sumeru? These are the things that ought to be asked; why do you ask about other matters?
How many bodies does each of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, Buddhas, and the most excellent sons [of the Buddha] possess? Why do you not ask this?
How many *aṇus* are there in a flame? How many *aṇus* are there in a wind? How many *aṇus* are there in each sense organ? And how many are there in a pore or a brow-hair?
[Wei Translation] Pratyekabuddhas, śrāvakas, and so forth, as well as all Buddhas and their sons—how many atoms compose their bodies?
Why do you not ask this? How many atoms are there in a flame? How many are there in a particle of wind? And how many atoms are there in each sense organ?
How many atoms are there in the eyebrows and the pores?
[Tang Translation: For the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, the Buddhas, and the sons of the Buddha—such as these, how many subtle atoms are there in their respective bodies?
How many atoms are there in the fire and wind [elements]? How many are there in each sense organ? And how many in the eyebrows and all the pores?
Furthermore, how many atoms compose each [of these]? Regarding such matters as these, why do you not ask me?
O King, Sovereign Lord of Wealth, Universal Monarch of Holy Kings—how does a king provide protection? And what constitutes liberation?
The detailed exposition and the exposition in verses—just as you have asked: regarding the various desires of sentient beings and their various kinds of food and drink;

[Wei Translation: By what cause does one become a sovereign, a wheel-turning sage-king, or a lord? By what cause is a king protected? Regarding liberation, both the extensive and the concise expositions;
the various desires of sentient beings—why do you ask me this? And by what cause are there various foods and drinks?
[The Tang Translation: How does one obtain wealth? How does one become a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin)?
How is a king protected? How does one attain liberation? What are long prose passages? [And what of] sensual desire and food and drink?
What is the Forest of Men and Women? What is the Mountain of Adamantine Solidity? How is it like an illusion or a dream? What is the analogy of the wild deer’s thirst?
What are the mountain deities and the adornments of the *gandharvas*?
[Wei Translation] For what reason is there the Forest of Men and Women? For what reason is there the Vajra Firm Mountain? Tell me, how is this so?
For what reason are they like illusions and dreams, and like the analogy of the wild deer’s thirst? For what reason do clouds exist? For what reason are there the six seasons?
By what cause are there various flavors? By what cause are there males, females, and those who are neither male nor female? By what cause are there all manner of ornaments?
O Son of the Buddha, for what reason do you ask? What are the various wondrous mountains? And how are the sages, music, and people adorned?
[The Tang Translation: What is the Forest of Men and Women? The Vajra and other mountains; the metaphors of illusion, dreams, and thirst—whence do these clouds arise?
How do the seasons come to be? By what cause are there various flavors? And what of women, men, and those who are neither?
The adornments of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; what are the various wondrous mountains? The adornments of seers and gandharvas;
where does liberation lead? Who is bound and who is liberated? What is the realm of dhyāna? Transformations and the non-Buddhists.
What is action without cause? What is action with cause? What is action both with and without cause, and what is that which is neither with nor without cause?
What is it for things to manifest and then cease? How are all perceptions purified? How do all perceptions transform, and how are all activities transformed?
How are all perceptions severed? How does one arise from samādhi? Who is it that destroys the three realms of existence?
Where and in what body [does this occur]? [Wei Translation: To what place does liberation go? Who is bound and how are they bound? What is the sphere of dhyāna?
Regarding nirvāṇa and the non-Buddhists: how is there creation without cause? By what cause can transformation be seen? By what cause are all cognitions purified?
By what cause do various perceptions arise? By what cause does one engage in activity? I pray that you will explain this to me:

by what cause are all conceptions severed? By what cause does one emerge from samādhi? Who is it that destroys the three realms of existence? By what cause does the body exist, and where is it located?
[The Tang Translation: To what place does liberation go? Who is bound and who is liberated? What is the realm of dhyāna?
Regarding transformations and non-Buddhists: how is it that some act without cause, and how is it that some act with cause? How are various views overturned?
How do conceptual constructions arise? How are conceptual constructions purified? How does that which is performed arise?
How does it proceed? How are all perceptions severed? How is samādhi produced? Who is it that destroys the three realms of existence? What is the body, and where is it located?
How is it that there are no sentient beings, yet one speaks of a self? How is it that worldly convention speaks thus? I pray you explain these extensively.
What are the characteristics of that which is asked about, and what is that which is asked about as "non-self"? What is the embryonic matrix (*garbha*), and what are the various different bodies?
[Wei Translation] What is meant by "no self" (anātman)? For what reason is it spoken of in reliance upon the world? For what reason do you ask about the characteristics of the self?
Why do you ask about non-self? What is the embryo (garbha)? For what reason do you ask about me?
[The Tang Translation: What is it that there is no self? How does one conform to worldly convention? You ask about the characteristics, as well as what you inquire regarding non-self.
What constitutes the embryonic matrix (*garbha*), and what are its other constituent parts?

What are the views of eternalism and nihilism? How does the mind attain concentration? Regarding speech and various forms of knowledge, the precepts, the spiritual lineage, and the sons of the Buddha—how are these established and discussed?
What is the relationship between teacher and disciple? And as for the various kinds of sentient beings—how do they come to be?
What constitutes food and drink? This was the question posed by the wise Māra. What are trees and climbing vines? This was asked by the Son of the Most Victorious One.
What are the various buddha-fields? This concerns the long ascetic practices of the ṛṣis. What constitutes a noble clan? From which teacher did you receive your training?
What constitutes ugliness? How does a person practice? Why is there no awakening in the desire realm? How is Akaniṣṭha established?
[Wei Translation] By what cause are the views of eternalism and nihilism severed? By what cause does the mind attain concentration? By what cause do speech and wisdom arise?

Regarding the nature of the realms, O Sons of the Buddha: how are teachers and disciples examined and understood? Among the various kinds of sentient beings, how is it that they consume the food of Māra?
Why is there the gift of space, clarity, and intelligence? Why are there forests? Son of the Buddha, why do you ask?
Why are there various realms? Why are there long-lived seers (*ṛṣi*)? Why are there various teachers? For what reason do you question me? Why is there ugliness?
Why do those who practice not wish for success? How is it that one attains the Way at the Akaniṣṭha heaven? Why do you ask me this?
[The Tang Translation: What are the views of eternalism and nihilism? What is one-pointedness of mind? What is the knowledge of verbal expression?

O Son of the Buddha of the lineage of precepts, how are the explanations given in accordance with principle? What constitutes a teacher and a disciple? And what are the differences in the lineages of sentient beings?
Food and drink, as well as space—these are the arrangements devised by the clever Māra. How is it that trees are distributed? This is what you have asked.

For what reason do all lands have various and differing characteristics? Why is it that some sages undergo long ascetic practices, while others are born into noble lineages and cause sentient beings to revere them;
yet others have bodies that are lowly and ugly, and are thus despised by others? How is this so?
In the desire realm, one practices but does not attain Buddhahood; it is only at the Akaniṣṭha heaven that one ascends to perfect enlightenment.
What is mundane supernatural power? What is a bhikṣu? What is a transformation Buddha (nirmāṇakāya-buddha)? What is a reward Buddha (saṃbhogakāya-buddha)?
"What is the Buddha of Suchness? What is the Buddha of Equal Wisdom? And what constitutes the Sangha? Thus did the Son of the Buddha inquire.
Regarding the lute, the waist-drum, and the flowers, as well as the lands devoid of light—these were his questions.
[Wei Translation] For what reason is there penetration in the world? For what reason is one a bhikṣu? What is a transformation-retribution Buddha?
For what reason do you ask me this? What is a Tathāgata-Buddha? What constitutes the Saṃgha? The lute, the drum, the flower-adorned lands.
How is it that one is free from light?
[Tang Translation] How is it that people of the world are able to attain supernatural powers (*abhijñā*)? For what reason is one called a *bhikṣu*?
What are transformation and retribution? Regarding the Buddha of True Suchness Wisdom (*tathatājñāna*), for what reason is he named Saṃgha? Or some are like a lute.
The waist-drum and various flowers; some are apart from light.
There are seven types of those who possess the ground of mind. All that you have asked is according to reality. This and many other things are what the sons of the Buddha should inquire about.
Each characteristic is in correspondence; one remains far removed from all views and errors. The *siddhānta* is beyond verbal expression; I shall now reveal it.
I shall establish the phrases in their proper sequence; O Son of the Buddha, listen well and attentively.
[Wei Translation] "What is the mind-ground? O Son of the Buddha, you ask me this, as well as many other things that a Son of the Buddha ought to inquire about.
Each of these corresponds to the correct characteristics, being free from all views and errors, and detached from the teachings of the non-Buddhists."
I say to you: listen attentively! I shall now speak of but a small portion. Son of the Buddha, listen well!
How is it that his mind comes to abide in the seventh stage? You have now asked me about this and its other meanings;
I shall explain each in accordance with their characteristics, free from all views and errors, and transcending the mundane.
I shall now explain for you the dharmas consisting of language; O Son of the Buddha, you should listen and receive them.
These one hundred and eight phrases are as spoken by all the Buddhas: the phrase of non-arising and the phrase of arising, the phrase of permanence and the phrase of impermanence.
The phrase of marks and the phrase of marklessness; the phrase of abiding and change and the phrase of non-abiding and non-change; the phrase of the momentary and the phrase of the non-momentary;
the phrase of intrinsic nature and the phrase of being free from intrinsic nature; the phrase of emptiness and the phrase of non-emptiness; the phrase of cessation and the phrase of non-cessation.
[Wei Translation] These one hundred and eight views, as taught by the Buddhas, are: the view of arising and the view of non-arising; the view of permanence and the view of impermanence;
the view of characteristics and the view of characteristiclessness; the view of abiding-change and the view of non-abiding-change; the view of momentariness and the view of non-momentariness;
the view of being devoid of self-nature and the view of not being devoid of self-nature; the view of emptiness and the view of non-emptiness; and the view of annihilation...
[This is] not the view of non-existence. [Tang Translation:
As previously taught by the Buddhas, there are one hundred and eight phrases. At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, what are these one hundred and eight phrases? The Buddha said to Mahāmati: "They are as follows: birth..."

The phrase of arising is not a phrase of arising; the phrase of permanence is not a phrase of permanence; the phrase of characteristics is not a phrase of characteristics; the phrase of abiding and changing is not a phrase of abiding and changing;
the phrase of the moment is not a phrase of the moment; the phrase of intrinsic nature is not a phrase of intrinsic nature;

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how many kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing are there for the various consciousnesses?
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "The various consciousnesses have two kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing, which are not to be known through discursive thought."

The various consciousnesses have two kinds of arising: namely, arising as a continuous flow (*pravāha-utpāda*) and arising as a phenomenal characteristic (*nimitta-utpāda*). They have two kinds of abiding:

namely, abiding as a continuous flow (*pravāha-sthiti*) and abiding as a phenomenal characteristic (*nimitta-sthiti*). They have two kinds of cessation: namely, cessation as a continuous flow (*pravāha-nirodha*) and cessation as a phenomenal characteristic (*nimitta-nirodha*).
[Wei Translation] At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, how many kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing are there for the various consciousnesses? The Buddha told the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva:

"Mahāmati, each of the various consciousnesses has two kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing, which cannot be known by those who lack deliberative reflection. Mahāmati, as for the various consciousnesses..."
There are two kinds of arising. What are the two? First, arising by way of characteristics; second, arising by way of continuity.
Mahāmati, the various consciousnesses have two kinds of abiding. What are the two? First, abiding by way of characteristics; second, abiding by way of continuity.
"Mahāmati, the various consciousnesses have two kinds of cessation. What are these two? First, the cessation of characteristics;
second, the cessation of continuity.
[Tang Translation] At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, all..."
“How many kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing do the consciousnesses have?

The Buddha said, “Mahāmati, the consciousnesses have two kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing, which cannot be known by those who rely on mere conjecture. They are: the continuity-arising and the characteristic-arising;
the continuity-abiding and the characteristic-abiding; and the continuity-ceasing and the characteristic-ceasing.”

Mahāmati, all consciousnesses have three kinds of characteristics: namely, the characteristic of transformation (*pariṇāma-lakṣaṇa*), the characteristic of activity (*karma-lakṣaṇa*), and the characteristic of reality (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*).
[Wei Translation: Mahāmati, there are three kinds of consciousness. What are the three? First, the consciousness of the characteristic of transformation;
second, the consciousness of the characteristic of activity; third, the consciousness of the characteristic of wisdom.

[The Tang Translation: "There are three kinds of consciousness: namely, the aspect of transformation (*pariṇāma-lakṣaṇa*), the aspect of activity (*karma-lakṣaṇa*), and the aspect of reality (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*).
Mahāmati, briefly stated there are three kinds of consciousness; explained in detail, there are eight aspects. What are the three?

They are the true consciousness (*tathatā-vijñāna*), the manifesting consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*), and the consciousness that discriminates phenomena (*vastu-vikalpa-vijñāna*). Mahāmati, it is like a bright mirror that holds all forms and images; such is the locus of the manifesting consciousness."
The present is also like this.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, there are eight kinds of consciousness; briefly stated, there are two kinds. What are these two?
First is the consciousness that discerns [objects]; second is the consciousness that discriminates phenomena. Mahāmati, it is like seeing various forms within a bright mirror.
Mahāmati, the consciousness that discerns is also like this: it perceives various reflected images.

[Tang Translation: Mahāmati, consciousness is explained extensively as being eightfold, but briefly there are only two: namely, the manifesting consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*) and the consciousness that discriminates phenomena (*vikaḷpa-vastu-vijñāna*).
Mahāmati, just as various forms and images appear within a clear mirror, so too is the manifesting consciousness.

Mahāmati, the manifesting consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*) and the consciousness that discriminates objects (*vastu-vikalpa-vijñāna*)—these two have the characteristics of being both perishable and imperishable, and they serve as mutual causes for one another.

[Wei Translation: Mahāmati, the consciousness of discernment (*vijñapti-vijñāna*) and the consciousness that discriminates objects (*vastu-vikalpa-vijñāna*)—those two kinds of consciousness have no distinct characteristics and mutually serve as causes for each other.

[The Tang Translation: "Mahāmati, the manifesting consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*) and the consciousness that discriminates objects (*vikaḷpa-vastu-vijñāna*)—these two consciousnesses are not different from one another and act as mutual causes.
Mahāmati, the inconceivable perfuming (*vāsanā*) and the inconceivable transformation (*pariṇāma*) are the causes of the manifesting consciousness."
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, the discerning consciousness has inconceivable perfuming and transformation as its cause.
[Tang Translation] Mahāmati, the manifesting consciousness takes inconceivable perfuming and transformation as its cause.
Mahāmati, the grasping of various objects and the perfuming of beginningless false discrimination are the causes of the *vijñapti-matratā-vijñāna* (consciousness that discriminates phenomena).

[Wei Translation: Mahāmati, the consciousness that discriminates phenomena discriminates and grasps objects; it is caused by the perfuming of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) from time immemorial.

[The Tang Translation: The *vijñapti-viṣaya-vikalpa-vijñāna* (the consciousness that discriminates objects) takes as its causes the discrimination of objective spheres and the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of beginningless conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

Mahāmati, if that true consciousness (*tathatā-vijñāna*) is covered over, then the various unreal and false [appearances] are extinguished, and all the sense-consciousnesses (*indriya-vijñāna*) [cease].

[Wei Translation: Mahāmati, when the various habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of false discrimination within the ālayavijñāna are extinguished, the sense faculties are also extinguished.

Mahāmati, as for the cessation of the continuity [of existence]: when the cause of the continuity ceases, the continuity ceases; when that from which it proceeds and its objective referent cease, the continuity ceases.
Mahāmati, why is this? Because these are its supports. "Support" refers to the habit-energy of beginningless false discrimination (*vikalpa*);
"referent" refers to the objects of consciousness, such as the manifestations of one's own mind, which are false discriminations.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, as for the cessation of the continuity: when the cause of continuity ceases, the continuity ceases;
when the cause ceases and the conditions cease, the continuity ceases. Mahāmati, this refers to that which relies on the dharma and relies on conditions.

"Relying on the dharma" means the perfuming of beginningless false conceptualization and deluded discrimination. "Relying on conditions" means the manifestation of objects by one's own mind-consciousness.

Mahāmati, it is like a lump of clay and its atoms, which are neither different nor not different. The same applies to gold and its ornaments.
Mahāmati, if the lump of clay were different from its atoms, it would not be produced by them; yet in reality, it is produced by them. Therefore, [they are neither different nor not different].
They are not different. If they were not different, then there would be no distinction between a lump of clay and its atoms.

In this way, Mahāmati, if the evolving consciousnesses were different from the true nature of the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), then the storehouse consciousness would not be their cause.
If they were not different, then when the evolving consciousnesses cease, the storehouse consciousness should also cease; yet its own true nature does not actually cease.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, if these evolving consciousnesses and the ālayavijñāna were of different characteristics, they would not arise from the ālayavijñāna.
If they were not different, then when the evolving consciousnesses cease, the ālayavijñāna should also cease.
However, the *ālayavijñāna* as its own characteristic does not cease.
[Tang Translation: "Mahāmati, if the evolving consciousnesses were different from the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), then the storehouse consciousness would not be their cause.
If they were not different, then when the evolving consciousnesses cease, the storehouse consciousness should also cease; yet its true characteristic does not cease."
Therefore, Mahāmati, it is not that the consciousness of its own true marks ceases; rather, it is only the aspect of karma that ceases.

Mahāmati, if the consciousness of its own true marks were to cease, then the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) would cease. Mahāmati, if the storehouse consciousness were to cease, that would be no different from the nihilistic theories of the non-Buddhists.

[Wei Translation] Therefore, Mahāmati, the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the various consciousnesses cease. When the specific characteristics cease, the activity-characteristic (*karmalakṣaṇa*) ceases.
If, Mahāmati, the specific characteristics were to cease, then the ālayavijñāna would have to cease.
If the ālayavijñāna were to cease, this would not differ from the conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) of the nihilistic view (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) of the non-Buddhists.

[The Tang Translation: "Mahāmati, the true characteristic of consciousness does not perish; only its karmic characteristic perishes. If the true characteristic were to perish, the ālayavijñāna would have to perish.
If the ālayavijñāna were to perish, that would be no different from the nihilistic doctrine of the non-Buddhists."
“Mahāmati, those non-Buddhists propound such a theory as this: they claim that when the grasping of objects ceases, the flow of consciousness also ceases.
If the flow of consciousness were to cease, then the beginningless flow would be severed. Mahāmati, the non-Buddhists speak of a cause for the arising of the flow;
they do not say it arises from the assembly of eye-consciousness, form, and light, but rather that there is another distinct cause. Mahāmati, as for that cause...”

Regarding "cessation": from beginningless time, the various consciousnesses ought to cease. Mahāmati, the non-Buddhists claim that the successive consciousnesses arise from a creator;
they do not say that consciousness arises based on the conjunction of the eye, form, space, and light, but rather assert the existence of a creator.
Mahāmati, who are these creators of the non-Buddhists? They are the Primal Being (Puruṣa), Īśvara, Time, and the atoms (paramāṇu).
This is the agent. [Tang Translation:
Mahāmati, those non-Buddhists speak thus: "The cessation of the consciousness that grasps the continuity of objective spheres is the cessation of the beginningless, continuous consciousness.
Mahāmati, those non-Buddhists say that the continuous consciousness arises from...

They assert that [consciousness] arises from a creator; they do not say that visual consciousness arises from the conjunction of form, light, and so forth, but rather maintain that only a creator serves as the cause of arising.
What is this creator? They conceive of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the person (*puruṣa*), the Lord (*īśvara*), time, and atoms as being the capable creators.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are seven kinds of self-nature (*svabhāva*). They are:

the self-nature of accumulation (*saṃgraha*), the self-nature of essence (*bhāva*), the self-nature of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the self-nature of the great elements (*mahābhūta*), the self-nature of cause (*hetu*), the self-nature of conditions (*pratyaya*), and the self-nature of accomplishment (*niṣpatti*).
[Wei Translation] Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are seven kinds of intrinsic nature (svabhāva) among the non-Buddhists.

What are these seven? First, the intrinsic nature of accumulation; second, the intrinsic nature of essence; third, the intrinsic nature of characteristics; fourth, the intrinsic nature of the great elements;
fifth, the intrinsic nature of cause; sixth, the intrinsic nature of conditions; and seventh, the intrinsic nature of accomplishment.
Intrinsic Nature.
[Tang Translation: Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are seven kinds of intrinsic nature:

namely, the intrinsic nature of accumulation, the intrinsic nature of essence, the intrinsic nature of characteristics, the intrinsic nature of the great elements, the intrinsic nature of cause, the intrinsic nature of conditions, and the intrinsic nature of accomplishment.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are seven kinds of ultimate reality (paramārtha):

namely, the realm of the mind (citta), the realm of discernment (prajñā), the realm of wisdom (jñāna), the realm of vision (darśana), the realm that transcends the two views, the realm that transcends the stages of the sons [of the Buddha], and the realm of the Tathāgata’s own self-attainment.
[Wei Translation] Furthermore, Mahāmati, I have seven kinds of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
What are the seven? First, the realm of the mind (*citta-viṣaya*); second, the realm of knowledge (*jñāna-viṣaya*); third, the realm of wisdom (*prajñā-viṣaya*); fourth, the realm of the two views;
fifth, the realm that transcends the two views; sixth, the realm that transcends the stages of the Buddha’s sons (*jinaputra-bhūmi*); and seventh, the entry into...
The internal sphere of practice within the stage of the Tathāgata. [Tang Translation:
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are seven kinds of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Namely: that which is the sphere of activity of the mind;

that which is the sphere of activity of wisdom (*jñāna*); that which is the sphere of activity of the two views; that which transcends the sphere of activity of the two views; that which transcends the sphere of activity of the stages of the sons [of the Buddha]; and that which is the sphere of activity of the Tathāgata.
It is the sphere of practice realized by the Tathāgata’s own noble wisdom.
Mahāmati, this is the mind of the ultimate reality of the intrinsic nature of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, future, and present.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, this is the mind of the ultimate reality of the intrinsic nature of all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, future, and present.

[The Tang Translation: Mahāmati, this is the mind of the ultimate reality and the intrinsic nature of phenomena (dharmasvabhāva-paramārthacitta) of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, future, and present.
By means of the mind of the ultimate reality of the self-nature of phenomena, one accomplishes the worldly, the world-transcending, and the supreme world-transcending dharmas of the Tathāgatas.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, relying on this mind of the ultimate reality of the self-nature of phenomena, all Buddhas and Tathāgatas...
Ultimately, one attains both the mundane and the supramundane.
[Tang Translation: By means of this mind, one accomplishes the supreme mundane and supramundane dharmas of the Tathāgata.

The noble eye of wisdom enters into the establishment of the specific and general characteristics [of phenomena]. As they are so established, they do not share in the evil views of the treatises of the non-Buddhists.
[Wei Translation: The eye of wisdom of all Buddhas establishes all phenomena according to their common and distinct characteristics; as they are so established...
Established. Not in common with the false views of external paths.
[Tang Translation: By means of the noble eye of wisdom, one enters into the various establishments of specific and general characteristics. That which is so established—
One does not associate with the evil views of non-Buddhists.
Mahāmati, what is meant by associating with the evil views of non-Buddhist treatises?
It refers to the false perception of one's own sphere of experience, failing to realize that it is a manifestation of one's own mind, and thus being limited by a lack of penetration.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, how is it that one does not share the same views as the heterodox outsiders?

It is because one perceives the false imaginings of the objective realm of one's own mind through discrimination, yet fails to realize that these are merely the perceptions of one's own mental constructs.
