It is just as with clay pots, threads, cloth, grass mats, seeds, sprouts, butter, and curd; all are likewise so.
This is called external conditions arising through successive transformation.

What are internal conditions? It refers to phenomena such as ignorance, craving, and karma which receive the name of "conditions," from which the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense bases (āyatanas) arise.
Dharma. It is that which arises conditioned by objects; it is without differentiation, yet it is falsely conceptualized by the ignorant. This is called the internal conditionally-arisen dharma.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, what is the characteristic of the internal collection of causes and conditions? Mahāmati, it refers to ignorance, karma, and craving.
Such dharmas as these are called the characteristic of the internal collection of causes and conditions. Mahāmati, because of ignorance and so forth, the aggregates [arise].

The elements (*dhātu*), bases (*āyatana*), and so forth, are designated as the characteristics of the collection of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-samudaya-lakṣaṇa*). Yet, ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) engage in false conceptualization (*abhūta-parikalpa*) and perceive them as distinct characteristics.

[Tang Translation: "Internal" refers to the arising of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements, and bases (*dhātu-āyatana*) through ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), karma (*karman*), and so forth; this is what constitutes the internal.
Regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*): this is merely a conceptual construction of the ignorant. Mahāmati, those causes are of six kinds:
namely, the cause of what is to be (the future), the cause of continuity, the cause of characteristics, the efficient cause, the cause of manifestation, and the expectant cause.
As for the cause of what is to be: once the efficient cause has acted, internal and external phenomena arise. As for the cause of continuity: having acted...
Having攀緣 (ālambana) internal and external dharmas, the seeds of the aggregates (skandha-bīja) and so forth arise. Regarding the "causal condition" (nimitta-hetu):

it produces an uninterrupted succession of arising. Regarding the "acting cause" (kāraṇa-hetu): it performs the function of sovereignty, like a universal monarch (cakravartin). Regarding the "manifesting cause" (pradarśana-hetu):

once the objects of false discrimination have arisen, it manifests the appearance of what has been produced, like a lamp illuminating forms and the like. Regarding the "waiting cause" (pratīkṣā-hetu): it acts at the time of cessation, causing the succession to be severed.
It does not arise from the nature of false conceptualization.
[Wei Translation: Mahāmati, there are six kinds of causes. What are the six? First, the primary cause;
second, the continuous cause; third, the characteristic cause; fourth, the productive cause; fifth, the revealing cause; sixth, the dependent cause.
"Mahāmati, as for the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*): having acted as a cause, it is able to produce internal and external phenomena. Mahāmati, as for the continuity condition (*sambandha-hetu*):
it is able to take internal and external phenomena, the aggregates (*skandhas*), seeds, and so forth, as its objects. Mahāmati, as for the characteristic condition (*lakṣaṇa-hetu*):

it is able to produce the sequence of continuity and perform its functions without interruption. Mahāmati, as for the creative condition (*kāraka-hetu*): it is able to act as a dominant condition (*adhipati-hetu*)."

Mahāmati, it is like a wheel-turning monarch. As for the "cause of manifestation" (*parijñā-hetu*), it is that which can reveal the phenomena produced by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), just as a lamp illuminates forms and so forth.

Mahāmati, as for the "dependent cause" (*apekṣā-hetu*), it is that at the time of cessation, one does not perceive the arising of false dharmas, because the continuity of those phenomena has been severed.

[The Tang Translation: "Mahāmati, there are six kinds of causes: namely, the cause of future existence (*bhaviṣyaddhetu*), the cause of connection (*sambandhahetu*), the cause of characteristics (*lakṣaṇahetu*), the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*), the cause of manifestation (*vyañjanahetu*), and the cause of dependence (*apekṣāhetu*).
Mahāmati, the cause of future existence refers to internal and external phenomena acting as causes to produce effects.
The cause of connection refers to internal and external phenomena acting as objects of perception (*ālambana*) to produce the seeds of the aggregates (*skandha*)."
Regarding these, the *samanantarapratyaya* (equal-and-immediate condition) produces an uninterrupted arising and brings about a continuous result.

The *kāraṇahetu* (efficient cause) refers to that which acts as a dominant influence (*adhipati*) in producing a result, like a universal monarch (*cakravartin*). The *vyañjanahetu* (manifesting cause) refers to that which, through discrimination, gives rise to and manifests the characteristics of an object, like a lamp illuminating things.
The *apekṣāhetu* (contingent cause) refers to the cessation at the time of extinction, wherein the continuity is severed and conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) ceases.
"Mahāmati, for those foolish people who are deluded by the marks of their own false imaginings, things do not arise gradually, nor do they arise simultaneously. Why is this?

If they were to arise simultaneously, there would be no distinction between the agent and the object, because the characteristic of causality could not be established. If they were to arise gradually..."
This is because they cannot be characterized as "I. They arise gradually or do not arise at all; just as there is no designation of a "father" if no son is born.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, in this way, all dharmas are the false conceptualizations of the ordinary person's own mind. Mahāmati!
These phenomena do not arise sequentially, nor do they arise simultaneously. Why is this?

Mahāmati, if all phenomena were to arise simultaneously, there would be no distinction between cause and effect, because one would not perceive the specific characteristics of the causal and resultant bodies.

If they were to arise sequentially, as long as the characteristics of the body have not yet been attained, one cannot speak of sequential arising; it would be like being unable to call someone "father" before a son exists.
[Tang Translation] Mahāmati, this is merely the conceptual construction of the ignorant; it is neither sequential arising nor...

They arise instantaneously. Why is this? Mahāmati, if they were to arise instantaneously, there would be no distinction between the agent and the action, because one could not find any causal characteristics upon investigation.
If they were to arise gradually, their essential nature could likewise not be found;
it would be like calling someone a "father" before a son has even been born.
"Mahāmati, the notion that there is a gradual arising through a continuous succession of skillful means is not so; it is merely a product of false discrimination (*vikalpa*).

This is because what is produced and that which produces it arise from conditions such as objective referents (*ālambana*), sequential conditions (*anuloma-pratyaya*), and dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*). Mahāmati, gradual arising does not occur because of attachment to the characteristics of the self-nature of false discrimination.

Neither gradual nor simultaneous arising occurs, because [all things] are the manifestation of one's own mind and are experienced as such. External objects, whether characterized by specific or general marks, do not exist."

It is not a nature, Mahāmati. Neither gradual nor simultaneous production occurs, except for the manifestation of signs arising from the deluded conceptualization that fails to perceive that [the world] is a manifestation of one's own mind.
Therefore, regarding the characteristics of causal conditions, functional activity, and skillful means, one should abandon views of both gradual and simultaneous [production].
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, foolish ordinary people observe with their own minds that because successive continuity is inconsistent, they speak thus:

"The causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) are able to produce all phenomena.
Mahāmati, in this manner, phenomena are not produced through succession. Mahāmati, [they] grasp through false discrimination.
Regarding the characteristics of the essence of dharmas: they are produced neither simultaneously nor sequentially.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, because one perceives within one’s own mind the body and the objects of livelihood, Mahāmati, external dharmas—whether by way of specific or general characteristics—do not exist.
Therefore, they are not produced either sequentially or simultaneously. Mahāmati, it is merely that false consciousness arises as the perception of one’s own mind. Mahāmati, you should...
One should abandon the occurrence of things produced by the conditions of improper views. Regarding the successive production of dharmas at one time:

[The Tang translation states: "Those who engage in conceptual construction claim that through the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), the immediate condition (*anantara-pratyaya*), the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), and so forth, the produced and the producer are mutually connected;
however, the principle of their successive production cannot be established. All [of these views are untenable].
This is because it is a characteristic of attachment to false conceptualization. Mahāmati, neither gradual nor sudden [arising] occurs at all;

it is merely the manifestation of mind, body, and resources. This is because external, self-, and common-characteristics are all devoid of intrinsic nature, except for the arising of consciousness which produces its own discriminative views.
Therefore, Mahāmati, one should abandon the notions of gradual and sudden within the characteristics of conjunction produced by causes and conditions.
The Arising of Views.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "All things are entirely without arising, And there is no extinction through causes and conditions.
Within that arising and extinction, One gives rise to the notion of causes and conditions. It is not to deny extinction followed by arising, But rather [to show] their continuity."

The arising of causes and conditions exists solely to sever the delusive conceptualizations of the ignorant and foolish. This dharma of dependent origination, characterized by neither existence nor non-existence, is entirely devoid of birth;
yet, through the confusion of habitual tendencies, the three realms of existence manifest from it.
[Wei Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse: "Because of causes and conditions, nothing is not produced; because it is not produced, it does not perish.
The causes and conditions of production and destruction are empty; there is neither production nor destruction. To refute these various causes and conditions, fools grasp at them as false.
Since there is no production from existent or non-existent conditions, all phenomena do not arise. Because they are perfumed within the triple world..."
Habituation to the deluded mind.
[Tang Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One further spoke in verse: "All phenomena are without arising, and likewise without cessation.
Within those various conditions, one discriminates the characteristics of arising and ceasing. This does not negate the convergence of conditions; thus it is."
Ceasing and then arising again, this occurs only within the deluded attachments of the ignorant. Whether phenomena exist or do not exist within conditions, they are all devoid of arising.
It is through the mind’s deluded revolution driven by habitual tendencies that the manifestation of existence arises from this.
In reality there is no arising of conditions, nor is there any cessation. One should contemplate all conditioned phenomena as being like flowers in the sky.

they falsely cling to the notions of identity, difference, both, neither, existence, non-existence, neither existence nor non-existence, permanence, and impermanence, thereby giving rise to all phenomena.
[The Tang Translation: Mahāmati, it is like those with cataracts who see the appearance of floating hairs and say to one another, "This is a marvel!
Yet these floating hairs are neither existent nor non-existent, because they are seen by some and not seen by others. It is the same with the heterodox teachers:

through their evil views and conceptual discriminations, they cling to such notions as identity, difference, both, or neither; thus they slander the True Dharma, bringing ruin upon themselves and others.
For example, a fire-wheel is not a wheel, yet the foolish perceive it as a wheel; the wise do not.

In this same way, the evil views and aspirations of the outsiders arise from the perceptions of oneness and difference, bothness and neitherness, existence and non-existence, and permanence and impermanence, whereby all natures are produced.
[Chinese Translation] Mahāmati, it is like a fire-wheel, which in reality is not a wheel; it is grasped by the ignorant, not by the wise.
It is the same with the non-Buddhists: through their evil views and desires, they cling to [the notions of] identity, difference, both, or neither regarding the arising of all phenomena.
For example, a bubble on the water resembles a mani jewel. A foolish person lacking wisdom conceives the notion that it is a mani jewel; they become attached to it and pursue it.
Yet that bubble is neither a mani jewel nor not a mani jewel, depending on whether it is grasped or not grasped.

In this same way, those of external paths, perfumed by the habitual tendencies of false discrimination and evil views, speak of "arising" regarding what does not exist due to conditions, while those who hold to existence speak of "cessation."
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, it is like raindrops produced by the falling rain that resemble crystal beads.
Foolish ordinary people, through false perception, become attached to them, giving rise to the notion that they are beads and running hither and thither in pursuit of them.
Mahāmati, those raindrops are neither precious beads nor non-beads. Why is this? Because there is grasping and non-grasping. Mahāmati, as for those...
The various non-Buddhists, due to the habitual perfuming of their deluded minds, are likewise in this regard:
they assert that non-existent phenomena arise dependent upon causes and conditions, while others claim that existent phenomena undergo cessation.
[The Tang Translation: "Mahāmati, it is like a bubble on water that resembles a crystal bead. Fools, grasping at it as real, run after it to seize it.
Yet that bubble is neither a bead nor not a bead, because it is neither grasped nor not grasped. The same is true of the non-Buddhists."
Perfumed by the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of false views and conceptual discrimination, they assert that what does not exist arises and destroy the existence of conditions.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the five-membered syllogism (*pañcāvayava-vākya*); having established each of these, one attains the self-realization of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*).
They falsely conceptualize and cling to the existence of intrinsic nature in things that are devoid of the two kinds of self-nature.
[Wei Translation] Furthermore, Mahāmati, those non-Buddhists establish three types of valid cognition and the five-membered syllogism.
And they speak thus: "There truly exists the Dharma realized within by the Noble Ones, which is free from the two types of self-nature and from false discrimination.
[Tang Translation:
Furthermore, Mahāmati, having established the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [it is shown that] within the internal realization of noble wisdom, one is free from the two.
Regarding the dharmas of intrinsic nature, there arises the discrimination of existence.

Mahāmati, when the transformation of mind, intellect, consciousness, body, and mental objects occurs, all false imaginings that grasp at the internal manifestations of one's own mind as subject and object are severed.
In the stage of the Tathāgata, which is the noble wisdom of self-realization, the practitioner does not form conceptions of existence or non-existence regarding that state.
If, however, a practitioner were to give rise to the grasping of marks of existence or non-existence toward such an object, they would be grasping at nourishment and grasping at a self and a person.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, by transcending mind, thought, and consciousness, one transforms the basis and immediately attains the body of the noble lineage.
In the practice of all activities, there is no such [deluded] mind, because one is free from the false objects of grasped and grasper as seen by one’s own mind.
Entering the stage of the Tathāgata, one personally advances toward the realization of noble wisdom. For one who practices according to reality, it is not...
Because birth-existence is devoid of mind, Mahāmati. A practitioner who cultivates according to reality will necessarily attain such a state.
Mahāmati, if one grasps at the existence or non-existence of phenomena, that constitutes the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, and the mark of a life-span.

[The Tang Translation: Mahāmati, all practitioners who transform the mind, intellect, and consciousness, becoming free from the grasping of subject and object, abide in the stage of the Tathāgata and the self-realized noble Dharma;
they do not give rise to the conception of existence or non-existence.
Mahāmati, if practitioners give rise to the attachment to existence or non-existence regarding objective realms, they will then cling to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.

Mahāmati, if one speaks of the self-nature and the specific or general characteristics of those natures, all such things are spoken by *nirmāṇa-buddhas* (transformation buddhas), not by *dharma-buddhas*.
Furthermore, all verbal expressions arise from the expectations and views of the foolish;

they do not establish a distinct path for the sake of those who have attained the dwelling in the bliss of samādhi through the self-realization of noble wisdom. [Such teachings] are merely conceptual displays.

[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, to speak of the existence or non-existence of self-characteristics and common characteristics is called the teaching of the *nirmāṇa-buddha* (transformation Buddha), not the teaching of the *dharma-buddha* (Dharma Buddha).
Furthermore, Mahāmati, the *nirmāṇa-tathāgata* teaches such dharmas in accordance with the views and minds of ignorant ordinary beings, causing them to practice;
it is not for the purpose of establishing the practice of reality (*yathābhūta*), but is merely a manifestation.
Because it is the practice of the bliss of samādhi through the noble wisdom realized within oneself.
[Tang Translation] Mahāmati, the specific and general characteristics of all dharmas are taught by the *nirmāṇa-buddha* (transformation Buddha), not by the *dharma-buddha* (Dharma Buddha).
Mahāmati, the teachings spoken by the *nirmāṇa-buddha* merely conform to the views arising from the minds of ordinary fools; they do not serve to reveal [ultimate reality].
This demonstrates the realm of the bliss of samādhi of self-realized noble wisdom.
It is like the reflection of a tree appearing in water; it is neither a reflection nor not a reflection, neither the form of a tree nor not the form of a tree.
Likewise, the false conceptualizations and attachments of non-Buddhists, perfumed by their habitual tendencies, rely upon [the notions of] identity, difference, both, or neither.
There are notions of existence, non-existence, neither existence nor non-existence, permanence, and impermanence; yet one is unable to know that these are merely the manifestations of one's own mind.
It is like a bright mirror which, according to conditions, displays all forms and images without conceptual construction. That mirror is neither the image nor not the image.
Yet one perceives what is not an image as an image; thus do deluded fools, through their false imaginings, form the notion of an image. Such is the evil view of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas):

they falsely conceptualize and cling to images appearing from their own minds, based on views of identity, difference, both, or neither, existence, non-existence, neither existence nor non-existence, permanence, or impermanence.
It is like the sound produced by the conjunction of wind and water; it is neither a nature nor a non-nature. Thus it is.

The false imaginings of the evil views of the non-Buddhists rely upon the notions of oneness and difference, bothness and not-bothness, existence and non-existence, neither-existence-nor-non-existence, permanence and impermanence.
It is like a vast expanse of earth where no grass or trees grow, yet where mirages appear as flowing rivers, surging with great waves like clouds;

these are neither entities nor non-entities, because of the presence of craving and the absence of craving. Thus it is with the foolish: they are driven by the habitual tendencies of beginningless falsehood.

The perfuming of false conceptualization and attachment—based on arising, abiding, and ceasing; on unity and difference; on conjunction and non-conjunction; on existence and non-existence; on being neither existent nor non-existent;
and on permanence and impermanence—occurs through the gateway of its own inherent objects, just like those shimmering mirages and waves.
It is, for example, like a person using incantations and mechanical devices to cause a *piśāca* ghost, which is not a sentient being, to move and shake through skillful means.
It is for the sake of those who, being ordinary and foolish, are attached to the delusions of coming and going;

such are the evil views and aspirations of the outsiders (*tīrthika*), which rely on the views of identity, difference, both, or neither, existence, non-existence, or neither existence nor non-existence, and the views of permanence or impermanence. They are attached to conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and establish what is unreal.

Therefore, Mahāmati, if you wish to attain the reality of the noble wisdom of self-realization (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*), you should abandon [the notions of] arising, abiding, and ceasing, as well as identity and difference.
The false conceptualizations of evil views—such as both [existence and non-existence], neither existence nor non-existence, permanence and impermanence, and so forth.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, it is like a person seeing the reflection of a tree in water. Mahāmati, that is neither a reflection nor not a reflection.
Why? Because when there is a tree, there is [a reflection]; when there is no tree, there is none. Mahāmati, those various outsiders...
The way in which the path is defiled by the habitual tendencies of false views and deluded thoughts is likewise so.

One discriminates between identity and difference, bothness and neitherness, existence and non-existence, being and non-being, permanence and impermanence; this is due to the discrimination of deluded thoughts. Why is this?

It is because one does not realize that what is seen is merely the manifestation of one’s own mind. Mahāmati, it is like a clear mirror which, according to conditions, allows one to see a single [image].
All forms and images are without a discriminating mind. Mahāmati, they are neither images nor non-images. Why is this?

Because they are seen when there are conditions for seeing them, and not seen when there are no such conditions. Mahāmati, ignorant ordinary people see the existence or non-existence of images through the discrimination of their own minds.
Mahāmati, the same applies to the mirror-images produced by the false conceptualizations of the minds of all outsiders.
It is so. This is because one perceives them as identical, different, both, or neither.

Mahāmati, it is like various echoes that are heard through the conjunction of mountains, rivers, water, wind, space, and houses; those echoed sounds are neither existent nor non-existent. Why is this?

“Because of the sound of the śrāvakas, Mahāmati, all non-Buddhists [perceive] through the habitual tendencies of their own minds’ false discrimination the views of oneness and otherness, bothness and not-bothness, existence and non-existence, neither-existence-nor-non-existence, permanence and impermanence.
Mahāmati, it is like a place where there are no grasses, trees, gardens, or forests; when sunlight and dust particles come together, [a mirage appears].”
One sees the movement of waves upon water, yet those waves neither exist nor do not exist. Why is this?
Because they cause sentient beings to experience both joy and lack of joy. Mahāmati, all non-Buddhists and deluded ordinary people are likewise like this.

Due to the habitual perfuming of the afflictive mind since beginningless time, conceptual proliferations arise regarding arising, abiding, and ceasing; oneness and difference; bothness and neitherness;
existence and non-existence; being and non-being; and permanence and impermanence. Within the gateway of the realized wisdom of the noble ones' internal realization, [these do not exist].
It is for the purpose of manifesting the phenomenon of mirages and thirst. Mahāmati, it is like a person who, through the power of incantations, raises a corpse;
or like a wooden automaton that lacks the essence of a sentient being, yet performs the acts of coming and going through the power of a piśāca spirit or the skill of a craftsman.
Yet foolish ordinary people cling to these as truly existent because they see them moving.
For this reason, Mahāmati, the deluded ordinary people and the various non-Buddhists likewise fall into the mind of false views.
This is because they cling to the false notions of oneness and difference, bothness and not-bothness, existence and non-existence, neither-existence-nor-non-existence, permanence and impermanence.
Therefore, Mahāmati, because ordinary people and non-Buddhists falsely establish such dharmas, [they fall into error]. Thus it is, Mahāmati.
You should remain far removed from views concerning arising, abiding, and ceasing; oneness and difference; bothness and not-bothness; existence and non-existence; neither-existence-nor-non-existence;
and permanence and impermanence, because these are distinctions made by the noble wisdom realized within one's own body.
[The Tang Translation: "Mahāmati, it is like the reflection of a tree appearing in water; it is neither a reflection nor not a reflection, neither the form of a tree nor not the form of a tree.
It is the same with the non-Buddhists: permeated by various views, they do not understand that [all things] are their own mind."
They give rise to conceptual discriminations regarding identity, difference, and so forth. For example, a clear mirror is devoid of discrimination;
it manifests various forms and images in accordance with various conditions. Those images are neither images nor non-images, yet one perceives them as both image and non-image.
Foolish people discriminate and form the notion that they are images. The same is true for the heterodox: regarding the various forms and images manifested within their own minds, they...
They grasp at the characteristics of identity, difference, both, or neither. Mahāmati, it is like an echo, which arises from the conjunction of wind, water, and the sounds of people;
it is neither existent nor non-existent, because what is heard is neither sound nor non-sound. It is the same with the heterodox teachers:
through the power of the habitual tendencies of their own mental discrimination, they give rise to views of identity, difference, both, or neither. Mahāmati...
Wisdom. For example, where there is no grass or trees upon the great earth, when sunlight strikes it, shimmering water-waves appear;
these are neither existent nor non-existent, because they arise from inverted perception rather than true perception. So too it is with foolish ordinary beings:

permeated by the evil habits of beginningless conceptual proliferation, they perceive arising, abiding, and ceasing within the gateway of the dharmatā that is personally realized through noble wisdom.

"Whether they are identical or different, existent or non-existent, both or neither—Mahāmati, it is like a wooden puppet or a reanimated corpse that moves, turns, and acts incessantly through the power of a piśāca mechanism.
Foolish people take these to be real. So too it is with ignorant ordinary beings; they follow after the outsiders and give rise to various evils."

They perceive and cling to false discourses such as identity and difference. Therefore, Mahāmati, within the dharma realized by noble wisdom, you should abandon all conceptual discriminations, such as arising, abiding, and ceasing;
identity and difference; existence and non-existence; both and neither, and so forth.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

"Like a phantom, a dream, a reflection in water, a tree reflected in a mirror, a mass of hair, or a mirage in the heat—thus one should contemplate the three realms of existence; by doing so, one ultimately attains liberation.
Just as a thirsty deer, with a flickering and deluded mind, perceives a mirage as water while in reality there is no substance of water—so too does the seed of consciousness flicker."

When perceiving objects, the deluded ordinary person gives rise to false conceptualization. Like being obscured by a cataract, they cling to and grasp at the nature of things throughout beginningless birth and death.
Just as one drives out a wedge with another wedge, one must abandon the grasping of craving.

Like illusions, spells, mechanical devices, floating clouds, dreams, or flashes of lightning—by contemplating these, one attains liberation and forever severs the three continuities. Regarding those [objects], there is no agent; it is just like...
Like a flame in empty space—thus one should know all phenomena; then there is nothing to be known. Verbal teachings are merely provisional names, and they possess no inherent marks.

To give rise to deluded conceptualization regarding them is like [seeing] the aggregates and formations as falling hairs, like a painting of falling hairs, an illusion, a dream, a city of the Gandharvas, a whirling firebrand, or a mirage in the heat;
these appear to sentient beings though they do not exist. [Concepts such as] permanence and impermanence, unity and difference, both and neither...
The same applies to both. Through the beginningless continuity of faults, the deluded and ignorant give rise to false conceptualizations.
Just as various forms appear within a bright mirror, water, clear eyes, or a wondrous mani jewel, yet in reality nothing exists there; so too do all natures manifest.
Like a mirage in the heat of the day, various forms appear, yet like a dream, they have no existence.
[Wei Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse: "The five aggregates and consciousness are like the reflection of a tree in water;

they are like what is seen in illusions and dreams. Do not rely on mental consciousness to grasp them. All phenomena are like the optical illusion of floating hairs, like the delusion of a mirage or water in a flame.
Contemplate the three realms: all are like illusions and dreams. If one can contemplate in this way, practice..."
Practice leads to liberation. Like a summer animal craving water, the agitated and deluded mind perceives water where no water exists;
through false imagination, it sees what is not there. Just as the seeds of consciousness produce perceptions when stirred by objects, the ignorant grasp them as real.
Those phenomena arise like visual distortions (*timira*); due to ignorance since beginningless time, one grasps at things as if embracing them, just as one might grasp a wedge.
Removing the wedge; deceiving the ordinary person to enter the Dharma; like a phantom, a reanimated corpse, or a mechanical device; like a dream, lightning, or clouds—always thus.
Contemplate the world in this way: sever existence to attain liberation. Like a mirage in the empty sky, there are no cognitions that know.
Contemplate all phenomena in this way: do not cling to any phenomena. All cognitions exist only as names, for all characteristics are empty and non-existent.
One perceives the aggregates (*skandha*) like a mass of floating hairs. Within what phenomena does one differentiate?

Like paintings, masses of floating hairs, illusions, dreams, *gandharva*-cities, fire-wheels, and water in a mirage—though non-existent in reality, they appear as existent. Whether permanent or impermanent, one or both, or neither;
bound by causes from beginningless time, the deluded minds of ordinary beings perceive these various things appearing within mirrors, jewels, water, and the eyes.
Various forms; one falsely perceives various colors, like a dream or the son of a barren woman.
All phenomena lack reality, like the mirage-water craved by deer.
[Tang Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse: "The aggregates of consciousness are five, just like water."
The shadows of trees; what is seen is like a phantom or a dream—do not engage in false conceptualization.
The three realms of existence are like a mirage, a phantom, a dream, or the optical illusion of falling hairs. If one can contemplate in this way, one will ultimately attain liberation.
Just as a mirage in the heat causes the agitated and deluded mind to perceive water, while in reality no water exists, so too is the seed of consciousness.

Moving and turning, one perceives objective realms; like what is seen by one with cataracts, the foolish give rise to attachment. Within beginningless birth and death, they are shrouded and enveloped by such attachment.

To cause them to relinquish it and attain liberation is like using a wedge to extract a wedge, or like that which is produced by illusions, spells, and mechanical devices—like floating clouds, dreams, and flashes of lightning.
One should contemplate the world as always being thus, forever severing the three continuities. Within this...
There is nothing at all; it is like a mirage in the sky. To know all phenomena in this way is to have nothing to know.

The aggregates are like the appearance of falling hairs; within them, one falsely discriminates. They are merely provisional designations and names; when sought for their characteristics, they cannot be found.
Like painted hanging hair, a magical illusion, a dream, a city of the Gandharvas, a fire-wheel, or a mirage in the heat—though non-existent, they appear as if real.
In this same way, through beginningless bondage, the foolish engage in false conceptualization regarding permanence and impermanence, identity and difference, or both and neither.
Just as forms and images appear within a clear mirror, water, a pure eye, or a wondrous mani-jewel, yet in reality [they have no inherent existence].
There is nothing that exists. Mind and consciousness are likewise; they universally manifest all forms and signs, like a dream, a mirage in the sky, or the son of a barren woman.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, when a Bodhisattva-Tathāgata teaches the Dharma, he is free from these four positions: namely, identity, difference, both, and neither.

Neither existent nor non-existent, neither eternal nor non-eternal, free from the conceptual proliferation of existence and non-existence, affirmation and denial, and discrimination, it is the ultimate truth, dependent origination, the path, cessation, and liberation.
When the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma, he takes this as the primary principle.

He does not teach that things arise from a primal nature (*prakṛti*), nor from a creator god (*īśvara*), nor from no cause, nor from atoms (*paramāṇu*), nor from time, nor from self-nature (*svabhāva*), nor from a continuous succession; rather, he teaches the Dharma in this way.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, in order to purify the obstacles of afflictions (*kleśa*) and cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), one should— like a caravan leader—
gradually establish the non-existence of the one hundred and eight propositions, and skillfully discern the characteristics of the various vehicles (*yāna*) and the stages (*bhūmi*).
[Wei Translation] Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, teach the Dharma free from four kinds of views;
that is, they are free from [the views of] identity, difference, both, and neither. They are far removed from the establishment of existence and non-existence.

Mahāmati, all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, teach the Dharma based upon the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), tranquility (*śānti*), and liberation (*vimukti*). Mahāmati, all the Buddhas...
The Buddha, the Tathāgata, teaches the Dharma based on the ultimate realm; he does not teach the Dharma by relying on causes such as self-nature, Īśvara, non-causality, atoms, or time.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Buddhas teach the Dharma free from the two kinds of obstructions:
the afflictive obstruction and the cognitive obstruction. Just as a great caravan leader leads a multitude of people and places them in succession [at their destination],...

They reach the previously unseen state of ultimate peace and tranquility, and are gradually established therein so that they may thoroughly understand and know the distinct characteristics of the vehicles and the stages.
[Tang Translation: Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Dharma taught by all Buddhas is free from the four propositions; that is, it is free from identity and difference.
"Mahāmati, establishing [theories] such as both [existence and non-existence], neither, or existence and non-existence, leads to slander.

Mahāmati, when the Buddhas teach the Dharma, they take the truths, dependent origination, cessation, the path, and liberation as its primary focus. It is not associated with [theories of] a supreme spirit (pradhāna), a creator lord (īśvara), past actions (pūrvakṛta), spontaneity (svabhāva), time (kāla), atoms (paramāṇu), and so forth.
Mahāmati, the Buddhas teach the Dharma for the sake of purifying the afflictions and the cognitive obscurations."
Because of these two kinds of hindrances, he leads them step by step to abide within the one hundred and eight phrases of the signless Dharma,
skillfully discerning the characteristics of the various vehicles and stages, just as a caravan leader skillfully guides a multitude.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of dhyāna. What are the four? They are:
the dhyāna practiced by fools, the dhyāna that examines meanings, the dhyāna that takes suchness as its object, and the Tathāgata-dhyāna. What is the dhyāna practiced by fools?

It refers to the practitioners of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and non-Buddhists who contemplate the selflessness of persons, the specific and general characteristics [of phenomena], the skeleton, and impermanence and suffering.
Taking attachment to the signs of impurity as primary, one contemplates these signs without distinction;
because these signs do not cease even as one progresses through successive stages, this is called the dhyāna practiced by fools.
[Wei Translation] Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of dhyāna. What are the four? First, the dhyāna practiced by ignorant ordinary beings;
second, the dhyāna that contemplates meaning; third, the dhyāna of mindfulness of *tathatā*;
and fourth, the dhyāna of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas. What is the dhyāna practiced by ignorant ordinary beings? It refers to the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
The practitioners of the non-Buddhist paths (tīrthika) contemplate the selflessness of persons through the specific and general characteristics of the skeleton;
they grasp at various marks, such as impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity.

Because these [graspings] are thus and thus, determined and ultimately not otherwise, they proceed through this sequence—from the preceding contemplations, ascending step by step, even unto the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
This is called the dhyāna of foolish ordinary people, non-Buddhists, and śrāvakas.
[Tang Translation] Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of dhyāna. What are the four? They are:
the dhyāna practiced by ordinary people, the dhyāna that examines meanings, the dhyāna that takes true thusness as its object, and the dhyāna of all Tathāgatas. What is the dhyāna of the foolish?

The Dhyāna practiced by the ignorant refers to those practitioners among the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas who realize the selflessness of persons and perceive the interconnected skeletons of their own and others' bodies as being entirely impermanent, suffering, and impure.

Observing in this manner with firm attachment and without relinquishing it, they gradually progress toward excellence until they reach the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) characterized by non-perception. This is called the dhyāna practiced by the ignorant.

What is the dhyāna of examining meaning? It refers to when, having realized that persons lack self-nature—both in their individual characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)—and that externalists’ notions of self, other, or both lack intrinsic nature, one examines the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).
As the meaning of the characteristics of those stages progressively advances, this is called the dhyāna of examining meaning.

[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, what is the dhyāna of examining the meaning? It refers to observing the self-characteristics and common characteristics of the non-existence of a personal self (*pudgala-nairātmya*).
It is seeing that the self-characteristics and common characteristics, as well as the characteristics of self and other, of foolish ordinary beings and non-Buddhists are without reality.
Because it observes the meaning of the sequential stages of practice regarding the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), Mahāmati, this is called the dhyāna that observes meaning.

[Tang Translation: What is the dhyāna that observes meaning? It refers to knowing the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) and the selflessness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*). Furthermore—

Free from the non-Buddhist views of creation by self, other, or both, one observes in accordance with the meaning of the characteristics of the stages (*bhūmi*) regarding the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*);
this is called the meditation on the observation of meaning.

What is the meditation on the suchness of objects (*tathatālambana*)? It refers to the non-arising of delusion within the state of reality, wherein the two kinds of selflessness are seen as mere mental constructions (*parikalpita*).
This is called the meditation that takes suchness as its object.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, what is the meditation that contemplates true suchness?

It refers to observing the causes and conditions of false discrimination, knowing the two kinds of selflessness as they truly are, and correctly discerning that all dharmas lack any substantial reality.
[Aspect]. At that time, one attains the realm of tranquility within a mind free from conceptualization. Mahāmati, this is called the dhyāna of contemplating *tathatā* (suchness).
[Tang Translation]: What is the dhyāna that takes *tathatā* as its object? It refers to when one realizes that the dualistic conceptualization of non-self is empty.
Delusive thoughts. If one knows them as they truly are, so that those thoughts do not arise, this is called the meditation on *tathatā* (suchness).
What is the Tathāgata-meditation? It refers to entering the stage of the Tathāgata and attaining the three kinds of blissful abidings characterized by the noble wisdom of self-realization.
Accomplishing inconceivable deeds for the sake of sentient beings—this is called the Tathāgata-dhyāna.
[Wei Translation] What is the Tathāgata-dhyāna of contemplation? It refers to entering the stage of the Tathāgata as it truly is;

it involves entering the characteristics of the noble internal wisdom of the body, the three kinds of emptiness, and the three kinds of blissful practice, thereby being able to accomplish what must be done for sentient beings.
"Inconceivable, Mahāmati! This is called the Tathāgata-dhyāna. [Tang Translation: "What is the dhyāna of all Tathāgatas?
It refers to entering the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*), abiding in the realization-wisdom (*pratyātma-jñāna*) of one's own ground, and experiencing the three kinds of bliss.
Performing inconceivable deeds for the sake of all sentient beings—this is called the dhyāna of all Tathāgatas."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

"The dhyāna practiced by fools, the dhyāna of observing the characteristics of objects, the dhyāna of relying on reality as it is, and the pure dhyāna of the Tathāgata— these are like the forms of the sun and moon, like the lotus, the deep abyss, or like space and the extinction of fire.
The practitioner observes these various kinds of signs; [thus do] the non-Buddhists [view them]."
The Way penetrates Chan; yet one may likewise fall into the realms of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. Abandoning all of those, there is then nothing at all.
All Buddhas of all lands, with inconceivable hands, simultaneously stroke the crown of one’s head, causing one to enter accordantly into the mark of Suchness.
[Wei Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse: “Ordinary people practice the dhyāna of conduct; They practice the dhyāna of observing the characteristics of meaning;
They practice the dhyāna of true mindfulness of *tathatā*; And they practice the dhyāna of the ultimate purity of the Buddha.

Like the forms of the sun and moon, The appearance of the *padma* lotus and the ocean, And the appearance of fire extinguished in space— The practitioner contemplates in this way. These various kinds of appearances lead to falling [into conceptualization].”
Regarding the teachings of non-Buddhists, as well as the practices of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and the like— one who abandons all these enters into that which is non-existent.
At that time, throughout the lands of the ten directions, the Buddhas touch the crown of that practitioner’s head with their hands of True Suchness (*tathatā*),
causing them to enter True Suchness, which is signless.
[The Tang Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"The dhyāna practiced by fools, the dhyāna observing the characteristics of meaning, the dhyāna taking true suchness as its object, and the pure dhyāna of the Tathāgata.

When practitioners are in meditative concentration, they perceive forms such as the sun and moon, the *pātala* flower, deep abysses, empty space, fire, and paintings— such various signs as these lead them to fall [into error]."
They have fallen away from the teachings of the non-Buddhists and also from the realms of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

Having abandoned all these, they abide in the objectless state. Then all the infinite Buddhas throughout the lands of the ten directions extend their hands of light and stroke the crown of this person’s head;
thus, they are able to enter accordingly into the true mark of suchness.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, regarding parinirvāṇa, what dharma do you teach when you speak of it as nirvāṇa?"
[Wei Translation] At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, regarding what is called 'nirvāṇa,' what dharma is taught when one speaks of nirvāṇa? What is named nirvāṇa?"
[The Tang Translation: At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, regarding the nirvāṇa spoken of by all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas—what dharma do they designate as 'nirvāṇa'?"

The Buddha told Mahāmati: "The transformation of all self-nature, habitual tendencies, the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), the manas, and the mental consciousness (manovijñāna), as well as the habitual tendencies of views—this is called nirvāṇa.
The nirvāṇa of all Buddhas and myself is the realm of the objective reality of the emptiness of self-nature."
[Wei Translation] The Buddha addressed the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva, saying: "Nirvāṇa is the transformation and cessation of the essential nature and characteristics of the various consciousnesses;
it is the transformation of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of views; it is the transformation of the habitual tendencies of the dharmas of the mind, the intellect, and the *ālayavijñāna*.
This is called nirvāṇa, Mahāmati. I and all the Buddhas speak of such a dharma-nature as nirvāṇa."
Because the objective sphere is empty.

[Tang Translation] The Buddha told Mahāmati: "When the habit-energies of the self-nature of all consciousnesses, as well as the habit-energies of the views of the *ālayavijñāna* and the *manovijñāna*, have been transformed, I and the Buddhas call this 'nirvāṇa. This is precisely the sphere of the emptiness of the nature of all dharmas."
The Elements.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, as for nirvāṇa, it is the realm of self-realization through noble wisdom, free from the false imaginings of permanence and annihilation, and beyond the nature of existence and non-existence.
Why is it not permanent? Because it is free from the false imaginings of specific and general characteristics, it is not permanent. Why is it not annihilated? [Because...]
This means that because all noble ones—past, future, and present—attain self-awakening, it is not annihilation.
[Wei Translation] Furthermore, Mahāmati, what is called *nirvāṇa* refers to the sphere of practice of the noble internal wisdom;
it is because one is free from the false discrimination of existence and non-existence. Mahāmati, why is it not eternal? It is because it is free from...

Because one discriminates between phenomena according to their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), it is therefore not eternal. Mahāmati, why is it not annihilated?
It is because all noble ones (*ārya*) of the past, future, and present have realized it within their own bodies; therefore, it is not annihilated.
[The Tang Translation: Furthermore, Mahāmati, nirvāṇa is the sphere of activity of the noble wisdom of self-realization;

it is far removed from the extremes of annihilation and permanence, as well as existence and non-existence. Why is it not permanent? Because it is free from all conceptual constructions regarding specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
Why is it not annihilated? Because it is the sphere of activity of the self-realized wisdom of all noble ones in the past, future, and present.
Therefore, Mahāmati, nirvāṇa is neither destroyed nor does it die. If nirvāṇa were subject to death, it would have to undergo the continuity of rebirth;

if it were subject to destruction, it would fall into the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). For this reason, nirvāṇa is free from destruction and free from death. Therefore, the practitioner—
The place of refuge.
[Wei Translation: Mahāmati, parinirvāṇa is neither death nor extinction.
Mahāmati, if parinirvāṇa were a phenomenon of death, there would necessarily be the bondage of birth. Mahāmati, if parinirvāṇa were a phenomenon of extinction...
Because it would otherwise fall into the category of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*). Therefore, Mahāmati, parinirvāṇa is neither death nor extinction;
it is the refuge for those who practice according to reality.
[The Tang Translation: Furthermore, Mahāmati, Great Parinirvāṇa is neither destroyed nor does it die.
If it were subject to death, it would undergo rebirth; if it were subject to destruction, it would be conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). Therefore, Nirvāṇa is neither destroyed nor does it die;
it is the ultimate refuge for all practitioners.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, nirvāṇa is neither abandonment nor attainment; it is neither annihilation nor permanence;
it is neither a single meaning nor manifold meanings. This is called nirvāṇa.
[Wei Translation] Furthermore, Mahāmati, that which is called *nirvāṇa* is neither to be grasped nor to be abandoned;
it is not in this place nor in that place; it is neither annihilation nor permanence; it is neither a single meaning nor manifold meanings. For these reasons, it is named *nirvāṇa*.

[The Tang Translation: Furthermore, Mahāmati, because there is neither abandonment nor attainment, because it is neither annihilation nor permanence, and because it is neither identical nor different, it is called nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, as for the nirvāṇa of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas: it is the realization that their own-characteristics and common-characteristics do not involve proximity to objective realms;
because they possess non-perverted views, false conceptualization does not arise. They, regarding that state, form the realization of nirvāṇa.

[Wei Translation] Furthermore, Mahāmati, as for the nirvāṇa of the śrāvakas: it is called the nirvāṇa of the śrāvakas because they perceive all dharmas by examining their specific and general characteristics.
Mahāmati, as for the nirvāṇa of the pratyekabuddhas: they take no delight in bustle and clamor;
they see that all objective realms are impermanent, suffering, selfless, and impure, and thus do not give rise to inverted perceptions. This is...
Therefore, śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas give rise to the notion of nirvāṇa regarding what is not the ultimate state.
[Tang Translation: Furthermore, Mahāmati, śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas recognize their own and common characteristics and abandon the clamor of worldly distraction.
They do not give rise to perversion, nor do they give rise to conceptual discrimination; regarding that [state], they conceive the notion of nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are two kinds of characteristics of self-nature. What are the two? They are:

attachment to the characteristic of the self-nature of verbal expression, and attachment to the characteristic of the self-nature of things. Regarding attachment to the characteristic of the self-nature of verbal expression: it arises from beginningless verbal expression.

The arising of attachment to the habitual tendencies of falsehood occurs through attachment to the characteristics of the self-nature of things. This is because one fails to realize the limits of what is manifested by one's own mind.
[Wei Translation] Furthermore, Mahāmati, I shall explain to you the essential characteristics of two dharmas. What are these two?
The first is attachment to the essential characteristics of verbal expression; the second is attachment to the essential characteristics of worldly affairs.
Mahāmati, what is attachment to the characteristics of verbal expression? It arises from the habitual perfuming of beginningless attachment to the conceptual proliferation of verbal expression.
Mahāmati, what is attachment to the characteristics of worldly affairs? It is the failure to know, as it truly is, that [the world] is nothing but one's own mind.
Because one perceives external objects.
[Tang Translation: Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are two kinds of characteristics of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*). What are the two? They are:

the characteristic of intrinsic nature consisting in attachment to verbal expression, and the characteristic of intrinsic nature consisting in attachment to all phenomena (*dharma*). Attachment to the intrinsic nature of verbal expression...
Characteristics arise due to the habitual tendencies of beginningless conceptual proliferation and attachment to verbal expression;
they arise from the attachment to the intrinsic characteristics of all phenomena, which occurs because one does not realize that these are manifestations of one's own mind.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Tathāgata establishes the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas through two kinds of spiritual powers (ṛddhi-bala), so that they may prostrate before the Buddhas and listen to and receive the meaning of their teachings. What are these two kinds of spiritual power? They are:
the spiritual power of manifesting all bodies, faces, and speech through the correct reception of samādhi; and the spiritual power of the hand-consecration (abhiṣeka).

[Wei Translation] Furthermore, Mahāmati, because they are sustained by two kinds of power of aspiration, the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas prostrate themselves before the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and inquire about matters of doubt.
Mahāmati, what are these two kinds of power of aspiration that sustain them? The first is the sustaining power based on samādhi and samāpatti.

Second is the attainment of bliss throughout the entire body. This refers to the power of the Buddha-Tathāgata’s conferral of rank and sustenance through the stroking of the crown of one's head with his hand.

[Tang Translation: Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are two kinds of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) by which the Buddhas sustain bodhisattvas, causing them to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet and inquire about various meanings. What are these two? They are: causing them to enter samādhi, and [empowering] the body.
They appear before him and pour water upon his crown.
Mahāmati, at the first stage of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, he abides by the spiritual power of the Buddhas;
that is to say, he enters the bodhisattva mahāyāna illumination samādhi. Having entered this samādhi, all the Buddhas of the worlds in the ten directions [bestow their power].
By means of their supernormal powers, they manifest all manner of bodies, faces, and speech,
such as the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha and other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who have likewise accomplished such marks and virtues.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas dwell in the first stage, by virtue of being sustained by the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of all Tathāgatas,

they are said to have entered the Bodhisattva Samādhi of the Radiance of the Great Vehicle. Mahāmati, once these Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have entered the Samādhi of the Radiance of the Great Vehicle,
at that time, the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones of the ten directions...
One should correctly and fully understand this, for it is through the sustaining power of the bodhisattvas that they manifest in body, speech, and mind.
Mahāmati, it is like the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha and other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who have accomplished such marks of merit.
[Chinese Translation] Mahāmati, because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the first stage receive the sustaining power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of all Buddhas,
they enter the Bodhisattva samādhi called "Luminosity of the Great Vehicle. Having entered it, the Buddhas of the ten directions universally manifest before them,
bestowing empowerment through their bodies and speech, just as Vajragarbha and other Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have accomplished such marks of merit.
"Sa" means, Mahāmati,
this is called the first bodhisattva stage. Having attained the power of the bodhisattva’s samādhi and meditative absorption,
which is accomplished through the accumulation of roots of goodness over hundreds of thousands of kalpas, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva successively applies the remedies for each of the stages.

Having thoroughly mastered the characteristics of what is to be remedied, they reach the ultimate stage and dwell in the subtle and wondrous palace of the Great Lotus upon the Dharma-Cloud Ground (*dharmameghā bhūmi*).

Seated upon a great lotus jewel-lion throne, surrounded by a retinue of similar Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, their bodies are adorned with various precious necklaces, shining like the radiance of gold, *campaka* flowers, the sun, and the moon. From these most excellent sons...
From the ten directions, they come and confer the empowerment upon the crown of his head while he sits upon the throne of the Great Lotus Palace.
It is like the empowerment conferred upon a sovereign universal monarch or the crown prince of Śakra, Lord of Devas. This is called the Bodhisattva’s power of hand-conferred empowerment.
Mahāmati, these are called the two kinds of spiritual powers of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva abides in these two kinds of spiritual power, they will see the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, face to face; if it were not so, they would be unable to see them.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, it is thus that these Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, by virtue of abiding in the power of samādhi and samāpatti within the first stage (bhūmi),
and by virtue of the power of cultivating roots of goodness for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas,
successively and in accordance with reality know the characteristics of the dharmas that serve as the antidotes for each stage. When the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva reaches...
On the stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*), he sat upon a lion throne within a palace of a great jewel lotus-king, surrounded by a retinue of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of similar rank.

His body was adorned with jeweled crowns and necklaces, possessing a radiance like that of Jāmbūnada gold, campaka flowers, the sun and moon, and the luster of superior lotuses. At that time, all the Tathāgatas of the ten directions...

Each extended their hand from afar and stroked the crown of the head of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva upon the Lotus King throne, just as Śakra, the King of the Sovereign Gods, or a Wheel-Turning King, sprinkles the water of consecration upon the crown of a crown prince to confer his position. Mahāmati!

Those Bodhisattvas who have received their position, along with their retinue of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, experience bliss throughout their entire bodies by virtue of the Tathāgata’s hand touching the crown of their heads.
Therefore, it is said that the power of sustaining [them] consists of the hand touching the Bodhisattvas’ crowns.
Mahāmati, these are called the two kinds of sustaining powers of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. Mahāmati, all Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas...
"Mahāmati, by virtue of these two kinds of sustaining power, one is able to perceive the bodies of all Tathāgatas.
Mahāmati, if these two kinds of sustaining power did not exist, one would not be able to see the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas."

[The Tang Translation: "O Mahāmati, once this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has entered samādhi through the sustaining power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Buddha, he has accumulated all roots of goodness over hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
Gradually entering the various stages (*bhūmi*), he becomes thoroughly proficient in discerning the characteristics of that which is to be remedied and its remedy.
Reaching the Dharma-Cloud Stage (*dharmameghā bhūmi*), he dwells in a subtle and wondrous palace of a great lotus flower, seated upon a jeweled throne, together with those of his own kind."
Surrounded by bodhisattvas, he wears a jeweled crown; his body is like the color of gold and campaka flowers, and like the full moon, he radiates great light.
The Buddhas of the ten directions extend their lotus hands and consecrate him upon his seat.
Just as the crown prince of a wheel-turning monarch attains sovereign power after receiving the consecration, so too does this one.
It is the same for all bodhisattvas; this is called the second [condition].
Because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are sustained by these two kinds of sustenance, they are able to see all buddhas directly, whereas otherwise they could not.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, whatever analytical practices of samādhi, psychic powers (ṛddhipāda), and all other dharmas a bodhisattva-mahāsattva performs, all of these abide entirely within the two kinds of supernatural power (adhiṣṭhāna) of the Tathāgata.

Mahāmati, if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva were able to expound [the Dharma] apart from the Buddha’s supernatural power, then all ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) should also be able to speak it. Why is this?
Why? It is because he does not abide in supernatural power (*ṛddhi*).

Mahāmati, by the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata entering a city, mountains, rocks, trees, musical instruments, cities, and palaces all spontaneously produce the sounds of music; how much more so for sentient beings?
Those with countless sufferings—such as the deaf, the blind, and the mute—all attain liberation. Such is the Tathāgata’s [power].
[They possess] such immeasurable supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) as to benefit and bring peace to sentient beings.

[Wei Translation: Mahāmati, if bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas were able to preach the Dharma apart from the power of the two kinds of sustaining support (*adhiṣṭhāna*), then foolish ordinary people (*bālapṛthagjana*) should also be able to preach the Dharma. Why is this? Because they would not have attained the various...
"By the power of the Buddha’s sustaining grace (*adhiṣṭhāna*), Mahāmati.

Relying on the sustaining grace of all Tathāgatas, Mahāmati, mountains, rivers, stone walls, grasses, trees, gardens, groves, as well as various kinds of music, cities, towns, villages, palaces, and dwellings are all able to produce the sound of the Dharma being preached;
they naturally all produce the sounds of music. Mahāmati, how much more so for those who [possess it]?"

The mind is deaf, blind, and mute. O Mahāmati, immeasurable sentient beings are freed from all suffering and affliction through the power of the Buddha-Tathāgata’s sustaining presence, which brings immeasurable benefit, peace, and happiness to sentient beings.

[The Tang Translation: Furthermore, Mahāmati, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas enter into samādhi, manifest supernatural powers, and preach the Dharma—all such things are due to the two kinds of sustaining power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Buddhas.
Mahāmati, if Bodhisattvas were able to preach the Dharma apart from the Buddha’s sustaining power, then ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) should also be able to preach it. Mahāmati!

In mountain forests, grasses, trees, cities, palaces, and various musical instruments, wherever the Tathāgata goes, he causes the sound of the Dharma to resonate through the power of his Buddha-holding (buddhadhāraṇī).
How much more so for those with minds! Those who are deaf, blind, or mute are freed from suffering and attain liberation. Mahāmati!
The Tathāgata’s power of sustenance possesses such vast functions as these.

Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, by what causes and conditions do the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas bestow their empowerment upon Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas when they abide in samādhi-samāpatti, and at the time of consecration in the stages of supreme advancement?”
Regarding that supernormal power, the Buddha told Mahāmati: "In order to leave behind the karma of Māra and the afflictions;
to avoid falling into the meditative states of the Śrāvaka stage; to attain the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-realization;

and to further advance in the dharmas already attained—for these reasons, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas all establish [the path] through their supernormal powers. If the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas..."
Those who rely on supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) fall into the false views and delusions of external paths, as well as the expectations of the various *śrāvakas* and Māras;
consequently, they do not attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
For this reason, all the Buddhas and Tathāgatas universally sustain the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas through their supernatural powers. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this, said:
Thus, he spoke these verses: "The Honored One among Men, by his supernormal powers, has completely purified his great vows;
through the empowerment of samādhi, he traverses from the first bhūmi to the tenth."
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, for what reason do the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas exercise their power of sustaining support when the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas enter samādhi, samāpatti, and the various stages (bhūmi)?
The Buddha told Mahāmati: “It is in order to protect them from the activities of Māra and the afflictions (kleśa).”
Because of a distracted mind; so that they do not fall into the meditative absorption stage of the Śrāvakas;
so that they may personally realize the stage of the Tathāgata within their own bodies; and so that they may increase the realization of the Dharma within their own bodies.

Mahāmati, for these reasons, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the Samyaksaṃbuddhas, provide the sustaining power for all Bodhisattvas. Mahāmati, if the Tathāgatas did not [provide this power]...

If a bodhisattva exerts the power of maintenance [of their own views], they will fall into the states of various non-Buddhists, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and māras, and thus fail to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
For this reason, the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, out of their great compassion, embrace all bodhisattvas. At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse: "Bodhi..."
Relying upon his own person, through the purity of the power of his original vow, he enters samādhi and receives his station;
from the first ground to the tenth, all Buddhas, the Honored Ones among men, empower and sustain him through their spiritual power.
[The Tang Translation: Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"For what reason does the Tathāgata, by means of his sustaining power, cause all bodhisattvas to enter into samādhi and the sublime stages, and personally bestow the empowerment upon their heads? The Buddha said:

Mahāmati, it is for the purpose of causing them to distance themselves from the karmic activities of Māra and all afflictions; for the purpose of preventing them from falling into the stage of the Śrāvakas;
for the purpose of causing them to enter far into the stage of the Tathāgatas; and for the purpose of causing the Dharma they have attained to increase manifold.
The Buddhas sustain all bodhisattvas through the power of their empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
Mahāmati, were it not for this, those bodhisattvas would fall into the realms of the non-Buddhists, the śrāvakas, and Māra, and would thus fail to attain unsurpassed enlightenment.
Therefore, the Tathāgata gathers in all bodhisattvas through the power of his empowerment. At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again:
The verse says: "The World-Honored One’s pure vows possess the power of great empowerment. Within the stages from the first to the tenth, there are samādhis and empowerments.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the Buddha has spoken of dependent origination..."

This teaching on dependent origination is not spoken by following one's own path. World-Honored One, the non-Buddhists also speak of dependent origination, saying that all these natures arise from a supreme lord, time, or atoms.
Yet, regarding the World-Honored One’s discourse on the arising of all natures through dependent origination, there is the *siddhānta* with intervals and the *siddhānta* without intervals.
[Wei Translation] At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has taught, the twelve links of dependent origination arise from causes to produce effects;

it is not said that they arise through the power of the false conceptualization and discrimination of one's own mind. World-Honored One, if that were so, then the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) would also say that effects arise from causes."
"World-Honored One, the non-Buddhists claim that all phenomena arise from causes such as primal nature (*prakṛti*), the Lord (*īśvara*), time, or atoms.
Yet the Tathāgata also says that all phenomena arise in dependence upon causes and conditions; he does not say that there exists any phenomenon established by itself."
[The Tang Translation: At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, the Buddha has taught that dependent origination arises through activity and not from its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Yet non-Buddhists also claim that all phenomena arise from the Primal Nature (*prakṛti*), the Lord (*īśvara*), Time (*kāla*), the Self (*ātman*), or atoms (*aṇu*). Now, World-Honored One, you merely describe 'activity' by using different names."
[The opponent] says: "There is no difference in meaning.
The Blessed One, like the non-Buddhists, speaks of arising from existence and non-existence. The Blessed One also says that what has not yet arisen does not arise, and what has already arisen ceases.
As the Blessed One has said: 'With ignorance as condition, there are volitional formations, and so on, up to old age and death. This, then, is the Blessed One’s teaching of causelessness."
This is not a teaching based on [inherent] causes; the Blessed One established this teaching by saying, "Because this exists, that exists.
He did not establish it as a gradual arising. When compared with the teachings of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), the former is superior, not the latter.

Why is this so? Blessed One, the causes taught by the non-Buddhists give rise to things without depending on conditions. The Blessed One, however, teaches that one observes the effect through the cause, and observes the cause through the effect.
Thus, causes and conditions are disordered; thus, they revolve in succession without end.
[Wei Translation] World-Honored One, the non-Buddhists also say that all phenomena arise from existence and non-existence.

The World-Honored One says that all phenomena are originally non-existent, yet arise through the four conditions, and having arisen, they again cease. The World-Honored One says they arise from non-existence...
It clarifies the conditions for formations (*saṃskāra*) up to existence (*bhava*), and how all phenomena arise based on eye-consciousness and so forth. As the Blessed One has said:
"There are also phenomena that arise without a cause. Why is this? Because they do not arise from a cause; they are simultaneous, lacking priority or posteriority. [One might argue:
"Because this phenomenon arises from that phenomenon," yet the Blessed One himself stated that it arises from a false cause (*abhūta-hetu*).
“World-Honored One, because dharmas do not arise sequentially. If that were so, World-Honored One, the Dharma taught by the non-Buddhists would be superior and that of the Tathāgata would not be.
Why is this? World-Honored One, the non-Buddhists teach that causes can produce effects even without conditions;

whereas the Tathāgata teaches that causes depend upon effects and effects also depend upon causes. If that were so, then causes and conditions would be without cause and without effect, World-Honored One.”
If that were so, the mutual causality between this and that would be infinite. Yet the Blessed One has said:
"From this dharma, that dharma arises. If that were so, dharmas would arise without a cause.
[The Tang Translation: "World-Honored One, the non-Buddhists also say that because there is a creator, existence arises from non-existence.
World-Honored One, you also say that because of causes and conditions, all dharmas originally do not exist but arise, and having arisen, they return to extinction.
As the Buddha has taught: 'Ignorance conditions volitional formations,' and so on, up to 'old age and death. This teaching [of yours] is one of causelessness; it is not a teaching of having a cause."

The World-Honored One has said: "Because this exists, that exists. If this were established as occurring simultaneously rather than through sequential dependence, its meaning would not be established.
Therefore, the doctrine of the non-Buddhists is superior, not that of the Tathāgata. Why is this?
The non-Buddhists claim that causes produce effects without arising from conditions; whereas what the World-Honored One teaches is that the effect depends upon the cause.

If one cause requires another cause, there would be the fault of infinite regress through such successive dependencies. Furthermore, regarding the statement "because this exists, that exists," it would then follow that there is no cause at all.

The Buddha told Mahāmati: "I do not teach that things are causeless, nor do I teach a confusion of causes and conditions; rather, I say 'because this exists, that exists' [in the sense of dependent origination]."
This refers to the non-existence of the grasper and the grasped. It is the realization that [all things] are merely the manifestation of one's own mind.

Mahāmati, if one is attached to the grasper and the grasped and fails to realize that they are the manifestation of one's own mind, then external objects—whether existent or non-existent—will lead to such errors.
This is not what I call dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). I always say that all phenomena arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions; they do not arise without a cause.
[Wei Translation] The Buddha told Mahāmati: "I shall now explain that this dharma arises from that dharma;
it is not like the cause-and-effect established by the non-Buddhists. Even dharmas without a [prior] cause arise from causes. I do not hold such a view.
I teach that all dharmas arise from causes and conditions; they do not arise without causes and conditions, nor are they disordered, nor do they arise through mutual succession."
This leads to the fault of infinite regress. Why is this? Because there would be no such things as the grasper (*grāhaka*) and the graspable (*grāhya*).
Mahāmati, because the non-Buddhists do not understand that what appears is their own mind, they cling to the dharmas of the grasper and the graspable;

they neither know nor realize that internal and external phenomena are merely the manifestations of their own minds. Mahāmati, those non-Buddhists do not understand the internal objects of their own minds.
Because of the realms, one perceives the existence or non-existence of things; therefore, such faults belong to the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), not to me.
I have always taught that all phenomena arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions, and do not arise without a cause.
[The Tang Translation: The Buddha said, "Mahāmati, I have realized that all phenomena are manifestations of mind alone, devoid of both the grasper and the grasped.
When I speak of 'this exists because that exists,' it is not a fault of being causeless or having defective causes and conditions.
Mahāmati, if one does not understand that all phenomena are manifestations of mind alone, but instead calculates the existence of a grasper and a grasped, one clings to the external."
