Because all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, having followed the Buddha's teaching and become weary of and detached from the world, are unable to attain liberation by themselves, I therefore teach the single vehicle.
Mahāmati, śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have not yet realized the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya), nor have they attained the inconceivable [wisdom].
[The Buddha] deliberated upon the transformation of birth. For this reason, I have taught the One Vehicle path for the sake of the śrāvakas.
[Tang Translation: Mahāmati said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, for what reason do you speak of three vehicles and not one vehicle?
The Buddha said: "Mahāmati, because śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas lack the nature of attaining parinirvāṇa by themselves, I speak of the One [Vehicle]."
Vehicle. Because they attain liberation by practicing according to the discipline and renunciation taught by the Tathāgata, rather than through their own independent attainment;

and because they have not yet eliminated the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and the habitual tendencies of karma (*karmavāsanā*), have not yet awakened to the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), and have not yet attained what is called the inconceivable transformation-death (*acintyapariṇāmikī cyuti*); for these reasons, I speak of them as three.

Mahāmati, when all those afflictions, faults, and habitual tendencies have been severed, and one realizes the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), then all those afflictions, faults, and habitual tendencies are severed.
This is not a state of attachment to the flavor of the bliss of samādhi; rather, it is the realization of the untainted realm (*anāsravadhātu*). It is realization.
Having further entered the supramundane, most excellent, untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*), and having fulfilled all requisites,
one shall attain the Tathāgata’s inconceivable and sovereign Dharma-body.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, if Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are free from all habitual tendencies of faults, they shall attain...
One realizes the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*). At that time, one is free from all faults.

Having awakened from the intoxication of the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) states of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one cultivates all the merits within the supramundane uncontaminated realm (*lokottarānāsravadhātu*).
Having so cultivated, one attains the inconceivable, sovereign *dharmakāya*.

[The Tang Translation: If they are able to eliminate all habitual tendencies of faults by awakening to the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), at that time they depart from the intoxication of samādhi and attain awakening within the untainted realm (*anāsravadhātu*).
Having attained awakening, they cultivate various merits within the supramundane, supreme, and untainted realm, universally bringing them to fulfillment and attaining inconceivable autonomy.
Within the Dharmakāya.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

"The vehicle of the devas and Brahmās, The vehicle of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, And the vehicle of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas— I have taught all these vehicles. As long as the mind continues to turn, So shall there be various vehicles."
It is not ultimate. If that mind is extinguished, there is neither vehicle nor rider, and no establishment of vehicles; I speak of this as the One Vehicle.
[Wei Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One further spoke in verse: "The celestial vehicle and the Brahma vehicle, the Śrāvaka and the Pratyekabuddha..."
The Vehicle of Awakening, the Vehicle of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas—I have taught these various vehicles because the mind undergoes arising and ceasing;
thus, these vehicles are not ultimate. If that mind were extinguished, there would be no vehicle nor any who ride it; there would be no differentiation among vehicles.
I teach this as the One Vehicle.
[The Tang Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"The vehicle of the gods and the vehicle of Brahmā, The vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, And the vehicle of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas— These various vehicles have been taught by me.

As long as the mind continues to arise, The vehicles are not yet ultimate. Once that mind has been transformed and extinguished, There is neither vehicle nor one who rides it; There is no establishment of a vehicle. My.

It is taught as the One Vehicle for the sake of guiding sentient beings; yet, for the purpose of leading them on, various vehicles are distinguished. There are three kinds of liberation, as well as the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).
When afflictions and wisdom are both transcended, one is liberated—just like a piece of wood floating upon the ocean, which constantly turns with the waves.

The same applies to the delusion of the śrāvakas: tossed about by the winds of signs, they give rise to afflictions and their cessation; yet they remain deluded by the residual habits of those afflictions. [Wei Translation:
In order to guide sentient beings, I have provisionally taught the various vehicles. There are three kinds of liberation, as well as the two types of selflessness.
Without being free from the two kinds of obstacles, one is far removed from true liberation. It is like a piece of wood floating on the ocean.

Just as waves roll on, so it is with the śrāvakas: tossed about by the winds of signs, they remain bound by the latent tendencies of afflictions, even though they are free from manifest secondary afflictions.

[The Tang Translation: In order to guide the foolish, the distinctions between the various vehicles are taught. There are three kinds of liberation, as well as the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).
This refers to being free from all afflictions and attaining liberation through the wisdom of equality. It is like wood in the ocean.

Constantly turning with the waves, so too is the mind of the śrāvaka. Driven and tossed by the winds of signs, though they have extinguished the arising of afflictions, they remain bound by habitual tendencies.
Relishing the bliss of samādhi, they dwell in the untainted realm (anāsrava-dhātu). Having no ultimate destination, yet neither do they fall back.
Having attained the body of various samādhis, they remain unawakened for as long as an eon; they are like a person who is intoxicated, who only awakens once the wine has worn off.
Their realization of the Dharma is likewise so; they attain the supreme body of a Buddha.
[Wei Translation] They savor the bliss of samādhi and abide in the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*). There is no ultimate destination, nor do they ever regress.
Having attained the bodies of various samādhis, they remain unawakened for immeasurable eons, like a person who is dazed and intoxicated.
Only after the wine has worn off does one awaken; thus one attains the unsurpassed body of the Buddha, which is my true *dharmakāya*. [Tang Translation:
Intoxicated by the wine of *samādhi*, one dwells in the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*). That is not the ultimate destination, yet one does not regress either.
Having attained the body of *samādhi*, one remains unawakened for as long as an eon. It is like a person who is deeply intoxicated.
Only after the wine has been digested does one awaken; the Śrāvakas are likewise. After awakening, they shall become Buddhas.
*Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, Compiled Translation, Volume Two, Part Two;
*Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, Compiled Translation, Volume Three, Part One.
Originally translated by Guṇabhadra, the Tripiṭaka Master from India during the Song dynasty;
retranslated by Bodhiruci, the Tripiṭaka Master from India during the Wei dynasty;
and subsequently translated by Śikṣānanda, the Tripiṭaka Master from Khotan during the Tang dynasty.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Yuanke of the True Lineage of Linji during the Ming Dynasty.
Chapter Three (Part One) of the "Essence of the Heart of All Buddha-Speech.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, saying: "The characteristics of the differentiation and penetration of the mind-made body."
"I shall now speak; listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well. Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "Excellent, World-Honored One! We shall indeed receive your instruction.
The Buddha told Mahāmati, "There are three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*). What are the three? They are: the mind-made body produced by the correct reception of the bliss of samādhi;
the mind-made body produced by the realization of the self-nature of dharmas; and the mind-made body of the same class [as the Buddhas]."

They give rise to a body born of mental construction (*manomaya-kāya*) that is free from volitional activity. The practitioner clearly understands the characteristics of the progressively higher advancements from the first stage upward and attains these three kinds of bodies.
[Wei Translation] At that time, the Buddha addressed the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva, saying: "Mahāmati, I shall now, for your sake..."
“You have asked about the distinctions in the cultivation of the mind-made body (*manomayakāya*). Mahāmati, listen closely, listen closely; I shall explain it for you.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, “Excellent, World-Honored One! We shall indeed receive your instruction.
The Buddha told Mahāmati, “There are three kinds of mind-made bodies. What are the three? The first is the mind-made body that has attained the bliss of samādhi and *samāpatti*.”
First is the birth-body (*janma-kāya*). Second is the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*) that realizes the characteristics of all phenomena as they truly are.

Third is the mind-made body of effortless activity born of the lineage (*gotra*). From the first stage (*bhūmi*) onward, the bodhisattva practices according to reality and attains the marks of the realized wisdom of the progressively higher stages.
[The Tang Translation: At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, saying:

"I shall now explain for you the various characteristics of the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*). Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well. Mahāmati replied: "Yes, [I shall do so]."
The Buddha said, "Mahāmati, there are three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*). What are the three? They are: the mind-made body consisting of the bliss of entering samādhi;
the mind-made body consisting of the realization of the self-nature of dharmas; and the mind-made body consisting of the spontaneous manifestation of the species.
These are realized progressively by practitioners after they have entered the first stage (*bhūmi*)."
Mahāmati, what is the mind-made body born of the meditative absorption in the bliss of samādhi?

It refers to the third, fourth, and fifth stages, where, through the meditative absorption in the bliss of samādhi, the various manifestations of one’s own mind become tranquil. One abides in the ocean of the mind, and the marks of the waves of consciousness do not arise.
Knowing that the nature of the objects appearing from one’s own mind is neither existent nor non-existent—this is called the mind-made body born of the meditative absorption in the bliss of samādhi.
Body. [Wei Translation] Mahāmati, what is the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*) obtained by Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas through the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) of the bliss of samādhi?
It refers to the cultivation of the seeds of practice for the tranquility of one's own mind within the third, fourth, and fifth stages.

The various types of practice, the ocean-like mind, the waves of the evolving consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*), and the bliss of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) are called the arising of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

Because one perceives the objects of one’s own mind, one knows, as they truly are, the characteristics of existence and non-existence. Mahāmati, this is called the characteristic of the mind-made body (*manomayakāya*).
[The Tang Translation: "Mahāmati, what is the body produced by mind that enters the bliss of samādhi?

It refers to the third, fourth, and fifth stages where one enters samādhi, becoming free from various mental states and remaining tranquil and unmoving. The ocean of the mind does not give rise to the waves of the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).
One realizes that objects are manifestations of the mind and that they are entirely non-existent. This is called the body produced by mind that enters the bliss of samādhi."
Mahāmati, what is the mind-made body that realizes the self-nature of dharmas?
It refers to the transformation of body and mind in the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), having observed and realized that all phenomena such as illusions are entirely non-existent.
One attains the illusion-like samādhi and other gateways of samādhi, as well as immeasurable marks, powers, masteries, and clarities, adorned like exquisite flowers, swift as one wishes, just like—
Like illusions, dreams, the moon in water, and reflections in a mirror, they are neither created nor derived from what is created, yet they appear as if created and derived.
Possessing all forms with their various limbs fully adorned, they enter into all buddha-fields and great assemblies, for they have realized the nature of phenomena.
This is called the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*) that realizes the self-nature of dharmas.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, what is the mind-made body that realizes the characteristics of all dharmas as they truly are?
It refers to the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, within the eighth stage, investigate and realize them, attaining the signlessness of all dharmas which is like an illusion.

All such phenomena are entirely non-existent. Through the transformation of body and mind, one attains the Illusion-like Samādhi (*māyopama-samādhi*) and other immeasurable gateways to the bliss of *samāpatti*.

One possesses immeasurable marks, powers, masteries, and supernormal faculties (*abhijñā*), adorned with exquisite flowers, swift as one wishes, and like illusions, dreams, the moon in water, or reflections in a mirror—neither born of the four great elements yet resembling them.
Endowed with the marks of greatness and complete physical proportions, they attain mastery at will through all spiritual practices and enter the great assemblies in the lands of all Buddhas.
Mahāmati, this is called the mind-made body that realizes the characteristics of all phenomena as they truly are.

[The Tang Translation: What is the mind-made body that realizes the self-nature of dharmas? It refers to the transformation of the basis of the mind in the eighth stage, having realized that all dharmas are like illusions and are devoid of characteristics.
Abiding in the illusion-like samādhi and other samādhis, one is able to manifest immeasurable sovereign supernormal powers.
These are as swift as the blooming of a flower and as one wishes, being like an illusion and like a dream.
Its shadow is like a reflection; it is neither the primary elements nor their derivatives, yet it resembles them.

It is fully adorned with all marks of physical form, universally enters all Buddha-fields, and thoroughly realizes the nature of all phenomena. This is called the "body made of mind through the realization of the intrinsic nature of dharmas."
Mahāmati, what is the body born of mental construction that is spontaneously produced along with its class and is without effortful activity?

It refers to the realization of all Buddha-dharmas through the characteristic of the joy of self-attained gnosis. This, Mahāmati, is called the body born of mental construction that is spontaneously produced along with its class and is without effortful activity. Mahāmati, [this is it].
One should observe, realize, and train in those three types of bodies.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, what is the mind-made body born of the lineage that is unconditioned?

It refers to the internal realization of all dharmas within one's own body, because of the joy in the true nature of phenomena and the joy in the characteristics of phenomena. Mahāmati, this is called the "lineage."

The body born of transformation, which is spontaneously produced and free from volitional effort, is the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*). Mahāmati, you should observe and thoroughly understand these three types of bodily characteristics.
[Tang Translation] What is the mind-made body that is spontaneously produced and free from volitional effort? It refers to the thorough realization of all...
The Buddha’s own realization of the characteristics of dharmas is called the "spontaneously born, effortless, mind-made body" (*manomaya-kāya*) arising from its own kind.
Mahāmati, you should diligently investigate the characteristics of these three bodies.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "My vehicle is not the Great Vehicle;
it is neither speech nor letters. It is not the truths, nor is it liberation; yet it is not without a sphere of activity.
Thus one mounts the Mahāyāna, possessing mastery over samādhi, with various mind-made bodies adorned with the flowers of sovereignty."
[Wei Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses again: "My vehicle is not a Great Vehicle; it is neither speech nor letters.
It is not the truths, nor is it liberation, yet it is not without a sphere of activity.
Nevertheless, by means of the Mahāyāna, one attains mastery over samādhi and various mind-made bodies, adorned with the flowers of sovereignty."
[The Tang Translation: At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse: "My Mahāyāna is neither a vehicle, nor a sound, nor even syllables;
It is not the truths, nor liberation, nor even the realm of signlessness.
Yet, by mounting the Mahāyāna, one attains mastery over samādhi, And various mind-made bodies adorned with the flowers of sovereignty."
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has said, if a man or a woman commits the five deeds of immediate retribution, they do not enter the Avīci Hell.

World-Honored One, how is it that a man or a woman who commits the five deeds of immediate retribution does not enter the Avīci Hell? The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Listen attentively, listen attentively..."
"Listen well and reflect upon this; I shall explain it for you. Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "Excellent, World-Honored One!

We shall indeed receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati, "What are the five acts of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*)? They are: killing one's father, killing one's mother, harming an Arhat, causing a schism in the Saṃgha, and shedding the blood of a Buddha with an evil mind."
[Wei Translation] At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has said, 'If a son of good family or a daughter of good family commits the five deeds of immediate retribution (pañcānantaryakarma), World-Honored One, what are these five deeds of immediate retribution by which a son of good family or a daughter of good family, having committed them, enters the Avīci hell'? The Buddha [replied].
The Buddha addressed the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva, saying: “Excellent, excellent, excellent, Mahāmati! Listen attentively, listen attentively;
I shall explain it for you. Mahāmati said to the Buddha: “Excellent, World-Honored One! We shall do as we are instructed. The Buddha told Mahāmati:
“As for the five acts of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*): first is killing one’s mother; second is killing one’s father; third is killing an Arhat...”
Arhat. Fourth, causing a schism in the Saṃgha. Fifth, with an evil mind, drawing blood from the body of a Buddha.
[Tang Translation] At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has spoken of the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya-karma*), what are these five? If a person commits them, they shall fall into the Avīci Hell."
The Buddha said, "Listen attentively; I shall explain it for you. Mahāmati replied, "Yes. The Buddha told Mahāmati, "The five acts of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*) are:
namely, killing one's mother, killing one's father, killing an Arhat, causing a schism in the Saṃgha, and with a mind of malice and rebellion, drawing blood from the body of a Buddha."
Mahāmati, what is the mother of sentient beings? It is craving for renewed existence, which, conjoined with greed and delight, stands as the condition like a mother.
Ignorance is the father who gives birth to the village of the sense-bases. To sever these two roots is called "killing one's parents."
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, what is the mother of sentient beings? It is that which, through craving and delight, gives rise to subsequent rebirth;
it is established as the mother by way of conditions. Mahāmati, what is the father? It is ignorance, which acts as the father to produce the village of the six sense bases.
Mahāmati, to sever those two roots capable of producing [rebirth] is called "killing one's parents."
[The Tang Translation: Mahāmati, what is the mother of sentient beings? It is that which draws forth craving, accompanied by greed and delight, nurturing them like a mother.
What is the father? It is ignorance, for it causes birth within the village of the six sense bases.
To sever these two roots is called "killing one's parents."
Those latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) do not manifest; they are like the outbreak of rat-poison. To utterly sever those dharmas is called "killing an Arhat.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, what is meant by "killing an Arhat"? It refers to the latent tendencies being like the outbreak of rat-poison.
To uproot the very root of the enemy that is the latent tendencies so that they do not arise again—Mahāmati, this is called "killing an Arhat."
[The Tang Translation: What is meant by "killing an arhat"? It refers to the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) acting as enemies, like the onset of rat-poison;
to completely sever them is therefore called "killing an arhat."

What is the schism of the Saṃgha? It refers to the ultimate severance of the accumulation and aggregation of the various aggregates (skandhas) characterized by distinct marks; this is called the schism of the Saṃgha.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, what is the schism of the harmonious Saṃgha? It refers to the accumulation and aggregation of the five aggregates, which possess distinct characteristics.
The aggregate. To definitively sever that is called "schism in the Saṃgha.
[Tang Translation: What is meant by "schism in the harmonious Saṃgha"? It refers to the accumulation and aggregation of the various aggregates (skandhas) with their distinct characteristics.
To definitively sever that is called "schism in the Saṃgha."

Mahāmati, when one fails to realize that the external world—consisting of specific and general characteristics—is merely the manifestation of one’s own mind, and instead perceives the seven bodies of consciousness through the three liberations as being tainted by impure conceptions, one ultimately severs those seven kinds of consciousness.
This, Mahāmati, is called shedding the blood of a Buddha with an evil mind.
If a man or woman commits this act of immediate retribution, it is called the fifth *ānantarya* (immediate) offense, and it is also termed "equal to the immediate."
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, what is "shedding the blood of a Buddha with an evil mind"?

It refers to seeing the specific and general characteristics of external objects as the manifestations of one's own mind—the eightfold collection of consciousnesses—and, by relying on the three gates of liberation that are free from outflows, ultimately severing the Buddha who is the eightfold collection of consciousnesses.
This, Mahāmati, is called "shedding the blood of a Buddha with an evil mind. Mahāmati, this is termed the five kinds within the internal body.
"Uninterrupted. If a son or daughter of good family practices this uninterrupted [path], they are named "uninterrupted.
One is named "uninterrupted" because they have realized the Dharma as it truly is.

[The Tang Translation: What is meant by "shedding the Buddha's blood with an evil mind"? It refers to the eight consciousnesses (vijñānakāya) falsely giving rise to conceptual thoughts, perceiving self-characteristics and common characteristics as existing outside of one's own mind.

By means of an untainted evil mind regarding the three gates of liberation, one ultimately severs that Buddha of the eight consciousnesses; this is called "shedding the Buddha's blood with an evil mind. Mahāmati, these are the five internal [factors].
"Immediate. If there is one who acts, they shall immediately realize and manifest the true Dharma.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there is an external immediacy which I shall now explain;
having heard this meaning, you and the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas will not fall into delusion in future ages. What are the five immediacies? They are as previously stated..."
It speaks of the "immediate" (ānantarya). If one practices this, one will not attain the dharma of immediate realization (abhisamaya) regarding each of the three liberations.

Apart from these, there are other manifestations of transformative power that appear as immediate realization; namely, the transformative power of śrāvakas, the transformative power of bodhisattvas, and the transformative power of Tathāgatas.
These are for the purpose of removing the doubts and regrets of others who have committed immediate transgressions, and for the purpose of exhorting and inspiring them.
Therefore, through the transformations of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), he manifests the realization of non-interruption (*ānantarya*).

There is nothing that exclusively constitutes an uninterrupted act such that one would fail to attain non-interruption, except for the failure to realize that all is merely the manifestation of one's own mind, to remain free from the false discriminations regarding body and possessions, and to remain free from the grasping of "I" and "mine.
At times, encountering a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), one is liberated from the false discriminations of the continuity of other realms of existence.
[Wei Translation] Furthermore, Mahāmati, I shall explain to you the characteristics of the five external acts of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*).
Having heard this teaching, the Bodhisattvas will not give rise to doubt in future ages. Mahāmati, what are these five external acts of immediate retribution?
They are: killing one’s father, mother, or an Arhat; causing a schism in the Saṃgha; and shedding the blood of a Buddha.
Regarding blood: those who commit this immediate transgression (*ānantarya*) are unable to realize any of the three gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*).

However, with the exception of those Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas who abide through the sustaining power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Tathāgata’s transformation, the Tathāgata’s spiritual power acts for the sake of the five types of offenders to repent their doubting minds;
by severing these doubts, it causes them to give rise to roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*). For...

That sinner speaks with intentional transformation. Mahāmati, if one has committed the five kinds of *ānantarya* (immediate) sins, one will ultimately never be able to realize entry into the factors of the path, except for those who see that their own mind is merely illusory, who are free from the body, the means of subsistence, and the place of dwelling, and who have abandoned the conceptualized views of "self" and "what belongs to self.
Even after immeasurable and boundless eons, they may encounter a virtuous...
Knowledge. It is the separation from the body of heterodox paths and from the false views of one's own mind.

[Tang Translation: Furthermore, Mahāmati, I shall now explain for you the five external immediate transgressions (*pañca-ānantarya*), so that you and other bodhisattvas, having heard this meaning, will not give rise to doubt or confusion in future ages. What are the five external immediate transgressions?
"Immediate" (ānantarya) refers to what is described as "immediate" in other teachings. If there were such a person, they would be unable to realize the three doors of liberation;

however, with the exception of the Tathāgatas, great Bodhisattvas, and great Śrāvakas, when they see someone committing an act of immediate retribution, they employ supernatural powers to manifest the same actions in order to exhort them and cause them to reform.
Seeking [the truth], they immediately repent and eliminate [their offenses], realizing liberation. All of these are manifested through transformation and are not actual deeds.
If there were those who had actually committed the karma of the immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*), they would never attain liberation in their present body.

This is excepted only for those who awaken to the fact that the bodies, resources, and dwellings appearing before them are but manifestations of their own minds, and who thus depart from the views of conceptual attachment to "I" and "mine," or [who do so] in a future life.
Taking birth in the realms of existence, one encounters a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) and, by departing from the fault of conceptual discrimination, finally realizes liberation.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: “Craving and attachment are called the mother; Ignorance is the father.

The consciousness that awakens to objects is the Buddha; The various latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are the Arhats. The accumulation of the aggregates (*skandha*) is called the Saṃgha. [In] the Avīci [hell]...
They are severed in succession; that is to say, these five immediate transgressions do not lead to the Avīci Hell.
[Wei Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse: "Craving is called the mother; ignorance is the father.
Consciousness that discerns objects is the Buddha; the various latent tendencies are the Arhats. The collection of aggregates is called the Saṃgha; the immediate..."
The continuity is severed; there is no further interval of karma, and one attains the uninterrupted state of *tathatā*.
[Tang Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse: "Craving is called the mother; ignorance is the father.
Consciousness that cognizes objects—this is called the Buddha. The latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are the Arhat; the collection of aggregates (*skandha*) is the heap."
The harmonious Saṃgha is severed by him without remainder; this is called an immediate transgression (*ānantarya-karma*).
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for us the Buddha’s knowledge and awakening."
“World-Honored One, what is the awakening of a Buddha? The Buddha told Mahāmati:

“To realize the selflessness of persons and phenomena, to fully understand the two obstacles, to be free from the two kinds of death, and to sever the two afflictions—this is called the awakening of a Buddha.
If Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas attain this Dharma, they too are called Buddhas. For these reasons, I teach the One Vehicle. At that time, the World-Honored One...

Venerable One, wishing to restate this meaning, I speak these verses: Thoroughly knowing the two kinds of selflessness, Severing the two obstructions and the afflictions, And forever departing from the two kinds of death— This is called the Buddha’s awakening.
[Wei Translation] At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for me the characteristics of the realization and awakening of all Tathāgatas. The Buddha said to the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva:
"Mahāmati, one who knows person-non-self (pudgala-nairātmya) and dharma-non-self (dharma-nairātmya) as they truly are, is able to know these two as they truly are."
Because of these various obstacles, one remains far removed from the two kinds of afflictions. Mahāmati, this is called the Tathāgata’s knowledge of reality as it is.
Mahāmati, those Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas who attain this Dharma are also called Buddhas.
Mahāmati, for this reason I teach the One Vehicle. At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse: "Thoroughly knowing the two kinds of selflessness..."
When the two obstacles and the two afflictions are eliminated, one attains inconceivable transformation; this is called the Buddha’s awakening.
[Tang Translation] At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for me the essential nature of all Buddhas.
The Buddha said: "Mahāmati, by awakening to the two kinds of selflessness and removing the two types of obstacles..."
Being free from the two kinds of death and having severed the two afflictions is the essential nature of a Buddha.
Mahāmati, when Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas realize this Dharma, they too are called Buddhas; it is for this reason that I teach only the One Vehicle.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses: “Thoroughly knowing the two kinds of selflessness, Eliminating the two obstructions and the two afflictions, As well as inconceivable death...”
For this reason, he is called the Tathāgata.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, for what reason did the World-Honored One proclaim these words in the midst of the great assembly:
'I am all the Buddhas of the past and have undergone various births; at that time, I was Mañjuśrī'?"
The *Śatasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* speaks of such things as King Cakravartin, the six-tusked great elephant, the parrot bird, Śakra Devendra,
and the seer Sunetra, across hundreds of thousands of lifetimes.
[Wei Translation] At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, for what reason did the World-Honored One speak these words in the midst of the great assembly:
'I was all the Buddhas of the past,' and why did he speak of various Jātaka sūtras, saying: 'At that time, I was King Mūrdhaja, the six-tusked great elephant, and the parrot'?"
The Ṛṣi Vyāsa, Śakra-rāja, the Bodhisattva Sunetra, and others—hundreds of thousands of such sūtras all speak of past lives (*jātaka*).
[Tang Translation: At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as..."
With what underlying intention did you come to proclaim these words in the midst of the great assembly, saying,
"I am all the Buddhas of the past," and recounting hundreds of thousands of *jātaka* tales, such as when I was King Mūrdhaja,
the Great Elephant, the Parrot, Candraprabha, Sunetra, and so forth?
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Because of four kinds of equality, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, proclaims these words in the midst of the great assembly:
'In that time, I was Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, and Kāśyapa Buddha. What are the four equalities?

They are the equality of letters, the equality of speech, the equality of dharmas, and the equality of bodies. These are called the four equalities. It is because of these four kinds of equality [that he speaks thus]."
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, proclaims these words among the great assembly.
[Wei Translation: The Buddha addressed the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, saying:
"Mahāmati, based upon four kinds of equality, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, proclaims these words among the great assembly: 'I, at..."
At that time, they were Krakucchanda Buddha, Kanakamuni Buddha, and Kāśyapa Buddha.
What are these four? First, equality of name; second, equality of speech; third, equality of dharma; and fourth, equality of body.
Mahāmati, it is by relying on these four kinds of equal dharmas that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, abide among the multitudes.
In the middle [of this passage], it is stated as follows:

[Tang Translation] The Buddha said: "Mahāmati, because of the fourfold secret intention of equality, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, spoke these words in the midst of the great assembly: 'In a former time, I was the Buddha Krakucchanda.'"
Regarding the Buddhas Kanakamuni and Kāśyapa: what are the four? They are the equality of letters, the equality of speech, the equality of body, and the equality of Dharma.

What is the equality of syllables? If the syllables that designate me as a Buddha also designate all Buddhas, and if those syllables are by nature without distinction, this is the equality of names. What is the equality of speech?
It means that the sixty-four types of vocal qualities and linguistic characteristics produced by my voice are likewise present in the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.

The characteristics of the Brahma-voice and speech arise in such a way that they neither increase nor decrease and possess no differentiation. They have the nature of the Brahma-voice of the kalaviṅka bird.

How is it that the bodies and so forth are identical? It means that there is no difference between myself and all Buddhas regarding the Dharma-body and the marks and signs of the Form-body, except for the manifestation of various [forms] in order to subdue sentient beings who differ according to their respective realms of existence.
The differentiated form-body is called the equality of body, and so forth. What is the equality of dharma?
It refers to myself and those Buddhas attaining the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; briefly stated, it is the unobstructed wisdom of the Buddha-dharmas. These are called the four equalities.
Therefore, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, proclaims these words amidst the great assembly. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate...
Proclaiming this meaning, he spoke in verse: "Kāśyapa, Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, and I—through these four who are equal, I have taught for the sake of my sons."
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, what is the equality of names? It means that whatever name was used for the Buddhas of the past as "Buddha," I am likewise named "Buddha" by that same name.
This name does not transcend those [past names]; it is equal to them, without difference or distinction. Mahāmati, this is the equality of names.
Mahāmati, what is the equality of the speech of all Buddhas? It means that having passed beyond...
The Buddhas of the past possessed sixty-four kinds of exquisite Brahma-voices with which they preached the Dharma;
I, too, possess sixty-four kinds of subtle Brahma-voices with which I preach the Dharma.
Mahāmati, the Buddhas of the future will likewise preach the Dharma with sixty-four kinds of subtle Brahma-voices, neither increasing nor decreasing, no different and without distinction.
It is distinct. O Mahāmati, the Brahma-voice of the kalaviṅka bird is exquisite and beautiful; this is called the equality of the speech of all Buddhas.

O Mahāmati, what is the equality of the bodies of all Buddhas? O Mahāmati, my Dharma-body and form-body, with their marks and signs of excellence, are without difference or distinction from those of all other Buddhas, except as they depend upon the various dispositions of the sentient beings to be converted. O Mahāmati, it is according to the respective lineages of those sentient beings...
In various places of birth, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, manifest various bodies. Mahāmati, this is called the equality of the bodies of all Buddhas.

Mahāmati, what is the equality of the dharmas of all Buddhas? It means that those Buddhas and I have attained the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and so forth. Mahāmati, this is called the equality of the dharmas of all Buddhas.
"Mahāmati, it is based on these four kinds of equality that the Tathāgata makes such a declaration in the midst of the great assembly:
'I was King Mūrdhaja and others in the past. At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
'Kāśyapa, Krakucchanda, and Kanakamuni—these were I. I speak thus to the sons of the Buddha and others, based upon the fourfold equality.'"
[The Tang Translation: What is the equality of names? It means that my name is "Buddha," and all Tathāgatas are also named "Buddha.
That the name "Buddha" is without distinction is what constitutes the equality of names. What is the equality of speech?
It means that I produce the sixty-four kinds of Brahma-sounds, and all Tathāgatas likewise produce this speech—the *kalaviṅka*-like Brahma-voice.
The nature of sound is neither increasing nor decreasing and is without distinction; this is called the equality of speech. What is the equality of the body?

It means that my dharma-body, its physical marks, and its secondary signs are no different from those of all Buddhas, except for manifesting bodies that conform to various types of beings in order to subdue them. This is called the equality of the body. What is the equality of the Dharma?
"Equal," etc., means that I and all Buddhas have equally realized the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
This is called "equality of phenomena. Therefore, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, makes such a declaration in the midst of the great assembly.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse: “Kāśyapa, Krakucchanda, and Kanakamuni are myself.
Relying upon the fourfold equality, I speak for the sake of all sons of the Buddha.”
Mahāmati spoke again to the Buddha, saying: "As the World-Honored One has said:
'From the night I attained supreme perfect enlightenment until the night I enter parinirvāṇa, in the interval between them, not even a single word has been spoken;
nor have I spoken, nor shall I speak. That which is not spoken is not the teaching of the Buddha. World-Honored One, for what reason do the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas speak?"
"It is said that what is not spoken by me is the teaching of the Buddha. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "I speak thus because of two dharmas.
What are these two dharmas? They are the dharma of self-attainment and the dharma of primordial abiding. These are called the two dharmas.
It is because of these two dharmas that I speak in this way."
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the Tathāgata has said:
'In the very night I realized Great Bodhi, and in the very night I entered Parinirvāṇa, I did not speak a single word in the interval.
World-Honored One, based on what meaning do you say such words as 'the Buddha speaks' and 'the Buddha does not speak'?"
The Buddha said to Mahāmati: "Mahāmati, the Tathāgata speaks these words based upon two kinds of dharmas.
What are the two? I say they are as follows: first, the dharma of internal self-realization; second, the dharma of primordial abiding.
It is based on these two dharmas that I speak thus."
[The Tang Translation: At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has said:
'On such-and-such a night I attained supreme perfect enlightenment, and on such-and-such a night I shall enter parinirvāṇa.'"
"In that interval, not a single word was spoken; nor has anything been spoken, nor will it ever be spoken.

This which is called 'the Buddha's teaching'—World-Honored One, with what underlying intention (*abhiprāya*) did you speak these words? The Buddha said: "Mahāmati, it is based on two secret dharmas that I have spoken thus.
What are these two dharmas? They are the dharma of self-realization (*pratyātma-dharma*) and the dharma that has existed from the beginning (*paurāṇa-sthiti-dharma*)."
What is the dharma realized through one's own attainment? It is that which the Tathāgata has attained, which I too have attained, without increase or decrease.
This is the ultimate realm of the dharma realized through one's own attainment, free from verbal conceptualization and free from the two courses of letters.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, what is meant by the dharma realized through internal personal realization?
It refers to the dharma realized by those past Buddhas and Tathāgatas, which I have likewise realized, neither increasing nor decreasing.
This is the practice of the realms of internal personal realization, which is free from the marks of verbal conceptualization and devoid of the two kinds of syllables.
[The Tang Translation: What is the dharma of self-realization? It refers to that which all Buddhas have realized, which I likewise realize—neither increasing nor decreasing.

It is the domain of realized wisdom, free from the characteristics of verbal expression, free from the characteristics of conceptual discrimination, and free from the characteristics of names and designations.
What is the primordially abiding dharma? It refers to the ancient path of the sages, which is like the nature of gold, silver, and so forth—the dharmadhātu is eternally abiding.
Whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, the dharmadhātu remains eternally abiding, just like the road leading to a city.
For example, it is like a man traveling through a vast wilderness who sees a level, direct path leading toward an ancient city; he then follows it into the city and experiences what he desires.
"Mahāmati, what do you think? Did he create those paths and the various pleasures within the city? Mahāmati replied, "No, Blessed One.
The Buddha told Mahāmati, "It is the same with me and all past Buddhas: the *dharmadhātu* is eternally abiding. Therefore, it is said:
'From the night I attained supreme perfect enlightenment until the night I enter *parinirvāṇa*...'"
Nirvana. Between these two, not a single word has been spoken; nor has anything been spoken in the past, nor will anything be spoken in the future.

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse: From the night I attained enlightenment until the night of my parinirvāṇa—between these two, I have said nothing at all.
Because the Dharma I have realized abides by itself, I have made this statement. It...
The Buddha and I are entirely without distinction.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, what is the primordial abiding of the Dharma? Mahāmati, it refers to the level path of original practice;
it is like gold, silver, pearls, and other treasures existing in that place. Mahāmati, this is called the primordial abiding of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*).

"Furthermore, Mahāmati, whether the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, appear in the world or do not appear in the world, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), the stability of phenomena (dharmaniyāmatā), the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa), and the realization of phenomena (dharmasamavasaraṇa) remain eternally constant, like the original path leading into a city. Mahāmati, it is, for example, as if someone were traveling through a vast wilderness."
Seeing the level, straight path leading back to his original city, he immediately follows it and enters the city.
Having entered that city, he experiences various pleasures and performs various activities. Mahāmati, what do you think? Did that person first create that path as he followed it into the city?
Or did he first create the various ornaments? Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "No, World-Honored One."

Mahāmati, for myself and all past Buddhas, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), the stability of phenomena (dharmaniyāmatā), the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa), and the realization of phenomena (dharmasākṣātkriyā) are likewise eternally abiding.
Mahāmati, it is based on this meaning that I have declared in the midst of the great assembly:
"The night in which I attained Great Enlightenment and the night in which I entered Parinirvāṇa—between these two," [the nature of phenomena remains unchanged].
In the interval, not a single word was spoken; nor has anything been spoken, nor will it be spoken, nor is it being spoken now. At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"On what night did I attain enlightenment? On what night shall I enter parinirvāṇa? Between these two moments, I have said nothing at all.
The nature of phenomena is realized within; It is based on this that I speak. The Buddhas of the ten directions and I— all [are thus]."
Dharmas are without differentiation.
[Tang Translation] What is the primordially abiding dharma? It refers to the intrinsic nature of dharmas, such as gold existing within ore.
Whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, dharmas abide in their fixed positions; the dharma-realm and the dharma-nature are all eternally abiding. Great.
"Mahāmati, it is like a person traveling through a vast wilderness who sees an old, level road leading toward an ancient city;
he immediately follows it, enters, rests, and enjoys himself there. Mahāmati, what do you think?
Did that person create that road and the various things within the city? He replied, "No, Blessed One. The Buddha said, "Mahāmati, this is how I and all the Buddhas..."
The realization of *tathatā* (suchness) and the eternally abiding *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) are likewise thus.
Therefore, it is said that from the moment of attaining Buddhahood until entering *nirvāṇa*, not a single word was spoken in the interim; nor has anything been spoken, nor shall anything be spoken.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse: "On the night I attained perfect enlightenment, On that very night I entered *parinirvāṇa*."
Between these two, I have said nothing at all. Because it is the self-realized, primordially abiding Dharma, I have uttered this esoteric word:
"There is not the slightest difference between me and all the Tathāgatas."
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again requested of the World-Honored One:

"I pray that you will explain for me the characteristics of existence and non-existence regarding all dharmas, so that I and other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas may depart from the characteristics of existence and non-existence and swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall now explain it for you."
"You have spoken. Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "Excellent, World-Honored One! We shall indeed receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati, "In this world there are two kinds of reliance:
namely, reliance on existence and non-existence, which falls into the categories of being and non-being. This desire to see does not depart from the characteristics of what is to be abandoned."
[Wei Translation] At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva again entreated the Buddha, saying:

"I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain the characteristics of existence and non-existence regarding all dharmas, so that I and the great assembly of other bodhisattvas, having heard this, may depart from the characteristics of existence and non-existence and swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. The Buddha addressed the noble one:
The Bodhisattva Mahāmati said: "Excellent, excellent, excellent, Mahāmati! Listen attentively, listen attentively;
I shall speak for your sake. Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying: "Excellent, World-Honored One! We shall indeed receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati:
Most people in the world fall into two views. What are these two views? First, the view of existence; second, the view of non-existence.
Because they perceive the existence of phenomena and perceive the non-existence of phenomena, they conceive the notion of ultimacy regarding that which is not ultimately real.
[The Tang Translation: At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain the characteristics of existence and non-existence of all dharmas, so that I and the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas may depart from these characteristics and swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. The Buddha said: "Listen attentively; I shall explain it for you."
Mahāmati said, “Yes. The Buddha said, “Mahāmati, the sentient beings of the world mostly fall into two views, namely the view of existence and the view of non-existence.
Because they fall into these two views, they do not perceive that they have emerged from them, even though they have emerged.”
Mahāmati, what is meant by the world depending on existence? It means that the world exists; it arises from causes and conditions and is not non-existent.
It arises from existence and not from the arising of non-existence. Mahāmati, those who speak in such a manner are asserting that the world is without cause. Mahāmati, [this is so].

What is meant by the world depending on non-existence? It means that after having experienced the nature of greed, hatred, and delusion, one subsequently engages in false conceptualization and attachment regarding whether the nature of greed, hatred, and delusion exists or does not exist.
Mahāmati, if one does not grasp at the existence of a nature, then the characteristics of that nature are quiescent;
therefore, the Tathāgatas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas do not grasp at the nature of greed, hatred, and delusion as being either existent or nonexistent.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, how is it that the world falls into the view of existence?
It is to say that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions that truly exist, and not from those that do not truly exist; that truly existent dharmas arise, and not non-existent dharmas.
Mahāmati, when people of the world speak in this way, they are said to be propounding causelessness and conditionlessness, and they are slandering the world. This is causelessness.
"Mahāmati, all phenomena arise without a [perceptual] object. How is it, Mahāmati, that people in the world fall into the view of non-existence?
It is by saying that although greed, hatred, and delusion exist as real entities, one then says that greed, hatred, and delusion do not exist—thus discriminating between existence and non-existence.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, if someone were to say that no phenomena exist because they are not perceived..."

Because they are the characteristics of all things, Mahāmati. Furthermore, Mahāmati, if someone were to say that Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are free from greed, hatred, and delusion, yet further claim that these [defilements] previously existed;
[The Tang Translation: What is the view of existence (*astitva-dṛṣṭi*)? It means that phenomena arise from truly existent causes and conditions, and are not non-existent.
Truly existent phenomena arise from causes and conditions; it is not the case that phenomena arise from non-existence. Mahāmati, one who speaks in this way is speaking of causelessness (*ahetu*).
What is the view of non-existence (*nāstitva-dṛṣṭi*)? It means that after knowing [the presence of] greed, hatred, and delusion, one falsely conceptualizes and says:
"No, Mahāmati. Furthermore, although they conceptualize the existence of signs, they do not accept that phenomena exist.
Moreover, there are those who, while knowing the nature of all Tathāgatas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas to be free from greed, hatred, and delusion, nevertheless reckon them to be non-existent."

"Mahāmati, what herein is meant by 'one who destroys'? Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, if one takes up the nature of greed, anger, and delusion, and subsequently does not take them up again.
The Buddha told Mahāmati, "Excellent, excellent! You understand it thus.
Mahāmati, it is not only the nature or non-nature of greed, anger, and delusion that constitutes 'one who destroys'; this also applies to the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Buddhas."
This is the destroyer. Why is this so? Because neither the internal nor the external can be apprehended; because the nature of the afflictions is neither different nor non-different.
[Wei Translation] Regarding these two types of persons, which one is superior and which one is inferior? Mahāmati Bodhisattva...
Saddha said: "If a person says that greed, hatred, and delusion existed previously but are absent at a later time, this person is not like [the Buddha].
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Excellent, excellent, excellent, Mahāmati! You have understood my question.

Mahāmati, it is not only because one says that greed, hatred, and delusion truly existed previously but are absent at a later time that one is the same as the Vaiśeṣikas and others; for that reason, such a person is not like [the Buddha]."
Mahāmati, it is not merely that [the Buddha-nature] does not resemble the extinction of all the dharmas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

Why is this? Mahāmati, because in reality there are no internal or external dharmas; because they are neither identical nor different; and because the various afflictions are neither identical nor different.
[The Tang Translation: "In this regard, who is it that destroys? Mahāmati replied:
'One who, having possessed the nature of greed, hatred, and delusion, subsequently grasps at their non-existence is called a destroyer. The Buddha said: 'Excellent! You have understood my question.
Such a person is not merely one who lacks greed, hatred, and delusion who is called a destroyer; they also destroy the Tathāgatas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas. Why is this?"
Therefore, because afflictions cannot be apprehended either internally or externally, and because their essential nature is neither different nor not different [from suchness].
Mahāmati, greed, hatred, and delusion cannot be apprehended whether internally or externally, because the nature of greed, hatred, and delusion is bodiless and without grasping.
It is not the Buddhas, Śrāvakas, or Pratyekabuddhas who destroy them; for the Buddhas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas are by their very nature liberated.
Therefore, Mahāmati, because both bondage and its cause lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), if there were one who is bound, there would have to be bondage, as it is the cause of that bondage.
Mahāmati, such a teaching that [bondage] is destroyed is called the characteristic of non-existence.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, the dharmas of greed, hatred, and delusion cannot be found within one's own body, nor can they be found among external phenomena, because they lack substantial reality.
Therefore, I do not admit them. Mahāmati, my non-admission means that I do not admit the existence of greed, hatred, and delusion.
For this reason, such persons destroy the teachings of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. Why is this? Because the Buddhas...
The Tathāgata knows the dharma of tranquility because Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas do not perceive dharmas; this is because there is no cause for that which binds or that which is bound.
Mahāmati, if there were that which binds, there would necessarily be that which is bound; if there were that which is bound, there would necessarily be a cause for that which binds.
Mahāmati, one who speaks in such a manner is said to annihilate all dharmas. Mahāmati, this is called the non-existence of dharmas.
[Characteristics].
[Tang Translation: Mahāmati, the nature of greed, hatred, and delusion—whether internal or external—is unobtainable.
This is because they lack intrinsic nature and are devoid of anything to be grasped. Śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and Tathāgatas are by their very nature liberated. There is no...
Because there is that which binds and the cause of binding, Mahāmati. If there were that which binds and the cause of binding, then there would be that which is bound.
To speak in such a manner is called being a nihilist; this is the characteristic of non-existence.

"Mahāmati, for this reason I say it would be better to hold a view of a personal self as large as Mount Sumeru than to give rise to the view of emptiness born of the overweening pride of non-existence.
Mahāmati, those who possess the overweening pride of non-existence are said to be destroyers;

they fall into views that hope for self-characteristics and common characteristics, failing to understand that all is merely the manifestation of one's own mind. They perceive external natures as impermanent, perishing moment by moment in a continuous succession."

The continuous flow and transformation-extinction of the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas) is free from the conceptualization of the marks of words; this is what is called "destruction.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, it is based on this meaning that I have said in other sūtras:

"It would be better to give rise to a view of self as large as Mount Sumeru than to give rise to arrogance and claim that all dharmas are empty and non-existent. Mahāmati, this refers to those of overweening pride.

When people say that all phenomena (*dharma*) are non-existent, they are negating all phenomena because they fall into the view of specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

This is because they see phenomena as the manifestations of their own mind; because they see external objects as impermanent; because they see various characteristics as mutually distinct and differentiated from one another; and because they see the continuity of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) as entities produced through the successive succession of various causes. Because of this... [self-]... (Note:

The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a philosophical commentary on Yogācāra thought, likely from a Chinese translation of a Sanskrit treatise such as the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* or a related work. The ellipsis at the end indicates the original text was cut off.)
The mind engages in false conceptualization; therefore, Mahāmati, such persons destroy the Buddha-dharma.
[Tang Translation: It is with this meaning and intentional terminology that I have spoken: "It would be better to give rise to a view of self as large as Mount Sumeru."
They do not give rise to the view of emptiness, yet harbor overweening pride (*adhimāna*). If they were to give rise to such a view, they would be called "destroyers.

They fall into the midst of attachment to views of selfhood and commonality; failing to understand that all phenomena are manifestations of mind-only, and because they fail to understand this, they perceive external phenomena as momentarily impermanent, characterized by the successive differentiation of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, which arise in a continuous flow.
"Having already returned to cessation, false discrimination is free from the marks of words; it is neither arising nor perishing.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "Existence and non-existence are two extremes, as are all things up to the realm of the mind.
By purifying those realms, the mind becomes equanimous and quiescent. There is no grasping at the nature of objects; this is the cessation of non-existence."
There is nothing that exists; all phenomena are entirely suchness (tathatā), like the realm of the noble ones. Without seeds, there is arising; having arisen, they again perish.

Conditioned by causes and conditions, they are both existent and non-existent. They do not abide within my teaching, nor are they outside the path of the Buddha; they belong neither to me nor to others.
Since they arise through the gathering of causes and conditions, how could they be non-existent? Who gathers these causes and conditions so that they exist, and yet...
They speak of non-existence; such is the discourse of false views regarding the arising of phenomena. Through deluded conceptualization, they reckon existence and non-existence.
If one knows that nothing arises, then likewise nothing ceases. Contemplating all this as entirely empty and quiescent, one is free from both existence and non-existence.
[Wei Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse: Existence and non-existence are two extremes, serving as the objects of the mind.
Free from all objective realms, the mind is equal and tranquil. Without grasping at objective phenomena, one extinguishes both existence and non-existence.
As suchness is primordially present, that is the realm of the noble ones. That which was originally non-existent arises; this arising...

Having returned, it again ceases; its arising is neither existent nor non-existent. Such a person does not abide in my teaching; they are neither a non-Buddhist nor a Buddha, neither I nor anyone else.
Since things are not established through causes and conditions, how can one say they exist? If they do not arise from causes and conditions, how can one say they do not exist?
Those with false views debate the nature of arising phenomena, delusively calculating existence and non-existence. If one knows that there is no [inherent existence]...
They know that what is produced is likewise without cessation; they contemplate the world as entirely empty and quiescent, and thus do not fall into the extremes of existence or non-existence.
[Tang Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse: "Existence and non-existence are two extremes, even unto the range of mental activity.
Having purified that range of activity, the mind of equanimity is extinguished. Not grasping at objective realms, it is not a mere extinction."
There is nothing whatsoever. Yet there exists the wondrous reality of *tathatā* (suchness), which is the sphere of practice for all the noble ones. It was originally non-existent and yet arises;
having arisen, it again ceases. Whether through conditions it exists or does not exist, that [reality] does not abide within my teaching, nor is it of the outsiders, nor is it of the Buddha.
Neither the self nor any other being can bring existence into being through conditions; how then could it become non-existent?
Who could bring existence into being through conditions and yet claim it becomes non-existent? Such evil views speak of "arising," while false imaginings calculate "existence" and "non-existence.
If one knows that nothing is produced, then there is likewise nothing that ceases. Contemplating the world as entirely empty and quiescent, one is free from both existence and non-existence.

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for me and for all bodhisattvas the characteristics of the penetration of the fundamental principle (*siddhānta-yukti*).
If the characteristics of the penetration of the fundamental principle are skillfully distinguished, I and all bodhisattvas shall thoroughly comprehend these characteristics;
having thoroughly comprehended these characteristics, we shall swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi and not follow after [erroneous] perceptions."
Regarding perceptions, the various Māras, and non-Buddhists, the Buddha told Mahāmati: "Listen closely, listen closely, and reflect upon this well; I shall explain it for you.
Mahāmati replied to the Buddha, "Yes, I shall receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati:

"All Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas have two kinds of general characteristics: namely, the penetration of the principle (*tathatā-praveśa*) and the penetration of the teaching (*deśanā-praveśa*)."
[Wei Translation] At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, I pray that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Teacher of Gods and Humans, will establish for me and for all bodhisattvas the characteristics of the true dharma of cultivation.
May I and all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas thoroughly understand the practice of cultivation."

Having understood the characteristics of the True Dharma (*saddharma*), one will swiftly attain the realization of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, because one does not fall into the demonic activities of all false conceptualizations and discursive thoughts (*vitarka-vicāra*). The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Mahāmati:
"Excellent, excellent, excellent, Mahāmati! Listen attentively, listen attentively; I shall speak for you. Mahāmati said: "Excellent, World-Honored One..."
“Venerable One, we shall indeed receive your instruction. The Buddha said to Mahāmati:
“Mahāmati, there are two kinds of dharmas by which the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas establish the characteristics of the cultivation of the True Dharma.
What are these two? First, the characteristic of establishing the True Dharma; second, the characteristic of explaining the establishment of the True Dharma.”
[The Tang Translation: At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again requested of the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for us the characteristics of the fundamental tenets, so that I and the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas may thoroughly understand this meaning and not follow any of the various false and deluded interpretations, thereby swiftly attaining Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
“Listen attentively, Mahāmati; I shall explain it for you. Mahāmati replied, “Yes, Blessed One.
The Buddha said, “Mahāmati, all those of the two vehicles and the bodhisattvas have two kinds of doctrinal characteristics (*siddhānta-dharmanimitta*). What are the two?
They are the characteristic of the ultimate goal (*abhiprāya*) and the characteristic of verbal expression (*deśanā*).”

Mahāmati, as for the penetration of the principle (siddhānta-naya): it refers to the characteristics of supreme advancement attained through personal realization; it is far removed from the delusions of speech, words, and letters;

it proceeds toward the outflow-free realm (anāsrava-dhātu) and the specific characteristics of the stage of self-realization; it is far removed from all false and delusive perceptions; it subdues all externalists and hordes of Māras;
and it radiates the brilliance of the path of self-realization. This is called the characteristic of the penetration of the principle.

[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, what is the characteristic of establishing the True Dharma? It refers to the characteristics of the various supreme dharmas realized within one’s own internal experience, which are free from words, language, and phrases;
it is the ability to grasp the characteristics of the dharma of practicing through the stages (*bhūmi*) and realizing the untainted (*anāsrava*) Right Precepts;
and it is that which is free from the false conceptualizations (*vitarka-vicāra*) of all non-Buddhists and the realms of all Māras, thereby subduing them all.
"Mahāmati, when non-Buddhists and various Māras manifest their own internally realized dharmas and practice them according to reality,
this is called the characteristic of establishing the True Dharma."

[The Tang Translation: Regarding the characteristics of the ultimate tenet (*siddhānta-lakṣaṇa*): it refers to the distinguished characteristic of what is personally realized, which is free from the conceptualization of words and language;
it enters the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*) and accomplishes the practice of one's own stage;
it transcends all improper thoughts and reflections, subdues Māras and non-Buddhists, and gives rise to the light of wisdom. This is called the characteristic of the ultimate tenet.

What is the characteristic of the penetration of teaching? It refers to the teaching of the various doctrines of the ninefold canon, which is free from characteristics such as difference and non-difference, existence and non-existence, and so forth.

By means of skillful expedients, it accords with sentient beings; it teaches the Dharma as appropriate so that they may attain liberation. This is called the characteristic of the penetration of teaching.
Mahāmati, you and the other bodhisattvas should practice and study this.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, what is the characteristic of establishing the teaching of the Dharma?

It refers to the exposition of the various teachings of the nine divisions of scripture, which are free from the grasping at characteristics of oneness, difference, existence, or non-existence. First, one employs skillful means in order to lead sentient beings into the state they delight in;
that is, according to the faith of sentient beings in this or that dharma, one expounds that particular dharma. Mahāmati.
This is called establishing the characteristics of the teaching of the Dharma. Mahāmati, you and the other Bodhisattvas should cultivate and study such a true Dharma.

[Tang Translation: As for what is called the characteristics of the teaching of the Dharma, it refers to the exposition of the various teachings of the nine divisions of scripture, which are free from the [extreme of] oneness.
It is distinct from such characteristics as existence and non-existence; by means of skillful expedients, it causes sentient beings to enter this Dharma according to their mental dispositions.
This is called the teaching of the characteristics of phenomena. You and all other bodhisattvas should diligently practice and study it.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

"The characteristics of the fundamental doctrine and the communication of the teaching, The conditions, the self-nature, and the instructional methods— Those who see them well and discern them well Do not follow after various conceptualizations."
[Wei Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:

"Establishing the Dharma of internal realization and the names of the characteristics of dharmas—if one can skillfully discriminate these, one will not follow the characteristics of others' teachings."

[The Tang Translation: At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse: "The fundamental import and its verbal expression, self-realization and the teaching—if one can skillfully know and see these, one will not follow the false interpretations of others."
There is no true reality, as imagined by the ignorant. How can such imagination arise? Liberation consists in the absence of intrinsic nature.
[Wei Translation] Truly there are no external dharmas, as ordinary people discriminate. If all dharmas are illusory, for what reason do they seek liberation?
[The Tang Translation: As the ignorant discriminate, so it is not the true characteristic. How could they not seek a means of measurement?
Yet no dharma can be obtained.
Observing all conditioned phenomena as a continuity of arising and ceasing, they increase the two views; being inverted, they possess no knowledge.
The first is the True Reality (*tattva*). Nirvāṇa is the state of being without fault. One observes the delusions of the world as being like illusions, dreams, and plantains.

[Wei Translation] One observes all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), which are bound by the characteristics of arising and ceasing, and which increase the two views while failing to understand causes and conditions.
Nirvāṇa is free from consciousness; this alone is the one true Dharma. One contemplates the world as empty and false.
Like a phantom, a dream, or a plantain tree—thus one observes all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as a succession of arising and ceasing. This increases the two views;
being inverted, there is no true knowledge. Nirvāṇa is free from mind and mental objects; this alone is the single reality. One observes that the world is entirely illusory.

Like a phantom, a dream, or a plantain tree, although there are greed, hatred, and delusion, in reality there is no person. From craving arise the aggregates; all that exists is like a phantom or a dream.
[Wei Translation] Although greed, hatred, and delusion exist, there is no agent. From craving arise the aggregates;
all that exists is like an illusion or a dream.
[Tang Translation] There is no greed, anger, or delusion, nor is there any person. From craving arise the aggregates, like [an illusion].

Regarding what was seen in the dream, at that time Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, we pray that you will explain the characteristics of unreal conceptualization (*abhūta-parikalpa*).
How does unreal conceptualization arise? What kind of phenomena are called unreal conceptualization? In what respect..."
"Regarding unreal conceptualization within the Dharma," the Buddha said to Mahāmati, "Excellent, excellent! You are able to ask the Tathāgata about such a meaning;
it will bring great benefit and great peace to many, out of compassion for all devas and humans in the world.
Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall explain it for you. Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "Excellent, World-Honored One, please do so."
Nevertheless, he accepted the instruction. The Buddha said to Mahāmati: "Various meanings and various unreal false imaginings arise from attachment to false imaginings.
Mahāmati, through attachment to the grasped and the grasper, one fails to know that all is a manifestation of one's own mind;

one falls into the views of existence and non-existence, increases the views of the non-Buddhists, and, due to the habitual tendencies of false imagination, becomes attached to various external objects. This is the false imagining of the mind and its mental factors."
[Arising] from attachment to "self" and "what belongs to self.
[Wei Translation: At that time, the noble Bodhisattva Mahāmati again requested of the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, we pray that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, will explain for the sake of the bodhisattvas the unreal conceptualization (*abhūtaparikalpa*). Within which phenomena does it arise?"
"Regarding unreal conceptualization, the Buddha said to Mahāmati Bodhisattva: 'Excellent, excellent, excellent, Mahāmati!

For the sake of bringing peace to all sentient beings, for the benefit of all sentient beings, for the happiness of all sentient beings, and out of compassion for all the world—including gods and humans—you have requested this matter of mine. Mahāmati, listen attentively, listen attentively.'"
"I shall explain it for you. Mahāmati said, "Excellent, World-Honored One! We shall surely receive your instruction.
The Buddha told Mahāmati, "All sentient beings who cling to unreal, false conceptualizations do so because they arise from perceiving various false dharmas.
Because they are attached to the false objects of the grasped and the grasper, they enter into the perceptions of their own minds and give rise to falsity."
Because of false conceptualization, they fall into the factional assemblies of non-Dharma characterized by the two views of existence and non-existence.
Because they increase and accomplish the habitual tendencies of the false and divergent views of externalists, Mahāmati, they grasp at the meanings of external discursive proliferations.
They arise from false mental states and their associated factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*).
Just as one might differentiate between "I" and "mine" within a bundle of grass, Mahāmati, it is for this reason that unreal conceptualization (*abhūta-parikalpa*) arises.
[The Tang Translation: At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
