"World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain to me the characteristics of false discrimination (*abhūta-parikalpa*). How does this false discrimination arise? From what does it arise?
By what cause does it arise? By whom is it produced? For what reason is it called 'false discrimination'? The Buddha—
The Buddha said: "Excellent, excellent, Mahāmati! You have asked about this meaning out of compassion for the world of gods and humans;
it will be of great benefit and great peace. Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well;
I shall explain it for you. Mahāmati replied, "Yes. The Buddha said: "Mahāmati, all sentient beings, regarding various objects..."
Having fully realized that what appears is the manifestation of one's own mind, yet they falsely cling to the duality of grasper and grasped;

they give rise to various conceptual discriminations and fall into the views of existence and non-existence, thereby increasing the habitual tendencies of the false views of externalists. When the mental states and their concomitants arise in association, [they do so in this manner].
To grasp at external objects as being variously perceivable, and to be attached to the notions of "self" and "what belongs to self"—this is called false discrimination.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, if these various objects are merely various unreal conceptualizations and attachments to the false..."

Perception arises from the attachment to the grasped and the grasper; it fails to recognize that these are merely manifestations of one’s own mind. It falls into the views of existence and non-existence, thereby increasing the views of the non-Buddhists.

Through the attachment to various external objects, which are actually the habitual tendencies of false imagination, there arise the false imaginings of the mind and mental factors, along with the attachment to "I" and "mine.
World-Honored One, if such various external characteristics of objects fall into the marks of existence and non-existence, they are devoid of intrinsic nature.

"World-Honored One, it is not that the nature [of things] is free from the characteristics of views. World-Honored One, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is likewise free from the characteristics of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), sense organs (*indriya*), parts (*avayava*), examples (*dṛṣṭānta*), and logical reasons (*hetu*).

World-Honored One, why is it that in one place, false discrimination arises through attachment to various natures based on unreal objects, whereas in another place, discrimination does not arise through attachment to the characteristics of the ultimate truth?
Is it not the case, World-Honored One, that you are propounding a theory of false causes? Thus he spoke.
"One arises and one does not arise.

[Wei Translation] Mahāmati said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, if sentient beings cling to unreal, false conceptualization, they give rise to the perception of various false phenomena, clinging to the false grasper and the graspable."
Regarding all objective realms, one enters into the perceptions of one’s own mind, giving rise to false conceptualizations.

One falls into the midst of the partisan discrimination of the two views of existence and non-existence, thereby increasing and perfecting the habitual tendencies of the false and divergent views of externalists.
By grasping at the meanings of external discursive proliferations—which are unreal and false—one gives rise to false minds and mental factors. Just as...
“World-Honored One, it is like taking up a bundle of grass while grasping at ‘self’ and ‘what belongs to self.

World-Honored One, just as those who rely on various external objects and various characteristics fall into the partisan views of existence and non-existence, one should likewise remain free from the characteristics of the views of existence and non-existence.

World-Honored One, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) should also be thus: it is far removed from the teachings spoken by the Noble Ones in the *āgamas*, far removed from the sense-faculties, and far removed from...”

World-Honored One, apart from the three kinds of dharmas—metaphors, causes, and characteristics—how is it that in a single locus various conceptualizations and attachments arise, and various false imaginings are produced?
Why do they not adhere to the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), yet produce further conceptualization through false discrimination?
World-Honored One, when the World-Honored One teaches the Dharma in this way, it is not a teaching of equality.
To speak without a cause—why is this? Because that which arises in one place does not arise in another.
If the Blessed One were to speak in such a manner, he would fall into two partisan positions, giving rise to conceptual discrimination through the attachment to views and false discrimination.
Because the World-Honored One has said that it is like a worldly illusionist who, relying on various causes and conditions, produces various forms and images;

because the World-Honored One’s own mind consists of false conceptualization; and because the World-Honored One’s words regarding various falsehoods—whether existent or non-existent—are inexpressible as they transcend conceptualization—in this way, the Tathāgata falls into worldly discourse and enters into error.
[Seeing that the mind gathers within its own factions.

[Tang Translation: Mahāmati said: "If it is so, then external various objects—whose nature is free from existence and non-existence and which give rise to the characteristics of various views—the World-Honored One, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is likewise so; it is free from the measures of the sense faculties and from propositions."

“By way of analogy, World-Honored One, for what reason do you speak of the arising of conceptual discrimination regarding various meanings, yet not say that it arises within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)?
Is it not the case that what the World-Honored One says contradicts reason, since you speak of ‘arising’ in one instance but not in another?
Furthermore, World-Honored One, you have said that false discrimination falls into the views of existence and non-existence, being like various illusory phenomena.”
It is not real; conceptualization is likewise devoid of both existence and non-existence. How, then, can it be said that one falls into the two views?
Does this statement itself not fall into worldly views?
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "It is not that false discrimination arises once and does not arise again. Why is this?

Because when the false discrimination of existence and non-existence ceases, one realizes that external appearances are neither existent nor non-existent, and that they are merely the manifestation of one's own mind; thus, false discrimination does not arise. Mahāmati!"

I speak thus because of the various marks of delusive conceptualization within the minds of other ignorant people. Based on these, attachments to the nature and characteristics of various conceptualizations arise as they stand before them.
How may ignorant people become free from the views of attachment to "self" and "what belongs to self," and how may they transcend the faults of causes, conditions, agents, and actions?
By awakening to the measure of their own delusively conceptualized mind, their body and mind undergo transformation, and they ultimately attain clear understanding of the One.
The entire realm of the Tathāgata’s self-realization is free from the delusive imaginings (*vikalpa*) regarding the five dharmas, the three natures (*svabhāva*), and the objects of perception.

For this reason, I say that delusive imaginings arise from attachment to various unreal meanings. By knowing the meaning as it truly is, one attains liberation from the various delusive imaginings of one's own mind.
[Wei Translation] The Buddha told Mahāmati: "I distinguish that false discrimination is neither born nor extinguished. Why?
Because it does not give rise to the marks of the discrimination between existence and non-existence, and because one does not perceive any external existence or non-existence.
Mahāmati, because one perceives the self-mind as it truly is, false discrimination is neither born nor extinguished. Mahāmati, this of mine..."
What has been taught is spoken solely for the sake of ignorant ordinary beings regarding the conceptualization of their own minds.
Various kinds of conceptualizations arise following prior moments of mind; various kinds of conceptualizations involve attachment to signs. Why is this?
If it were not taught, ignorant ordinary beings would not be free from the false cognitive awareness of their own minds, nor would they be free from attachment to the views of "I" and "mine."
One does not fall into the error of [denying] cause and effect or various conditions, because one awakens to the two kinds of mind as they truly are.
One thoroughly understands the characteristics of practice in all the stages (*bhūmi*), and thoroughly understands the internally realized realm of the Buddhas' own conduct.
By transforming the five dharmas and the perceived marks of discrimination, one enters the stage of the Tathāgata. Mahāmati, for these reasons, I speak of "one."
All sentient beings alike cling to unreal and false mental constructions, and through their own minds they differentiate various meanings.
For this reason, all sentient beings must realize the meaning as it truly is in order to attain liberation.
The Buddha said, "Mahāmati, discrimination does not arise nor does it cease. Why is this? Because it does not give rise to the marks of discrimination regarding existence and non-existence;
because all external phenomena that are perceived are non-existent; and because one realizes they are merely manifestations of one's own mind.
It is only because foolish people discriminate their own minds that they become attached to the various marks of diverse phenomena."
I speak thus so that they may know that all that is seen is but their own mind; so that they may sever all views and attachments regarding "self" and "what belongs to self";
so that they may abandon the various evil causes and conditions of agent and action; so that, by awakening to the fact that it is only mind, they may transform their mental dispositions;

so that they may clearly illuminate the stages and enter the realm of the Buddhas; and so that they may relinquish the five dharmas, the self-natures, and all views of conceptual discrimination. For this reason, I say: "Empty..."
The arising of various objects manifested from one's own mind occurs through false conceptualization and attachment;
by understanding them as they truly are, one attains liberation.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "From causes and conditions..."

Born into the world, they are deludedly attached to the four propositions and do not understand that which I have realized: that the world is neither born from existence, nor is it born from non-existence;
it is not born from both existence and non-existence, nor is it born from neither existence nor non-existence. How can the ignorant be so deluded regarding causes and conditions?
It is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent. By observing the world in this way, the mind is transformed.
One attains non-self. All natures are unarisen because they arise from conditions; all that is produced by conditions is not self-existent.
An entity does not produce itself as an entity, for there would be the fault of duality, and because there is no fault of duality, no nature can be apprehended.
[Wei Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse: "From causes and conditions, this world arises;

those who falsely imagine and cling to the four extremes do not understand my teaching. The world is neither born from existence nor non-existence, nor is it born apart from existence and non-existence.
How can the deluded discriminate? If one can see the world as phenomena arising through dependent origination, [one sees] existence..."
There is neither non-existence nor existence; by turning away from the deluded mind, one attains the true Dharma of non-self.

All phenomena are fundamentally unarisen, yet they arise in dependence upon causes and conditions. These very conditions are themselves the fruit; from the fruit, existence is not produced, and from the fruit, no further fruit is produced.
If it were so, there would be two fruits; if there were two fruits, it would be difficult to find a fruit within a fruit.
[The Tang Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse: "From various causes and conditions, this world arises;
It corresponds to the four propositions, yet those who do not know my Dharma Do not understand that the world is neither existent nor non-existent, Nor is it both, nor is it neither.
How is it that all foolish people Discriminate regarding dependent origination? It is neither existent nor non-existent..."
Furthermore, it is neither existent nor non-existent; thus one contemplates the world. When the mind turns toward this, one realizes selflessness (*anātman*).

All phenomena (*dharma*) are unarisen, because they arise from conditions. That which is produced by various conditions is not an arisen phenomenon, for a fruit does not produce itself as a fruit, as that would entail the fallacy of two fruits.
Since there are no two fruits, no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) can be found.

Observing all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), which are free from the grasper (*ālambaka*) and the grasped (*ālambana*), and which are a mind-measure (*citta-mātra*) devoid of mind—I call this "mind-measure.
This measure is the locus of self-nature; it is free from both the nature of the object and the subject. Its nature is ultimately wondrously pure; I call this by the name "mind-measure."

[Wei Translation] Contemplating all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), one is free from both thought and the object of thought. Seeing that all phenomena are but mind-only, I therefore teach "Mind-Only.
Beyond measure, substance, and form, and free from conditions and all dharmas, there exists ultimately the truly pure reality.
I have thus explained this measure:
observing all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) as being devoid of the grasper (*ālambaka*) and the grasped (*ālambana*), one realizes with certainty that they are nothing but mind (*citta*).
Therefore, I speak of the "measure of mind" (*cittamātra*). This measure, in its essential nature, is free from both the object and the subject; it is the ultimate, wondrously pure reality.
I describe this as the measure of mind (cittamātra).

The designation of a self in the conventional truth (saṃvṛti) lacks any real entity; likewise, the aggregates (skandha) and the designation of the aggregates lack any real entity. Thus it is for all things.
There are four kinds of equality: [equality of] characteristics, causes, and arising; third, the selflessness [of phenomena]; and fourth, the cultivation and the cultivator. [Wei Translation:
The "self" is a conventional designation in the worldly truth; it possesses no substantial reality. The aggregates and the "aggregates" are mere designations;
these designations are not real dharmas. There are four kinds of equality: characteristics, causes, arising, and selflessness. Such are the four equalities.
This is the dharma of the practitioner:
although one provisionally designates a "self," it is in reality unfindable. The aggregates (skandhas) are likewise merely provisional designations and lack any substantial reality.
There are four kinds of equality: equality of characteristics, equality of causes, equality of that which is produced, and non-self as the fourth.

The practitioner observes that as the habitual tendencies of false conceptualization transform, various states of mind arise, and objects manifest externally; this is the measure of the conventional mind.
Appearing externally yet not existing, the mind perceives these various things; establishing them as body and property, I call this the "Mind-Only" (cittamātra). [Wei Translation:
Bound by the habituation of discrimination, the mind arises dependent on various objects. Sentient beings perceive external objects; therefore, I say it is Mind-Only.
External phenomena that can be seen do not exist; the mind exhaustively perceives them in this way: as body, means of subsistence, and dwelling place.
Therefore, I teach that there is only mind (*cittamātra*).
Bound by the habitual tendencies of false discrimination (*vikalpa-vāsanā*), various things arise from the mind; sentient beings perceive them as external.
I declare this to be the measure of mind (*cittamātra*); that which is seen externally does not exist, yet the mind manifests in various ways as the body, its resources, and its dwelling place.
I declare this to be the measure of mind (*cittamātra*):
it is free from all views, and free from both the perceiver and the perceived; it is neither attained nor produced—this I declare to be the measure of mind.
Neither existence nor non-existence; it is entirely free from both existence and non-existence. This is what is called the liberation of the mind; I describe this as the Mind-only (cittamātra).
Suchness, the limit of emptiness, nirvāṇa, and the dharma-realm, as well as the various types of mind-made bodies—I describe these as the Mind-only.
[Wei Translation] It turns away all views and abandons conceptualization and discrimination. Because there is neither seeing nor arising, I speak of "Mind-only.
It is neither existent nor non-existent; it is free from all dharmas of existence and non-existence. Thus, it is free from both mind and dharmas.
Therefore, I teach that it is mind-only: suchness, emptiness, the limit of reality, nirvāṇa, and the dharma-realm; as well as the mental body, the physical body, and so forth.
Therefore, I teach that it is mind-only.
[The Tang Translation: Free from all views, as well as the discrimination of subject and object; neither attainment nor arising—this I call the measure of mind (*cittamātra*).
It is neither existent nor non-existent, being free from both existence and non-existence; likewise, the mind itself is free [from these extremes].
I declare that these are the measure of mind: suchness, emptiness, the reality limit, nirvāṇa, and the dharma-realm;
as well as the various types of mind-made bodies—I declare these to be the measure of mind.

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has taught, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should be skilled in speech and meaning (*vācārtha*).
What is meant by a bodhisattva being skilled in speech and meaning? What is speech? What is meaning? The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall explain it for you. Mahāmati replied: [Please do so.]
The Buddha said, "Excellent, World-Honored One! We shall indeed receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "What is speech?

It refers to the conjunction of words, letters, and conceptualization (*vikalpa*). It arises based on the throat, lips, tongue, teeth, gums, and cheeks, and is produced through the attachment to the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the conceptualization of 'self' and 'other' in discourse. This is called speech."
[Wei Translation] At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the Tathāgata has said:
'As I have taught, you and all bodhisattvas must not cling to the meanings of sounds and words.'"
“World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva not become attached to the meaning of words? World-Honored One, what is ‘word’ and what is ‘meaning’?
The Buddha addressed the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva, saying: “Excellent, excellent, excellent, Mahāmati!
I shall explain this for you. Mahāmati said: “Excellent, World-Honored One! We shall indeed receive your instruction. The Buddha said:
Mahāmati, what is sound? It refers to the discrimination based on the combination of speech, names, and words, which has been habituated since beginningless time;
arising from the movement and coordination of the throat, nose, teeth, cheeks, lips, and tongue, it produces that speech which discriminates all phenomena.
This is called sound.
[The Tang Translation: At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, the Tathāgata has said: 'As I have taught, you and the other bodhisattvas should not grasp the meaning based on the words.
World-Honored One, for what reason should one not grasp the meaning based on the words? What is meant by 'words,' and what is meant by 'meaning'?"

The Buddha said, "Listen attentively, and I shall explain it for you. Mahāmati replied, "Yes. The Buddha said, "Mahāmati, 'speech' refers to that which has the habitual tendencies of discrimination as its cause;
depending upon the throat, tongue, lips, palate, teeth, and cheeks, it produces various sounds and syllables through mutual discourse. This is what is called speech."
Mahāmati, what is meant by "meaning" (artha)? It refers to that which is free from all characteristics of conceptual construction and characteristics of verbal expression; this is called "meaning.

Mahāmati, regarding such meaning, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, in a solitary and quiet place, through the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, takes as his object the self-realized awakening directed toward the city of Nirvāṇa.
Once the body of habitual tendencies has been transformed, he observes stage after stage within the realm of self-realization.
The characteristic of the meaning of intermediate progress is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s skill in meaning.

[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, what is meant by "meaning"? It is when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, relying on the power of noble wisdom derived from hearing, reflection, and cultivation, sits alone in a secluded place and contemplates: "What is nirvāṇa? What is the path leading to nirvāṇa?"

One observes the internal body as the sphere of cultivation and cultivates the superior characteristics at each stage and in every place, thereby transforming the causes of beginningless habitual tendencies.
Mahāmati, this is called the Bodhisattva’s skillful understanding of the characteristics of meaning.

[The Tang Translation: What is meant by "meaning"? It is when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwells in solitary seclusion and, by means of the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, contemplates and examines the realm of self-knowledge on the path toward nirvāṇa, thereby transforming all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Practicing the various modes of conduct across the stages is what is called "meaning.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva skilled in the meaning of speech contemplates that speech and meaning are neither different nor not different;
he contemplates meaning and speech in the same way. If speech were different from meaning, then meaning could not be articulated by means of speech.
And entering into meaning through words is like a lamp illuminating forms.
[Wei Translation] Furthermore, Mahāmati, how does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva skillfully understand the meaning of words?

Mahāmati, the Bodhisattva perceives that words, sounds, and meanings are neither identical nor different; he perceives that meanings and words, sounds, and meanings are neither identical nor different.
Mahāmati, if words were separate from meaning, then meaning would not exist by virtue of those words and sounds;
yet, meaning is discerned in dependence upon those words. Mahāmati, it is just as [if one were to depend upon...]
"Mahāmati, a lamp discerns various forms. Mahāmati, it is like a person who lights a lamp to examine various precious jewels, thinking, 'In this place it is such-and-such;
in that place it is such-and-such. Mahāmati, because a bodhisattva relies on the lamp of the sound of words to enter the meaning of practice within their own inner realization, they transcend words."
[The Tang Translation: Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is skilled in the relationship between words and meaning.
He knows that words and meaning are neither identical nor different; the same applies to meaning and words.

If meaning were different from words, then meaning could not be revealed by means of words, yet one perceives meaning through words just as a lamp illuminates forms. Mahāmati, it is like this: [the analogy continues].
Just as when someone holds a lamp to illuminate an object, they know that this object is thus and in such a place, so too it is with the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
By means of the lamp of language, they enter the realm of self-realization that transcends verbal expression.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, regarding non-arising and non-ceasing, intrinsic nature, nirvāṇa, the three vehicles, the one vehicle, the mind, and self-nature—when one becomes attached to the meanings of these verbal expressions, one falls into the views of superimposition and denial.
This is the false imagination of constructing something different from what has been established.
Various delusive thoughts appear like illusions; for example, various illusions are produced by the delusive thoughts of ordinary, ignorant beings, not by the noble ones.
[Wei Translation] Furthermore, Mahāmati, all dharmas are neither born nor extinguished; their intrinsic nature is originally...
They enter into nirvāṇa. Regarding the three vehicles, the one vehicle, the five dharmas, the mind, and the essence of all phenomena, they are identical;
yet, through the sounds of speech and meaning, they rely on various conditions to grasp at signs. Thus they fall into the views of existence and non-existence and slander all phenomena.

They perceive the essence of phenomena as each abiding in distinct characteristics, and they differentiate these distinct characteristics. Having made such distinctions, they see the various marks of phenomena as being like illusions.
They perceive various kinds of conceptual distinctions. Mahāmati, it is like the various and diverse conceptualizations of a magical illusion;
it is not that the noble ones see what ordinary people see.
[Tang Translation] Furthermore, Mahāmati, if there are those who, regarding the unborn, the unceasing, and the self-nature of parinirvāṇa—

If one grasps at the meaning according to the words regarding the One Vehicle, the five dharmas, the various minds, and the self-nature of phenomena, one falls into the views of superimposition and denial.
This is because one gives rise to conceptual discrimination that differs from reality; it is like seeing a magical illusion and reckoning it to be real.
This is the vision of the foolish, not that of the noble ones.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "Those conceptualizations of verbal expression establish all phenomena.
Because of those establishments, one dies and falls into the hells. Within the aggregates there is no self; the aggregates are not themselves the self.
It is not as they are conceptually imagined, yet it is also not the case that there is no self. All things possess a nature, just as with ordinary people."
This is the deluded imagination of the ignorant. If things were as they are seen by them, then everyone would see the Truth;
all phenomena would be without intrinsic nature, and both purity and impurity would utterly not exist. They are unreal just as they are seen, yet they are not non-existent either.
[Wei Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse: "By discriminating the sounds of speech, one establishes all dharmas.
Because of those establishments, one falls into evil realms. Within the five aggregates there is no self; within the self there are no five aggregates.
It is not as they are falsely imagined, yet it is also not non-existent. Ordinary people falsely discriminate and thus perceive [them]."
All phenomena truly exist; if they were as they are perceived, then everything would be seen as real.
If all phenomena were non-existent, then both defilement and purity would likewise not exist. That perception is not like that, yet it is not a mere nothingness either.
[The Tang Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:

"If one grasps the meaning according to the words and establishes [concepts] regarding all phenomena, because of that establishment, one will fall into hell after death. Within the aggregates there is no self, nor is the non-aggregate the self;
it is not as they conceptualize, yet it is also not non-existent. It is like that which is conceptualized by the foolish. (1)
All things possess intrinsic nature. If it were as they perceive it to be, then all would see reality.
All phenomena, whether defiled or pure, are entirely devoid of substantial essence; yet they are not as they perceive them, nor are they non-existent.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, I shall now explain the characteristics of gnosis (*jñāna*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*).

If you and the other bodhisattvas skillfully discern the characteristics of gnosis and consciousness, you will be able to penetrate those characteristics and swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Mahāmati, that gnosis is of three kinds: namely, mundane, supramundane, and supremely supramundane.
What is mundane knowledge? It refers to all non-Buddhists and ordinary worldlings who cling to the notions of existence and non-existence. What is supramundane knowledge?
It refers to all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who fall into clinging to the expectations of self-characteristics and common characteristics.
What is the supreme supramundane knowledge? It refers to the Buddhas and bodhisattvas who contemplate the dharma of non-existence and perceive that which is neither born nor extinguished.
Having departed from the categories of existence and non-existence, one enters the stage of the Tathāgata;

this is attained through self-realization by means of the non-selfhood of persons and phenomena. [Wei Translation] Furthermore, Mahāmati, I shall now explain for you the characteristics of knowledge (*jñāna*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
You and the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas should thoroughly understand those characteristics of knowledge and consciousness, and practice accordingly in accordance with reality.
Therefore, one quickly attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Mahāmati, there are three kinds of knowledge.
What are the three? First, worldly knowledge; second, supramundane knowledge; and third, the supreme supramundane knowledge.
Mahāmati, what is worldly knowledge? It refers to that which is held by outsiders, ordinary persons, and others who are attached [to their views].
The existence or non-existence of all phenomena—this is called the characteristic of worldly knowledge (*laukika-jñāna*). Mahāmati, what is supramundane knowledge (*lokottara-jñāna*)?
It refers to the false discrimination of the self-characteristics and common characteristics by all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas;
this is called supramundane knowledge. Mahāmati, what is the supreme supramundane knowledge (*lokottarottara-jñāna*)? It refers to the Buddha-Tathāgata’s bodhi...
O Mahāsattva, observing that all phenomena are quiescent, neither arising nor ceasing, you have attained the stage of the Tathāgata and realized the dharma of non-self,
remaining free from the two views of the partisan extremes of existence and non-existence.
[Chinese Translation] Furthermore, Mahāmati, I shall explain to you the characteristics of knowledge (*jñāna*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
If you and the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas thoroughly understand the characteristics of knowledge and consciousness, you will swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Mahāmati, there are three kinds of knowledge: namely, worldly knowledge, supramundane [knowledge], and...
Wisdom. It is the supreme wisdom that transcends the world. What is mundane wisdom? It refers to the calculations of existence and non-existence held by all heterodox teachers and ordinary fools.
What is supramundane wisdom? It refers to [the wisdom of] all followers of the two vehicles who are attached to specific and general characteristics.

What is the supramundane, most excellent wisdom? It refers to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who contemplate all phenomena as being entirely without marks—neither arising nor ceasing, neither existent nor non-existent—and who, realizing the selflessness of phenomena, enter the stage of the Tathāgata.
Mahāmati, that which arises and ceases is consciousness (*vijñāna*); that which neither arises nor ceases is wisdom (*jñāna*).

Furthermore, that which falls into the categories of the characterized and the characterless, as well as the various causal signs of existence and non-existence, is consciousness; that which transcends the signs of existence and non-existence is wisdom.
Furthermore, that which nourishes and develops characteristics is consciousness; that which does not nourish or develop characteristics is wisdom.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, consciousness has the characteristic of arising and ceasing; wisdom has the characteristic of non-arising and non-ceasing.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, consciousness falls into the categories of having signs and being signless; it falls into the causes of various signs such as existence and non-existence. Mahāmati!

The characteristic of wisdom (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*) is that which is far removed from the characteristics of existence, non-existence, both existence and non-existence, and the causes of existence and non-existence;

this is called the characteristic of wisdom. Furthermore, Mahāmati, the gathering together of all phenomena is called the characteristic of consciousness (*vijñāna-lakṣaṇa*); the non-gathering of all phenomena is called the characteristic of wisdom.
[Chinese Translation] Furthermore, Mahāmati, arising and ceasing are consciousness (*vijñāna*); non-arising and non-ceasing are wisdom (*jñāna*).

That which falls into the various characteristics of signs and signlessness, as well as existence and non-existence, and which has these as its causes, is consciousness. That which is free from the characteristics of signs and signlessness, as well as the causes of existence and non-existence, is wisdom.
That which possesses the characteristic of accumulation is consciousness; that which lacks the characteristic of accumulation is wisdom.

Furthermore, there are three kinds of wisdom (*jñāna*): namely, knowing arising and ceasing; knowing specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*); and knowing non-arising and non-ceasing. Furthermore, the characteristic of being unimpeded is wisdom;

the various impeded characteristics of objects are consciousness (*vijñāna*). Furthermore, the characteristic of the skillful means (*upāya*) produced by the conjunction of the three factors is consciousness;
the characteristic of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the skillful means that is without objective entities is wisdom. Furthermore, the characteristic of attainment is...

Consciousness cannot grasp its own characteristics; this is wisdom (*jñāna*). It spontaneously attains the realm of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*), which neither issues forth nor enters. Therefore, it is like the moon in water.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, there are three kinds of wisdom. What are the three? The first is the observation of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
The same characteristic. Second, observing the characteristic of arising and the characteristic of ceasing. Third, observing the characteristic of neither arising nor ceasing.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, that which is called "wisdom" (jñāna) has the characteristic of being unobstructed; "consciousness" (vijñāna) is the characteristic of cognizing those various objective spheres.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, consciousness is the characteristic of consciousness when it arises through the conjunction of the agent and the object of action. It is unobstructed.

The characteristic of being in accord with the Dharma is called the characteristic of wisdom. Furthermore, Mahāmati, the characteristic of non-apprehension is called wisdom, because one practices by means of attaining noble wisdom through personal internal realization;
thus one enters and emerges from all phenomena like the moon in water.
This is called the characteristic of wisdom.
[Tang Translation] Mahāmati, furthermore, there are three kinds of wisdom: namely, the wisdom that knows specific and general characteristics;

the wisdom that knows arising and ceasing; and the wisdom that knows non-arising and non-ceasing. Clinging to the characteristics of objects is consciousness (*vijñāna*); not clinging to the characteristics of objects is wisdom (*jñāna*).
This is wisdom (*jñāna*). That which arises from the conjunction of the three is consciousness (*vijñāna*). That whose intrinsic nature is characterized by non-obstruction is wisdom;

that whose characteristic is attainment is consciousness; that whose characteristic is non-attainment is wisdom. It is the realm attained through the realization of one's own noble wisdom (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*), for it is like the moon in water—neither entering nor exiting.

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "The accumulation of karma constitutes consciousness (*vijñāna*); non-accumulation constitutes wisdom (*jñāna*).
By observing all phenomena and penetrating their non-existence, one attains the power of mastery;

this is what is called insight (*prajñā*). That which is bound to objective realms is the mind (*citta*); that which arises from awakened conceptualization is wisdom (*jñāna*). When there is neither non-existence nor superiority, it is insight (*prajñā*)."
From this it arises.
[Wei Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse: "Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is able to accumulate all karma; wisdom (*jñāna*) is able to discern and differentiate;
insight (*prajñā*) is able to attain the signless (*animitta*) as well as the realm of sublime adornment. Consciousness is bound by its objects; wisdom is able to..."
Having thoroughly understood all objects—both the signless and the supreme object—this is the dwelling place of wisdom.
[Tang Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse: "The accumulation of karma constitutes the mind; the observation of phenomena constitutes wisdom.
Wisdom is able to realize the signless and attain sovereign majestic radiance. Bound by its objects, it is the mind; awakening to their characteristics..."
Birth is wisdom; signlessness and preeminence arise therein as wisdom.
Mind, mentation, and consciousness are far removed from conceptualization; one attains the state of non-conceptual dharmas. Such is the Son of the Buddha, not a śrāvaka.
The patience of tranquil, supreme progress; the pure wisdom of the Tathāgata; born from the excellent ultimate truth; completely free from all spheres of activity.
[Wei Translation] Mind, thought, and consciousness are free from all conceptualizations.
The Śrāvakas who discriminate phenomena are not true disciples. The patience of tranquil, supreme progress; the pure wisdom of the Tathāgata; born from the excellent, sublime wisdom.
Far removed from all spheres of activity—mind, thought, and consciousness—they are free from all conceptual marks and attain the non-conceptual Dharma.
These sons of the Buddha, not śrāvakas, possess the sublime patience of tranquility; through the Tathāgata’s pure wisdom, they are born into the excellent ultimate truth.
Distant from all spheres of activity, I possess three kinds of knowledge.
The Noble One has revealed the reality; regarding that, one contemplates perceptions and fully grasps all natures.
It is not associated with the two vehicles; wisdom is detached from all that exists. Clinging to intrinsic nature arises from the śrāvakas;
transcending all mental constructs, the Tathāgata’s wisdom is pure.

[Wei Translation] I possess three kinds of wisdom. By relying upon them, one attains the name of "Noble One. One discriminates their characteristics and is able to hear [the teachings on] existence and non-existence.
Departing from the practices of the two vehicles, this wisdom is detached from objective realms; yet it grasps the marks of existence and non-existence.
Arising from all the śrāvakas, they enter only such a mind; it is the stainless characteristic of wisdom. [Tang Translation:
I possess three kinds of knowledge, which the Noble Ones can clearly illuminate; by discerning all characteristics, they reveal all dharmas.
My knowledge is free from all characteristics and transcends the two vehicles; this is because of the śrāvakas and others.
They cling to the existence of all phenomena; however, the Tathāgata’s wisdom is stainless because he has thoroughly realized that there is only mind (*cittamātra*).
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are nine types of theories of transformation among the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), from which their views on transformation arise. Namely:

transformation of shape and location, transformation of characteristics, transformation of cause, transformation of accomplishment, transformation of vision, transformation of nature, and transformation of conditions...
Manifest transformation, manifest transformation of what is produced, and transformation of phenomena—Mahāmati, these are called the nine kinds of views on transformation.
It is because of these that all outsiders give rise to theories of existence, non-existence, and production through transformation. What is meant by transformation of shape and location?
It refers to the perception of differences in shape and location; for example, when gold is transformed into various vessels, there arise diverse shapes and locations.
It appears; it is not that the nature of gold undergoes transformation. The transformation of all natures is likewise.

There may be non-Buddhists who form such false imaginings, even up to the false imagining of the transformation of things; this is because they falsely imagine what is neither identical nor different.
[Wei Translation] Furthermore, Mahāmati, the non-Buddhists have nine kinds of views regarding transformation (*pariṇāma*).
What are these nine? First, transformation of form; second, transformation of characteristics; third, transformation of cause; fourth, transformation of association;
fifth, transformation of view; sixth, transformation of substance; seventh, transformation of conditions and discernment...
Transformation. Eighth is the transformation of the discernment of the performance of actions. Ninth is the transformation of birth.

Mahāmati, these are called the nine kinds of views on transformation. Based on these nine kinds of views on transformation, all non-Buddhists speak of transformation arising from existence and non-existence.
Mahāmati, what is the transformation of form according to the non-Buddhists? Mahāmati, it is, for example, as follows:
Ornaments made of gold—such as rings, bracelets, and necklaces—are each distinct in their various forms; yet, although their shapes differ, the essence of the gold remains unchanged.
In the same way, when all non-Buddhists differentiate among phenomena, although their forms and characteristics undergo transformation, the underlying reality is likewise unchanging.
Mahāmati, furthermore, there are other outsiders who discriminate that all phenomena arise through the transformation of causes.
Mahāmati, yet those phenomena are neither thus nor not thus, because they are based on discrimination.
[The Tang Translation: Furthermore, Mahāmati, the various non-Buddhists have nine kinds of views regarding transformation (*pariṇāma*). Namely:

transformation of form, transformation of characteristics, transformation of cause, transformation of correspondence, transformation of view, transformation of substance, transformation of the clarity of conditions, transformation of the clarity of what is produced, and transformation of birth. These are the nine. All non-Buddhists...

Because of such views regarding the path, they give rise to theories of existence, non-existence, and transformation. Among these, "transformation of form" refers to the perception of distinct differences in form;
it is, for example, like fashioning ornaments from gold, such as rings, bracelets, and necklaces, which are variously different.
The shape may differ, yet the golden substance remains unchanged. All phenomena undergo transformation in this very same way.
The various conceptual attachments of other non-Buddhist outsiders are neither like this nor different from it; they arise solely through discrimination.
In this way, all transformations of nature should be understood as being like the ripening of milk into curd, wine, or fruit.
The transformations imagined by the non-Buddhists do not actually exist; whether existent or non-existent, they are external natures and non-natures manifested by one’s own mind.
Mahāmati, such things arise from the habitual cultivation of the false imaginings of ordinary, ignorant beings. Mahāmati, there is no dharma that is born.
If they cease, it is like seeing the arising of forms that are like dreams or illusions.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, you should know that all such transformations are likewise.
For example, just as milk, curd, wine, fruit, and the like undergo transformation one by one upon ripening, so too are the transformations conceptualized by all non-Buddhists.

This is so; yet there is no real dharma that can undergo transformation. Because one perceives existence and non-existence through one's own mind and discriminates between existence and non-existence, Mahāmati, all ordinary beings are likewise thus, relying on the discrimination of their own minds.
And thus all phenomena arise. Mahāmati, there is no phenomenon that arises, nor is there any phenomenon that evolves;

it is like seeing various forms and objects within a dream or an illusion. Mahāmati, it is as if one were to see all manner of things, or the birth and death of the son of a barren woman, within a dream.
[The Tang Translation: One should understand that all transformations are like the ripening of milk, curd, wine, fruit, and so forth.

The non-Buddhists claim that these all involve transformation, yet in reality, neither existence nor non-existence exists. This is because what is seen is one's own mind and there are no external objects.
All such [views] belong to ignorant and deluded ordinary beings who follow the habitual tendencies of their own conceptual discrimination.
Yet they arise. In reality, there is not a single dharma that is born or perishes. It is like the various forms seen in illusions and dreams;
it is like speaking of birth and death for the son of a barren woman.

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "The transformation of shape, location, and time, The four great elements, and the various sense faculties— The intermediate state (*antarābhava*) arises gradually;
Such deluded conceptions are not the wisdom of the enlightened. The Supreme One [teaches] dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) Is not like those deluded conceptions;
Yet worldly dependent origination Is like a city of the *gandharvas*."
[Wei Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:

"The transformation of time and form, the four great elements and the sense faculties, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the various graspings—such graspings are not wisdom. The world arises from causes and conditions;
the Buddha does not speak of it in such a way. Causes and conditions are themselves the world, like a city of the *gandharvas*."

[The Tang Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse: "The forms, locations, and temporal transformations of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and the sense faculties arise gradually in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
This is a false conceptualization, not the wisdom of the enlightened.
When one does not conceptually differentiate between dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and the world, one sees that the world of all conditions is like a city of the *gandharvas*."
The Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra: A Combined Translation, Fascicle Three, Part One.
The Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra: A Combined Translation, Fascicle Three, Part Two.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Yuánkē of Zhōudū during the Ming Dynasty’s Línjì Orthodox Lineage.
The Third Chapter, "The Heart of All Buddha-Speech," Part Two.

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for me the meaning of the continuity of all dharmas and the meaning of liberation.
If you skillfully distinguish the characteristics of the continuity and non-continuity of all dharmas, then I and [others]..."
All these bodhisattvas are well-versed in the skillful means of all continuities (*saṃtati*) and do not fall into the continuity of attachment to the literal meaning as it was taught.

They are skilled in the characteristics of the continuity and non-continuity of all phenomena (*dharma*), as well as in the awakening that transcends the delusive conceptualization of words, letters, and speech.
They travel through the immeasurable great assemblies in all buddha-fields, possessing mastery over powers and supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*).
Holding this seal, various transformations and radiant lights shine forth. His awakened wisdom skillfully enters the ten inexhaustible phrases.
His practice of non-expedient means is like the sun, moon, mani-jewel, and the four great elements. In all stages, he is free from the marks of his own deluded conceptualizations and views;
he perceives all phenomena as being like illusions, dreams, and so forth. He enters the body of the Buddha-ground and, throughout the realms of all sentient beings, according to...

He preaches the Dharma to them as is appropriate and guides them, causing them all to dwell securely in the realization that all phenomena are like illusions, dreams, and so forth—free from the categories of existence and non-existence, the delusions of arising and ceasing, and the meanings of divergent verbal expressions. Their bodies become increasingly sublime.
[Wei Translation] At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, I pray that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, will skillfully explain the characteristics of the continuity and non-continuity of all dharmas."
I pray that the Sugata will explain the characteristics of the continuity and non-continuity of all phenomena,

so that I and the entire assembly of bodhisattvas may thoroughly understand the characteristics of the continuity and non-continuity of all phenomena, and having understood them through skillful means, [attain liberation].
They do not fall into the attachment to the characteristics of the continuity or non-continuity of all phenomena.

Having abandoned the conceptualizations of words, letters, and speech regarding the continuity or non-continuity of all phenomena, they attain mastery over powers and spiritual penetrations (*abhijñā*) to travel and transform within the great assemblies of all Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions. They are sealed by the excellent seal of the *dhāraṇī* gates. Ten...
Bound by the fetters of the ultimate limit, various transformations shine with radiant light. Like the four great elements, the sun, the moon, and the *maṇi* jewel, they proceed spontaneously.
Sentient beings experience them while remaining detached from the various stages (*bhūmi*). These are merely the appearances of conceptualization seen by one's own mind.
They demonstrate that all phenomena are like illusions and dreams, and they show the entry into the refuge of all Buddhas.
On this stage, they teach the Dharma to the realm of sentient beings according to what is appropriate for them.

They gather them in and cause them to abide in the realization that all phenomena are like illusions and dreams, remaining free from the factions of existence and non-existence, and transcending the conceptual fabrications of arising and ceasing as well as the divergent meanings of verbal expressions.
They attain mastery over their rebirth and dwell in the supreme abodes.
[The Tang Translation: At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, we pray that the Tathāgata will explain for us the profound and secret meaning of all dharmas, as well as the characteristics of interpreting their meaning, so that I and the other Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas may thoroughly understand these teachings and not fall into the deep-seated attachment of grasping at meaning according to the literal expression."
Free from the false conceptualizations of words and speech, they universally enter all buddha-fields.
Sealed by the power of mastery over the *dhāraṇīs*, their awakened wisdom dwells well within the ten inexhaustible vows.
Through effortless and manifold manifestations, their radiance shines like the sun, moon, *maṇi* jewels, earth, water, fire, and wind, abiding in all...
The stage is free from discriminatory views; one knows all phenomena to be like illusions and dreams.

Entering the rank of the Tathāgata, one universally transforms sentient beings, causing them to know that all phenomena are empty, false, and unreal. One leaves behind the categories of existence and non-existence, severs attachment to arising and ceasing, does not cling to verbal expression, and effects the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
The Buddha said to Mahāmati, "Excellent, excellent! Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect well upon it;
I shall speak for your sake. Mahāmati replied to the Buddha, "Yes, I shall receive your instruction.

The Buddha told Mahāmati, "Regarding all immeasurable dharmas, there is a continuous attachment to the meaning as it is described—namely, the continuity of attachment to marks (*nimitta*), the continuity of attachment to conditions (*pratyaya*), and the continuity of [attachment to] nature (*svabhāva*)."

The continuity of attachment to the non-existence of intrinsic nature; the continuity of attachment to the false imagination of arising and non-arising; the continuity of attachment to the false imagination of cessation and non-cessation;
the continuity of attachment to the false imagination of vehicles and non-vehicles; the continuity of attachment to the false imagination of the conditioned and the unconditioned;
the continuity of attachment to the false imagination of the specific characteristics of each stage; and the uninterrupted false imagination of one's own [conceptual] constructions.

The continuity of clinging to conceptual marks; the continuity of clinging to conceptual marks based on the false imaginings of non-Buddhists who adhere to the positions of existence and non-existence;
and the continuity of clinging to conceptual marks through the uninterrupted false imaginings of the three vehicles and the one vehicle.
[Wei Translation] The Buddha addressed the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, excellent, Mahāmati! Listen attentively, listen attentively; I shall explain it for you. Mahāmati said to the Buddha: "Excellent, World-Honored One!
We shall indeed receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Regarding the characteristics of the continuity and non-continuity of all dharmas, it refers to..."
The continuity of attachment to signs such as [the sign of] characteristics; the continuity of attachment to objects of perception; the continuity of attachment to existence and non-existence;
the continuity of attachment to the conceptualization of arising and non-arising; the continuity of attachment to the conceptualization of cessation and non-cessation;

the continuity of attachment to the conceptualization of vehicles and non-vehicles; the continuity of attachment to the conceptualization of the conditioned and the unconditioned; and the conceptualization of the stages.
The continuity of attachment to the characteristics of the stages; the continuity of attachment to discrimination and self-discrimination;

the continuity of attachment to entering the factions of non-Buddhist paths through discriminating between existence and non-existence; and the continuity of attachment to the meaning [of teachings] by the śrāvakas.
[The Tang Translation: The Buddha said, "Listen attentively, and I shall explain it for you.
Mahāmati, regarding all dharmas, there are immeasurable instances of clinging to meanings as they are expressed in words, which are profound and subtle. These are namely:

clinging to marks (*nimitta*), clinging to conditions (*pratyaya*), clinging to existence and non-existence, clinging to arising and non-arising, clinging to cessation and non-cessation, and clinging to vehicles (*yāna*) and non-vehicles."
Attachment to the conditioned and the unconditioned; attachment to the specific characteristics of each stage; attachment to the realization of one's own conceptual constructions;
attachment to the categories of existence and non-existence in the tenets of non-Buddhist schools; and attachment to the three vehicles and the single vehicle.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, this and other ordinary, ignorant beings continue in the succession of their own false imaginings.

Because of this succession, the false imaginings of the ordinary and ignorant are like a silkworm spinning its cocoon; by the threads of false imagination, they entangle themselves and others. They are attached to the characteristics of the succession of existence and non-existence.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, in this way, foolish ordinary beings possess a continuous succession of countless diverse mental discriminations.

Relying on this succession, their deluded discrimination is like a silkworm spinning a cocoon; they rely on the threads of discrimination arising from the perceptions of their own minds to form a continuous succession.
Delighting in conjunction, they entangle themselves and entangle others, clinging to the continuous succession of the conjunction of existence and non-existence.

[The Tang Translation: Mahāmati, these various secret attachments are of immeasurable kinds; they are all secret attachments resulting from the self-discriminating grasping of the foolish and ignorant.
These discriminations are like a silkworm making a cocoon, binding themselves and others with the threads of their own false imaginings.
They cling to existence and non-existence, firmly adhering to their desires and pleasures.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, therein there is neither the characteristic of continuity nor the characteristic of non-continuity.
One perceives all phenomena as quiescent, and thus false conceptualization does not arise. Therefore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva perceives all phenomena as quiescent.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, having realized that external natures are without intrinsic nature and that the appearances manifested by one's own mind do not exist, one should conformingly contemplate what is manifested by one's own mind.
Through the measure [of valid cognition], one perceives that all natures, whether existent or non-existent, are without marks (*animitta*).

Because the continuity [of conceptualization] is stilled, there is neither a mark of continuity nor a mark of non-continuity regarding all phenomena. Furthermore, Mahāmati, therein there is neither bondage nor liberation;

others, however, who have fallen into [wrong views] and do not realize things as they truly are, perceive bondage and liberation. Why is this? It is because they [perceive] existence and non-existence regarding all phenomena.
Because no sentient beings can be apprehended.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, yet there is neither continuity nor the characteristic of continuity, because one perceives all dharmas as quiescent.
Mahāmati, because Bodhisattvas perceive all dharmas as being without the characteristic of discrimination, it is therefore called "seeing."
This is the gate of the dharma of quiescence for all bodhisattvas.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, one who is able to know, according to reality, that all external dharmas are free from existence and non-existence, and who realizes, according to reality, that the appearances seen are but one's own mind—because they have entered into the signless nature of their own mind—Mahāmati, because of seeing and discriminating between existent and non-existent dharmas, it is called "continuity" (*saṃtati*). Because of seeing all...
Because phenomena are quiescent, they are called "without continuity. Being without continuity, they lack the characteristics of all dharmas that possess continuity.
Mahāmati, there is neither bondage nor liberation; one falls into dualistic views [only] through the conceptualization of one's own mind, which imagines there is bondage and liberation. Why is this?
Because they cannot know whether phenomena exist or do not exist.

[Tang Translation: Mahāmati, herein there is truly no characteristic of secrecy or non-secrecy, because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas perceive all phenomena as abiding in tranquility and being free from conceptual discrimination. If one realizes that all phenomena are merely mind...
One sees that external objects do not exist and are all identical to the signless (*animitta*).

Following this, one observes that the subtle attachments to the conceptual discriminations of "existence" and "non-existence" are entirely quiescent. Therefore, there is neither the characteristic of subtlety nor the characteristic of non-subtlety.
Mahāmati, herein there is neither bondage nor liberation; it is only those who do not understand reality who perceive bondage and liberation. Why is this? Because all...
Because the essential nature of all phenomena—whether they exist or do not exist—cannot be found when sought.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are three continuities for the foolish: namely, greed, hatred, and delusion; and craving for future existence accompanied by delight.
Because of these continuities, there is the continuity of the realms of existence (*gati*). That continuity, Mahāmati, continues through the five realms of existence. Mahāmati, [this is so].
Regarding the severance of continuity: there is neither the characteristic of continuity nor the characteristic of non-continuity.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, when one clings to the conditions of the threefold conjunction as a means, consciousness arises in uninterrupted succession. Through clinging to such means, there is continuity;
but when consciousness is severed from the conditions of the threefold conjunction, and one perceives the three gates of liberation, all continuity ceases to arise.
[Wei Translation] Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are three kinds of continuities for foolish ordinary beings. What are the three?
They are greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as the arising of craving and attachment. Because of these continuities, there is future birth, Mahāmati.

“Continuity” refers to the continuity of sentient beings being born within the five destinies. Mahāmati, for one who has severed continuity, there is no continuity and no characteristic of continuity.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, because of attachment to the continuity of causes and conditions, one is born into the three realms of existence.
By means of the various consciousnesses continuing and revolving without interruption, one perceives the three gates of liberation and thereby turns away from and extinguishes attachment.
The consciousness that has the three realms of existence as its cause is called the severance of the continuity.
[Tang Translation: Furthermore, Mahāmati, ignorant ordinary beings have three kinds of secret fetters: namely, greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as craving.
Together with the craving for future birth and delight in greed, by means of these secret fetters, they cause all sentient beings to continue their rebirth.
The five destinies. If the secret bond is severed, then there is neither the characteristic of secrecy nor the characteristic of non-secrecy.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, if one clings to the conditions of the triple combination, the secret bonds of the various consciousnesses arise in succession. Because of clinging, there is a secret bond;
if one perceives the three liberations as being apart from the consciousness of the triple combination, all secrets [are eliminated].
None arise at all.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "Unreal conceptualization—this is called the characteristic of continuity.
If one knows that reality, the net of continuity is severed. Lacking knowledge of the various natures, one follows after words."

It is called "appropriation. For example, just as that silkworm spins a web and entangles itself, so too are fools bound by their own false conceptualizations, continuing in this way without observation.
[Wei Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One again spoke in verse: "Unreal and false discrimination is called 'characteristic' (nimitta)."
Regarding the continuity of phenomena: one who can know them as they truly are will sever the web of continuity. If one grasps at sounds as real, one is like a silkworm binding itself in its cocoon;
bound by the false imaginings of their own minds, ordinary people cannot perceive this.
[The Tang Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse: "Unreal and false conceptualization—this is called the 'hidden characteristic' (*guhyaka*).
If one can know it as it truly is, all nets of concealment will be severed. Ordinary fools cannot comprehend this;
they grasp at meanings according to the words alone. Like a silkworm dwelling within its cocoon, their own deluded imaginings bind them."
Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "As the World-Honored One has taught, by means of various conceptualizations one conceptualizes various natures;
yet those intrinsic natures do not exist, for they are merely the nature of conceptualization itself. World-Honored One, if they are merely the nature of conceptualization,"
"Regarding 'the nature of non-existence does not depend on mutual relativity': would this not be a fault for the Blessed One to state that the purification of afflictions is without intrinsic nature?
For all phenomena are of the nature of imagined self-nature and thus lack intrinsic existence."

[Wei Translation] Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "As the World-Honored One has taught, by means of various kinds of discriminative minds, one discriminates various kinds of phenomena;
yet those respective phenomena lack such-and-such an intrinsic nature or characteristic.
They are merely the discrimination of one's own mind. World-Honored One, if it is only the discrimination of one's own mind and not those [external phenomena]..."
Regarding the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*): as the World-Honored One has taught, all phenomena should be neither defiled nor pure. Why is this?
Because the Tathāgata has declared that all phenomena are seen through false conceptualization and lack any substantial reality.
[The Tang Translation: At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has taught, one discriminates all phenomena by means of various minds; it is not that these phenomena possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), for this is merely false conceptualization (*parikalpa*).
World-Honored One, if there are no phenomena because they are merely false conceptualizations, would it not follow that both defiled and pure phenomena do not exist?"
[It] is completely destroyed.

The Buddha told Mahāmati: "So it is, so it is, just as you have said. Mahāmati, it is not as the false imagination of the nature of self-nature (svabhāva-lakṣaṇa) by foolish people [regards it] as real.
This imagined self-nature does not possess the characteristics of a real nature."
[Wei Translation] The Buddha told Mahāmati: "It is so, it is so, just as you have said.
Mahāmati, all foolish commoners (*bāla-pṛthagjana*) discriminate among phenomena (*dharma*), yet those phenomena do not possess such characteristics.
They falsely discriminate them as being substantially existent. Mahāmati, that is the false discrimination of phenomena by foolish commoners."
Regarding their essential nature and characteristics: deluded cognition does not perceive them as they truly are.
[The Tang Translation states: The Buddha said, "Mahāmati, it is so, it is just as you have said.
All ordinary and ignorant people discriminate among all phenomena, yet the nature of these phenomena does not exist in that way; this is merely a false attachment to what has no inherent nature."
[The Buddha said:

"Characteristics. Mahāmati, just as there is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of noble wisdom, which is known by the noble ones, seen by the noble ones, and perceived by the eye of noble insight—in this way one knows that intrinsic nature.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha: "If it is as you say, through the noble ones' noble knowledge, noble vision, and the eye of noble insight [that this is known], then it is not..."
The divine eye is not the fleshly eye; its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is known in this way. It is not as the deluded commoners imagine it.

World-Honored One, how do the deluded commoners depart from such false imagination? Because they do not perceive the reality of the noble nature. World-Honored One, that [nature] is neither inverted nor non-inverted. Why is this?
Because they do not perceive the reality of the noble nature as its own intrinsic nature, and thus they do not see that which is free from [delusion].
Because it possesses the characteristic of existence and non-existence.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, just as the noble ones know the intrinsic nature and characteristics of all phenomena—
relying on the wisdom of the noble ones, relying on the vision of the noble ones, and relying on the eye of noble insight— they know the intrinsic characteristics of all phenomena as they truly are.

The Bodhisattva Mahāmati said: "World-Honored One, just as the various noble ones rely upon noble wisdom, rely upon noble vision, and rely upon the noble eye of insight—rather than the fleshly eye or the divine eye—they realize that the essence and characteristics of all phenomena possess no such characteristics, unlike the false conceptualizations of ordinary worldlings.
World-Honored One, how is it that ignorant ordinary worldlings [perceive them]?"
"Transforming the marks of false imagination. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "One who can realize the realm of the noble ones as it truly is transforms the false consciousness.
"World-Honored One," [Mahāmati asked,] "Is that ignorant ordinary person not possessed of perverted views, nor is he without perverted views? Why is this?
Because he cannot see the true nature of dharmas within the realm of the noble ones as it truly is; because he sees the transformation of existence..."
Because they are signless.
[Tang Translation: However, the noble ones perceive and know the self-nature of all phenomena as it truly is with their noble eye of wisdom.
Mahāmati said: "If the noble ones see the nature of all phenomena with their noble eye of wisdom, it is not..."
The divine eye and the fleshly eye are not the same as the conceptual distinctions made by the foolish ordinary people. How can the foolish ordinary people be free from such conceptualization?
Because they are unable to awaken to and comprehend the dharmas of the noble ones. World-Honored One, those [distinctions] are neither inverted nor non-inverted.
Why is this? Because they do not perceive the dharmas perceived by the noble ones. The noble eye is free from the marks of existence and non-existence.
World-Honored One, the noble ones do not perceive things in the manner of such conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), for they do not take the realm of self-characteristics as their objective domain.
World-Honored One, that too is the characteristic of the intrinsic nature of things; the nature of conceptual construction appears in this way, yet it is not said to have a cause.

Because it would be causeless; that is to say, because one would fall into the view of [inherent] nature and characteristics (*dharmatā-lakṣaṇa-dṛṣṭi*). Since other objects are not like those [imagined natures], there would be the fault of infinite regress.
World-Honored One, because they do not perceive the self-nature and characteristics of nature, the World-Honored One is also not the cause for the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Regarding that self-nature and characteristics of nature, how could they be either imagined or non-imagined? One must know the imagination as it truly is.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, even all the noble ones possess discrimination.
All the various kinds of phenomena do not possess such characteristics, because they are merely the appearances of objects perceived by one's own mind. World-Honored One," [he continued].
Those noble ones perceive the substantiality of phenomena and differentiate their characteristics; yet the World-Honored One neither says they have a cause nor says they are causeless.
Why is this? Because [to say so] would fall into the characteristic of existing phenomena. Other people perceive objects not in this way.
World-Honored One, if one speaks thus, there is the fault of infinite regress. Why is this? Because of a lack of awakening.
Because all dharmic characteristics lack intrinsic nature, World-Honored One, it is not because of conceptual differentiation that the intrinsic nature of dharmas exists;
rather, World-Honored One, how could they be differentiated? They should not be differentiated in the manner they are differentiated; they should be differentiated in accordance with reality.

[The Tang Translation: "O Blessed One, even the Noble Ones do not attain [reality] through such conceptual discrimination as ordinary beings do. This is because it is not a characteristic of the objective sphere within which they themselves move.
Furthermore, they too perceive the nature and characteristics of all phenomena, for these appear just like the nature they falsely cling to.
Since this does not speak of existence by cause or lack of cause, one falls into the view of the nature and characteristics of all phenomena."
Since their other spheres of experience are not like this, it would result in the fallacy of infinite regress.
Who, then, could truly understand the nature and characteristics of phenomena? World-Honored One, the nature and characteristics of all phenomena do not arise from conceptual discrimination;
why then do you say that phenomena exist because of conceptual discrimination?
“World-Honored One, conceptual construction is distinct; the characteristics of self-nature are distinct. World-Honored One, they have dissimilar causes.
How is it that those characteristics of the self-nature of conceptual construction are each not conceptual constructions, yet foolish people do not know them as they truly are?

Nevertheless, for the sake of causing sentient beings to abandon conceptual construction, you say that such characteristics of conceptual construction do not exist as they truly are. World-Honored One, why do you deny that sentient beings exist?”
There is the view of non-existence; attachment to the intrinsic nature of phenomena; and attachment to the sphere of activity of noble wisdom, which results in falling into the view of existence.
Thus, while teaching that dharmas are empty and lack intrinsic nature, one speaks of the intrinsic nature of the reality of noble wisdom.

[Wei Translation] "World-Honored One, there are the characteristics of conceptualization (*vikalpa-lakṣaṇa*), the characteristics of difference (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), and the characteristics of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*).
World-Honored One, these two kinds of causes are not similar; the intrinsic natures of those various conceptualized phenomena are distinct.

How is it that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) conceptualize in such a way? These causes do not establish [the objects] as they are perceived. The World-Honored One said: "I [teach this] in order to sever all..."
Because all sentient beings possess minds of false conceptualization, they speak in such a manner; yet for those ordinary people, there is no such dharma as they falsely conceptualize.
World-Honored One, for what reason do you refute the views of existence and non-existence held by sentient beings?
Yet they cling to real dharmas as the realm of noble wisdom. World-Honored One, this further causes all sentient beings to fall into the state of non-existence.
Why is this? Because you say that all dharmas are quiescent and signless, and because the essence of the dharma-body of noble wisdom is likewise signless.
[The Tang Translation: "World-Honored One, the characteristics of conceptualization are distinct and the characteristics of various phenomena are distinct;

since their causes are dissimilar, how can all phenomena arise from conceptualization? Furthermore, for what reason do ordinary, ignorant people conceptualize them as not being thus, yet speak in this way?
[The Buddha replied: "It is in order to cause sentient beings to abandon conceptualization that I teach that the characteristics of phenomena are as they appear through conceptualization."

There is no such dharma. World-Honored One, for what reason do you cause all sentient beings to abandon the dharmas clung to through the views of existence and non-existence, yet again cause them to cling to the realm of noble wisdom and fall into the view of existence? Why is this?
Because you do not speak of the dharma of quiescent emptiness and non-existence, but instead speak of the intrinsic nature of noble wisdom.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "It is not that I teach a dharma of emptiness that is non-existent, nor do I fall into the view of existence by speaking of the reality of the self-nature of noble wisdom.

Rather, it is in order to cause sentient beings to leave behind phrases that provoke terror that I speak of the dharma of emptiness. Since beginningless time, sentient beings have been attached to the signs of the self-nature of things;
they are attached to the signs of the self-nature of the reality of noble wisdom. Therefore, Mahāmati, I [teach emptiness]."
I speak of the characteristics of the self-nature of phenomena (*dharmasvabhāva*).

Mahāmati, it is I who abide in the reality of the emptiness of self-attainment, which is free from the appearances of delusive confusion, free from the views of existence and non-existence regarding what is manifested by one's own mind, and which is sealed by the seal of the reality of the three gates of liberation.
Thus, I abide in the observation of self-realized wisdom regarding the self-nature of phenomena, free from the views and signs of the entities of existence and non-existence.
[Wei Translation] The Buddha told Mahāmati: "I do not say that all dharmas are quiescent and signless, nor do I say that all dharmas are non-existent.
