Nor do I cause them to fall into the view of nihilism, nor do I cause them to become attached to the realm of the noble ones in such a manner.
Why is this? It is because I wish to free sentient beings from fear and terror."
Because of their dwelling [in false views]. Since beginningless time, all sentient beings have clung to the substantial existence of the essence and characteristics of all phenomena;
therefore, I say that while the noble ones know the essence and characteristics of phenomena to be substantially existent, they further teach that all phenomena are quiescent and signless.
Mahāmati, I do not speak of the existence or non-existence of the essence of dharmas. I speak of the dharma realized through one's own direct realization as it truly is.
By hearing my teaching and practicing the tranquility of all signless dharmas, one attains the vision of the signless realm of suchness.
Entering into the perception of phenomena as one's own mind, one remains far removed from views of the existence or non-existence of external phenomena.

Having attained the three gates of liberation, one then thoroughly seals all phenomena with the seal of reality (*yathābhūta-mudrā*). Through the wisdom of internal realization, one observes and becomes free from views of existence and non-existence.
The Buddha said, "Mahāmati, it is not that I do not teach the dharma of tranquil emptiness, which would lead to the view of existence.
Why is this? Because I have already taught the nature of the reality of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*).

For sentient beings who, since beginningless time, have been attached to existence, I have taught the tranquil dharma by means of the reality of the noble ones, so that upon hearing it, they will not give rise to fear."
They are fearless. They are able to realize the quiescent dharma of emptiness as it truly is; they leave behind the signs of delusion and enter the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only).
Knowing that what is perceived has no external phenomena, they awaken to the three gates of liberation and obtain the seal of reality (*yathābhūta-mudrā*).
Seeing the self-nature of dharmas, they comprehend the realm of the sages and remain far removed from all attachments to existence and non-existence.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should not establish the thesis that "all dharmas are unarisen. Why is this?
Because it would imply that all natures are non-natures, and because it involves the characteristic of arising from causes;
thus, the thesis that "all dharmas are unarisen" would be undermined. If that thesis—that all dharmas are unarisen—is undermined, then [the position fails].
Because their own thesis arises in dependence [on others], and because that thesis does not enter into all phenomena (*sarvadharma*), for it is the non-arising of unimpaired characteristics.
For one who establishes a thesis that all phenomena are non-arisen, that statement is then subverted.

Mahāmati, as for the thesis of the non-arising of existence and non-existence, that thesis enters into all natures (*sarvabhāva*), for the characteristics of existence and non-existence are unapprehendable. Mahāmati, if that thesis...
Non-arising. One establishes the thesis that all natures are non-arising; thus, that thesis is undermined because the characteristics of existence and non-existence do not arise.

Furthermore, one should not establish a thesis, because a five-membered syllogism contains many faults, because the successive causes have different characteristics, and because it is something produced.
One should not establish a thesis-part such as "all phenomena are non-arising," nor, likewise, "all phenomena are empty."
In this way, all phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
One should not establish a thesis [regarding their existence]. [Wei Translation: Furthermore, Mahāmati, a bodhisattva should not establish that all phenomena are unarisen. Why?
Because if one establishes a phenomenon, it is the same as having [the notion of] the existence of phenomena; if one does not do so, it is the same as the non-existence of phenomena. Furthermore...
Mahāmati, because one establishes that all phenomena exist, one speaks of "all phenomena. Within this establishment of phenomena, they are identical. Why?
Because that establishment is not different from the non-arising of all phenomena;
therefore, to establish and speak of "all phenomena" is a self-contradiction. Why? Because within the establishment itself, there is no such thing as that establishment. If not...
In that case, that establishment also does not arise, because it shares the same characteristic of non-differentiation as all phenomena.
Therefore, the establishment that all phenomena do not arise is called "self-subversion," because that establishment exists through the combination of the three factors and the five factors.
Apart from such establishment, neither existence nor non-existence arises. Mahāmati, that establishment enters into all phenomena.
In the middle, one does not perceive the existence or non-existence of phenomena.
Mahāmati, if one establishes that all phenomena are unarisen and then declares, "All things are unarisen," Mahāmati, such a proponent’s own establishment is undermined. Why is this?
Because they are free from the characteristics of existence and non-existence and cannot be apprehended. Mahāmati, for this reason, one should not establish that all phenomena are unarisen.
Mahāmati, because such an establishment would be identical to the essence of those very phenomena that are unarisen, one should not establish that all phenomena are unarisen;
for there are many faults [in doing so]. Mahāmati, furthermore, there is another...
One should establish that all phenomena are unarisen. Why? Because the causes for each of those three and five phenomena are different.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are cases where one should not establish that all phenomena are unarisen. Why?
Because those three and five phenomena constitute conditioned and impermanent things. Therefore, one should not establish that all phenomena are unarisen.
[Arising. In this way, one should not establish that all phenomena (*dharma*) are empty. All phenomena lack any substantial intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). [Tang Translation:
Furthermore, Mahāmati, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should not establish that all phenomena are entirely unarisen. Why?
Because all phenomena are fundamentally non-existent, as well as because of their own thesis and reason (*pakṣa-hetu*).
Because it possesses the characteristic of arising. Furthermore, Mahāmati, the statement that "all dharmas are unarisen" is self-contradictory.
Why? Because that thesis arises in dependence [upon other factors]. Moreover, that thesis itself falls within the category of all dharmas, for even the characteristic of non-arising does not arise.
Furthermore, that thesis is composed of various parts; thus, whether existent or non-existent, all [dharmas]...
[If you argue that] non-arising [is established], this very thesis enters into all phenomena, because the characteristics of existence and non-existence are likewise non-arising.

Therefore, the thesis that "all phenomena are non-arising" is self-contradictory; one should not establish such a position, as it involves many fallacies regarding the various members [of the syllogism].
Because they arise through a succession of differing characteristics. Just as no phenomena are produced, so too are all phenomena empty and devoid of intrinsic nature.
However, Mahāmati, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas describe all phenomena as being like illusions and dreams, because their characteristics appear and then do not appear.

Furthermore, because one perceives the faults of [subjective] cognition, it should be taught that all phenomena have the nature of illusions and dreams. This is excepted for the sake of providing a phrase to remove the fear of fools.
Mahāmati, fools fall into the views of existence and non-existence; do not cause them to become terrified and thereby abandon the Mahāyāna.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, it is for the sake of sentient beings that Bodhisattvas teach that all dharmas are like illusions and like dreams.
This is because they perceive the characteristics of what is seen and what is not seen, and because the characteristics of dharmas delude both vision and cognition.
Therefore, one should speak of them as being like illusions and like dreams, in order to exclude all ignorant worldlings and remove the ground for their fear. Mahāmati...

Wisdom. Because ordinary beings fall into the false views of existence and non-existence, and because ordinary beings experience terror upon hearing that things are like illusions and dreams, they abandon the Mahāyāna once they have become terrified by what they hear.

[The Tang Translation: Mahāmati, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should declare that all dharmas are like illusions and like dreams, because they are seen and yet not seen, and because they are all merely the marks of delusive confusion. This is excepted for the sake of preventing fools from giving rise to fear.
Mahāmati, ordinary people are ignorant and fall into the views of existence and non-existence; do not cause them to become terrified.
They remain far removed from the Mahāyāna.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

"Without intrinsic nature, without verbal expression, without objective entities, and without continuity—these are the deluded imaginings of fools, like the evil perceptions of a corpse. All dharmas are unarisen; they are not [produced] by them."
The tenets of the non-Buddhists maintain that, in the ultimate sense, nothing is produced; that things are established through the conditions of their nature;
and that all phenomena are unarisen, such that the wise do not form conceptualizations. Because those tenets arise from causes, the Awakened One has completely eliminated them.
[Wei Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse: "No intrinsic nature, no consciousness, No ālayavijñāna— The deluded falsely discriminate;
Their false views are like corpses. All phenomena are unarisen; Other views and consciousnesses are not established.
All phenomena are ultimately unarisen; Causal conditions cannot establish them. All phenomena are unarisen; do not [cling to them]."
Establishing such a dharma, it cannot be accomplished because its causes are not concordant; therefore, the establishment is destroyed.

[Tang Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One further spoke in verse: "Without intrinsic nature, without expression, Without objective entities, and without a basis— The foolish and ignorant engage in false discrimination;
Their evil conceptions are like corpses. All dharmas are unarisen; [this is not the view of] the non-Buddhists."
That which is established [as existing] is not produced by conditions; therefore, all phenomena are unproduced, and the wise do not conceptualize them.
Since that [opponent’s] thesis arises from production, this realization [of non-production] would be undermined.

Just as one with cataracts sees the false appearance of falling hair, so too do the ignorant, through their perverse conceptualization, cling to the nature of things and establish the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*).
Where no intrinsic nature of things exists, they establish the intrinsic nature of things; through such reflection, they give rise to delusive thoughts.

Based on signs and phenomena, verbal teachings are established; yet when the mind is agitated, it trembles violently. The Son of the Buddha is able to transcend this and remain far removed from all false conceptualizations.
[Wei Translation] It is like having a film over the eye, whereby one falsely perceives floating hairs; ordinary people likewise falsely perceive existence and non-existence through discrimination.
The three realms of existence are merely provisional names; there is no real essence to dharmas. Yet they cling to these provisional names as being real.
Ordinary beings give rise to conceptualization regarding signs, things, and provisional names; these are what the mind and consciousness experience.
The sons of the Buddha are able to remain far removed from them, dwelling in the practice of the realm of tranquility.
[The Tang Translation: It is like having a film over the eye, whereby one falsely perceives a mass of hairs. All phenomena are likewise; the foolish and ignorant engage in false conceptualization.
The three realms of existence are merely provisional names; there is no real essence to dharmas. It is by virtue of these provisional designations [that they appear].

Conceptualizing through false discrimination, they falsely designate the characteristics of all phenomena; these disturb the mind and consciousness, yet the sons of the Buddha completely transcend them and wander without discrimination.
To perceive what is not water as water is a sensation born of craving; such is the delusion of the foolish, but for the noble one it is not so.
The noble one perceives purity, which arises from the three liberations and samādhis; far removed from arising and ceasing, they wander in the state of non-existence.
Cultivating the practice of non-existence, there is neither nature nor non-nature; through the equality of nature and non-nature, the fruits of sagehood arise.
[Wei Translation: There is no water, yet they perceive the mark of water; the various beasts have deluded and false minds. Ordinary people see phenomena as such, but the sages do not.
The sages see them as pure, giving rise to the samādhis of the three liberations, far removed from arising and ceasing.
One attains unobstructed tranquility and practices the state of non-existence; yet one does not perceive even "non-existence.
Since existence and non-existence are equal, the fruits of the noble ones arise.
[The Tang Translation: To perceive water where there is no water arises from thirst and craving. Such is the way things appear to the ignorant;
for the noble ones, it is not so. The noble ones see purity, giving rise to the three doors of liberation, and remaining far removed from arising and ceasing.
Constantly practicing the realm of signlessness, cultivating the realm of signlessness, and furthermore being without even non-existence— wherein existence and non-existence are entirely equal—
one thereby gives birth to the fruit of holiness.

What is nature and what is non-nature? What is equanimity? It is said that when the mind does not know and is utterly tossed about by internal and external [objects], if one can destroy that [state of agitation], the mind will perceive with equanimity.
[Wei Translation] What is the nature of existence and non-existence? How is equality established? Because the mind cannot perceive it, internal and external phenomena are impermanent.
If one can extinguish those phenomena, one perceives the mind as being equal.

[The Tang Translation: What is the existence and non-existence of phenomena? How are they established as equal? If the mind does not comprehend phenomena, then both the internal and external are agitated and disturbed.
Once they are comprehended, there is equality; at that time, the signs of agitation cease.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has said:
'Just as when one grasps at an object, wisdom does not apprehend it; this is the establishment of the measure of designation (prajñapti-mātra).
That which is grasped has no intrinsic nature, and the grasping itself also has no intrinsic nature. Because there is no grasping, wisdom does not arise; it is merely a name by designation.'"
[Wei Translation] At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has said, through the observation of wisdom one cannot perceive external objects;

at that time, one rightly knows that these are merely the internal mind, and realizes the nature of the mind, intellect, and consciousness as it truly is. There is no object to be grasped, nor is there a grasper."
Therefore, wisdom is likewise unable to differentiate and grasp [it].
[Tang Translation: At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, as the Buddha has taught, if one knows that the objective realm is merely a provisional designation and is ultimately unobtainable, then there is nothing to be grasped."
Because there is nothing to be grasped, there is also no grasper. Since both the grasper and the grasped are absent, conceptual discrimination does not arise;
this is what is called "wisdom.
World-Honored One, is it because one does not perceive whether the intrinsic nature and the common characteristics are different or non-different that wisdom cannot be attained?
"Is it because wisdom cannot apprehend [an object] due to its being obscured by the various natures and characteristics of specific and general marks?

Or is it because wisdom cannot apprehend it due to obstructions such as mountains, crags, stone walls, earth, water, fire, or wind? Or is it because wisdom cannot apprehend it due to extreme distance or extreme proximity?
Or is it because wisdom cannot apprehend it due to old age, childhood, blindness, or the impairment of the sense faculties? World-Honored One, if..."

When one does not perceive whether the particular and universal characteristics (svalakṣaṇa and sāmānyalakṣaṇa) are different or non-different, and cognition does not apprehend them, it should not be called "cognition";

rather, it should be called "non-cognition," because there is an object that is not apprehended. Furthermore, this is because the nature of the various particular and universal characteristics is obscured by their own intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
“World-Honored One, that which is not apprehended by wisdom is neither wisdom nor the absence of wisdom. It is because there is an object of cognition (*ālambana*) that wisdom arises;
it is not the case that wisdom is named as such simply because it encounters a lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

If, regarding mountains, rocks, walls, earth, water, fire, or wind—whether extremely distant or extremely near—if wisdom does not apprehend them due to old age, childhood, blindness, or the impairment of the sense faculties, this too would not be wisdom. [It should rather be so.]
There is no wisdom, because there is nothing that can be apprehended.

[Wei Translation: World-Honored One, if it is said that wisdom cannot grasp, is it because one perceives the specific and general characteristics of all phenomena, and because the various distinct phenomena have different natures and are not identical, such that wisdom cannot know them?
Because the various essential natures and characteristics of all phenomena cannot be differentiated, wisdom is unable to know them.
Because they are obstructed by mountains, rocks, stone walls, curtains, forests, grasses, trees, earth, water, fire, and wind, wisdom is unable to know them.
Because they are at an extremely distant or extremely near location, wisdom is unable to know them. Because they are old or young... [or] because they are... [wisdom is unable to know them].
"Blinded and with sense faculties incomplete, wisdom is unable to know it, World-Honored One.
If all dharmas are distinct, and the characteristics of dharmas are distinct—because their individual essences and common characteristics are variously different—then wisdom is unable to know them."
"World-Honored One, if that is so, then that cognition is not cognition. Why? Because it cannot know the previously existing real object.

World-Honored One, if the various substantial bodies and characteristics of all phenomena do not appear as distinct from their own-characteristics and common-characteristics, and thus cognition cannot know them, then that cognition cannot be called 'cognition. Why? Because there is a real object."
Because it cannot be known, World-Honored One. That which can see the objects before one as they truly are is called wisdom (*jñāna*).
However, [this is obstructed] by mountains, rocks, stone walls, curtains, trees, forests, grasses, and woods, or by earth, water, fire, and wind, whether extremely distant or extremely near.

Those who are old, young, blind, deluded, or whose faculties are incomplete, and who are thus unable to know or see—such wisdom is not true wisdom, because they do not know the reality of the objective realm.
[Tang Translation: World-Honored One, for what reason does that wisdom fail to attain the object? Is it because it cannot fully comprehend it?
Is it because the self-characteristics and common characteristics of all phenomena are identical or different that they cannot be apprehended?
Or is it because the various distinct self-characteristics and common characteristics of all phenomena mutually obscure one another that they cannot be apprehended?

Or is it because they are covered and obstructed by mountains, rocks, stone walls, curtains, veils, and hangings that they cannot be apprehended? Or is it because of extreme distance, extreme proximity, or old age...?
Is it not that those who are small, blind, and ignorant, whose faculties are incomplete, fail to attain [it]?

If one says they do not attain it because they do not understand the meaning of the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena, as well as their identity and difference, then this is not called "knowledge" (*jñāna*), but rather a lack of knowledge (*ajñāna*).
This is because there is an object of perception (*viṣaya*) which they do not know. If, however, [one considers] the various different specific and general characteristics of all phenomena...
That which is obscured and thus not perceived is likewise not wisdom. Wisdom is defined by its knowing of objects;

it is not [wisdom] because of non-knowing. If one does not know due to being covered and separated by mountain crags, rocky walls, curtains, or screens, or due to extreme distance or proximity, or because of old age, youth, or blindness, that too is not wisdom, for wisdom exists only when there is an object.
Because they do not possess [this knowledge] and do not understand it.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "It is not that there is no wisdom; rather, it should be understood as wisdom, not as a lack of wisdom. I have not spoken with such concealment.

When the intellect cannot apprehend an object through its conditions, this is established as a conventional designation (*prajñapti-mātra*). One awakens to the fact that all is merely the manifestation of one's own mind."

There is knowledge that external existence and non-existence do not exist as such, yet no objective entity (*artha*) is apprehended. Because nothing is apprehended, cognition does not arise with respect to the object-field (*jñeya*).

Even the cognition conforming to the three gates of liberation is not apprehended. For one who is free from false discrimination, there is the knowledge that beginningless existence and non-existence are merely deceptive habitual cognitions;
this is knowing that which others do not know.
[Wei Translation] The Buddha told Mahāmati: "As for what you have said—that there is no such thing as wisdom—this meaning is not so. Why?
Because there is real wisdom. Mahāmati, I do not rely on your statement that objects do not exist and are merely the manifestation of one's own mind.
I teach that it is due to a lack of awakening that one perceives external things as being merely the manifestation of one's own mind."
Because of existence and non-existence, wisdom does not perceive objects. That which wisdom does not perceive does not function within the mind.
Therefore, I say that even when entering the three gates of liberation, wisdom does not perceive them. Yet, since beginningless time, ordinary beings have engaged in false conceptualization;
because their minds have been perfumed by the habitual tendencies of such frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*), they conceptualize in this way.
The Buddha said: "Mahāmati, this is indeed wisdom; it is not as you have described it. What I have taught is not a teaching of concealment.

When I say that objects are merely provisional designations and are unattainable, it is because one realizes that external phenomena—whether existent or non-existent—are but what is seen by one's own mind.
Within this, wisdom ultimately finds nothing to be attained. Because there is nothing [to be grasped]..."
Because this has been attained, cognitive objects do not arise; even the essence of wisdom that enters the three gates of liberation is forgotten.
This is unlike the habitual tendencies of beginningless conceptual proliferation belonging to all ordinary beings who possess discursive thought and perception.
Therefore, regarding external objects, their locations, characteristics, and the absence of intrinsic nature, his false conceptualization remains uninterrupted.

He establishes and speaks of the marks of "self" and "what belongs to self" based on the manifestations of his own mind, grasping and adhering to them. Failing to realize that these are manifestations of his own mind, he gives rise to false conceptualization regarding knowledge (*jñāna*) and the knowable (*jñeya*).
Because of this conceptualization, he fails to perceive through investigation that external natures have no inherent existence, thereby relying upon the view of annihilationism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*).

[Wei Translation] Seeing that external objects have forms and characteristics, whether existent or non-existent, one speaks of "all phenomena are but the manifestation of one's own mind" in order to abandon such false minds.
Because of clinging to "self" and "what belongs to self," one is unable to realize that these are merely the false discriminations of one's own mind—
that which is wisdom and that which is the object-field are both discriminated as wisdom and as the object-field.
Therefore, when one observes external phenomena and does not perceive them as either existent or non-existent, one does not fall into the view of nihilism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*).
[Tang Translation: To be attached to external phenomena as having various forms, whether existent or non-existent—in this way, such knowledge is called "not knowing.

It is because one does not understand that all phenomena are seen only as the mind, yet remains attached to a self (*ātman*) and what belongs to a self (*ātmīya*), thereby discriminating against objective objects.
Wisdom does not know whether external phenomena exist or do not exist, because its mind abides in the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).
To cause such conceptual discrimination to be abandoned, it is taught that all phenomena are established as being solely the mind.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"When there are objects of perception, yet wisdom does not examine them—this is called ignorance, not wisdom; so say those who harbor false imaginings.

When one does not examine with wisdom the nature of non-differentiation, nor the obstructions, nor the distant and the near, this is termed 'erroneous wisdom. The faculties of the old and the young are obscured, yet their wisdom..."
Wisdom does not arise, yet *jñeya* (the knowable) truly exists; this too is called false wisdom.
[Wei Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse: "There are various objective realms which wisdom cannot perceive;
those are neither wisdom nor non-wisdom, as spoken by those who hold false views. To say that all phenomena are immeasurable is wisdom."
One cannot know obstructions, nor distance, nearness, or farness; such is deluded cognition, not true wisdom.
When the faculties are obscured by old age or youth, one cannot produce wisdom, even though objects truly exist; that cognition is not real wisdom.
[The Tang Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"If one has an object of focus, yet wisdom does not perceive it, that is neither wisdom nor non-wisdom; it is called false conceptual attachment.

When boundaries, mutual concealment, obstructions, distance, and proximity prevent wisdom from seeing, this is called erroneous wisdom. Furthermore, when the faculties of the old and the young are obscured..."
Even when there is a real object, it cannot give rise to wisdom; this is called false wisdom.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, foolish ordinary people are turned around by beginningless, false, evil, and perverse conceptual constructions.
When turning back [to the ultimate], they do not properly understand the *svapravṛtti* (the realization of one's own school) and the *deśanā-pravṛtti* (the teaching).

Because they are attached to the external characteristics of the nature of what appears from their own minds, they cling to expedient teachings. They do not skillfully discern the pure common characteristics of the fourfold propositions (*catuskoṭi*) within their own school.

Mahāmati said to the Buddha: "It is exactly as Your Reverence has taught. I only pray that the World-Honored One will, for my sake, distinguish and explain the *deśanā-pravṛtti* and the *svapravṛtti*."
I and other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are skilled in the two penetrations (*abhijñā*); in future ages, ordinary persons, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas shall not find any deficiency in us.
[Wei Translation] Furthermore, Mahāmati, foolish ordinary persons rely on the afflictions of beginningless bodily conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
They discriminate afflictions and establish their own doctrines through illusory bodies.
They cling to external objects as seen by their own minds and cling to names, phrases, and verbal expressions, yet they are unable to know how to establish the True Dharma.
They do not cultivate right practice and depart from the pure Dharma that is free from the four positions. Mahāmati Bodhisattva said: "So it is, so it is."
"So it is, World-Honored One! Just as the World-Honored One has taught, may the World-Honored One explain for me the characteristics of the establishment of the teachings he has proclaimed.

Thus, I and all the bodhisattvas may, in future ages, skillfully understand the characteristics of the establishment of the teachings and not be deluded by the heterodox views of outsiders, nor by the incorrect views of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."
[The Tang Translation: Furthermore, Mahāmati, foolish ordinary beings are deluded by the false discriminations of beginningless vanity and evil heterodoxy.
Failing to understand reality as it is (*yathābhūta*) and the teachings of the Dharma, they conceptualize external signs apart from the mind and cling to expedient teachings.
They are unable to cultivate the pure, true Dharma that is free from the four extremes (*catuṣkoṭi*). Mahāmati said: "It is so."
It is exactly as Your Reverence has taught. I pray that you will explain for me the Dharma of reality (*tathatā*) and the Dharma of verbal expression (*deśanā-dharma*),
so that I and all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas may attain skillfulness in these two dharmas,
which cannot be entered by outsiders or those of the two vehicles.
The Buddha said to Mahāmati, "Excellent, excellent! Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect well upon it; I shall explain it for you.
Mahāmati replied to the Buddha, "Yes, I shall receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati, "The Tathāgatas of the three periods of time possess two kinds of dharma-attainment:

namely, the attainment of the teaching (*deśanā-prativedha*) and the attainment of one's own realization (*svapratyātma-gotra-prativedha*). As for the attainment of the teaching, it refers to that which accords with the inclinations of the minds of sentient beings."

To preach various sūtras concerning the manifold requisites is called the "communication of teaching" (deśanā-prativedha). As for the "thorough penetration of one's own school" (sva-siddhānta-prativedha), it means that a practitioner leaves behind the various delusive imaginings manifested by their own mind;
that is, they do not fall into the categories of identity, difference, both, or neither.

They transcend all mind, intellect, and consciousness (*citta-mano-manovijñāna*), and personally realize the noble realm of the sages, which is free from the characteristics of views produced by causes. [This applies to] all outsiders and... [Śrāvakas].
"It is that which those śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who have fallen into the two extremes cannot know. I call this the Dharma of the self-realized lineage (*svaprakṛti-siddhānta*).
Mahāmati, these are the characteristics of the self-realized lineage and the teaching-lineage (*deśanā*); you and the other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice and study them."
[Wei Translation] The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāmati, saying: "Excellent, excellent! Excellent, Mahāmati!
Listen attentively, listen attentively; I shall speak for you. Mahāmati said: "Excellent, World-Honored One! We shall indeed receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"There are two kinds [of teachings] concerning the past, future, and present Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas..."

The teaching of the Dharma. What are these two? First, the establishment of the characteristics of the teaching of the Dharma; second, the establishment of the characteristics of the Dharma as it truly is.
Mahāmati, what is the establishment of the characteristics of the teaching of the Dharma?
It refers to various merits, sūtras, and upadeśas, wherein one teaches the Dharma according to the faith and inclinations of sentient beings. Mahāmati, this is called "establishment."
I shall explain the characteristics of dharmas. Mahāmati, what is the establishment of the characteristics of dharmas as they truly are?
It refers to practicing correct conduct based on those dharmas, because one remains far removed from the false conceptualizations of all dharma-characteristics arising from one's own mind.

Thus, one does not fall into the factions of those who hold to positions of identity, difference, both, or neither; one transcends the mind, intellect, and consciousness, and dwells in the sphere of the inner realization of noble wisdom.
The realm [of reality] is free from the characteristics of views associated with various causes and conditions; it is free from all the false views of external paths;
it is free from all the views of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; and it is free from the partisan views of existence and non-existence.
Mahāmati, this is called the establishment of the true characteristic of dharmas. Mahāmati, you and the other bodhisattvas should practice and study this.
[The Tang Translation: The Buddha said, "Listen attentively; I shall explain it for you. Mahāmati, the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time possess two kinds of dharmas:

namely, the dharma of verbal expression and the dharma of reality as it is (*yathābhūta*). As for the dharma of verbal expression, this refers to the teaching of various skillful means (*upāya*) spoken in accordance with the minds of sentient beings.
As for the dharma of reality as it is, this refers to that which [is realized] by practitioners within the mind..."
Manifestly free from all conceptual discrimination, it does not fall into the categories of identity, difference, both, or neither.

It transcends all mind, thought, and mentation, and within the sphere of activity of the noble wisdom of self-realization, it is free from all views and characteristics associated with causal conditions.
This is what cannot be known by any heterodox practitioners, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas who have fallen into the two extremes;
it is called the Dharma as it truly is. You and all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should skillfully train yourselves in these two kinds of Dharma.

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses: "I speak of two kinds of penetration: the penetration of the ultimate principle and the penetration of verbal expression.
Verbal expression is taught to the ignorant; the ultimate principle is for the practitioner."
[Wei Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse: "I establish two kinds [of teaching]:
I preach the Dharma according to reality, and I preach the Dharma by means of names and conventions, for the sake of those who practice in accordance with reality."
[The Tang Translation: At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse: "I teach two kinds of dharmas: the verbal instruction and the suchness.
The verbal instruction is shown for the sake of ordinary persons; the suchness is for the practitioner."
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One once said:
'One must be careful not to study or associate with the various discursive arguments of worldly treatises; if one does so, it will lead to the grasping of desire and not the grasping of the Dharma.
World-Honored One, for what reason did you speak thus? The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Worldly discourse is of many kinds..."
Through the arrangement of phrases, meanings, causes, conditions, and parables, they entice and delude foolish ordinary people, leading them not to enter into the true self-realization.
Failing to awaken to all phenomena, they fall into the two extremes through false imagination and inversion;
thus, the ignorant and deluded destroy themselves, continuing through the various realms of existence without attaining liberation, unable to realize that all is a manifestation of their own minds.
These measures do not transcend the attachment to the imagined nature of external entities;

therefore, the various discursive explanations of worldly discourse do not escape birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction, and remain deceptive, delusive, and confusing.
[Wei Translation] At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has at one time said: 'The Lokāyatikas engage in various forms of sophistry;
if one associates with and makes offerings to such persons, one will receive the food of desire and not the food of the Dharma. World-Honored One, for what reason did he say this?"
They frequent and make offerings to the Lokāyatikas, who provide various eloquent expositions; they accept the food of desire but do not accept the food of the Dharma.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "The various rhetorical skills of the Lokāyatikas and their clever phrasing delude the world.
They do not speak in accordance with the Dharma, nor do they speak in accordance with the meaning; they merely follow the foolishness of worldly commoners."
Because it is what their emotions delight in, they speak of worldly matters; possessing only clever rhetoric and beautiful phrasing, they lose the true meaning.
Mahāmati, this is called the fault of the various eloquent discourses of the Lokāyata.
Mahāmati, such eloquence of the Lokāyata merely attracts the ignorant and foolish worldlings; it does not lead them into [the truth].
They preach the Dharma according to the true nature of phenomena, yet because they themselves do not realize all dharmas, they fall into the mass of false views regarding the two extremes.
Having lost the right path themselves, they cause others to lose it as well; therefore, they are unable to escape the various realms of existence.
Because they are unable to see that [all things] are merely their own mind, they conceptually discriminate and cling to external phenomena as having real characteristics.

For this reason, they do not escape false discrimination. Mahāmati, therefore I say that although the Lokāyata possesses various kinds of clever eloquence and delights in discoursing on all phenomena, because it has lost the correct principle, it cannot bring about liberation from birth, old age, and sickness.
The mass of all suffering, including death, grief, lamentation, and affliction, exists because people are deluded and deceived by skillful explanations using various names, phrases, and metaphors.
[Tang Translation] At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as..."
"I shall explain this all at once. The *Lokāyata* treatises on incantations and rhetoric can only procure worldly wealth and profit;
they do not yield the benefit of the Dharma. One should not associate with, serve, or make offerings to them. "Why, World-Honored One, do you speak thus?
The Buddha said, "Mahāmati, the treatises of the *Lokāyatas* merely adorn their phrasing to deceive."
They delude the foolish and ignorant, conforming to the world’s false and deceptive speech; it does not accord with reality nor correspond to principle.
They are unable to enter the realm of true reality, nor can they awaken to the understanding of all phenomena.

Constantly falling into the two extremes, they lose the right path for themselves and cause others to lose it as well, wandering through the various realms of existence without ever attaining liberation. Why is this?
Therefore, because they do not understand that all phenomena are seen only as the mind’s own projections, they cling to external objects and increase their conceptual discrimination.
For this reason, I say that the words and phrases of worldly treatises, though adorned with causes and analogies, merely deceive the foolish;
they cannot bring liberation from the afflictions of birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, grief, and so forth.
Mahāmati, Śakra Devendra was a master of many treatises and had himself composed a work on phonology (*śabda-śāstra*).
A disciple of that worldly philosopher went to the palace of Śakra, assuming the form of a nāga, and established a philosophical thesis: "I shall destroy Śakra’s thousand-spoked wheel;
if I am defeated, I will cut off one head for each spoke as a tribute for my failure. Having made this vow, he then...
The Śākya Dharma-Crusher defeated Śakra; having fallen into a position of defeat, he destroyed his chariot and returned to the human realm. Thus it is, Mahāmati:

even down to the animals, worldly discourse—adorned with causes and similes—is able to delude those gods and asuras with various phrases and expressions, causing them to cling to views of arising and ceasing; how much more so for humans? Therefore, Mahāmati...
Mahāmati, worldly discourse should be avoided; since it brings about the causes for the arising of suffering, one must be careful not to cultivate or frequent it.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, Śakra Devendra extensively explained various treatises and composed his own work on phonology. That Lu...
A disciple of Gayāśīrṣa had realized the mundane supernormal powers (*laukika-abhijñā*).
He went to the celestial palace of Śakra Devendra and established a formal debate, saying: "Kauśika, I shall engage in a discussion with you;
if I am defeated, I must submit to your authority, so that all devas and humans may know and see it. Thus they made a mutual agreement. "If I..."
"I shall defeat you; I must break your thousand-spoked wheel with blows. If I am not victorious, I shall sever my body from head to foot, limb by limb, as an offering to you.
Having made this vow, a disciple of the Lokāyata appeared in the form of a nāga and debated with Śakra Devendra.
By means of that method of debate, he was able to defeat him. Śakra...
Śakra caused him to be subdued; he then struck his thousand-spoked wheel-chariot in the heavens, reducing it to fine dust, and returned to the human realm.
Mahāmati, the Lokāyata Brahmins employ various such analogies, even manifesting as the bodies of animals under various names to delude the world’s devas and humans.
O Asura, because all sentient beings in the world cling to phenomena that arise and perish, how much more so is this true for humans?
Mahāmati, for this reason, you should distance yourself from the Lokāyata Brahmins.
Because it is said that such [teachings] give rise to a mass of suffering, one should not associate with, make offerings to,
honor, or consult with the Lokāyata Brahmins.
[Chinese Translation] Mahāmati, Śakra Devendra extensively understood various treatises and composed many of his own.
Among those proponents of worldly doctrines (Lokāyatika), there was a disciple who manifested in the form of a nāga and went to the celestial palace of Śakra to establish a philosophical position.
He made this solemn declaration: "Kauśika, I shall debate with you; if you are not my equal, I shall shatter your [thousand]..."
"If I am not as [skilled] as you regarding the wheel with its thousand spokes, I shall cut off each of my heads to atone for this defeat.
Having spoken these words, he immediately subdued Śakra by means of the methods of debate. Having shattered the thousand-spoked wheel, he returned to the human realm.
Mahāmati, worldly discourse is adorned with causes and analogies; it can even manifest the forms of animals through exquisite literary compositions.
They delude the various devas and asuras, causing them to cling to views such as arising and ceasing; how much more so for human beings?
Therefore, Mahāmati, one should not associate with, serve, or make offerings to them, because they can act as the cause for the production of suffering.

Mahāmati, those who propound worldly treatises (lokāyatika) speak only of the body, perception, and their objective spheres. Mahāmati, there are hundreds of thousands of such proponents of worldly treatises;
however, in a future time, during the final five hundred years, they will cause the destruction of the compilation [of the teachings].

This is because false perceptions and views will flourish, and evil disciples will accept them. Thus, Mahāmati, the proponents of worldly treatises will bring about the destruction of the compilation through various phrases and expressions.
Using analogies as adornments, he speaks of the matters of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Clinging to their own causal conditions, they lack any self-attained realization (*sva-prativedha*).

Mahāmati, those various non-Buddhists have no treatises of self-attained realization; regarding other worldly discourses (*loka-vāda*), they extensively expound immeasurable hundreds of thousands of categories of phenomena, yet they possess no self-attained realization, nor do they recognize that these are merely the worldly discourses of the ignorant.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, the Dharma taught by the Lokāyata brāhmaṇas perceives only the realm of the body and the intellect in the present life.
Relying on worldly designations, they expound various false doctrines.
Mahāmati, the treatises composed by the Lokāyata brāhmaṇas consist of hundreds of thousands of verses; in future ages and at the end of time, these will be divided into many schools.
Each has a different name because they are produced based on the perceptions of their own minds.
Mahāmati, among the Lokāyata Brahmins, there is no disciple capable of receiving their doctrine; therefore, in later generations, it split into many schools with various different names.
Mahāmati, because these non-Buddhists lack genuine understanding within their own minds, they rely on [their own] seeds...
Based on various causes, they produce diverse interpretations; following the fabrications of their own minds, they explain them to others.
Because they cling to such things as the cause of Īśvara, Mahāmati, there is no such teaching within the treatises composed by any of the non-Buddhists;
rather, these are all merely Lokāyata doctrines that expound hundreds of thousands of teachings through various causal gateways, yet they do not understand this.
Lokāyata. [Tang Translation:
Mahāmati, the worldly treatises (loka-vāda) speak only of the objects of bodily perception. Mahāmati, those worldly treatises consist of hundreds of thousands of words and phrases;
in the future degenerate age, they will be divided into many factions as evil views cause dissension and the heterodox assemblies fall apart.
Each school clings to its own cause. Mahāmati, no other non-Buddhist can establish a true teaching;
it is only the Lokāyata who, through hundreds of thousands of phrases, extensively explains immeasurable varieties of causal characteristics that do not accord with reality.
Furthermore, they do not even recognize themselves as merely deluding the world with such doctrines.
At that time, Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, if the various phrases and expressions of the worldly treatises of the non-Buddhists— adorned with causes and analogies—
are devoid of their own internal realization and involve attachment to their own particular objects, then the World-Honored One also speaks of worldly treatises.
For the sake of the various assemblies of devas, humans, and asuras gathered from different regions, you too extensively expound immeasurable varieties of phrases and expressions."
"Is this not my own established doctrine? Does it not also fall within the category of the wisdom and discourse of all non-Buddhists?
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "I do not speak of worldly treatises (*lokāyata*). There is neither coming nor going; I speak only of that which neither comes nor goes.
Mahāmati, 'coming' refers to gathering and arising; 'going' refers to dispersal and destruction. That which neither comes nor goes is neither born nor extinguished—this is what I teach."

This meaning does not fall within the categories of worldly discourse or false conceptualization. Why is this? It is because one does not cling to the existence or non-existence of external objects, which are merely manifestations of one's own mind.

One cannot be turned away by the false conceptualizations of the two extremes. Since the characteristics of objective realms have no inherent nature, when one realizes that these are manifestations of one's own mind, the false conceptualizations of those manifestations cease to arise.
When false conceptualizations do not arise, there is emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; thus one enters [the state of liberation].
The three gates of liberation are called "liberation.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, if all non-Buddhists speak only of *lokāyata*, relying on various worldly names, phrases, and metaphors to cling to them..."

“World-Honored One, as for the cause: when all sentient beings, devas, and asuras from the lands of the ten directions gather at the Tathāgata’s place, the Tathāgata also preaches the Dharma using various worldly names, phrases, and parables, yet does not speak of the Dharma realized through his own internal wisdom.
If that were so, it would be no different from what is taught by all the non-Buddhists.”
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "I do not speak of Lokāyata, nor do I say that all phenomena neither come nor go.
Mahāmati, it is I who say that all phenomena neither come nor go. Mahāmati, what is called 'coming'?"
Mahāmati, that which is called "coming" is termed "arising and gathering," because it arises through combination.
Mahāmati, what is called "going"? Mahāmati, that which is called "going" is termed "cessation. Mahāmati, I say that neither going nor coming is called "non-arising.
Mahāmati, I say this is not the same as the teachings of the various non-Buddhists. Why is this? Because...
They do not cling to the existence or non-existence of external objects, because they establish and teach that [all things] are but the manifestations of one's own mind.
They do not abide in the two extremes, nor do they engage in the conceptualization of various marks and objective spheres, because they know the manifestations of their own minds as they truly are.
Because they do not give rise to the conceptualizing views of their own minds, and because they do not differentiate any marks, they are able to enter emptiness.
The three gates of liberation—signlessness, wishlessness, and emptiness—are called "liberation.
[Tang Translation] At that time, Mahāmati said to the World-Honored One: "World-Honored One, if there are treatises composed by the Lokāyatas..."
Those who adorn their discourse with various letters, causes, and metaphors, yet cling to their own tenets as being the non-illusory reality, are called "non-Buddhists" (tīrthika).
Nevertheless, the World-Honored One also speaks of worldly matters, explaining them extensively through various phrases and expressions.
The multitudes of devas and humans from all lands in the ten directions have gathered here.
Is this not a teaching realized through one’s own wisdom? Does the World-Honored One also speak like the non-Buddhists? The Buddha said:

"Mahāmati, I do not speak according to worldly conventions, nor is there coming or going. I teach that all phenomena neither come nor go. Mahāmati, 'coming' refers to the gathering and arising [of conditions]; 'going'..."
This is the destruction [of grasping]. It neither comes nor goes; this is what is called "neither arising nor ceasing.

Mahāmati, my teaching is not like that of the non-Buddhists who fall into conceptual discrimination. Why is this? Because they have no attachment to the existence or non-existence of external phenomena.

Having realized that there is only one's own mind and not seeing the two graspings (subject and object), they do not engage with sense organs or objects, and thus do not give rise to discrimination. They enter...
Because they are liberated through the gateways of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
Mahāmati, I recall that once, while staying in a certain place, a world-theorizing Brahmin came to where I was;
without asking for leave, he immediately asked me: "Gautama, is everything created? I then replied to him: "Brahmin..."
“O Brahmin, the view that ‘everything is created’ is the first worldly doctrine.
He asked again, ‘Is everything uncreated? I replied, ‘Everything is uncreated. This is the second worldly doctrine.
He asked again, ‘Is everything eternal? Is everything impermanent? Is everything born? Is everything unborn? To this, I replied:”
This is the sixth world-theory (*loka-vāda*). Mahāmati, he further asked me: "Are all things one? Are all things different? Are all things both? Are all things neither?
Do all things manifest through birth based on various causes? I then replied to him: "This is the eleventh world-theory.
Mahāmati, he further asked: "Are all things indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)? Or are all things determinate (*vyākṛta*)?"
Is there a self? Is there no self? Does this world exist? Does this world not exist? Does another world exist? Does another world not exist?
Is there liberation? Is there no liberation? Are all things momentary? Are all things non-momentary?
Is it space? Is it analytical cessation? Is it nirvāṇa? Gautama, is it created? Is it uncreated? Does it exist?
"Is there an intermediate state (*antarābhava*), or is there no intermediate state? Mahāmati, I then replied:
"Brāhmaṇa, such statements are all merely worldly discourse; they are not what I teach. These are your own worldly doctrines."
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, I recall that in the past, while I was dwelling in a certain place, there came to me a Lokāyata great Brahmin who addressed me, saying: "Gautama, is everything created?
Mahāmati, I then replied: "Brahmin, 'everything is created'—this is the first [view of the Lokāyatas]."
"O Gāyadhā, the brāhmaṇa said, 'Gautama, is it that nothing at all is created?
At that time, I replied, 'Brāhmaṇa, "nothing at all is created" is the second Lokāyata.
Likewise, [the views that] everything is eternal, everything is impermanent, everything is born, and everything is unborn—at that time, I replied, "Brāhmaṇa, these..."
The sixth is the Lokāyata. Mahāmati, the Lokāyatika again asked me:
"Gautama, are all things one? Are all things different? Are all things both? Are all things neither?
All dharmas arise based on causes, for we see that they arise from various causes. Mahāmati, I then replied: "Brahmin..."
This is the eleventh Lokāyata. Mahāmati, he further asked me: "Gautama, are all things indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), or are all things determinate?
Is there a self (*ātman*), or is there no self? Does this world exist, or does it not exist?
Does a future world exist, or does it not exist? Is there liberation, or is there no liberation? One.
"Is everything empty? Is everything non-empty? Is everything void? Is it not through the cessation of conditions?
Is it nirvāṇa? Gautama, is it created? Is it uncreated? Is there an intermediate state (antarābhava)?
Or is there no intermediate state? Mahāmati, at that time I replied: "Brāhmaṇa, one who speaks in such a manner is entirely a Lokāyata."
"What I have spoken is the Dharma you preach.

[Tang Translation] "Mahāmati, I recall that once, while staying in a certain place, a world-theorizing Brahmin came to where I was and suddenly asked me: 'Gautama, is all this created? I then replied:"
He said, "Brahmin, 'everything is created' is the first worldly doctrine. Again he asked me, "'Is everything uncreated?
I replied at that time, 'Everything is uncreated'; this is the second worldly doctrine.
He asked again, "'Is everything eternal? Is everything impermanent? Is everything born? Is everything unborn?'"
"Yes. At that time, I replied: "This is the sixth worldly doctrine (*lokāyatavāda*). He asked again: "Is everything one? Is everything different?
Is everything both? Is everything neither? Does everything arise through various causes and conditions?
At that time, I replied: "This is the eleventh worldly doctrine. He asked again:
Are all things determinate (*vyākṛta*) or are they all indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)? Is there a self (*ātman*) or is there no self? Does this world exist or does it not exist?
Does another world exist or does it not exist? Is there liberation (*mokṣa*) or is there no liberation?
Are these things momentary (*kṣaṇika*) or are they non-momentary? [And what of] space (*ākāśa*), nirvāṇa (*nirvāṇa*), and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)? Are these...
"Is it created or uncreated? Is there an intermediate state (*antarābhava*) or is there no intermediate state? At that time, I replied:
"Brahmin, all such things are your worldly philosophy; they are not what I teach."
I teach only that the various evils of the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*) have their cause in beginningless, false, and delusive habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

Failing to realize that these are merely manifestations of one’s own mind (*svacittadṛśyamātra*), one gives rise to delusive thoughts and clings to external objects, as is the case with the doctrines of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

For example, they claim that cognition arises from the conjunction of the sense organs, the objects, and consciousness. I do not say this, O Brahmin; I do not speak of causes, nor do I speak of [conditions].
There is no cause. It is only said that dependent origination is established through the nature of the grasped and the grasper, which is a mere conceptual construction.
This cannot be realized by you or others who have fallen into the perception of a self-continuum. Mahāmati, nirvāṇa, space, and cessation do not actually exist as three kinds;
there are only three in terms of enumeration.
[Wei Translation] O Brāhmaṇa, I say that because of the habitual perfuming of afflictions arising from beginningless conceptual proliferation and false discrimination,
those three realms of existence are said to exist as the perception of one's own mind-only, which is not realized through awakening.
It is not that one perceives an external reality as the teachings of the non-Buddhists do. Mahāmati, the non-Buddhists say:
"The self, the sense organs, and the objects—through the conjunction of these three, cognition is produced. O Brahmin, it is not so for me. I do not speak of a cause, nor do I speak of no-cause;
I speak only of the perception of the graspable and the grasper within the conceptualization of one's own mind.
Regarding characteristics: I teach that all phenomena arise through the gathering of causes and conditions as mere conventional designations;

this is not within the scope of you Brahmins or others, for you have fallen into the view of self (*ātman*). Mahāmati, nirvāṇa, space, and the cessation of conditions do not constitute a triad of numbers;
how much less can one speak of them as being created, as having an agent, or as being uncreated?
[The Tang Translation: "O Brahmin, I say that the three realms of existence arise from the habitual tendencies of evil arising from beginningless conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Failing to realize that these are merely what is seen by one's own mind, one grasps at external phenomena, though in reality nothing can be apprehended."
As the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) say: "The self, the sense faculties, and the objects—through the conjunction of these three, [cognition] arises.

It is not so for me. I do not say there is a cause, nor do I say there is no cause; rather, based solely upon the deluded mind, I speak of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) in terms of the grasped and the grasper.
This cannot be fathomed by you or others who are attached to a self. Mahāmati, [this applies to] space, nirvāṇa, and that which is not through analytical cessation...
They cease; yet these three categories have no intrinsic nature from the beginning. How much less can one speak of "action" or "non-action"?
Furthermore, Mahāmati, at that time the Lokāyatika Brahmin again asked me:
"Is the triple existence caused by ignorance, craving, and karma, or is it without cause? I replied to him: "Both of these views are merely worldly discourse."
He asked again: "Do all natures enter into their own-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and common-characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)? I replied: "This too, O Brahmin, is worldly discourse (*lokavāda*).
Even the mental flow’s false conceptualization of external objects is all worldly discourse. Furthermore, Mahāmati,"
At that time, the Lokāyatika Brahmin asked me again, "Is there anyone who is not a Lokāyatika? I am the preeminent teacher among all non-Buddhists;
I speak with various phrases, flavors, causes, conditions, and parables as adornments.
I replied to him, "Brahmin, there is one who is not like you—neither possessing such [views], nor lacking a doctrine, nor failing to speak. "Does he not speak in various ways? I replied, "He does."
Regarding the phrasing and meaning: it is not that they do not employ ornaments of simile.
The Brahmin asked, "What is that which is neither worldly discourse (*loka-vāda*), nor non-doctrine, nor non-exposition?

I replied to him, "Brahmin, there is a discourse that is not worldly, which you followers of the external paths cannot know, because of your attachment to false imaginings regarding unreal external natures. That is to say, it is not [the realm of] false imagination."

Birth. One who has realized that existence and non-existence are merely the manifestations of one’s own mind, for whom false discrimination does not arise, and who no longer receives external objects so that false discrimination is forever stilled—this is called "non-worldly discourse. This is my teaching, not yours, O Brahmin.
To speak briefly of that consciousness: whether coming or going, dying or being born, pleasure or pain, drowning or seeing, contact or...
They cling to various marks—whether to marks of conjunction or continuity, or to clinging to [them as] objects of craving or causes.

O Brahmin, such things as these are your worldly discourses (*loka-vāda*); they are not my own. Mahāmati, when the Brahmins of worldly discourse ask me such questions, I answer them in this way; they then remain silent and withdraw without further argument, reflecting upon their own positions and thinking thus: [The text continues: ...clinging to various marks—whether to marks of conjunction or continuity, or to clinging to [them as] objects of craving or causes.

O Brahmin, such things as these are your worldly discourses; they are not my own. Mahāmati, when the Brahmins of worldly discourse ask me such questions, I answer them in this way; they then remain silent and withdraw without further argument, reflecting upon their own positions and thinking thus: [they are defeated].

He thought to himself: "The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have strayed outside of the Way; they preach non-arising, signlessness, and causelessness, [claiming that] one awakens to the fact that the manifestations of one's own deluded thoughts are merely deluded thoughts and do not arise."
[Wei Translation] "Mahāmati, furthermore, there was a Lokāyata Brahmin who came and asked me:
'Gautama, do these worlds arise from the causes of ignorance, craving, and karma within the three realms of existence, or are they without cause?
At that time, I replied: 'Brahmin, these two views belong to the Lokāyatas; they are not my teaching. Brahmin...
The gatekeeper asked me again, "Gautama, do all phenomena fall under their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) or their common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)?
I replied at that time, "Brahmin, this is Lokāyata; it is not my teaching.
Brahmin, whatever involves the mind, mentation, and consciousness clinging to external objects—all of that is Lokāyata; it is not my teaching."
"Mahāmati, the Lokāyata brāhmaṇa again asked me: 'Gautama, is there any dharma that is not Lokāyata?
Gautama, all the heterodox teachers establish various names, phrases, and sentences.'"
"Whatever is taught through parables is all my Dharma. At that time, I replied: "Brahmin, there is a Dharma that is not your Dharma;
yet it is not that I do not establish it, nor that I do not speak it in various names, phrases, and syllables, nor that I do not explain it based on the meaning and in accordance with the meaning.
However, this is not a Dharma established by the Lokāyata. Brahmin, there is such a Dharma."

This is not *lokāyata*, for all those dharmas are beyond the comprehension of any outsider, even unto you, because they falsely cling to external, unreal phenomena through conceptual proliferation. What, then, is meant by being "free from conceptualization"?
It is when the mind observes existence and non-existence and realizes, as it truly is, that the marks of what is seen are but one's own mind. Therefore—
One does not give rise to any conceptual discrimination, because one does not grasp at external objective phenomena.
When the discriminating mind ceases, one abides in its own natural state, the realm of tranquility. This is called non-Lokāyata;
it is my teaching, not yours, O Brahmin. One who abides in their own natural state neither arises nor ceases. Because they neither arise nor...
"O Brahmin, 'extinction' (nirvāṇa) means that no conceptualizing mind arises. O Brahmin, this is called what is not *lokāyata*.
O Brahmin, to speak briefly: in whatever state consciousness does not function, does not grasp, does not recede, does not arise, does not seek, does not cling, and does not delight;
wherein one does not see, does not behold, does not dwell, and does not touch—that is called 'abiding,' and it is called [Nirvāṇa]."
First, regarding the difference in meaning: O Brahmin, you cling to various marks and, through a self-identity, are attached to various causes.
This, O Brahmin, is the Lokāyata doctrine; it is not my teaching.
Mahāmati, when the Lokāyata Brahmin came to me and asked about such a doctrine, I then answered that Brahmin as follows:
When what had been said was finished, the brahmin departed in silence, without asking me to establish the true Dharma.
At that time, the Lokāyata brahmin thought to himself: "This śramaṇa son of the Śākyas is pitiable for being outside my own doctrine;
he teaches that all phenomena are without cause, without condition, and without the characteristic of arising. Only...

I teach that phenomena are seen through the conceptualization of one's own mind. If one can awaken to and know these marks as the visions of one's own mind, then the conceptualizing mind is extinguished.
[Tang Translation] O Mahāmati, at that time, the Brahmin of worldly discourse again asked me: "Ignorance and craving..."
"Is it because karma serves as the causal condition that the three realms of existence arise? Or are they without cause? I replied, "These two views are also worldly doctrines.
He asked me again, "Do all phenomena enter into their own-characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) and common-characteristics (sāmānyalakṣaṇa)?
I then answered, "This too is a worldly doctrine, O Brahmin. Even the slightest movement of mental consciousness is [a worldly doctrine]."
"Mahāmati, all other external objects are merely worldly discourse (*loka-vāda*). At that time, Mahāmati, that Brahmin again asked me:

'Is there anything that is not worldly discourse? All the verbal theories of the various non-Buddhists, adorned with diverse phrases, causes, and analogies—do they not all emerge from my own doctrine? I replied to him: 'There is; it is not yours.'"
What is accepted by us is not accepted by the world; it is not that we do not employ various phrases and expressions, for they are consistent with the underlying principles, not inconsistent.
He asked again, "Is there anything accepted by the world that is not the worldly treatise?
I replied, "There is, but it cannot be known by you or by any of the non-Buddhists. Why? Because regarding external phenomena, [they are] empty..."

Because attachment arises from false discrimination, if one can thoroughly realize that all phenomena—whether existent or non-existent—are entirely what is seen by one's own mind, then one will not give rise to discrimination and will not grasp at external objects.
One will abide in one's own place. To "abide in one's own place" means to not arise.
What does one not cause to arise? One does not cause discrimination to arise, such as thinking, "This is my dharma, not yours."
"It exists, O Brahmin. To speak briefly, wherever the mind and consciousness go, come, die, are born, seek, or yearn;
wherever they experience, perceive, contact, or abide; wherever they grasp various signs and continue in conjunction;
and wherever they give rise to attachment toward experiences and their causes—all these are your worldly doctrines (loka-vāda) and not my Dharma. Mahāmati, this is the worldly doctrine."
The Brahmin asked such questions, and I answered him thus.
He did not inquire about my own school’s true Dharma, but departed in silence, thinking to himself: "The śramaṇa Gautama has nothing worthy of respect;

he teaches that all phenomena are unarisen, without ideation, without cause, and without condition, being merely what is seen through the conceptual discrimination of one's own mind. If [he were able]...
"When this discrimination is understood, it does not arise.

Mahāmati, this is precisely what you asked me earlier: 'For what reason do you say that those who study worldly treatises and engage in various forms of sophistry embrace desire but do not embrace the Dharma?
Mahāmati said to the Buddha: 'World-Honored One, [what is] embracing desire?'"
"And what is the meaning of the term 'dharma'? The Buddha said to Mahāmati, "Excellent, excellent!
That you are able to contemplate and inquire about such meanings for the sake of future sentient beings—listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well;
I shall explain it for you. Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "Yes, I shall receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati, "As for what is called 'greed,' if..."
Whether grasping or abandoning, whether touching or tasting, one becomes fettered by external objects and falls into the views of the two extremes.
Thus, the aggregate of suffering—birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, pain, and despair—is produced. All such afflictions arise from craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
This results from associating with worldly treatises and those who follow worldly treatises; I and all the Buddhas call this "greed. This is called the appropriation of desire.
On the Grasping of the Dharma.

[Wei Translation] "Mahāmati, you have now asked me: 'For what reason do the various dialectical arguments of the Lokāyatikas lead those who approach, make offerings to, and revere them to grasp only the flavor of desire and not the flavor of the Dharma? Mahāmati replied:"
The Buddha said, "World-Honored One, what is meant by the meaning of the term 'food' (āhāra), and what is meant by the meaning of the term 'Dharma'?

The Buddha told Mahāmati, "Excellent, excellent, excellent, Mahāmati! That you are able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding these two meanings for the sake of future sentient beings is truly excellent, Mahāmati.
Listen attentively, listen attentively; I shall explain this for you. Mahāmati said, "I am listening, World-Honored One. The Buddha said:
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, “Excellent, World-Honored One! We shall indeed receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati, “What are these ‘foods’?

They are the taste of flavors and the taste of tactile sensations. To eagerly seek expedient means, to be craftily deceitful, to be attached to flavors, and to cling to external objects—such dharmas as these are called ‘different in expression but one in meaning,’ because they do not enter the dharma-gate of the non-dual realm.”
Furthermore, Mahāmati, that which is called "nutriment" refers to the arising of the aggregates (*skandha*) and the factors of existence (*bhava-aṅga*) based on false views;
it does not transcend birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction. Craving gives rise to existence; such phenomena as these are termed "nutriment."
Therefore, I and all the Buddhas declare that those who associate with and make offerings to the Lokāyata brahmins obtain the flavor of food,
but do not obtain the flavor of the Dharma.
[The Tang Translation: "Mahāmati, you have now likewise asked me about this matter:

for what reason do those who associate with worldly scholars obtain only material gain and not the gain of the Dharma? Mahāmati said, "What is the meaning of 'material' and 'Dharma' as you have spoken?
The Buddha said, "Excellent! You are indeed able to contemplate this matter for the sake of future sentient beings."
Listen attentively, listen attentively; I shall explain it for you. Mahāmati, that which is called "wealth" (artha) is tangible, graspable, receivable, and flavorful;
it causes attachment to external objects, leading one to fall into the two extremes, increasing craving and the suffering of birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, pain, and distress.
I and all the Buddhas designate this as "material gain" (artha-lābha), which is obtained through proximity to worldly treatises.

It is attained, Mahāmati. What is the grasping of the Dharma? It means to rightly awaken to the manifestation of one's own mind, to perceive the characteristics of the selflessness of persons and the selflessness of phenomena, for which conceptual construction no longer arises, to well understand the successive higher stages, and to be free from mind, thought, and consciousness. All...
The empowerment of the wisdom of all Buddhas fully encompasses the ten inexhaustible phrases. It is sovereign mastery over all phenomena without fabrication;
this is called the Dharma. That is to say, it does not fall into any views, any falsehoods, any conceptual proliferations, any natures, or any two extremes.
Mahāmati, there are many foolish outsiders who fall into these two [extremes].
The extremes of eternalism or nihilism do not belong to those of wisdom. To accept a doctrine of causelessness is to give rise to the view of eternalism;
to deny external causes and the nature of causal conditions is to give rise to the view of nihilism. Mahāmati, because I do not perceive arising, abiding, or ceasing, I speak of them as "dharmas.
Mahāmati, this is what is called desire and dharma. You and the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas should cultivate them accordingly.
[Study.
[Wei Translation: Mahāmati, what is the flavor of the Dharma? It refers to being able to know the two kinds of selflessness as they truly are.
By perceiving the characteristics of the selflessness of persons and the selflessness of phenomena, one consequently does not give rise to the marks of conceptual discrimination. As it truly is...

Because one is able to know the progressively superior wisdoms of the various stages (*bhūmi*), at that time one is able to leave behind mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
One enters the ground of receiving the position within the wisdom of all Buddhas and grasps the ultimate limit of all phrases.

To be able to know, as it truly is, the sphere of the sovereign power of all Buddhas is called the "flavor of the Dharma" (*dharmarasa*); it does not fall into any portion of false views or conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Distinguishing the two extremes: Mahāmati, the teachings of the non-Buddhists mostly cause sentient beings to fall into the two extremes;
they do not cause the wise to fall into the two extremes. Why is this? Mahāmati, it is because the various non-Buddhists frequently propound the views of annihilationism and eternalism.
Because of the absence of causes, one falls into the view of eternalism; because of seeing the cessation of causes, one falls into the view of nihilism.
Mahāmati, I teach the vision of reality as it is, which does not cling to arising or ceasing; therefore, I call this the "taste of the Dharma.
Mahāmati, this is what I call the taste of food and the taste of the Dharma. Mahāmati, you and all the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas should study this.
This Dharma.

[Tang Translation] What is the benefit of the Dharma? It means to realize that this Dharma is mind, to see the two kinds of selflessness (*nairātmya*), not to grasp at signs, and to be without conceptual discrimination.
To skillfully know the various stages (*bhūmi*) and to be free from mind, thought, and consciousness—this is what all Buddhas together [uphold].
Having received empowerment and fully practiced the ten inexhaustible vows, one attains mastery over all phenomena;
this is called the benefit of the Dharma. By means of this, one does not fall into any views, conceptual proliferations, or discriminations regarding the two extremes of eternalism and nihilism.
“Mahāmati, the worldly treatises of the non-Buddhists cause foolish people to fall into the two extremes, namely, eternalism and nihilism.
By accepting the doctrine of no-cause, one gives rise to the view of eternalism; by [asserting] that causes perish, one generates the view of nihilism.

I say that not seeing arising, abiding, or ceasing is called attaining the benefit of the Dharma. This is what is meant by the distinction between the two types of wealth: material wealth and the Dharma-wealth. You and all others...”
"A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should diligently investigate this.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "All worldly treatises are the false doctrines of non-Buddhists;
they are based on deluded views regarding cause and effect, and thus they possess no school of their own. Only I have my own true school, which is free from..."
The agent and the acted-upon are taught for the sake of disciples; they are far removed from all worldly treatises. The mind-only (*cittamātra*) is invisible; one does not examine the two minds.
