The grasped and the grasper lack intrinsic nature; it is free from both extremes of annihilation and permanence. As long as the mind continues to flow, this is considered a worldly treatise.
For one in whom false discrimination (*vikalpa*) no longer turns, that person perceives their own mind. That which comes is said to be the arising of phenomena; that which goes...
Phenomena do not manifest; one clearly knows the past and the future, and delusive thoughts no longer arise.
Permanence and impermanence, the created and the uncreated, this world and the other world—all these are encompassed by worldly discourse.
[Wei Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse: "I gather in sentient beings; relying on the precepts, I subdue all evils.
Through wisdom, I extinguish false views, and the three gates of liberation increase. The empty and false teachings of non-Buddhists are all merely worldly treatises;
they establish their doctrines based on false views of cause and effect, lacking right view. I establish the Dharma, which is free from [such errors]."
Based on false views as their cause, they teach for the sake of disciples that one must depart from worldly dharmas; [they claim] there is only mind and no external phenomena.
With a mind free from the two extremes, they [assert] the dharma of the grasper and the grasped.

Free from the views of annihilationism and eternalism, they hold that wherever the mind operates is entirely conventional discourse. If one can contemplate one's own mind, one will not see any falsehoods. Thus it is said: "The coming one sees."

They arise from causes. The goer perceives the cessation of the fruit; thus they know going and coming as they truly are, without discriminating between the false, the eternal, the impermanent, the created, the uncreated, or this and that object. All such phenomena are merely conventional discourse.
[The Tang Translation: At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse: "To subdue and gather sentient beings, one employs the precepts to overcome all evils;
through wisdom, all views are extinguished, and liberation is increased. The false teachings of non-Buddhists are all merely worldly treatises;
their arbitrary speculations regarding cause and effect cannot establish themselves. Only my own unique school..."
Attached to the subject and the object, [the Buddha] taught for the sake of his disciples so that they might leave behind worldly discourse (*lokavāda*).
The phenomena of the grasper and the grasped are merely mind; nothing exists [externally]. Both [subject and object] are manifestations of the mind; neither permanence nor annihilation can be found.
As long as the mind continues to fluctuate, this is considered worldly discourse. One who does not give rise to such conceptual discrimination sees their own mind. Thus speaks the one who has come.

When phenomena arise, the "goer" does not appear. One clearly understands coming and going without giving rise to conceptual discrimination regarding permanence and impermanence, the conditioned and the unconditioned, this world and the next, and so forth;
all such things belong to the methods of worldly discourse.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, regarding what is called 'nirvāṇa,' what dharma do you teach that is named nirvāṇa?
For the various non-Buddhists each give rise to false conceptualizations. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well;
I shall explain it for you. As for the nirvāṇa falsely conceptualized by the various non-Buddhists, it is not their [false]..."
[He] conceives of it as conforming to nirvāṇa. Mahāmati said to the Buddha, “Yes, I shall receive your teaching.

The Buddha told Mahāmati, “There are some non-Buddhists who [assert that there is liberation] through the cessation of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases; through detachment from objects; through seeing the impermanence of phenomena; and through the non-arising of the categories of mind and mental factors.”
They do not attend to the objects of the past, future, or present. All aggregates of sensation (vedanā-skandha) are exhausted like the extinguishing of a lamp or the destruction of a seed;

thus, false conceptualization (vikalpa) does not arise. Such individuals conceive of this state as nirvāṇa. However, Mahāmati, it is not by the mere cessation of views that one is said to have attained nirvāṇa.
[Wei Translation] At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, regarding what the Tathāgata calls 'nirvāṇa,' by what dharmas is nirvāṇa so named? Yet the various non-Buddhists each falsely discriminate regarding nirvāṇa.
The Buddha said to Mahāmati Bodhisattva: "Excellent, excellent, excellent!"
"Indeed, Mahāmati! Listen attentively, listen attentively; I shall explain it for you. The various non-Buddhists falsely discriminate the characteristics of nirvāṇa.
That which is discriminated by those non-Buddhists is not this nirvāṇa. Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "Excellent, World-Honored One!
We shall indeed receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati, "There are certain non-Buddhists who, being weary of..."
Regarding all objective realms: seeing the cessation of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, and that all phenomena are impermanent;
the non-arising of the mind and mental factors; being present before one without recollecting past, future, or present objects;

where the aggregates are exhausted like the extinguishing of a lamp flame, the destruction of seeds, or the stilling of the wind; and not grasping at signs or engaging in deluded conceptualization—this is called Nirvana. Great!
Wisdom. Yet those non-Buddhists perceive such phenomena and give rise to the notion of nirvana; it is not because they see cessation that it is called nirvana.
[Tang Translation] At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the Buddha..."
[The Buddha] speaks of *nirvāṇa*. Regarding what dharmas he speaks of as *nirvāṇa*, the various non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) engage in manifold conceptualizations.
The Buddha said: "Mahāmati, the various ways in which the non-Buddhists conceptualize *nirvāṇa* do not accord with the true characteristic of *nirvāṇa*.
Listen closely, listen closely; I shall explain it for you. Mahāmati, some non-Buddhists say: 'Seeing that dharmas are non-existent...'"
One is constantly free from craving for sense objects. The aggregates, elements, and bases cease, and mental states and their concomitants do not manifest before one.

One does not dwell upon past, present, or future objects. Like a lamp that has gone out, like a seed that has rotted, or like a fire that has been extinguished, no grasping arises and no conceptualization is produced;
one conceives the thought of nirvāṇa. Mahāmati, it is not by the destruction of what is seen that it is called nirvāṇa.
Mahāmati, some consider that moving from one direction to another is liberation, like the cessation of wind when the perception of objective realms has been extinguished.
Others consider that the destruction of the vision of the knower and the known is liberation. Still others conceive the idea of liberation by viewing the eternal and the non-eternal.
Having reflected thus, they perceive that the perception of various marks is the cause that brings about the arising of suffering; yet, having thought this, they do not correctly understand it.
It is the manifestation of one's own mind. Fearing signs, they perceive signlessness; they develop deep attachment and delight, conceiving it to be nirvana.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, there are some non-Buddhists who travel from place to place, calling this "nirvana. Mahāmati, [there are others who...]
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are other non-Buddhists who discriminate various objects like the wind; therefore, they designate such discrimination as nirvāṇa.
Again, Mahāmati, there are other non-Buddhists who speak thus: "Not perceiving the arising and ceasing of the objects of the seer and the seen is called nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are other non-Buddhists who speak thus: "Not perceiving [the parts]..."
To perceive permanence and impermanence as distinct is called nirvāṇa. Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are other outsiders who speak thus:

"The conceptualization of various diverse characteristics gives rise to all suffering. Because one perceives all characteristics through the false discrimination of one's own mind, one becomes terrified of these characteristics;
seeing the signless (animitta), one develops a deep-seated love and delight for it."
They conceive the notion of nirvana.
[The Tang translation states: Or they say that reaching a certain destination is called attaining nirvana; the cessation of the perception of objects is like the stilling of the wind.
Or they say that not perceiving the subject who awakens and the object awakened to is called nirvana. Or they say that the non-arising of conceptual discrimination is permanence.
The perception of impermanence is called attaining nirvana. Some say that the conceptualization of various marks gives rise to suffering;

yet, they fail to realize that these are manifestations of their own minds. Because they do not understand this, they fear marks and seek the markless, developing a deep attachment to it and grasping at it as nirvana.

Some perceive that the internal and external dharmas, with their specific and general characteristics, possess an indestructible nature throughout the past, future, and present, and thus conceive the notion of nirvāṇa.
Others claim that the self, persons, sentient beings, life-span, and all dharmas are subject to destruction, and thus conceive the notion of nirvāṇa.
Or, because their wisdom has been scorched by the evil of non-Buddhist paths (tīrthika), they perceive primordial nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa).

They hold that there is an interval between these two, and that what is produced by the person is called "nature. Like the transformation of the gunas through comparison with primordial darkness (avyakta), they regard the gunas as the agent and conceive the notion of nirvāṇa.
Or they claim it is the exhaustion of merit and demerit; or the exhaustion of all afflictions (kleśa); or they claim it is wisdom. Or...
They perceive Īśvara as the true creator of birth and death, and they conceive the notion that this is *nirvāṇa*.
[Wei Translation] Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are other non-Buddhists who perceive all phenomena—both their specific and general characteristics—as being neither arising nor ceasing;
they conceptually discriminate that past, future, and present phenomena exist, and they designate this as *nirvāṇa*.
...the term "parinirvāṇa. Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are other outsiders who perceive the non-extinction of the self, the person, sentient beings, life-span, the soul, and all phenomena;
their false conceptualization is what they call nirvāṇa. Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are yet other outsiders...
Because they lack wisdom, they conceptualize the self-nature of what is perceived; they conceptualize the transformation of human life and call this transformation "nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are other non-Buddhists who speak thus: "The exhaustion of sins and the exhaustion of merit is called nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are other non-Buddhists who say that it is the exhaustion of the afflictions.
It is called nirvāṇa by virtue of wisdom. Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are other non-Buddhists who speak as follows:
they see that Maheśvara creates sentient beings, and this false discrimination is what they call nirvāṇa.

[The Tang Translation: Some claim that they perceive the intrinsic and common characteristics of all internal and external phenomena, and that their existence persists without destruction throughout the past, future, and present;
thus they conceive the notion of nirvāṇa. Others calculate that the self, persons, sentient beings, life-span, and all phenomena are indestructible and non-perishing;
thus they conceive the notion of nirvāṇa. Furthermore, there are non-Buddhists who lack wisdom and calculate that [existence] exists...
Some take the transformation of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the person (*puruṣa*), and the qualities (*guṇa*) into all things as *nirvāṇa*.
Some non-Buddhists reckon it to be the exhaustion of merit and demerit; some reckon it to be the exhaustion of the afflictions without relying on wisdom;
and some reckon that Īśvara is the real creator, taking this to be *nirvāṇa*.
Some claim that birth and death arise through a continuous succession of mutual production and that there is no other cause for them;
such a view is an attachment to a cause, yet those fools are unable to perceive this. Because they do not understand it, they conceive the notion of *nirvāṇa*.

Or there are non-Buddhists who, upon attaining the path of True Reality, conceive the notion of *nirvāṇa*; or they perceive the union of qualities and that which arises from qualities as being either identical or different.

Whether in combination or not, they conceive the notion that this is nirvāṇa; or they perceive the nature of the variegated patterns of a peacock’s plumage, various miscellaneous jewels, sharp thorns, and so forth arising from self-nature, and having seen these, they conceive the notion that this is nirvāṇa.
[Wei Translation] Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are other non-Buddhists who say that all sentient beings arise through mutual causality and not from any other cause.
Like those non-Buddhists who are attached to their views regarding causes and lack understanding or awakening, they engage in deluded, dull, and false conceptualization, which they call "nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are other non-Buddhists who speak of realization...
The false discrimination regarding the truths and the path is called nirvāṇa. Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are other non-Buddhists who speak thus:
"There is an agent and an object of action which, being in mutual conjunction, are seen as identical, different, both, or neither;
this false discrimination is called nirvāṇa. Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are other non-Buddhists who say that all dharmas are self-...
Nevertheless, they arise just as a magician produces various forms and images;
one sees various things such as jewels and thorns arising spontaneously. This false discrimination is what is called "nirvāṇa."
[The Tang Translation: Some claim that sentient beings arise from one another in succession, and taking this as their cause, they maintain there is no other cause.
Because they lack wisdom, they are unable to realize this; because they do not understand it, they cling to it as *nirvāṇa*.

Or they calculate that the realization of the Truths and the Path is a false discrimination, which they take to be *nirvāṇa*. Or they calculate that the *guṇas* and the possessor of the *guṇas* [are such].
They then collectively and harmoniously maintain that both identity and difference, their coexistence and non-coexistence, constitute *nirvāṇa*.

Alternatively, they speculate that all things arise spontaneously (*svabhāva*): such as the variegated patterns of a peacock’s plumage, the sharpness of a thorn, or the production of various jewels from the places where they are found.
They ask, "Who could have created such things? and thus they maintain that spontaneous arising itself is *nirvāṇa*.

Mahāmati, there are some who perceive twenty-five principles; or there are kings who, while protecting their kingdoms, study the *Ṣaḍguṇya-śāstra* (Treatise on the Six Virtues) and conceive the notion that this is nirvāṇa.
Or there are those who see time as the creator, thinking that time and the seasons constitute the world; such perceivers conceive the notion that this is nirvāṇa.
Or they speak of "nature" (*prakṛti*), or they speak of "non-nature"; or they speak of knowing nature and non-nature; or they see the existence of perception and nirvāṇa.
...the distinctions of the wheel. They conceive of this as *nirvāṇa*.
[Wei Translation] Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are other non-Buddhists who say: "All phenomena are produced by time;
one perceives that time alone exists. This false discrimination is called *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are others...

The Way says: To perceive the existence of things, to perceive the non-existence of things, and to perceive both the existence and non-existence of things—such conceptual discrimination is called *nirvāṇa*.
[Tang Translation:
Some say that by being able to understand the twenty-five principles (*pañcaviṃśati-tattva*), one immediately attains *nirvāṇa*. Others say:
One who is able to receive the six parts and protect sentient beings attains nirvana. Some say that when one is born into the world, at that very moment one enters nirvana.
Some cling to the existence of things as being nirvana; some reckon the non-existence of things as being nirvana;
some reckon both the existence and non-existence of things as being nirvana; or some reckon all things with...
Nirvāṇa has no differentiation; yet they form conceptions of nirvāṇa.
Such various false imaginings as these, spoken of by the non-Buddhists, neither establish what is to be established nor are they abandoned by the wise.
Mahāmati, all such [views] fall into the two extremes and are conceived as nirvāṇa. Such are the false imaginings of nirvāṇa held by these outsiders;
within them, there is absolutely no arising or ceasing. Mahāmati, regarding each and every nirvāṇa of those outsiders:
In their own treatises, these [proponents] have nothing established whatsoever when examined with wisdom.
Like the wandering, coming and going, drifting, racing, and flowing of the deluded mind and intellect, there is not a single one among them who attains nirvāṇa.

[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, furthermore, there are various non-Buddhists who, with false views and discursive thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), propound various treatises that do not accord with the true Dharma as it is; these are shunned and censured by the wise.
Mahāmati, such non-Buddhists all fall into the dualistic extremes of false discrimination and lack true *nirvāṇa*. Mahāmati, first—
All non-Buddhists thus falsely discriminate regarding nirvāṇa: "No person dwells in the world; no person enters nirvāṇa. Why is this?
Because all non-Buddhists rely on their own mental discourses and falsely discriminate, lacking knowledge as it truly is.
Just as those non-Buddhists discriminate within their own minds, such phenomena do not exist; there is no coming or going, nor any movement.
There is such a nirvāṇa of these non-Buddhists.
[Tang Translation: Mahāmati, those various non-Buddhists engage in false conceptualization; they are rejected by those who accord with the principle of wisdom (*jñāna*).
They all fall into the two extremes and conceive the notion of nirvāṇa, yet therein there is neither abiding nor emerging. They...
All non-Buddhists give rise to false cognitions based on their own respective tenets;
they contradict the true principle and achieve nothing, merely causing the mind and consciousness to wander and fluctuate. Not a single one among them attains nirvana.
"Mahāmati, as for what I have called 'nirvāṇa,' it means the thorough awakening to the manifestation of one's own mind, non-attachment to external natures, and freedom from the four extremes.
It is seeing the state of reality as it is, not falling into the two extremes of the false imaginings of one's own mind-manifestations, where neither the grasped nor the grasper can be found.
Since no object of proof is seen through any form of measurement, the foolish should not grasp at what is real."

Having abandoned those [states], one attains the noble Dharma of self-realization; knowing the two kinds of non-self and being free from the two kinds of afflictions, one purifies the two obstructions and is forever liberated from the two kinds of death.
On the successive stages up to the stage of a Tathāgata, there are profound samādhis such as the shadow-like and illusion-like.
Being free from mind, thought, and consciousness, this is called nirvāṇa. Mahāmati, you and the other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should...
One should practice and swiftly distance oneself from all views of nirvana held by non-Buddhists.
[Wei Translation] Furthermore, Mahāmati, other proponents of established doctrines say that those who see according to reality perceive only their own mind;
they do not grasp at external objects and, free from the four kinds of dharmas, see all things.

The Dharma abides as each respective phenomenon. One does not perceive the marks of one's own mental construction; one does not fall into the two extremes. One does not perceive the realms of the grasper and the grasped.
One sees that all worldly establishments are unreal and deluded regarding the Dharma as it truly is.
Because one does not grasp at phenomena, they are called "real. This is the Dharma of the noble wisdom realized within oneself. As...
Realizing the two kinds of selflessness, one becomes free from the stains of the two kinds of afflictions;
purifying the two obstacles, one is able to know the characteristics of the progressively higher stages as they truly are.

Entering the stage of the Tathāgata, one attains the illusion-like samādhi and remains far removed from the conceptualizations of mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). Such a vision is called nirvāṇa. Mahāmati, you and [the others...]
All Bodhisattvas and others should remain far removed from all the false nirvāṇas of the non-Buddhists.
[Tang Translation: Mahāmati, furthermore, there is something different from what those non-Buddhists have taught.

By means of the Great Lion’s Roar of All-Knowing Wisdom, one can thoroughly comprehend that which is manifested as mind-only and does not grasp at external objects; thus one remains far removed from the four extremes.

Seeing things as they truly are, one does not fall into the two extremes and remains free from the grasped and the grasper. One does not enter into the various means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and does not cling to reality.

Abiding in the Dharma realized through noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*), one awakens to the two kinds of selflessness, becomes free from the two afflictions (*kleśa*), and purifies the two types of obstructions (*āvaraṇa*).
One proceeds through the successive stages (*bhūmi*), enters the stage of a Buddha, attains the great samādhis such as "like an illusion," and forever transcends.
"The mind (citta), the intellect (manas), and the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) are what are called 'attaining nirvāṇa. You and all bodhisattvas should remain far removed from this.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "The views of nirvāṇa held by the non-Buddhists are each born of false imaginings.
These arise from the conceptualizing mind; they lack the skillful means for liberation. They are fools regarding bondage and those who are bound; [you] should remain far removed from them."
Skillful means and the liberation-concept of non-Buddhists—liberation never arises from these. The various wisdoms of different paths are all that is seen by non-Buddhists;
they possess no liberation at all, because of their deluded and false imaginings.
[Wei Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse: "The views of nirvāṇa held by the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) each give rise to conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*).
All arise from the production of mental states (*cittanimitta*) and lack the means for liberation.

Not being free from the bonds and that which binds, they distance themselves from all true means while falsely conceiving themselves to have attained liberation; yet in reality, there is no liberation. The dharmas established by the non-Buddhists..."
Their wisdoms each grasp differently; none of them possess liberation. They are merely deluded and false discriminations.
[Tang Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse: "The views of nirvāṇa held by the non-Buddhists are each distinguished differently;
they are nothing but false imaginings and lack the means for liberation. Being far removed from all such means, they do not reach it."
In that which is without bondage, they falsely conceive the notion of liberation, yet in reality there is no liberation. This is what is established by the non-Buddhists;
each according to their own intelligence grasps it differently, but none of them possess liberation. It is merely the deluded conceptualization of the ignorant.
All foolish non-Buddhists falsely perceive agent and action; their discourses on existence and non-existence lead none to liberation.
The ignorant delight in false conceptualization and do not hear the wisdom of reality. Language is the root of the three sufferings; reality is the cause for extinguishing suffering.
Just as an image in a mirror appears yet does not exist, so too, in the mirror of the deluded mind, the ignorant perceive duality.
Failing to recognize the mind and its objects, they give rise to dualistic conceptualization; by thoroughly understanding the mind and its spheres, such conceptualization no longer arises.
The mind is manifold; it is far removed from the signifier and the signified. Though phenomena appear, they do not truly exist, yet the ignorant falsely conceptualize them as such.
[Wei Translation: All deluded non-Buddhists falsely perceive the agent and the acted-upon; therefore, there is no liberation, for they speak of existence and non-existence.
Ordinary people delight in frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*) and do not hear the wisdom of reality. Language is the root of the triple world.
Knowledge as-it-is extinguishes suffering; it is like an image in a mirror: though seen, it does not exist. The mind, conditioned by habitual tendencies, perceives [objects];
ordinary people say there are two [subject and object], not knowing that these are seen only by the mind. Therefore, they conceptualize duality.
When one knows truly that it is only mind, conceptualization does not arise. Mind is called "the manifold"; it is free from the seer and the seen, and is the characteristic of seeing.
Nothing is visible; it is the deluded discrimination of ordinary beings. [Tang Translation:
All foolish non-Buddhists falsely perceive the agent and the acted-upon; they all cling to the views of existence and non-existence, and therefore there is no liberation.
The ignorant delight in discrimination and do not give rise to true wisdom; verbal expression is the root of the triple world.
The true cause for the cessation of suffering is like an image in a mirror: although it appears, it is not real.
Within the mirror-mind of habitual tendencies, the ignorant perceive duality. Failing to understand that this is a manifestation of mind-only, they give rise to dualistic discrimination.
If one knows that these are merely mind, then discrimination will not arise. Mind itself is the manifold; it is free from both the signifier and the signified, just as with the ignorant.
That which is discriminated is seen, yet there is no seeing.
The three realms of existence are merely false imagination; external objects do not exist at all. False imagination manifests in various ways, yet the deluded and ignorant cannot comprehend this.
The sūtras repeatedly state that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) never transcends names. If one is separated from verbal expression, there is likewise nothing to be expressed.

[Wei Translation: The three realms of existence are merely conceptual construction; external objects do not truly exist. Through conceptual construction, various things are perceived, yet ordinary people cannot understand this.
The sūtras repeatedly explain that these various distinct names are all conceptual discrimination; apart from the dharma of language, there is nothing at all.
It may be said that [the object] is unattainable. [Tang Translation:

The three realms of existence are mere conceptualization; external objects do not exist at all. Various appearances manifest through false imagination, yet the ignorant and foolish cannot perceive this.
The sūtras repeatedly state that conceptualization is nothing more than a different name for the same thing. If one is free from verbal expression, [conceptualization ceases].
Its meaning cannot be apprehended.
*Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, Compiled Translation, Volume Three, Part Two;
*Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, Compiled Translation, Volume Four, Part One.
Originally translated by Guṇabhadra, the Tripiṭaka Master from India during the Song dynasty;
retranslated by Bodhiruci, the Tripiṭaka Master from India during the Wei dynasty;
and subsequently translated by Śikṣānanda, the Tripiṭaka Master from Khotan during the Tang dynasty.
Translated by the śramaṇa Yuankuo of the Zhongdu Monastery during the Ming Dynasty.
Chapter Four: The Essence of the Mind of All Buddhas.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for us the state of a Samyaksaṃbuddha."
"I and other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas wish to become skilled in the self-nature of the Tathāgata, awakening to it for ourselves and awakening others to it.
The Buddha said to Mahāmati, "Ask whatever you desire; I shall explain to you according to your questions.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, something created, or is he uncreated? Is he an effect, or is he a cause?"
Is it the characteristic? Or is it that which is characterized? Is it the teaching? Or is it that which is taught?
Is it the awakening? Or is it that which is awakened to? Regarding such phrases as these, are they different or not different?
[Wei Translation] At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, we pray that you will expound the Dharma of internal realization personally attained by yourself.
By what dharma is the 'Dharmakāya' designated? May I and all other bodhisattvas thoroughly understand the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata."
[The marks. Both oneself and others enter into them without doubt. The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Mahāmati:
"Excellent, excellent, excellent, Mahāmati! You have a doubt; ask whatever you wish, and I shall analyze it for you.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha: "Excellent, World-Honored One! Indeed, we shall receive your instruction. He then addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the Tathāgata..."
Regarding the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha: is it a conditioned phenomenon (saṃskṛta-dharma) or an unconditioned phenomenon (asaṃskṛta-dharma)?
Is it a cause or a fruit? Is it the seer or the seen? Is it that which speaks or that which can be spoken?
Is it wisdom or that which is awakened to by wisdom? Regarding such phrases as these, for the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata...
"Are they different or not different?
[Tang Translation: At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for me the self-realized nature of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, so that I and all other Bodhisattvas may..."
“...the Bodhisattva attains skillfulness in self-awakening and awakening others. The Buddha said, “Mahāmati, regarding what you have asked, I shall explain it for you.
Mahāmati replied, “Yes, World-Honored One; the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, is he something created or uncreated?”
"Are they fruit or cause? Are they characteristic or the characterized? Are they the teaching or the taught? Are they the awakening or the awakened?
Are such things as these different or not different?
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, regarding such terms and phrases, is neither a thing nor..."
Because of this cause. Why is that? Because both positions entail faults. Mahāmati, if the Tathāgata were a conditioned thing, he would be either created or impermanent.
Because he would be impermanent, all things would consequently be the Tathāgata; this is something neither I nor the Buddhas desire.

If it were not something produced, there would be nothing to be attained, and thus skillful means would be empty—identical to a rabbit’s horn or the son of a barren woman—because they do not exist at all.
Mahāmati, if there were no object and no cause, then it would be neither existent nor non-existent.
If it were neither existent nor non-existent, it would transcend the four propositions (*catuskoṭi*). These four propositions are worldly discourse; if one transcends the four propositions...
A phrase does not fall into the four extremes; because it does not fall into the four extremes, it is that which is grasped by the wise.
The meaning of the phrases of all Tathāgatas is also like this; those with wisdom should know this.

[Wei Translation] The Buddha told Mahāmati: "The characteristics of the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—such phrases as these—are neither conditioned phenomena nor unconditioned phenomena; they are neither cause nor fruit. Why?
Because both extremes entail faults. Mahāmati, if one were to say that the Tathāgata is a conditioned phenomenon, then he would be impermanent."
If that which is impermanent were the Tathāgata, then all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) would be the Tathāgata;

however, the Buddha, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, does not admit this doctrine. Mahāmati, if the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata were not a conditioned phenomenon, it would be bodiless.
To say that there is one who practices immeasurable merit and all practices would be false, Mahāmati.
If there were no agent, it would be like a rabbit’s horn or the son of a barren woman, for there would be neither a cause for action nor a body.

Mahāmati, if a dharma is neither cause nor effect, neither existent nor non-existent, and if the essence of that dharma is free from these four characteristics, Mahāmati, those four types of dharmas are merely worldly conventions.
Mahāmati, if a dharma does not transcend these four types of dharmas, that dharma exists only as a name, like the son of a barren woman. Mahāmati, as for the son of a barren woman—
These are merely dharmas of names and phrases, explained as being identical to the four dharmas. If one falls into these four dharmas, the wise do not grasp them.
All such questions addressed to the Tathāgata should be understood by the wise in this way.
[The Tang Translation: The Buddha said, "Mahāmati, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is neither created nor uncreated;
neither effect nor cause; neither characteristic nor that which is characterized; neither speech nor that which is spoken; neither awakening nor that which is awakened.
Why is this? Because both [positions] entail faults. Mahāmati, if the Tathāgata were something created, he would be impermanent."
If all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) were impermanent, they would have to be the Tathāgata; this is something neither I nor the Buddhas can accept.

If he were not a conditioned phenomenon, he would lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and the skillful means (*upāya*) practiced for his sake would be entirely empty and useless—like a rabbit’s horn or the son of a barren woman—because he would not be established through causal activity.
If he is neither cause nor effect, then he is neither existent nor non-existent.

That which is neither existent nor non-existent transcends the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). As for what are called the "four propositions," they exist only as conventional expressions following worldly usage.
If one transcends the four propositions, then that which remains is merely a verbal expression, like the son of a barren woman, O Mahāmati.
The son of a barren woman exists only as a verbal expression and does not fall within the four logical alternatives. Because he does not so fall, he cannot be measured.
All wise ones should understand all the meanings of the Tathāgata’s words in this same way.
Regarding what I have taught—that all phenomena (*dharma*) are without self—you should understand this meaning: the nature of selflessness is itself selfless.

All phenomena possess their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and do not possess the nature of another, just as with an ox or a horse. Mahāmati, for example, the nature of a non-ox is not the nature of a horse, nor is the nature of a non-horse the nature of an ox;
in reality, they are neither existent nor non-existent. Yet, they are not without their own intrinsic nature. In the same way, Mahāmati, all [phenomena]...

All phenomena do not lack their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*); they possess their own specific characteristics. However, these are not what can be known by deluded fools due to their false conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
Thus, one should understand that all phenomena are empty, unarisen, and without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
[Wei Translation] The Buddha again addressed Mahāmati: "I teach that all dharmas are without self.
You should listen attentively to the meaning of 'no-self. Now, as for 'no-self,' it means that within the internal body there is no self; therefore, it is called 'no-self. Mahāmati!"
All phenomena exist as their own nature and do not exist as the nature of another, just like an ox or a horse.
Mahāmati, for example, the body of an ox is not the body of a horse, and a horse is likewise not an ox; therefore, one cannot say that they either exist or do not exist.
"Is it not the case that their own essence (*svabhāva*) does not exist? Mahāmati, all dharmas are likewise:

they do not lack an essential characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), yet they possess an essential characteristic. Foolish ordinary beings do not understand that all dharmas lack a self-essence as their characteristic."
Mahāmati, it is by means of a discriminating mind, not by a non-discriminating mind. In this way, all phenomena are empty;
all phenomena are unarisen; and likewise, all phenomena are without intrinsic nature or characteristics.
[The Tang Translation: "Mahāmati, as I have taught that all dharmas are without self, it is because there is no nature of self within all dharmas that they are said to be 'without self.
It is not that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all dharmas does not exist. Mahāmati, you should know that the meaning of the Tathāgata’s words is likewise.
Mahāmati, for example, a cow lacks the nature of a horse, and a horse lacks the nature of a cow; yet it is not that they lack their own intrinsic nature."
All phenomena are likewise thus: they possess no intrinsic nature (*sva-lakṣaṇa*), yet they are not non-existent;
they exist as suchness. This is not something that ordinary, foolish people can know. Why do they not know it? Because of their conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*). All phenomena are empty.
All phenomena are unarisen; all phenomena lack intrinsic nature—all are likewise so.
In this way, the Tathāgata and the aggregates are neither different nor not different. If he were not different from the aggregates, he would be impermanent.
If they were different, then skillful means would be empty. If there were two [distinct entities], there should be a difference between them.
For example, because the horns of a cow are similar, they are not different; yet because of the distinction between long and short, they are different. All phenomena are likewise, Mahāmati.

Just as the right horn of a cow is different from the left horn and the left horn is different from the right horn, so too are length, shortness, and various colors each distinct from one another, Mahāmati.
The Tathāgata is neither different from nor not different from the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), and sense-bases (āyatana).
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is also like this; within the five aggregates, it is neither one nor different.
Mahāmati, if the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata were one with the five aggregates, it would be impermanent, because the five aggregates—

Because these are phenomena produced by action, Mahāmati. If the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body and the five aggregates were different, there would be two distinct dharmas with dissimilar essential natures and characteristics.
It is like the two horns of a cow, which are similar and not different, yet when one observes them, they appear to have separate entities and seem different in their length.
Mahāmati, if this were the case, all phenomena would lack any characteristic of difference, yet they possess characteristics of difference. As it is said:
The left horn of an ox differs from the right horn, and the right horn differs from the left horn.

Thus, length and shortness are distinct in their mutual dependence, just as various colors differ from one another. Mahāmati, in this same way, the characteristic of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body cannot be said to be identical to, nor different from, the five aggregates.
[Chinese Translation] Mahāmati, the Tathāgata is neither different from nor non-different from the aggregates (*skandha*).

If he were not different, he would be impermanent, because the phenomena of the five aggregates are produced. If he were different, it would be like the two horns of an ox, which are both different and non-different:
they are non-different because they resemble each other, and they are different because they differ in length. For example, as with the right horn of an ox...
The left corner differs from the right; length and shortness are not the same, and their color and characteristics are each distinct. Yet, they are also not different.
As it is with the aggregates (*skandha*), so it is with all phenomena (*dharma*) such as the elements (*dhātu*) and the sense bases (*āyatana*).
In this way, the Tathāgata’s liberation is neither different nor not different [from him]. Thus, the Tathāgata is designated by the name "liberation.
If the Tathāgata were different from liberation, he would be constituted by material form (*rūpa*); because he would be constituted by material form, he would be impermanent.

If they were not different, then when a practitioner attains the mark [of liberation], there should be no conceptual differentiation; yet practitioners are seen to engage in conceptual differentiation. Therefore...
Neither different nor non-different.
[Wei Translation: Within liberation, it cannot be said to be one, nor can it be said to be different. Within nirvāṇa, it cannot be said to be one, nor can it be said to be different.
It is in this way, by relying upon liberation, that it is called the Tathāgata-dharma.
Regarding the characteristics of the body, Mahāmati: if the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body were different from liberation, it would be identical to material form and thus impermanent.
If the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body were not different from liberation, there would be no distinction between the subject that realizes and the object realized.
Yet, Mahāmati, practitioners perceive both the subject that realizes and the object realized; therefore, this is not [the case].
1. [Tang Translation] Mahāmati, the Tathāgata speaks in reliance upon liberation. The Tathāgata and liberation are neither different nor not different.
If they were different, the Tathāgata would be associated with the marks of form (*rūpa-nimitta*); to be associated with the marks of form is...
It is impermanent. If they were not different, the practitioner’s perceptions would have no distinction; yet, because there is a distinction, they are not non-different.
In this way, wisdom (*jñāna*) and the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) are neither different nor non-different. Mahāmati, wisdom and the object of knowledge are neither different nor...
That which is not different is neither permanent nor impermanent; it is neither an agent nor an object of action; it is neither conditioned nor unconditioned;

it is neither the subject of cognition nor the object of cognition; it is neither a characteristic nor that which is characterized; it is neither the aggregates nor distinct from the aggregates; it is neither speech nor that which is spoken;
it is neither one nor different; it is neither both nor neither. Because it is neither one, nor different, nor both, nor neither, it is entirely free from all [conceptual constructs].
All means of valid cognition.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, thus one knows that the object of knowledge is neither identical to nor different [from the cognition].
Mahāmati, if a phenomenon is neither eternal nor non-eternal, neither cause nor effect, neither conditioned nor unconditioned, it is not an object of awakening.
It is not non-awakening; it is neither the seer nor the seen; it is neither apart from the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, nor identical with the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases;
it is not a name, nor an objective realm; it is neither one nor different; it is neither simultaneous nor non-simultaneous;
it is neither continuous nor non-continuous; it transcends all dharmas.
[The Tang Translation: Thus, wisdom and the object of knowledge are neither different nor not different.
If they are neither different nor not different, then they are neither permanent nor impermanent; neither agent nor acted upon; neither conditioned nor unconditioned;

neither the knower nor the known; neither the characteristic nor that which is characterized; neither the aggregates nor distinct from the aggregates; neither the speaker nor that which is spoken. Not...
It is neither identical nor different; it is neither simultaneous nor non-simultaneous. For this reason, it transcends all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Being free from all means of valid cognition, it is beyond verbal expression. Being beyond verbal expression, it is without arising. Being without arising, it is without cessation.

Being without cessation, it is quiescent extinction (*śānti*). Quiescent extinction is the nirvāṇa of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-nirvāṇa*). That which is the nirvāṇa of intrinsic nature is without object and without cause.
When there is no object and no cause, there is no攀緣 (ālambana, objective support). When there is no objective support, one transcends all falsity.
To transcend all falsity is to be a Tathāgata. A Tathāgata is a Samyaksaṃbuddha. Mahāmati, this is called the Buddha who is a Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Mahāmati, as for the term "Buddha who is a Samyaksaṃbuddha," it refers to one who is free from the one [extreme].
The Measure of Cutting Off the Root.

[Wei Translation: If all phenomena transcend [reality] and possess nothing but names, and if those phenomena do not arise because they possess only names, then because they do not arise, those phenomena do not perish;
and because they do not perish, those phenomena are equal to empty space.
"Mahāmati, space is neither cause nor effect. If a phenomenon is neither cause nor effect, that phenomenon cannot be observed.
That which cannot be observed transcends all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
That which transcends all conceptual proliferation is called the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body. Mahāmati, this is what is meant by the Tathāgata, the Arhat..."
The characteristic of the *dharmakāya* of the Perfectly Awakened One (*samyaksaṃbuddha*) transcends the spheres of all sense faculties.
[Tang Translation: Because it transcends all measures, it is merely a matter of verbal expression; because it is merely a matter of verbal expression, there is no arising;
because there is no arising, there is no cessation; because there is no cessation, it is like space. Great.
Wisdom. Space is neither created nor produced; because it is neither created nor produced, it is free from objective grasping.
Because it is free from objective grasping, it transcends all phenomena of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). That which transcends all phenomena of conceptual proliferation is the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata is the essence of perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). One who has attained perfect enlightenment is forever free from [conceptual proliferation].
Regarding all sense faculties and their objects:
at that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "Completely free from the measure of the sense faculties, there is neither object nor cause.

Having already transcended the perceiver and the perceived, one also transcends the characteristic and the characterized. The aggregates, conditions, and so forth—these are the Perfectly Awakened; they are neither identical nor different."
None are able to see it. If there is no seer, how can there be discrimination? It is neither created nor uncreated; it is neither an effect nor a cause.
It is not the aggregates (*skandha*), nor does it reside within the aggregates, nor is it something else distinct from them, nor does it possess various natures.
Just as it is seen through false imagination, one should know that it is not non-existent either. This Dharma and its phenomena are likewise so.
[Wei Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse: "Detached from all dharmas and the sense faculties, neither effect nor cause;
Already detached from the awakening and the awakened, detached from the seer and the seen; Regarding all conditions and the five aggregates, the Buddha does not perceive a single dharma.
If there is no dharma to be seen, how could one engage in discrimination? Neither created nor uncreated, neither..."
The cause is not the fruit; it is neither the aggregates nor separate from the aggregates, nor does it exist elsewhere. By what kind of mind is it conceptualized?
Conceptualization cannot perceive it. That dharma is not non-existent; such is the very nature of all dharmas.
[The Tang Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse: "Transcending the measure of all faculties, it is neither fruit nor cause.

Thus, it is entirely free from characteristics and the objects of characteristics. Regarding the aggregates, conditions, and perfect enlightenment, one cannot perceive them as being either identical or different.
Since there is no perceiver, how could conceptualization arise? It is neither created nor uncreated."
Causes are not non-causes; they are neither aggregates nor non-aggregates, nor are they separate from other things.
There is no single entity of a dharma as it is perceived through conceptual construction, yet it is also not non-existent. Such is the nature of all phenomena.
Because of existence there is non-existence; because of non-existence there is existence. If it were non-existent, one should not grasp it; if it were existent, one should not conceptualize it.
Whether regarding self or non-self, those who linger in the domain of verbal expression become immersed in the two extremes; thus they destroy themselves and destroy the world.
Liberated from all faults, one correctly observes the penetration of the self; this is called right contemplation. One does not disparage the Great Teacher. [Wei Translation:
To say "non-existent" when it previously existed, or to say "existent" when it previously did not exist—therefore, one does not speak of non-existence, nor can one speak of existence.
Those who are deluded regarding self and non-self merely cling to sounds; they fall into the two extremes.
Those who falsely speak destroy the world; those who are free from all faults can see my Dharma—this is called right view.
Such persons do not slander the Buddhas.

[The Tang Translation: Existence is established in dependence upon non-existence; non-existence is established in dependence upon existence. Since non-existence cannot be grasped, existence likewise should not be spoken of.
Failing to understand self and non-self, they cling merely to words; thus they are submerged in the two extremes.
One who destroys themselves destroys the world; yet if one can see this Dharma, they will be free from all faults. This is called right contemplation;
such a person does not disparage the Great Teacher.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has taught that the sūtras uphold the doctrine of non-arising and non-ceasing, and as the World-Honored One has further stated that 'non-arising and non-ceasing' is another name for the Tathāgata—how is it, World-Honored One?
Do you speak of non-arising and non-ceasing because of the absence of intrinsic nature, or is it indeed another name for the Tathāgata? The Buddha told Mahāmati:
“Mahāmati, I teach that all dharmas are neither arising nor ceasing; the categories of existence and non-existence do not appear.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, if all dharmas are non-arising, then the apprehension of dharmas cannot be obtained, because all dharmas are non-arising.
If there are dharmas within names, I pray that you will explain them for me. The Buddha told Mahāmati, “Excellent, excellent!”
"Excellent! Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well. I shall analyze and explain it for you. Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "So be it;
we shall receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "I do not say that the Tathāgata is without nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Nor is he unarisen and undestroyed.
Because he encompasses all phenomena and does not depend on conditions, he is neither born nor destroyed. Furthermore, this is not without meaning."
[Wei Translation] At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, I pray that the World-Honored One will explain this for me; I pray that the Sugata will explain this for me.

The Tathāgata has stated in various places that all dharmas are neither born nor extinguished. World-Honored One, you have further stated that 'neither born nor extinguished' is a name for the Tathāgata."

It is the Dharma-body; therefore, it is said to be neither born nor extinguished. World-Honored One, when the Tathāgata speaks of being "neither born nor extinguished," does this mean that because there is no dharma, it is called neither born nor extinguished?
Or is "neither born nor extinguished" another name for the Tathāgata?
Furthermore, the Buddha-Tathāgata constantly teaches that all dharmas are neither born nor extinguished, because he is free from the conceptual construction of existence and non-existence.
World-Honored One, if all dharmas are unborn, then one cannot speak of "all dharmas," because all dharmas are unborn.
If this name exists based on some other dharma, World-Honored One, you should explain it to me.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāmati, saying: "Excellent, excellent, excellent, Mahāmati! Listen attentively, listen attentively; I shall explain it for you.
The Bodhisattva Mahāmati said to the Buddha: "Excellent, World-Honored One! We shall indeed receive your instruction."
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "The Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is not a non-entity. Nor is it the case that all phenomena are neither arising nor ceasing.
One cannot say it exists by depending on causes and conditions, nor is it a false statement that it is neither arising nor ceasing."
[The Tang Translation: At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, as analyzed and taken up in the Buddha’s sūtras, non-arising and non-ceasing are said to be alternative names for the Tathāgata."
"Bhagavān, please explain this to me: if 'non-arising and non-ceasing' refers to a non-existent dharma, how can it be said to be another name for the Tathāgata?
As the Bhagavān has taught, if one holds that all dharmas are non-arising and non-ceasing, one should know that such a person falls into the view of existence and non-existence.
Bhagavān, if a dharma does not arise, it cannot be grasped; since there is not even the slightest dharma [to be found], who—"
"This is the Tathāgata. I pray only that the World-Honored One will proclaim it for me. The Buddha said, "Listen attentively; I shall explain it for you.
Mahāmati, when I speak of the Tathāgata, it is not a non-existent thing, nor is it the grasping of that which is neither born nor extinguished;
it does not depend on conditions, nor is it without meaning."

"Mahāmati, what I call the Tathāgata’s designation of the 'mind-born Dharma-body'—that which is unborn—is not within the realm of any outsiders, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or Bodhisattvas of the seventh stage, Mahāmati.
Mahāmati, that 'unborn' is simply another name for the Tathāgata. Mahāmati, it is like the various things such as Indra, Śakra, and Praṇidara."
Each one has many names, yet these many names do not imply a multiplicity of natures, nor is it that they lack intrinsic nature.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, I have always said that what is called "unborn and undying" is the mind-made body (*manomayakāya*).
This is because the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is not within the realm of non-Buddhists, Śrāvakas, or Pratyekabuddhas. It is realized by Bodhisattvas dwelling on the seventh stage.
"Even the *sattva* is not its domain. Mahāmati, what I call 'unborn' and 'unceasing' is simply another name for the Tathāgata.
Mahāmati, it is like Śakra, Devendra, Purandara, Bala-dhara, Haste-nakha-śarīra, Dharanimdhara, and Ākāśa;
though these various names differ, their meaning is one. It is not [otherwise]."
Is it because of many names that there are multiple entities such as Śakra and so forth?
[The Tang Translation states: "I say that non-arising is itself another name for the Tathāgata’s mind-made Dharma-body."
All non-Buddhists, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas of the seven stages do not understand its meaning.
Mahāmati, it is like the many names given to each individual thing, from Śakra’s earth and space down to his hands and feet.
It is not that there are multiple entities because there are many names, nor is it that there is no entity at all.
In this way, Mahāmati, I have three hundred thousand *asaṃkhyeya* names in this Sahā world.
Fools hear all these names and each speaks of them as my name, yet they do not understand that these are the various epithets of me, the Tathāgata.
Mahāmati, there are some sentient beings who know me as the Tathāgata; some know me as the Omniscient One; some know me as the Buddha;
some know me as the Savior of the World; some know me as the Self-Awakened One; some know me as the Guide; some know me as the Universal Guide; and some know me as the One... [text ends]... One.
Among those who lead all beings, there are some who know him as the Rishi, some who know him as Brahmā, some who know him as Viṣṇu,
some who know him as Īśvara, some who know him as Jina, some who know him as Kapila, some who know him as Bhūtakoṭi,
some who know him as the Moon, some who know him as the Sun, some who know him as the King, and some who know him as the Unborn and the Undying.
There are those who know emptiness; there are those who know suchness; there are those who know the truths; there are those who know the limit of reality;
there are those who know the nature of phenomena; there are those who know nirvana; there are those who know the eternal; there are those who know equality; there are those who know non-duality;
there are those who know signlessness; there are those who know liberation; there are those who know the path; and there are those who know the mind-born.
"Mahāmati, such as these three hundred thousand *asaṃkhyeya* names—neither increasing nor decreasing—I am known throughout this world and all other worlds.
Like the moon in water, I neither emerge nor enter."
[Wei Translation] “Mahāmati, it is the same with me. Within this Sahā world, there are three hundred thousand *asaṃkhyeya* names.
Although ordinary people speak of them, they do not know that these are alternative names for the Tathāgata. Mahāmati, there are some sentient beings who know [him as] the Tathāgata;
some who know [him as] the Sovereign (*Īśvara*); some who know [him as] the Omniscient One (*Sarvajña*); and some...”
Some know him as the Savior of the World; some know him as the Guide; some know him as the General;
some know him as the Victorious One; some know him as the Sublime One; some know him as the World-Honored One; some know him as the Buddha; some know him as the Bull-King;
some know him as the Lion; some know him as the Rishi; some know him as Brahmā; some know him as Nara.
As for "Elder" (Āyuṣmat): some know him as Jina, some know him as Kapila,
some know him as Niṣṭhāgata, some know him as Ariṣṭanemi, some know him as Candra, some know him as Sūrya,
some know him as Śalona, some know him as Vināśa, some know him as Śakra, some know him as Bala, and some know him as Samudra.
There are those who know non-arising; there are those who know non-extinction; there are those who know emptiness;

there are those who know *tathatā* (suchness); there are those who know the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); there are those who know *nirvāṇa*; there are those who know the *dharmadhātu*; there are those who know the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*);
there are those who know permanence; there are those who know equality; there are those who know non-duality; there are those who know non-existence.

As for these characteristics: there are those who know the conditions, those who know the body of the Buddha, those who know the cause, those who know liberation, those who know the path, those who know the true truths, those who know the omniscient one, and those who know the mind-born body.
Mahāmati, such various names and titles as these belong to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
In the Sahā world and in other worlds, his three hundred thousand *asaṃkhyeya* names neither increase nor decrease;
all sentient beings know them, just as the moon in water neither enters nor exits.
[Chinese Translation] Mahāmati, it is the same with me. In this Sahā world, I have three hundred thousand *asaṃkhyeya* names.
Although all foolish commoners hear them and speak of them, they do not know that these are different names for the Tathāgata.
Among them, there are some who know [me as] the Tathāgata, some who know [me as] the Self-Taught One (*asvayaṃbhū*), some who know [me as] the Teacher (*śāstṛ*), and some who know...
He who knows the supreme guide; he who knows the universal guide; he who knows the Buddha; he who knows the Bull-King (Vṛṣabha);
he who knows the Brahma-King; he who knows Viṣṇu; he who knows the Sovereign (Īśvara); he who knows the Victorious One (Jina); he who knows Kapila; he who knows the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi);
he who knows the inexhaustible; he who knows the auspicious signs; he who knows that which is like the wind; he who knows that which is like fire.
He knows Kubera; he knows him who is like the moon; he knows him who is like the sun; he knows him who is like a king;
he knows him who is like a rishi; he knows Śuka; he knows Indra; he knows the Morning Star; he knows the Great Powerful One.
To know it as being like water; to know it as being without cessation; to know it as being without arising; to know it as being empty of intrinsic nature;

to know it as being suchness; to know it as being truth; to know it as being the true nature; to know it as being the limit of reality; to know it as being the dharma-realm; to know it as being nirvana;
to know it as being eternally abiding; to know it as being equality; to know it as being non-dual; to know it as being signless; to know it...
The One of Quiescent Extinction; the Knower of Endowed Marks; the Knower of Causes and Conditions; the Knower of Buddha-nature; the Knower of Instruction;
the Knower of Liberation; the Knower of the Path; the Knower of All-Knowledge; the Knower of the Most Supreme;
the Knower of the Mind-made Body. Such names as these, numbering three hundred thousand *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, are fully complete—neither more nor less.

[It] diminishes. Within this and other worlds, there are those who can know me as being like the moon in water—neither entering nor exiting—yet those foolish people cannot know me because they fall into the two extremes; nevertheless, they all pay me respectful homage and make offerings to me.
They do not skillfully understand the meaning and intent of words and phrases; they do not discern names, nor do they understand their own internal realization.
They become attached to various verbal expressions and textual passages, conceiving of non-arising and non-ceasing as being without intrinsic nature.

They do not know the distinctions among the Tathāgata’s various names—such as Indra, Śakra, and Brahmā—and they do not understand how these lead back to the ultimate through one's own internal realization.
They adhere to verbal designations regarding all phenomena;
[the Wei translation reads: yet ordinary beings do not perceive or understand this, as they fall into the continuity of the two extremes.
Nevertheless, they all respectfully honor and make offerings to me; yet they do not skillfully understand the meaning of names and phrases.

Grasping at differentiated characteristics, they are unable to know themselves. Because they cling to names, they engage in false conceptualization, asserting that "that which is neither born nor extinguished" is called "non-existence.
They do not realize that this is merely a distinction in the naming of the Tathāgata, just as [the same being may be called] Indra.
Śakra, King Brahmā, Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, and others are unable to definitively establish names as being identical to reality;
likewise, grasping at dharmas by following after names and sounds is also thus.
[The Tang Translation: However, the minds of all ordinary and ignorant beings are submerged in the two extremes and cannot understand [this].

Nevertheless, they respect, serve, and make offerings [to the Buddha], yet they do not skillfully comprehend the meaning of names and phrases. Clinging to the literal teachings, they are obscured regarding the ultimate reality;
they claim that "non-arising" and "non-ceasing" mean there is no essential nature, failing to realize that these are merely the Buddha’s various designations.
Indra, Śakra, and others, being deluded regarding the true reality by their faith in verbal teachings, grasp the meaning of all phenomena according to the words themselves.
Mahāmati, those foolish people speak thus: "The meaning is identical to the verbal expression; there is no difference between the meaning and its description. Why is this?
Why is this? It is because meaning has no body; apart from verbal expression, there is no further meaning, for it is merely verbal expression itself.

Mahāmati, those whose wisdom is scorched by evil do not know the self-nature of verbal expression, nor do they know that while verbal expression arises and ceases, its meaning neither arises nor ceases.
Mahāmati, all verbal expressions fall into the realm of letters, but meaning does not fall [into it], because it is free from both existence and non-existence.
There is neither rebirth nor a body. Mahāmati, the Tathāgata does not teach a dharma that falls into words, because the existence or non-existence of words cannot be apprehended.
This excludes only that which does not fall into words.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, in future ages foolish ordinary people will speak these words:
"As the name is, so too is the object. Yet they do not understand that there are objects distinct from names. Why is this? Because objects have no intrinsic nature or characteristics.
Furthermore, they will say: "There is no object apart from the sounds of names; the sounds of names are themselves [the object]."
This is the meaning. Why is this? Because they do not understand the essential nature and characteristics of names.
Mahāmati, those deluded people do not understand that sounds arise and perish moment by moment, whereas the meaning neither arises nor perishes.

Mahāmati, the nature of sound falls within the realm of names, yet the meaning does not fall within the realm of names because it is free from existence and non-existence; thus, it is without arising and without [perishing].
Because it is the essence. Mahāmati, when the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma, he speaks based on his own voice and does not perceive the various syllables;
because [the essence] is neither existent nor non-existent, he does not cling to names.
[Tang Translation: Those foolish commoners speak thus: "The meaning is like the verbal expression; there is no difference between the meaning and the verbal expression."

Why is this? Because meaning has no substantial entity. Such a person does not understand the intrinsic nature of speech and sound, claiming that words are themselves the meaning and that there is no separate entity for meaning.
Mahāmati, that person is deluded; they do not know that while speech arises and ceases, meaning neither arises nor ceases.
Mahāmati, all speech falls within the realm of letters, whereas meaning does not fall therein, as it is free from existence.

Because they are free from non-existence, and because that which is unarisen has no essence. Mahāmati, the Tathāgata does not speak of dharmas that fall into words, for existence and non-existence regarding words cannot be apprehended; this is excepted only for those who do not fall into words.
Mahāmati, if anyone were to say that the Tathāgata teaches a dharma that falls within the realm of words, they would be speaking falsely, for the Dharma is free from words.
Therefore, Mahāmati, we Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not speak a single word nor answer with a single word. Why is this?
Because the Dharma is free from words. It is not that there is no benefit in the teaching of the meaning; rather, it is through speech [that the meaning is conveyed].
This is because of the deluded conceptualizations of sentient beings, Mahāmati. If all dharmas were not taught, the teaching would perish.
If the teaching perishes, there would be no Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, or Śrāvakas. If these did not exist, who would teach and for whom?
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, if a person clings to names and speaks, that person is not called one who speaks the Dharma well.

Why is this? Because dharmas have no names. Mahāmati, for this reason, I have said in my sūtras that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, do not speak even a single word nor indicate a single name. Why is this? Because all dharmas are without [names].
Names depend on meanings, yet there is no verbal expression; they are spoken based on conceptual differentiation.

Mahāmati, if the Dharma were not taught, the wheel of the Dharma of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas would be extinguished. If the wheel of the Dharma were extinguished, there would likewise be no śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattvas.
If there were no śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattvas, for what kind of person, what kind of Dharma, and for what purpose would one teach?
[Chinese Translation] Mahāmati, if a person preaches the Dharma by falling into the trap of words and letters, that is false and deceptive speech.
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is free from words and letters.
Therefore, Mahāmati, I have stated in my sūtras that I, along with all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, do not speak a single word nor answer a single word. Why is this? Because...
Because all phenomena are devoid of words. It is not that one does not analytically explain them in accordance with their meaning.
Mahāmati, if they were not explained, the teaching would be severed. If the teaching were severed, there would be no śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, or buddhas.
If these were all non-existent, who would speak for whom?
Therefore, Mahāmati, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should not be attached to verbal expression.
They should extensively expound the Dharma through skillful means according to what is appropriate, because the inclinations and afflictions of sentient beings are not uniform.

I and the Buddhas teach all dharmas for the sake of those sentient beings with various differing understandings, so that they may become detached from mind, thought, and consciousness; it is not for the sake of attaining the noble self-realization.
The Abode of Wisdom.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, for this reason, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should not become attached to speech, words, or names.
Mahāmati, because names, phrases, and sentences are not fixed dharmas, they are taught in accordance with the minds of sentient beings by the Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
I teach various dharmas according to the faith of sentient beings in order to cause them to distance themselves from mind, thought, and consciousness;
I do not establish the dharmas based on my own self-realized noble wisdom.
Therefore, Mahāmati, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should not cling to words but should preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate.
Both I and all the Buddhas expound the teachings by following the various differences in the afflictions, understandings, and desires of sentient beings.
This is to transform the mind, intellect, and consciousness, and not for the sake of establishing a realm of noble self-realization.
Mahāmati, regarding all phenomena as non-existent, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas awaken to the manifestation of their own mind’s measure and remain free from the two kinds of false conceptualization.
They rely on the meaning and not on the words. If good sons or good daughters rely on the words, they will destroy the ultimate truth for themselves and be unable to awaken others;
they will fall into a continuity of evil views and act as leaders for the masses.

It is said: Those who do not correctly understand all phenomena, all stages, and all characteristics, and who do not know the words and phrases, are different from those who are skilled in all phenomena, all stages, and all characteristics, who penetrate the words and phrases, and who are fully endowed with the nature and meaning of reality.
The latter are able to delight themselves with the true bliss of signlessness and establish sentient beings in the equal Mahāyāna.

[Wei Translation] Because they are able to know all dharmas as they truly are in their state of quiescence, they see only the dharmas known by the awakening of their own minds, free from the characteristics of dualistic mental discrimination. It is not so stated, Mahāmati:
a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva relies on the meaning and not on the words. If a son or daughter of good family follows the literal text...
Such a speaker falls into false views; they destroy the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) for themselves and likewise ruin others by preventing them from realizing it.
Mahāmati, all the non-Buddhists (tīrthika) each rely on their own treatises and speak according to their divergent views. Mahāmati!
You should thoroughly understand the characteristics of all stages (*bhūmi*). You should thoroughly understand eloquence in speech, rhetoric, and phrasing.

Having thoroughly understood the characteristics of all stages, you shall advance to acquire the eloquence of names, phrases, and joyful speech. You should thoroughly understand the characteristics of the correspondence between the meanings of all phenomena (*dharma*).
At that time, your own person will experience the blissful sensation within the joy of signless phenomena (*animitta-dharma*), abiding in the Great [Vehicle].

Within this vehicle, one causes sentient beings to know that all phenomena are what is seen by one's own mind and that there are no external objects; thus they are freed from dualistic discrimination.
Mahāmati, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should follow the meaning and not rely on the words; for those who rely on the words...
Falling into wrong views, they cling to their own tenets and engage in verbal disputes;

unable to properly comprehend the characteristics of all phenomena, nor their terminology and phrasing, they harm themselves and others alike, and are unable to cause others' minds to attain realization.
If one can skillfully know the characteristics of all phenomena and achieve thorough mastery of their terminology, phrases, and meanings, then...
It enables one’s own self to experience the bliss of signlessness (*animitta-sukha*), and it also enables others to abide securely in the Mahāyāna.
Mahāmati, to embrace the Mahāyāna is to embrace all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas.
To embrace all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas is to embrace all sentient beings. To embrace all...
Sentient beings are those who uphold the true Dharma. Those who uphold the true Dharma ensure that the lineage of the Buddhas is not severed.
When the lineage of the Buddhas is not severed, one is able to understand and attain the sublime state of entry.

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who know how to attain this sublime state of entry are constantly born by transformation, establish the Mahāyāna, manifest various forms through the ten powers of mastery, and possess supernatural penetration.

One penetrates the forms, categories, aspirations, afflictions, and various characteristics of sentient beings and teaches the Dharma according to reality. That which is "according to reality" (yathābhūta) is not otherwise;
that which is according to reality is characterized by neither coming nor going, wherein all fabrications cease—this is called "according to reality.
Mahāmati, sons and daughters of good family should not grasp at or adhere to verbal explanations, for the truth is free from words.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, those who embrace the Mahāyāna are those who embrace all Buddhas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas.
Those who embrace all Buddhas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas are those who embrace all sentient beings.
Those who embrace all sentient beings are those who embrace the sublime and wondrous Dharma-treasury. To embrace [the Dharma-treasury]...
The "Dharma-treasury" means not severing the lineage of the Buddhas.
Not severing the lineage of the Buddhas means not severing all superior and sublime places of birth, because bodhisattvas vow to be born in those superior places.

It means establishing all sentient beings within the Mahāyāna Dharma and, through the ten powers of mastery, being able to manifest in accordance with the forms, colors, and dispositions of sentient beings.
I teach the Dharma as it truly is. Mahāmati, what is the Dharma as it truly is?

The Dharma as it truly is is that which is non-different and non-distinct, neither grasped nor abandoned, and free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); this is called the Dharma as it truly is.
Mahāmati, sons and daughters of good family must not cling to words or sounds, for all dharmas are devoid of words.
[Chinese Translation] If one can cause others to abide securely in the Mahāyāna, one will receive the protection and acceptance of all Buddhas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas.

If one receives the protection and acceptance of all Buddhas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas, one will then be able to embrace and sustain all sentient beings. If one can embrace [them]...
All sentient beings are thus able to embrace all the true Dharma. If they can embrace all the true Dharma, they will not sever the lineage of the Buddhas.
If they do not sever the lineage of the Buddhas, they will attain a supreme and wondrous state.
