Mahāmati, when Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are born into such a supreme and wondrous state, they desire to establish sentient beings in the Mahāyāna by means of the ten [self-]...
The Tathāgata manifests various forms and images through his power, expounding the true Dharma according to what is appropriate for each being.
As for the true Dharma, it is without difference or distinction; it neither comes nor goes. All conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) are completely stilled. Therefore, Mahāmati:
Good sons and good daughters should not cling to the meaning according to the literal expression. Why is this?
Because the true Dharma is free from words and letters.
Mahāmati, it is like using a finger to point at an object for a fool; the fool looks only at the finger and does not perceive the actual object. Thus it is.
Fools follow the pointing finger of verbal expression; they grasp at it and become attached to it, never relinquishing it until the very end.

Consequently, they are ultimately unable to attain the ultimate reality that transcends the pointing finger of verbal expression. Mahāmati, it is like an infant who should eat food that is cooked and should not eat what is raw.
If one eats raw food, it causes madness because one does not know the sequential methods for cooking it.
Mahāmati, in this way, that which is neither born nor extinguished becomes unwholesome if one does not skillfully cultivate its practice; therefore, one should skillfully cultivate the methods.
Do not follow after verbal expressions, just as one looks at the fingertip.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, it is like a person who, in order to show an object to others, points with a finger;
yet that foolish person clings to the finger itself and does not grasp the object indicated by the finger. Mahāmati, such is the case for ignorant ordinary beings.

It is likewise in this case. Because they hear sounds and cling to the finger of names and words, even unto death they are unable to abandon the finger of letters to grasp the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Mahāmati, it is like the name "grain" for ordinary people's food;
if it has not been pounded or cooked, it cannot be eaten. If there is someone who has not prepared it as food, it is merely called by that name.
It would be like madness. One must proceed through the stages until it is cooked before it can become food.
Mahāmati, non-arising and non-ceasing are also like this; those who do not cultivate skillful wisdom and expedient means cannot fully adorn the Dharmakāya.
Mahāmati, those who cling to names and claim to have attained the meaning are like that foolish person who does not know.

To pound grain for cooking yet eat only the husks of the grain of words without obtaining the nourishment of its meaning—for this reason, one should study the meaning and not be attached to the words.
[Tang Translation: Mahāmati, it is like a person pointing at an object with a finger; a small child looks at the finger and does not look at the object.
Regarding objects, foolish ordinary people are likewise: they give rise to attachment following the pointing finger of verbal expression.
Even unto the end of their lives, they are unable to relinquish the finger of the letter to grasp the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*).
Mahāmati, it is like an infant who should eat cooked food; if someone, not understanding the method of cooking, feeds them raw food, then—
It gives rise to madness and confusion. Non-arising and non-ceasing are likewise thus: if one does not skillfully cultivate them, it is unwholesome.
Therefore, one should properly cultivate skillful means; do not follow mere words, like one who gazes only at the tip of a finger.
Therefore, Mahāmati, you should practice skillful means regarding the ultimate truth (*tattvārtha*). The ultimate truth is subtle, tranquil, and is the cause of nirvana.
Discursive speech, however, is associated with false conceptualization (*vikalpa*); false conceptualization is that which accumulates birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Mahāmati, the ultimate truth is obtained from those who have heard much (*bahuśruta*). Mahāmati, "having heard much" refers to being skilled in the meaning, not being skilled in discursive speech.
One who possesses the excellence of meaning does not follow any of the scriptures or treatises of the non-Buddhists; neither does he follow them himself, nor does he cause others to follow them.
This is what is called being a person of great virtue and vast learning. Therefore, those who seek the meaning should draw near to such vast learning—namely, the excellence of meaning.
That which is contrary to this, namely attachment to mere words, should be avoided.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, that which is called "meaning" (artha) is named nirvāṇa.

That which is called "names" (nāman) refers to the arising of worldly understanding through the bondage of conceptualizing marks. Mahāmati, meaning is obtained from those who have heard much (bahuśruta).
Mahāmati, those who have heard much are said to possess skillful means regarding meaning, not skillful means regarding sounds. Mahāmati, as for skillful means regarding meaning:
It is free from all the false teachings of external paths and is not mixed with them.
One who speaks in this manner does not fall into the false dharmas of external paths themselves, nor do they cause others to fall into those external dharmas.
Mahāmati, this is called the skillful means of much hearing that possesses meaning. Mahāmati, one who wishes to attain this meaning should draw near to and serve those who are learned and wise.
One should cultivate reverence. Those who are attached to names and words should be kept at a distance and not associated with.
[Tang Translation] Mahāmati, the true meaning is subtle and tranquil; it is the cause of nirvāṇa.

Discursive speech, however, is conjoined with false conceptualization and causes one to transmigrate through birth and death. Mahāmati, the true meaning is attained through extensive learning; it is through extensive learning that one realizes it.

This refers to one who is skilled in the meaning (*artha*) rather than skilled in verbal expression. One who is skilled in the meaning does not follow any of the evil views of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*);
they do not follow them themselves and cause others not to follow them either. This is what is called "much learning regarding the meaning.
Those who seek the meaning should draw near to such a person. Conversely, those who are attached to the mere letter (*vyañjana*) should be swiftly abandoned.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva, further empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, there is nothing extraordinary in the World-Honored One’s demonstration of non-arising and non-ceasing. Why is this? World-Honored One, all non-Buddhists also claim that their causes are neither born nor extinguished.
World-Honored One, they likewise speak of space, cessation not through deliberation, and the realm of nirvana as being non-arising."

“Extinction! World-Honored One, the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) teach that causes give rise to all worlds. The World-Honored One also teaches that ignorance, craving, karma, and false discrimination serve as conditions for the arising of all worlds.
These causes and these conditions differ only in name. The same applies to external objects and their causes and conditions.
There is no difference between the World-Honored One’s discourse and that of the non-Buddhists regarding atoms, primordial matter (pradhāna), the Supreme Lord (īśvara), or the Self (puruṣa).”

The Lord and others [have taught that] these nine substances are neither born nor extinguished. The World-Honored One has also said that all natures are neither born nor extinguished, and that existence and non-existence cannot be apprehended.
The non-Buddhists likewise say that the four great elements are indestructible and that self-nature is neither born nor extinguished.
The four great elements are eternally the four great elements; even as they circulate through the various realms of existence, they do not abandon their own nature.
What the World-Honored One has taught is likewise so. Therefore, I say there is nothing extraordinary about it.

I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain the reason why there is a distinction such that [the Buddha's teaching] is superior to and more extraordinary than all other heterodox paths. If there were no distinction, then all heterodox paths would also be [the truth].
Because Buddhas are neither born nor extinguished, the World-Honored One has said that it is impossible for many Buddhas to appear in a single world-system.
As previously stated, there would have to be many Buddhas in a single world-system because they are without distinction.
[Wei Translation] At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva, empowered by the strength of all Buddhas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, it is not considered extraordinary for the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, to teach that all dharmas are neither born nor extinguished. Why is this?
All non-Buddhists also teach that their various causes are neither born nor extinguished; the Tathāgata likewise teaches that space is non-substantial."
The conditions cease, and the realm of nirvāṇa is neither born nor extinguished. World-Honored One, the various non-Buddhists also say that all sentient beings arise based on causes and conditions.
The Tathāgata likewise says that the world arises based on the causes and conditions of ignorance, craving, karma, and discrimination.
If this is so, then although the Tathāgata speaks of causes and conditions, the names and characteristics differ; he relies upon external causes and conditions.
They can give rise to all phenomena. Non-Buddhists also say that all phenomena arise based on external causes and conditions.
Therefore, there is no difference between the Tathāgata’s teaching and the teachings of the non-Buddhists.

World-Honored One, the non-Buddhists—relying on atoms, the Supreme Lord (Īśvara), Brahmā, and so forth, along with nine other types of external causes and conditions—claim that all phenomena are neither born nor extinguished. As...
Furthermore, it is taught that all phenomena are neither born nor extinguished, and that existence and non-existence cannot be apprehended.

This is because the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are not extinguished, and their intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are neither born nor extinguished. Although the Buddha-Tathāgata provides various different explanations, they do not diverge from what is taught by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
For the non-Buddhists also teach that the great elements do not depart from the essence of the great elements. Worldly...
“World-Honored One, the various non-Buddhists analyze the great elements (*mahābhūta*); the Tathāgata likewise analyzes the great elements.

World-Honored One, for this reason, what the Tathāgata teaches is no different from that of the non-Buddhists. If they were not the same, the Tathāgata should have explained the characteristics by which they differ.
If there were distinct characteristics, it should be known that [the teaching] would differ from what is taught by the non-Buddhists. World-Honored One, if...”

If the Buddha-Tathāgata did not teach the mark of excellence within his own Dharma, then the various non-Buddhists would also be Buddhas, for they too speak of all phenomena as neither arising nor ceasing.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata has constantly taught that it is impossible for many Buddhas to appear simultaneously in a single world-system.
As previously stated, [if there were no distinction], there would have to be [many Buddhas] in a single world-system.
There are many Buddhas. Why is this? Because there is no distinction between existence and non-existence regarding the causes that have been taught.
Since what the Buddha has spoken is without falsehood or error, why does the World-Honored One not explain the superior characteristics within his own Dharma?
[The Tang Translation: At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, empowered by the Buddha’s majesty, addressed the Buddha once more, saying:
“World-Honored One, it is not extraordinary for the Tathāgata to proclaim that there is neither arising nor ceasing. Why is this?
All non-Buddhists also speak of a creator who is neither born nor extinguished. World-Honored One, you likewise speak of space and nirvāṇa.”

Furthermore, there is non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), which is neither arising nor ceasing. Non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) also say that the world arises from a creator as its causal condition;
the World-Honored One also says that all worlds arise from ignorance, craving, and karma. Both are causal conditions, differing only in name.
The causal conditions of external things are likewise so. Therefore, there is no difference between what the Buddha teaches and what the non-Buddhists teach.

There is a distinction. The non-Buddhists claim that the nine entities—the atoms, the Primal Matter (Prakṛti), the Supreme Lord (Īśvara), and the Lord of Beings (Puruṣa)—are neither produced nor destroyed.
The World-Honored One also says that all phenomena are neither produced nor destroyed, and that whether they exist or do not exist, they are both unobtainable.
World-Honored One, the great elements are indestructible because they are not produced by way of their own characteristics.
It is not extinguished; it circulates through the various realms of existence without abandoning its own nature.

Although the World-Honored One’s analysis shows slight variations, everything is nothing other than what has already been taught by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Therefore, the Buddha-dharma is identical to that of the non-Buddhists.

If there is any difference, we pray that the Buddha will expound it for us. For what reason do you say that the Buddha’s teaching is superior? If there is no distinction, then the non-Buddhists [are the same].
The Buddha [objects]: "Because you also speak of non-arising and non-ceasing, the World-Honored One has always taught that there are not many Buddhas in a single world-system;
yet according to what you have just said, there would indeed have to be."
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "When I speak of non-arising and non-ceasing, it is not the same as the non-arising and non-ceasing of the externalists. Why is this?
Those externalists maintain that there is a self-nature (*svabhāva*) which attains the characteristics of non-arising and immutability.

I do not fall into such categories of existence or non-existence. Mahāmati, my teaching is free from the categories of existence and non-existence, and free from arising and ceasing; it is neither a nature nor a lack of nature."
Just as various illusions and dreams appear, they are not without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Why are they without intrinsic nature?

It is because form lacks the characteristic of being grasped, whether it appears or does not appear, and because of its being grasped or not grasped. For this reason, all natures are neither without nature nor not without nature;

rather, when one realizes that which is the manifestation of one’s own mind, false discrimination (*vikalpa*) does not arise, and there is peace, happiness, and the eternal cessation of worldly affairs.
[Wei Translation] The Buddha addressed Mahāmati, saying:

"Mahāmati, that which I teach as neither-arising-nor-ceasing is not the same as the 'neither-arising-nor-ceasing' of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), nor is it the same as their doctrine of the impermanence of non-arising.
Why is this? Mahāmati, the various non-Buddhists assert that there exists a real essence and nature that is unarisen and immutable; I do not..."
In this way, one falls into the factions and assemblies of existence and non-existence.

Mahāmati, I teach that which is free from existence and non-existence, free from the characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing—neither existent nor non-existent. One perceives all various forms and images as being like an illusion or a dream;
therefore, one cannot say they are either existent or non-existent. Mahāmati, why is it that one cannot say they are existent or non-existent?

This is because the essential nature and characteristics of form (rūpa) involve being visible or invisible, and being grasped or not grasped. Mahāmati, for this reason I say that all dharmas are neither existent nor non-existent.
Mahāmati, it is because they do not realize that [all things] arise from the conceptualization of their own minds that they perceive them as such;
in truth, all worldly dharmas are fundamentally neither born nor extinguished.

[The Tang Translation: The Buddha said, "Mahāmati, what I teach regarding non-arising and non-ceasing is not the same as the non-arising and non-ceasing of the outsiders, nor their theory of the non-arising of impermanence.
Why is this? What the outsiders teach is that there exists a real nature and characteristic that does not arise and is unchanging.
I do not fall into such categories of existence and non-existence; the Dharma I teach is neither existent nor non-existent."
It is not that there is no arising and no ceasing. Why is it not non-existent? Because forms are seen in their various ways, like illusions and dreams.
Why is it not existent? Because the intrinsic nature of the characteristics of form is not existent; because they are seen and not seen; because they are grasped and not grasped.
Therefore, I say that all phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent.
If one realizes that these are merely what is seen by one's own mind and abides in suchness, where conceptual discrimination does not arise, then all worldly activities will be forever stilled.
Foolish worldlings engage in activities through false conceptualization; this is not the case for the noble ones.
Unreal conceptualization is like a city of the Gandharvas or a magically conjured person.

Mahāmati, just as various beings, merchants, and others enter and exit a city of the Gandharvas or a magical illusion, the deluded imagine they are truly entering and exiting, yet in reality there is no one who enters or exits.
However, it is due to their false conceptualization, Mahāmati, that foolish ordinary people give rise to delusions regarding arising and non-arising.
For them, there is neither the conditioned nor the unconditioned; they are like a person born of illusion, who in reality neither arises nor ceases.
Because their nature and lack of nature are non-existent, all phenomena are likewise free from arising and ceasing—yet this is not realized by foolish ordinary people.
Falling into what is not as it truly is, they give rise to the delusive thoughts of arising and ceasing;
this is not the case for the noble sages. [Wei Translation: Yet ordinary worldlings give rise to discrimination; is this not the case for the noble ones?
Mahāmati, those who, with deluded minds, discriminate regarding unreal objects are like ordinary worldlings who see a city of the Gandharvas or the illusions created by a magician.
Seeing various illusory people and various elephants and horses entering and exiting, one engages in false discrimination, saying:
"They enter in such and such a way; they exit in such and such a way. However, Mahāmati, in reality there is no person entering or exiting there;
it is merely the deluded discrimination of one's own mind that perceives them. The same is true for the phenomena of arising and non-arising.
Mahāmati, in that true state there are no such conditioned or unconditioned dharmas, just as with the illusory feats performed by a magician;
yet that magician is neither born nor extinguished. Mahāmati, the existence or non-existence of all dharmas is likewise devoid of purpose, because they are free from arising and ceasing.
It is only ordinary people who, fallen into inverted minds, conceptually discriminate arising and ceasing.
This does not refer to the noble ones.
[Tang Translation: "Discrimination is the affair of ordinary fools, not that of the wise and noble.
Mahāmati, the false mind discriminates unreal objects, like a city of the Gandharvas or a person created by illusion. Mahāmati, it is just as, for example, a small...
A child sees a city of the gandharvas and illusory merchants entering and exiting; with a deluded mind, he discriminates and says there are real things.
What ordinary fools perceive regarding birth and non-birth, the conditioned and the unconditioned, is all likewise so.
As an illusory person is born and an illusory person ceases, yet that illusory person in reality neither arises nor ceases, so too are all phenomena, free from arising and ceasing.
Mahāmati, it is the deluded ordinary beings who give rise to views of arising and ceasing; this is not the case for the noble ones.
It is not so for those who do not see things as they truly are. The false imagination (*parikalpita*) regarding the self-nature of phenomena (*svabhāva*) is not different from that [reality].

If the false imagination were different, one would be attached to all self-natures of phenomena and would not perceive tranquility. Not perceiving tranquility, one never leaves behind false imagination.
Therefore, Mahāmati, the vision of signlessness (*animitta-darśana*) is superior, not the vision of signs (*nimitta-darśana*), because the vision of signs is the cause for receiving rebirth.
Excellent, Mahāmati. As for "signlessness," it is the non-arising of false discrimination; I declare that which neither arises nor ceases to be nirvāṇa.

Mahāmati, as for nirvāṇa, it is the vision of reality as it truly is. It is the attainment of the Tathāgata’s noble wisdom of self-realization, free from the previously existing mind and mental factors of false discrimination. This, I say, is nirvāṇa.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, inversion is like the conceptualization of the mind: "This dharma is thus and thus," while "that dharma is not thus and thus.
Furthermore, it is not that there is no inverted conceptualization; rather, inversion consists in the attachment to all dharmas as being either existent or non-existent.
This is because one does not see tranquility. Those who do not see tranquility are unable to transcend [inversion].
It is false conceptualization. Therefore, Mahāmati, seeing tranquility is called the supreme characteristic;
seeing various marks is not called the supreme characteristic, because it cannot sever the marks that cause birth.
Mahāmati, what is called "signlessness" is the distancing from all conceptualizing minds. That which is without birth and without marks is what I have taught as the [supreme] name.
Nirvāṇa. Mahāmati, that which is called nirvāṇa refers to seeing all dharmas as they truly abide;

it is the distancing from the mind and mental factors of conceptual discrimination; it is the realization within one's own internal body through noble wisdom attained by practicing according to the sequence of reality as it is. It is this that I call nirvāṇa.
[The Tang Translation: That which is called "falsehood" arises as a perverted view contrary to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

A perverted view consists in clinging to the existence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and failing to perceive cessation (*śānti*). Because one does not perceive cessation, one is unable to distance oneself from false conceptualization (*abhūta-vikalpa*).
Therefore, Mahāmati, the vision of signlessness (*animitta-darśana*) is superior, not the vision of signs (*nimitta-darśana*). Signs are the cause of birth. If...
Where there are no marks, there is no discrimination. That which is neither arising nor ceasing is nirvāṇa.
Mahāmati, what is called "nirvāṇa" refers to seeing the state of reality as it is and abandoning the mind and mental factors of discrimination;
it is the attainment of the Tathāgata’s inner-realized noble wisdom. This, I say, is the quiescent nirvāṇa.

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "I have taught such a Dharma as this, which eliminates the theory of arising and establishes the principle of non-arising;
yet the foolish are unable to understand it. All dharmas are unarisen, devoid of intrinsic nature, and non-existent.

Like a *gandharva-city*, a magical illusion, or a dream, those who claim things possess intrinsic nature do so without cause. Since they are unarisen and lack intrinsic nature, what cause could there be?"
Emptiness shall now be explained. Because it is free from combination, the nature of cognition does not manifest; therefore, emptiness is unarisen.
I teach that there is no intrinsic nature, meaning that while the nature appears when each factor is combined, it does not exist [independently]. When analyzed, there is no combination;
this is not like the views of the non-Buddhists.
[Wei Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse: To prevent the arising of all phenomena, I establish the dharma of non-arising.
I teach that dharmas have no cause; ordinary people cannot understand this. All dharmas are unarisen, yet one must not say they are non-existent.
Like a *gandharva-city*, a magical illusion, or a dream, all dharmas exist without a cause. All dharmas are empty and signless. How...?
Why do I speak thus? Apart from all composite conditions, wisdom cannot perceive them. Because they are empty and fundamentally unarisen, they are said to have no intrinsic nature.
When each individual condition is combined, the object perceived cannot be found; since the combination itself cannot be found, this is not what is seen by the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
[The Tang Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse: "To eliminate attachment to birth, I establish the meaning of non-arising.
I teach the doctrine of causelessness, which the ignorant cannot comprehend. All phenomena are without arising, yet they are not non-existent.
Like a city of the Gandharvas, a phantom, or a dream, they exist yet lack a cause. They are empty, unarisen, and devoid of intrinsic nature."
Why do I speak thus? Because apart from all combined conditions, wisdom cannot perceive them. For this reason, I say they are empty, unarisen, and without intrinsic nature.
Though they appear when individual conditions combine, they do not truly exist. When analyzed, there is no combination;
this is not as the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) perceive it.
Like dreams, illusions, floating hairs, mirages, and the city of the gandharvas, the various phenomena of the world appear without cause.

To refute those who argue for the existence of causes, the meaning of non-arising is proclaimed. When the meaning of non-arising is proclaimed, the stream of Dharma flows on forever without interruption.
The blazing doctrine of causelessness terrifies all the non-Buddhists.
Like dreams, illusions, the hair-tufts seen by those with cataracts, gandharva-cities, and mirages—these are perceived falsely without a cause;
worldly phenomena are likewise so. By subduing the doctrine of causelessness, one can establish the meaning of non-arising. One who can establish non-arising [is a true teacher].
My Dharma is not subject to destruction. When I teach the doctrine of causelessness, the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) are struck with terror. [Tang Translation:
Like illusions, dreams, falling hairs, mirages, and the city of the Gandharvas—these appear falsely without a cause;
all worldly phenomena are thus. By refuting the theories of those who maintain causes, I proclaim the principle of non-arising. If this meaning of non-arising is preserved...
"The Dharma-eye is eternally unextinguished; I proclaim the doctrine of causelessness (*ahetuvāda*). All the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) are filled with alarm and fear.
At that time, Mahāmati asked in verse: "What is it? What is its cause? For what reason does it arise?
In what place do they conjoin to formulate this doctrine of causelessness?"
At that time, the World-Honored One again replied in verse: "Observing conditioned phenomena, one sees they do not exist without a cause, but have a cause;
thus, the views of those who propound arising and ceasing are extinguished."
[Wei Translation] What kind of person, by what cause, and in what place [perceives this]?

That all phenomena are without cause, that they are neither caused nor uncaused—if a wise person can see this, they can abandon the view of arising and ceasing. There is no phenomenon that arises or does not arise; this is because there are no causal conditions.
[The marks. [Tang Translation: What is it? What is its cause? For what reason does it arise? In what place is it combined?
Why do you propound the theory of no-cause?
Observing conditioned phenomena as neither having a cause nor being causeless, the views of those who propound arising and ceasing are thereby extinguished.
At that time, Mahāmati spoke a verse in question: "What is meant by 'non-arising'? Is it the absence of intrinsic nature? Or is it [a matter of]..."
Observe all conditions. There is a dharma called "non-arising. A name should not be without meaning; it is taught solely for the sake of analytical discrimination.
[Wei Translation] If it were merely a name for a dharma, please explain to me what its meaning is.
[The Tang Translation: "Because it is non-existent, there is no arising; because it depends upon various conditions; because it exists as a name but lacks reality—please explain this to me.

At that time, the World-Honored One replied again in verse: "It is not that there is no arising due to the absence of intrinsic nature, nor is it that [arising] regards various conditions, nor is it that [things] exist..."

It is named according to its nature; yet the name is not without meaning. It is not within the realm of any of the non-Buddhists, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or those at the seventh stage—this is called the characteristic of non-arising.
[Wei Translation] It is not that dharmas arise from existence or non-existence, nor do they depend on causes and conditions. It is not that prior dharmas have names;
this is also called the teaching of non-emptiness. It is not the domain of Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or outsiders; it resides in the seventh stage.
In that state, there is no characteristic of arising.
It is not that non-existent things do not arise, nor is it by depending on conditions. It is not a thing that is given a name, nor is it a name without an object.
This is not the sphere of activity for any of the outsiders, the śrāvakas, the pratyekabuddhas, or those at the seventh stage.
This is the characteristic of non-arising:
it is far removed from all causes and conditions and detached from all phenomena; there is only the subtle mind abiding, free from both the perceiver and the perceived.
The transformation of its body—this I call "non-arising.
[Wei Translation] Detached from all dharmas of causes and conditions, and in order to negate all causes and conditions, I teach the establishment of "Mind-Only" and name this "non-arising.
All dharmas are without causes and conditions; they are free from conceptualization and that which is conceptualized, and free from the factions of existence and non-existence.

I call this "non-arising. When the mind is free from the phenomena of views and free from the essence of these two dharmas, and when the body is transformed to rely upon the marks of the true [dharmakāya], I call this "non-arising."
[The Tang Translation: Far removed from all causes and conditions, there is no agent whatsoever. Established solely by the mind, I declare this to be non-arising.
All phenomena do not arise from causes; they are neither non-existent nor existent. They are free from the dualistic discrimination of subject and object.
I declare this to be non-arising: it is mind-only with nothing perceived, and it is also free from the two natures.
When the basis is thus transformed, I declare this to be non-arising.
There is no external nature nor non-nature, nor is there any mental grasping. Having severed all views, I declare this to be non-arising.

Thus, regarding the absence of intrinsic nature, emptiness and so forth should be distinguished. It is not because of being empty that it is called "empty," but because of being non-arisen that it is called "empty."
[Wei Translation] External objects are neither real nor unreal, nor are they what the mind apprehends.

Like illusions, dreams, the hair-tufts [seen by those with cataracts], gandharva-cities, and mirages, they are free from all views; this is called the characteristic of non-arising. Such are the dharmas of emptiness and so forth.
One should understand that all phrases [expressing] non-arising and emptiness do not themselves possess the emptiness of arising.
[Tang Translation: External objects exist and yet do not exist; the mind has nothing to grasp. All views are completely severed—this is the characteristic of non-arising.
Such is the meaning of all phrases such as "emptiness" and "selflessness": it is not by means of emptiness that there is emptiness.
Because there is no arising, it is said to be empty.
Through the combination of various causes and conditions, there is arising and ceasing; apart from these various causes and conditions, there is no separate arising or ceasing.
Apart from the enumeration of causes and conditions, there is no other distinct nature. To speak of identity or difference is the false imagination of the non-Buddhists.
The nature of existence and non-existence does not arise; it is neither existent nor non-existent. Apart from the transformation of these enumerations, none of these can be apprehended.

[Wei Translation] There is arising and there is cessation. Through the conjunction of various causes and conditions, things arise; apart from these causes and conditions, there is neither arising nor cessation.
Apart from causes and conditions, no dharma exists; apart from conjunction, nothing can be attained. These are the false discriminations of the non-Buddhists.
Yet one perceives a distinction between existence and non-existence; however, phenomena are not produced through existence or non-existence, for existence and non-existence cannot be apprehended.
It is only through the conjunction of all dharmas that one perceives arising and ceasing.
Through the gathering together of causes and conditions, there is thus arising and ceasing. When separated from causes and conditions, arising and ceasing do not exist.
Apart from all causes and conditions, no further phenomena exist; neither identity nor difference.
That which is discriminated by the ignorant—existence, non-existence, and the unborn nature of phenomena—is likewise so for that which is neither.
Only when various conditions converge does one perceive arising and ceasing therein.
There are only various conventional designations that link together like a chain of hooks; apart from that causal chain, the meaning of "arising" cannot be found.

Since arising lacks intrinsic nature, it does not occur, thereby avoiding the errors of the non-Buddhists. I speak only of this causal chain of links, yet the foolish and ignorant are unable to comprehend it.
If there were a nature of arising that existed apart from conditions linked like a chain, this would be the doctrine of causelessness and would destroy the meaning of the chain-like linkage.

Just as a lamp reveals various forms, if the manifestation of the chain-like linkage were such [as you claim], then there would be various natures existing separately, apart from the chain-like linkage itself.
[Wei Translation] There are only names, which link together like a chain. Apart from that causal chain, the phenomenon of arising cannot be found.
Since the phenomenon of arising is not seen to arise, one is free from the errors of the non-Buddhists; one speaks only of the chain of conditions.
Ordinary beings do not understand this. If one were to depart from the chain of conditions, there would be no other distinct phenomenon;

this would then be a doctrine of causelessness, which destroys the meaning of the chain of conditions. Just as a lamp reveals various forms, so too does the chain of conditions give rise to phenomena.
If it were otherwise, and there were a phenomenon arising separately apart from the chain of conditions, [it would be causeless].

[The Tang Translation: Following worldly convention, one employs provisional designations; causes and conditions link together like a chain. If one were to depart from the chain of causes and conditions, the meaning of "arising" could not be established.
I teach that there is only this chain; since arising does not exist, there is no birth. Thus, one is free from the faults of the non-Buddhists.

This is not understood by the ignorant. If there were dharmas that arise separately, apart from the chain of conditions, this would be a doctrine of causelessness (*ahetuvāda*) that destroys the meaning of the chain.
Just as a lamp can illuminate objects, if the chain were manifest in such a way, then there would be various dharmas existing separately, apart from the chain.
There is no nature and no arising; it is like the intrinsic nature of space. If one is free from the hook and the chain, wisdom has nothing to differentiate.

Furthermore, there is another non-arising, the dharma attained by the noble ones (*ārya*): that which is both arising and non-arising is precisely the patience toward non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
[Wei Translation] Phenomena that arise have no inherent substance; their self-nature is like empty space. Seeking the Dharma apart from the hook and the chain, the foolish have no knowledge of it.

Furthermore, there is another non-arising, the Dharma attained by the Sages. That which is both arising and non-arising— *Note: This passage reflects the translation style of the Wei dynasty (c. 220–265 CE), characterized by archaic terminology and a focus on the ontological emptiness of phenomena.*
This is the patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

[Tang Translation: Non-arising is the absence of intrinsic nature; its essence and characteristics are like empty space. To seek the Dharma apart from hooks and chains is the conceptualization of the foolish.

Furthermore, there is another non-arising, the Dharma attained by the various sages. That which is both arising and non-arising— [Note: The bracketed portion "Tang Translation" indicates that the following is a variant reading from the Tang dynasty translation.]
This is the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
If one were to observe the interlocking chain of all worlds, one would find that everything is free from such chains; from this, one attains samādhi.
Ignorance, craving, various karmas, and so forth—these constitute the internal chain. The fire-drill, the lump of clay, the potter’s wheel, seeds, and so forth are called external.
If these were to arise from causes and conditions while possessing an intrinsic nature belonging to another, they would not have the meaning of a "chain," and thus they would not be established.
If that which arises lacks intrinsic nature, for whom would there be this chain of links? Because they arise through mutual succession, one should understand the meaning of causes and conditions.
[Wei Translation: If one perceives all worlds, this is seeing the chain of links. All things are chains of links; thus the mind attains concentration.
Ignorance, craving, karma, and so forth—these are the internal chain of links. Like the pulling and spinning of a lump of clay on a wheel.

The seed is the great hook-and-chain. If there were any other phenomena that arise from causes and conditions yet are devoid of the principle of the hook-and-chain, they would not abide within the Noble Teaching.
If the arising phenomenon were non-existent, for whom would it be a hook-and-chain?
Because they arise in mutual succession, this is called the meaning of dependent origination.
[The Tang Translation: All worlds are nothing other than chains and locks. If one can understand them in this way, this person’s mind attains concentration.
Ignorance, craving, and karma—these are the internal chains and locks. Seeds, mud, the potter’s wheel, and so forth [are the external ones].

This is what is called "external. If one claims that there are other phenomena produced from causes and conditions that are devoid of the principle of mutual dependence (the hook-and-chain logic), this is not consistent with the scriptural teachings or reasoning.
If the phenomena that arise do not exist [independently], for whom would they serve as causes and conditions?
That they arise through a reciprocal succession is the true meaning of causes and conditions.

The dharmas of solidity, moisture, heat, and motion—fools give rise to false imaginings regarding them. Apart from these enumerations, there is no other dharma; thus it is said that they lack intrinsic nature. [Wei Translation:
The dharmas of solidity, moisture, heat, and motion—fools give rise to discrimination regarding them. Apart from these designations, there is no further dharma;
therefore it is said they have no essence.

[The Tang Translation: Solidity, moisture, heat, motion, and so forth are what the ignorant discriminate. Since they take as their objects only non-existent dharmas, they are said to lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
Just as a physician treats various illnesses without having a fixed number of theories, but devises diverse remedies according to the differences in the diseases, [so too does the Buddha teach].
For the sake of those sentient beings, I destroy all afflictions; knowing the superiority or inferiority of their faculties, I preach for them the gateways of liberation.
It is not that there are various dharmas due to differences in afflictions or faculties; I preach only the Single Vehicle Dharma, and this is precisely the Mahāyāna.

[Wei Translation] Just as a physician treats various illnesses by prescribing remedies according to the specific disease, yet the medical treatise itself remains undifferentiated—only because the diseases differ do the prescriptions vary—so too do I contemplate all sentient beings who are defiled by the faults of afflictions;
knowing the differences in their faculties and powers, [I teach accordingly].

I grant predictions according to what they are capable of receiving; my Dharma is without distinction. I teach various doctrines according to differences in faculties and ailments, yet my vehicle is but the One Vehicle, the purity of the Eightfold Noble Path.
[The Tang Translation: Just as a physician treats various illnesses with a medical treatise that remains undifferentiated, yet employs diverse prescriptions and medicines because the ailments differ;
so too do I, for the sake of all sentient beings, eliminate the diseases of affliction by discerning the superior or inferior capacities of their faculties.
I expound various Dharma gates; it is not that the roots of affliction differ, such that there are diverse teachings.
There is only this single Great Vehicle, the eightfold path of purity and coolness.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, all non-Buddhists give rise to the false discrimination of impermanence. World-Honored One, you also say that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent and are subject to arising and ceasing.
What is the meaning of this? Is it erroneous or correct? And how many kinds of impermanence are there?"
[Wei Translation] At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, the World-Honored One speaks of impermanence. Yet, all non-Buddhists also speak of impermanence.

World-Honored One, the Tathāgata relies upon names, phrases, and syllables to speak these words: 'All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are dharmas subject to arising and ceasing. World-Honored One..."
"Is this dharma real or is it false? World-Honored One, furthermore, how many kinds of impermanence are there? [Tang Translation:
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, all non-Buddhists falsely proclaim impermanence. World-Honored One, you also say: 'All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are dharmas of arising and ceasing.'"
I do not yet know whether this teaching is false or correct. Furthermore, how many kinds of impermanence are there? The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"All non-Buddhists maintain seven kinds of impermanence; these do not belong to my Dharma. What are the seven?
Some among them say that once something has been created and is then abandoned, this is called impermanence. Others say that the destruction of form and location is called..."
Regarding impermanence (*anityatā*): some say that form itself (*rūpa*) is impermanent;

others say that the interval during which form undergoes transformation is called impermanence, wherein it subsequently disintegrates of its own accord—just as the intermediate stages of the transformation of milk into curd are invisible.
Impermanence destroys all natures (*bhāva*). Some say that nature itself is impermanent; some say that both nature and non-nature are impermanent; and some say [it is] one.
"All phenomena are unborn; impermanence enters into all phenomena.
[Wei Translation] The Buddha addressed the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva, saying: "Excellent, excellent, excellent, Mahāmati!
All non-Buddhists, through false discrimination, speak of eight kinds of impermanence. What are these eight? First..."
That which initiates activity yet does not perform it is called impermanence. What is meant by "initiation"?
It refers to the arising of phenomena and non-arising phenomena, as well as permanent phenomena and impermanent phenomena; this is called the impermanence of initiation.
Second, the cessation of form and characteristics is called impermanence. Third, form and so forth are themselves impermanent. Fourth, the transformation of form [is impermanent].
1. Change and transformation constitute impermanence; all phenomena (*dharma*) cease spontaneously within their own continuity, like the transformation of milk into curd.
Not perceiving this transformation nor perceiving this cessation in any phenomenon is called impermanence. 2.
Furthermore, there are other non-Buddhists who claim that because things do not exist, it is called impermanence. 3. There are those who speak of existence and non-existence.
Yet all are impermanent. Because all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen, they are called "impermanent.

Because impermanent dharmas are conjoined within them, they are therefore impermanent. Seventh, there are further non-Buddhists who claim that what was originally non-existent and later comes into existence is called "impermanence."
[The Tang Translation] The Buddha said: "Mahāmati, non-Buddhists speak of seven kinds of impermanence, which do not belong to my teaching.

What are these seven? Some say that the very moment of initial arising is itself abandonment; this is called impermanence, because once produced, there is no further production, being of the nature of impermanence.
Others say that the transformation and destruction of form and location is called impermanence. Others say that form itself is impermanence."
"Permanence. Some say that the transformation of form (*rūpa*) is called impermanence (*anitya*). All phenomena (*dharma*) continue in an uninterrupted succession;
they cause transformation and naturally lead to extinction, just as milk and curd undergo successive transformations.
Although these are invisible, they exist within phenomena and destroy all things. Some say that "things" are impermanent; others say that there are neither "things" nor "non-things."
It is impermanent. Some say that non-arising is impermanence, which pervades all phenomena.
Mahāmati, as for the impermanence of existence and non-existence, it refers to the destruction of the specific characteristics of the four great elements and their derivatives;
since the self-nature of the four great elements cannot be apprehended, they are non-arisen.

[Wei Translation] It refers to the cessation of the characteristics produced by the primary elements (*mahābhūta*). Not perceiving the non-arising [of things] apart from the substance of the continuum is called impermanence.

[Tang Translation] Regarding "the impermanence of entities and non-entities therein": it refers to the cessation of the characteristics of both the primary elements (*bhūta*) and their derivatives (*bhautika*).
Destruction. The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the great elements is originally without arising.
That which is non-arising impermanence is not [the impermanence of] constant change; it is the non-arising of all phenomena, whether existent or non-existent.
Even when analyzed down to the level of atoms, they cannot be perceived. This meaning of non-arising is not [mere] production; this is called the characteristic of non-arising impermanence. If...
Those who do not realize this fall into the view of all non-Buddhists that birth is impermanent.
[Wei Translation] Eighth is the impermanence of non-arising. This means that because it is not permanent, it is impermanent.

One perceives that all phenomena have both arising and non-arising; yet, even when examining them down to the finest atom, one does not perceive the arising of any phenomenon. Therefore, it is called "non-arising."
"Arising! Yet all dharmas do not arise, Mahāmati. This is called the characteristic of non-arising impermanence.
However, the non-Buddhists do not understand why those dharmas do not arise; therefore, they conceptually construct that all dharmas do not arise and thus speak of impermanence."
[The Tang Translation: Regarding "non-arising impermanence": this refers to phenomena such as permanence and impermanence, existence and non-existence, and so forth;
all such things are without arising. Even when analyzed down to the level of subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*), nothing is perceived.
Because they do not arise, they are called "unborn" (*anutpāda*). This is the characteristic of non-arising impermanence. If one does not understand this, then...
This falls into the view of outsiders who assert that birth is impermanent.
Mahāmati, as for the impermanence of intrinsic nature, it is a conceptual construction of one's own mind, not the actual nature of permanence or impermanence. Why is this so?
This means that the nature of impermanence itself is indestructible. Mahāmati, this is the matter of the impermanence of all things and their lack of intrinsic nature.
Apart from impermanence, there is nothing else capable of rendering all dharmas devoid of intrinsic nature, such as a staff, a tile, or a stone might destroy various objects.
[Wei Translation] Furthermore, Mahāmati, the non-Buddhists (tīrthika) discriminate regarding impermanent phenomena, asserting that they exist as entities.
Those non-Buddhists falsely discriminate within their own minds that the impermanent is permanent, or that it is not impermanent, on the grounds that there are such entities.
Why is this? Because their intrinsic nature does not perish. That which does not perish in its intrinsic nature is the permanence of the essence of impermanence.
Because they are not extinguished, Mahāmati. If impermanent phenomena were substantial entities, then all phenomena would arise, for that impermanence would act as their cause.
Mahāmati, if all phenomena were not separate from impermanence, then the existence and non-existence of all phenomena would have to be perceived.
Why? Because, like a staff, wood, tiles, or stones, they are capable of breaking and destroying what is destructible.
All things are utterly destroyed. [Tang Translation:
Regarding those things that are impermanent: this refers to the arising of conceptual discrimination regarding that which is neither permanent nor impermanent.
What is the meaning of this? They establish that impermanence itself does not perish or disintegrate, yet it is capable of destroying all phenomena. If it were not...
Impermanence destroys all phenomena, yet phenomena do not ultimately perish into non-existence.
Just as a staff, a mallet, a tile, or a stone can destroy other objects while remaining unharmed themselves, so it is with this as well.

It is directly perceived that each is not different; this nature is an impermanent phenomenon (*anitya-vastu*). There is no distinction between the agent and the acted-upon, such that one could say "this is impermanence" and "this is the phenomenon.
If there were no difference between the agent and the acted-upon, all natures would be eternal and devoid of causality. Mahāmati!
The fact that all natures are without nature has a cause, which is not known by ordinary, ignorant people.
Because they perceive various and diverse characteristics, they [erroneously] hold that the cause of impermanence is the non-existence of all dharmas;
yet it is neither a cause nor a fruit. Mahāmati, there are further faults, for that cause and fruit do not exist.
Because of their distinction, one cannot say that this is impermanent while that is its fruit; for since cause and fruit are distinct, one cannot say that all phenomena are eternal.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, because all phenomena are without cause [in the sense of being unconditioned], [one cannot say they are eternal].
All phenomena have causes, yet ordinary worldlings do not perceive or know this.
[Tang Translation: Mahāmati, it is directly perceived that there is no distinction between impermanence and all phenomena as agent and object;
for there is no differentiation such that "this is impermanence" and "this is the produced object. Thus, agent and object...
They should both be eternal, for no cause is seen that could cause all phenomena to become non-existent.
Mahāmati, although the destruction of all phenomena does indeed have a cause, it is simply beyond the comprehension of the foolish and the ignorant.
It does not arise from causes that are dissimilar. If it were to arise [from such], then all natures would be entirely impermanent, which is a dissimilarity.
There would be no distinction between the agent and the acted-upon, yet a distinction is clearly perceived. If nature were impermanent, it would fall into the characteristic of being a causal agent;
if it were to fall [into that], then all natures would be non-ultimate, as all natures would fall into the characteristic of being a causal agent.
[If that were so,] then that which is itself impermanent would have to be impermanent; yet because impermanence is impermanent, all natures would not be impermanent, but rather must be permanent.
[Wei Translation: Because a different cause cannot produce a different effect, Mahāmati, if a different cause could produce a different...
As for "fruition": if it were produced by a distinct cause, then all phenomena would arise [from that single cause]. If that were so, there would be yet another fault:

one would perceive a distinction [in the effect] corresponding to the distinction [in the cause]. Mahāmati, if that which is impermanent were a substantial entity, it should be identical to the causal substance and its performed function.
Furthermore, there would be yet another fault: within a single phenomenon, everything would have to be fully contained.
All phenomena [would be identical], because there would be no distinction between their causes, effects, actions, and characteristics as they perform all functions alike.
Furthermore, there is another fault: they would inherently be impermanent, because impermanence would possess the essence of impermanence. Yet there is yet another fault:
all phenomena, being impermanent, would consequently have to be permanent.
[The Tang Translation: Mahāmati, a dissimilar cause should not produce a dissimilar effect.
If it could so produce one, then all dissimilar phenomena would arise simultaneously from one another; there would be no distinction between those phenomena as the producer and the produced.
Yet we clearly perceive such distinctions. How, then, could a dissimilar cause produce a dissimilar effect? Mahāmati, if the nature of impermanence were an existent entity...
As for "dharmas": if that which is produced were inherently impermanent, then because it is inherently impermanent, all impermanent dharmas would have to be permanent.
If impermanence were to enter into all natures, they would fall into the three periods of time. That past form is co-existent with destruction; [it has not yet...]

It does not arise from the future, because form (*rūpa*) does not arise. Present form is co-existent with the characteristic of disintegration. Form is a specific accumulation of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the four great elements and their derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) is indestructible, because it is free from being either different or non-different.

For all non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), the four great elements are indestructible. All four great elements and derived matter within the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*) exist as objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) and possess arising.
Cessation. Apart from the derived matter of the four great elements, what nature do all non-Buddhists contemplate as impermanent?
It is that the four great elements are unarisen, for their intrinsic nature and characteristics are indestructible.
[Wei Translation] Furthermore, there is another fault. If impermanence were identical to all phenomena, it would fall under the category of the dharmas of the three periods of time.
Mahāmati, because past form is identical to impermanence, it has already ceased; future dharmas have not yet arisen, and because they are identical to the impermanence of form, they do not arise;
present existing dharmas are not separate from form, for form [is composed of] those great elements (mahābhūta).
Characteristics. Because they depend upon the five great elements (*mahābhūta*) and their objects, they do not perish; for those [elements and objects] are mutually inseparable.
Mahāmati, all non-Buddhists do not admit the impermanence of the great elements; they maintain that the three realms depend upon the great elements and subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*).
Therefore, based on those dharmas, they speak of arising, abiding, and ceasing. Mahāmati, apart from these dharmas, there are no other four great elements or various objects.
Regarding the Dharma: because those non-Buddhists engage in false conceptualization, they maintain that there is impermanence existing apart from all phenomena.
Therefore, the non-Buddhists assert that the great elements are neither produced nor extinguished, because their own essential nature is eternally indestructible.
[The Tang Translation: "Mahāmati, if the nature of impermanence were to abide within all phenomena, it would follow that it, like the phenomena themselves, falls within the three periods of time.
It would have already perished simultaneously with past form; it would not arise in the future; and it would perish together with the present.
As for those among the various non-Buddhists who reckon that the essential nature of the four great elements is indestructible, this is merely a differentiation of the great elements."
Because the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) are neither different nor non-different, their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) likewise does not perish.
Mahāmati, within the three realms of existence, there is nothing among the creators and the created that is not characterized by arising, abiding, and ceasing.
How could there be any other nature of impermanence that could produce things without itself ceasing?

Regarding those who deny the impermanence of initial creation: it is not that there are other elements distinct from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), for the four great elements each possess their own distinct characteristics and specific natures;
thus, no differentiation can be found. Since they lack such differentiation, these [elements] do not undergo further creation, nor do they act through the two types of skillful means (*upāya*).
One should know that this is impermanent.
[Wei Translation] Therefore, it is said that when an activity has been initiated but is not yet being performed in the interim, this is called impermanence.

Among the great elements (*mahābhūta*), there is further the initiation of great elements; there are no distinct or common characteristics therein that are subject to non-arising or non-ceasing phenomena.
Because one perceives that all phenomena are neither arising nor ceasing, the wisdom of impermanence arises regarding them.

[Tang Translation: That which is impermanent as being created and immediately abandoned does not mean that the primary elements (mahābhūta) create other primary elements, because they are distinct from one another.
Nor do they create themselves, because there is no difference [in their nature]. Nor do they create together, because they are disjoined. It should be understood...
One should know that this is not the beginningless impermanence.

Regarding that impermanence which is the destruction of form and location: it means that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) do not undergo destruction; they remain ultimately indestructible.

Mahāmati, "ultimately" means that even when analyzed down to the subtlest atoms (*paramāṇu*), the four great elements and the derived matter are observed to be destroyed only in terms of their differences in shape and location.

One cannot perceive length or shortness [in them]. They are not the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). Although the four great elements do not destroy the locus of form, they appear as if destroyed; thus one falls into the Sāṃkhya school.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, what is called the impermanence of the cessation of form? It refers to the primary causes and their effects...

Regarding the perception of forms: seeing forms as distinct—such as long and short—and perceiving the transformation of the forms of the great elements (*mahābhūta*) without the great elements themselves being extinguished, such a person falls into the system of the Sāṃkhya.

[The Tang Translation: Regarding the impermanence of the destruction of shape (*saṃsthāna*): this is not the destruction of the primary elements (*bhūta*) and their derivatives (*bhautika*), but rather the destruction of shape alone.
What is the meaning of this? It means that when matter is analyzed down to its subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*), one merely ceases to perceive shapes such as long and short;
it does not destroy the essential substance of the primary and derivative elements. This view falls within the Sāṃkhya school.
"Form is impermanent" means that form itself is impermanent; it is the spatial configuration that is impermanent, not the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

If the four great elements were impermanent, it would not be a conventional designation. If conventional designations were not of the nature [of reality], one would fall into the worldly view (*lokāyata*), seeing all natures as being merely verbal expressions and failing to see the manifestation of their own-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, furthermore, regarding the impermanence of form and appearance: this refers to those who claim that "form" itself is called impermanent.
Such people perceive only the impermanence of form and appearance, yet they do not recognize that the great elements (*mahābhūta*) are themselves impermanent phenomena.

If the great elements were impermanent, then all worldly discourse concerning mundane affairs would be impossible. Yet, if such discourse on mundane affairs does indeed occur, [it follows that the great elements must be permanent].
They fall into the faction of the Lokāyata heresy; for while they claim that all phenomena are merely names, they nevertheless perceive the intrinsic characteristics of the self-nature of phenomena.
[The Tang Translation states: "That 'form is impermanent' means that this refers to the impermanence of shape, not of the great elements."
Regarding the element-lineage (*gotra*): if even the great elements (*mahābhūta*) were impermanent, then there would be no worldly affairs.

One should know that where there are no worldly affairs, one falls into the Lokāyata view, because it perceives all phenomena as being merely verbal designations for the characteristics of their own-nature (*svalakṣaṇa*).

Regarding impermanence as transformation (*pariṇāma-anityatā*): this refers to the manifestation of a different state of form (*rūpa*) that is not the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). It is like gold being fashioned into an ornament;

while the ornament manifests through transformation, the nature of the gold itself is not destroyed. Rather, it is only the spatial configuration of the ornament that is destroyed. The same applies to the transformation of other natures and so forth.

[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, regarding "impermanence as transformation," this refers to seeing the various differing characteristics of all forms, yet not the transformation of the great elements themselves.
It is like seeing gold fashioned into ornaments: although the shape and appearance have transformed, the essence of the gold remains unchanged.
The transformation of other phenomena is likewise so.
[The Tang Translation: Regarding transformational impermanence: this refers to the transformation of the substance of form (*rūpa*), and not of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
For example, when gold is fashioned into ornaments, the ornaments undergo change while the gold itself remains unaltered; this case is likewise so.

Such are the various false conceptions of the non-eternalism held by the outsiders. When the fire burns the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are not burned.
If each of these specific characteristics were to perish, then the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) produced from the four great elements would necessarily be severed.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, in this way, the heterodox teachers falsely discriminate and perceive phenomena as impermanent.
Fire does not burn the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), nor does it burn their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because those primary elements possess distinct intrinsic natures.
Mahāmati, the heterodox teachers say that if fire were able to burn the primary elements, then those primary elements would be annihilated; therefore, it does not burn them.
[The Tang Translation: "Mahāmati, such various non-Buddhists as these falsely discriminate and perceive impermanence.
They assert: 'Fire cannot burn the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the great elements; they merely disperse from one another.
If fire were able to burn them, then both the primary elements (*bhūta*) and their derivatives (*bhautika*) would be utterly annihilated.'"
Mahāmati, in my teaching, arising is neither eternal nor non-eternal. Why is this? It is because external objects are not established as real;

I teach that the three realms of existence are mind-only (*cittamātra*), and do not speak of the arising and ceasing of various marks, nor of the distinctions among the four great elements and their derivative forms.
One should understand that the two kinds of imagined things—the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*)—are both false.
[The Buddha said: "Perception. It is free from the two kinds of views regarding external existence and non-existence.
[Wei Translation: "Mahāmati, I say that the Great [Self] and all sense-objects are neither eternal nor impermanent. Why is this?"
I do not say that external objects exist. I teach that the three realms are merely one's own mind;

I do not say that the various marks (lakṣaṇa) are real. Therefore, I speak of them as neither arising nor ceasing. They are merely the combination of the causes and conditions of the four great elements (mahābhūta);
neither the elements nor the sensory objects (viṣaya) are substantially existent dharmas. This is because the deluded mind discriminates these two kinds [of subject and object].
One grasps the dharma of the grasper and is able to know the two kinds of discrimination as they truly are; therefore, one is free from the marks of the views of external existence and non-existence.
[Tang Translation] Mahāmati, I say that all dharmas are neither permanent nor impermanent. Why is this? Because one does not grasp at the external.
Because it is the Dharma; because the three realms are mind-only; because various characteristics are not spoken of;
because the various distinctions of the great elements, their natures, and their locations are neither produced nor extinguished; because there is no distinction between the creator and the created;
because both the nature of the grasper and the grasped arise entirely from conceptual construction; and because one knows the nature of the two graspings as they truly are.

Those who realize that the measure of what appears to one's own mind is but a false construction (vikalpa) give rise to thought and mental activity; it is not that they do not engage in such activity.
Free from the false construction of a self-nature or a lack of nature within the mind, all dharmas—mundane, supramundane, and the supreme supramundane—are neither eternal nor impermanent.
Those who do not realize that these are the measure of what appears to their own minds fall into the continuity of dualistic extremes and evil views; this is the case for all non-Buddhists.
One awakens to one's own false imaginings; these ordinary people have no fundamental basis.
That which is called the mundane, the supramundane, and the supreme supramundane arises from the discourse on false imaginings; it is not something perceived by the ignorant and deluded.

[Wei Translation] It is solely the activity of the conceptualization of one’s own mind that is called "arising," yet karma does not arise, because it is free from the dualistic conceptualization of existence and non-existence.
Mahāmati, why is it neither eternal nor non-eternal?
Because there are mundane and supramundane dharmas of the highest order; therefore, it cannot be said to be eternal. Why?
Therefore, they are not impermanent, because one can realize that these are merely the perceptions of one’s own mind’s discrimination; for this reason, they are not impermanent.
Yet, the various non-Buddhists fall into false views by clinging to the two extremes, failing to understand that they are the false discriminations of their own minds.
It is not that the noble ones discriminate impermanence. Mahāmati, all dharmas in total...
There are three kinds. What are these three? First, the characteristics of worldly dharmas; second, the characteristics of supramundane dharmas;

and third, the characteristics of the most supreme dharmas that transcend the world. Although various dharmas are taught by relying on words and speech, ordinary beings do not perceive or understand them.

[The Tang Translation: Because one thoroughly realizes that [all things] are merely manifestations of one's own mind, and because one is free from the two views of external existence and non-existence;
being free from the view of existence and non-existence, one does not conceptualize the agent and the object created.
Mahāmati, all dharmas—mundane, supramundane, and those superior to the supramundane—are merely one's own mind; they are neither eternal nor impermanent. It is impossible...
One thoroughly understands that [these views] fall into the evil views of the two extremes held by non-Buddhists.
Mahāmati, all non-Buddhists are unable to comprehend these three kinds of dharmas; the realm of linguistic discrimination is not something that ordinary, foolish people can know.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

"Detached from the created, as well as from differences in form and location, and regarding nature and color as impermanent—these are the deluded false imaginings of the outsiders. All natures are indestructible; the Great Elements abide in their own self-nature.
Yet the outsiders harbor notions of impermanence, submerged in various views. Those various outsiders lack [true understanding]."
If birth were to cease, the nature of the Great Elements would be eternal; what then would be meant by the perception of impermanence? All is merely the measure of the mind (*cittamātra*).
Two kinds of mind revolve: the grasper (*grāhaka*) and the grasped (*grāhya*). There is no self (*ātman*) nor anything belonging to a self (*ātmīya*).
Brahmā is the root of the tree; its branches extend everywhere. Thus have I taught: it is solely that measure of the mind.
[Wei Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:

"Free from initial creation and distinct from form and characteristics, 'The impermanent' is a name for existing things—thus do the non-Buddhists falsely discriminate. All phenomena have no cessation;
the primary elements abide in their own nature. Falling into various views, the non-Buddhists proclaim impermanence. Those various non-Buddhists say..."
Dharmas are neither born nor extinguished; the great elements are themselves eternal. What dharma is impermanent?
All worlds are but mind, yet the mind perceives two objects: the grasped and the grasper. The dharmas of "self" and "mine" do not exist.
The dharmas of the three realms, from the highest to the lowest—I say they are all mind. Apart from these mental dharmas, nothing else can be found.
[The Tang Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse: "Abandoning what was first created, The form undergoes transformation;

Material things and so forth are impermanent— Such are the false discriminations of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). All phenomena are without destruction; The primary elements abide in their own nature.
The various views of the non-Buddhists Thus speak of impermanence. All those multitudes of non-Buddhists..."
I speak of neither arising nor ceasing; the nature of the great elements is itself eternal. What dharma could be impermanent?
Both the grasper and the grasped appear from the mind; all is but mind. There is no self and nothing belonging to a self.
The dharmas such as Brahmā and others—I say they are but mind. Apart from the mind, nothing at all can be found.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, we pray that you will explain for us the sequential continuity of the cessation-samādhi (nirodha-samāpatti) of all bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas.

If one is skilled in the characteristics of the sequential continuity of the cessation-samādhi, I and the other bodhisattvas shall never recklessly abandon the gateway to the bliss of cessation-samādhi, nor fall into [the state of] one-vehicle."
[All] Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and followers of external paths are deluded.
[Wei Translation: At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, we only pray that the World-Honored One will explain for us how all Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas enter..."

Regarding the sequential characteristics of the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*): if I and all other bodhisattvas skillfully master the expedient means for knowing the sequential characteristics of entering the attainment of cessation,
we shall not fall into the bliss of the samādhis and samāpattis of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or the attainment of cessation,
nor shall we fall into the delusions of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
The Dharma of Delusion.
[Tang Translation] At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for me the characteristics of the sequential continuity of the entry into cessation of all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, so that I and [others may understand it]."
Once the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have thoroughly understood this, their minds will not be deluded regarding the bliss of the samādhi of cessation;
they will not fall into the errors of the two vehicles or those of the various non-Buddhist paths.
The Buddha said to Mahāmati, "Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect well upon it; I shall explain it for you.

Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain it. The Buddha told Mahāmati, "Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the sixth stage, as well as śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the seventh stage and above enter meditative absorption in every thought-moment, free from..."
The meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) on the characteristics of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is not [the domain] of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.

All Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas fall into the meditative absorption that extinguishes the grasped and the grasper within the sphere of conditioned activity and conceptualization. Therefore, in the seventh stage, it is not the meditative absorption of mindfulness.

They do not attain the undifferentiated characteristic of all phenomena as their portion; rather, they attain various characteristics and natures, perceiving the wholesome and unwholesome natures of all phenomena.
This is the meditative attainment of signs (*nimitta-samāpatti*). Therefore, in the seventh stage, there is no meditative attainment of wholesome mindfulness (*kuśala-smṛti-samāpatti*).

Mahāmati, in the eighth stage, the conceptualizations of mind, thought, and consciousness (*citta-mano-manovijñāna-vikalpa-lakṣaṇa*) are extinguished for the Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas.
[Wei Translation] The Buddha addressed the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva, saying: "Excellent, excellent, excellent, Mahāmati!
Listen attentively, listen attentively; I shall explain it for you. Mahāmati Bodhisattva said to the Buddha: "Excellent, World-Honored One!
We shall indeed receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "From the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the sixth stage, the bodhisattva enters..."
Regarding the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*): Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas also enter the attainment of cessation.

However, Mahāmati, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas enter the attainment of cessation in every thought-moment throughout the seven stages (*bhūmi*), because all Bodhisattvas are able to remain far removed from the marks of existence and non-existence regarding all phenomena.
Mahāmati, Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are not able to [do so] in every thought-moment.

They contemplate entering the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). However, because Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas enter the absorption of cessation by means of conditioned activities (*saṃskṛta-karma*), they remain within the sphere of the grasped object (*grāhya*) and the grasping subject (*grāhaka*). For this reason, Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are unable to enter the absorption of cessation in every moment throughout the seventh stage;
for Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas give rise to thoughts of terror, fearing that they might fall [into lower realms].
