Because all dharmas lack distinct characteristics, one enters the meditative absorption of cessation by awakening to the various distinct characteristics of dharmas—whether they be existent or non-existent, wholesome or unwholesome—and by entering into their common and distinct characteristics. For this reason, the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas [do not attain it].
They are unable to enter the cessation samādhi (nirodha-samāpatti) at every thought-moment within the seventh stage because they lack the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).
Mahāmati, it is because in the seventh stage, bodhisattvas transform and extinguish the mind (*citta*), intellect (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
[The Tang Translation: The Buddha said: "Listen attentively; I shall explain this for you.

Mahāmati, when Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas reach the sixth stage, as well as Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, they enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). Bodhisattvas of the seventh stage enter it constantly in every thought-moment because they have abandoned the characteristics of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena;
this is not the case for those of the two vehicles. The two vehicles involve effort and fall into [the duality of] subject and object."

Regarding the grasped object: one does not perceive the undifferentiated characteristics of all dharmas; having realized the specific and general characteristics of the wholesome and unwholesome, one enters the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

For this reason, one cannot enter it constantly at every moment. Mahāmati, for Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage, as well as for Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, the conceptualizations of mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are extinguished.

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas from the first stage through the seventh stage contemplate the extent of mind, thought, and consciousness within the triple world. They are free from the notions of "I" and "mine.
Yet, they observe how their own false imaginings lead them to fall into the various external characteristics of objective natures;

how fools are caught by the two aspects of their own minds—the grasper and the grasped—and how they are directed toward ignorance and lack of awakening, being permeated by the habitual tendencies of false delusions and the evils of beginningless transgressions.

[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas from the first stage through the sixth stage perceive that the triple world is merely their own mind—consisting of the mind, the intellect, and consciousness—and is devoid of the dharmas of "self" and "what belongs to self. It is solely the discrimination of one's own mind;
they do not fall into the various marks of external phenomena. It is only due to the internal ignorance of ordinary beings that they fall into [such views].

Due to ignorance regarding the phenomena of the grasped and the grasper, those with dualistic views fail to realize that all dharmas arise from the habitual tendencies of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and afflictions (*kleśa*),
which have been produced by the false imaginings (*vikalpa*) of body, speech, and mind since beginningless time.
[The Tang Translation: From the first stage up to the sixth stage, one observes that all things within the three realms arise solely from the discrimination of mind, thought, and consciousness.
One sees that they are devoid of self and what belongs to a self, and that there are no various external phenomena.
Fools and ignorant ones do not understand this; due to the habitual perfuming of faults and evils since beginningless time, [they perceive] transformations produced within their own minds.
One gives rise to attachment toward the characteristics of the grasper and the grasped.
Mahāmati, the nirvāṇa of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas at the eighth stage is sustained by the awakening of samādhi.
Therefore, they do not enter parinirvāṇa due to the bliss of the gate of samādhi. If it were not so sustained, [they would enter] the stage of the Tathāgata.
They are not satisfied, for they abandon all conditioned activities for the sake of sentient beings; thus, the lineage of the Buddhas would be severed.

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, manifest the inconceivable and immeasurable merits of the Tathāgata so that śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—who, being led by the pursuit of their own pleasure, conceive the notion of nirvāṇa—may realize it is not true liberation.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, within the eighth stage, all bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas conceive the notion that they have entered nirvāṇa.
Mahāmati, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, by virtue of their own minds, samādhi, and the power of the Buddhas, [realize this].
They do not enter the gate of the bliss of samādhi, nor do they dwell in nirvāṇa, because they are not yet satisfied with the stage of a Tathāgata.

If those bodhisattvas were to abide in the portion of samādhi, they would cease their liberation of all sentient beings, sever the lineage of the Tathāgatas, and extinguish the family of the Tathāgatas.
It is for the sake of demonstrating the inconceivable realms of the Tathāgatas that [they do so]. Therefore...
They do not enter nirvana. Mahāmati, because śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas fall into the gate of the dharma of the bliss of samādhi, they give rise to the notion of nirvana.
[The Tang Translation: "Mahāmati, the samādhi attained by Bodhisattvas at the eighth stage is identical to the nirvāṇa of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
However, because they are sustained by the empowerment of all Buddhas, they do not enter nirvāṇa within that gate of samādhi.
If they were not so sustained, they would fail to transform and deliver all sentient beings and would be unable to fulfill the stage of a Tathāgata."
This would also sever the lineage of the Tathāgatas.

For this reason, the Buddhas proclaim the inconceivable great merits of the Tathāgatas, so that they may ultimately not enter nirvāṇa. Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas become attached to the bliss of samādhi;
therefore, they conceive the notion of nirvāṇa within that state.

Mahāmati, I have established the divisions of the seven stages (*bhūmi*) for the purpose of skillfully cultivating the characteristics of mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*);

for skillfully cultivating the grasping of "self" and "mine," as well as the selflessness of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharmanairātmya*), and the characteristics of arising and ceasing, and of specific and general marks (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*); and for skillfully [attaining] the four unhindered powers (*pratisaṃvid*), the power of certainty, and the successive continuity of the stages of the gateways of samādhi, thereby entering the dharmas of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*).
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the seventh stage, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).
They contemplate the perceptions of mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*); they remain far removed from the grasping at signs of "self" and "what belongs to self.

They contemplate the emptiness of self (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*); they contemplate common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) and specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), and they are well-versed in the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*).
The meaning of skillful means: mastery and certainty in entering the stages (*bhūmi*) and the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
[Tang Translation: Mahāmati, Bodhisattvas of the seventh stage are well able to examine the mind, thought, and consciousness, as well as the grasping at self and what belongs to self;
they [understand] the arising and ceasing of phenomena, their specific and general characteristics, and the four kinds of unimpeded eloquence.

Skillfully making determinations, they attain mastery over the gates of samādhi; gradually entering the various stages (*bhūmi*), they are endowed with the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
They ensure that Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not fail to perceive their own and common characteristics, nor fall into the evil paths of externalists at the seventh stage.

Therefore, the sequence of the stages is established. Mahāmati, in reality there is neither arising nor ceasing, apart from what is merely the manifestation of one's own mind—namely, the succession of the sequence of stages and the various activities within the triple world, which are not perceived by the ignorant.
That which is not perceived by the ignorant refers to what I and the Buddhas teach regarding the succession of the sequence of stages and the teaching of the triple world.
Various Practices.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, if I were not to explain the dharmas of the common and distinct characteristics of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
all bodhisattvas would not know the sequence of the stages as they truly are, and I fear they would fall into the errors of the heterodox paths.

Because they perceive phenomena as equal, I have explained the characteristics of the stages (*bhūmi*) in their proper sequence. Mahāmati, if a person enters the stages in sequence, they do not fall into other paths.

When I speak of the sequential characteristics of the stages, I mean that the sequence of the stages and the various modes of activity within the triple world are merely the perceptions of one’s own mind; yet ordinary beings neither realize nor understand this.

Because ordinary beings do not realize this, I and all the Buddhas have taught the sequential characteristics of the stages (*bhūmi*) and established the various modes of activity within the triple world (*tridhātu*).

[The Tang Translation: "Mahāmati, I have spoken thus because I fear that bodhisattvas might not skillfully understand specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), might not know the sequential progression of the stages (*bhūmi*), and might consequently fall into the various evil views of the non-Buddhists."
“Mahāmati, in reality there is neither arising nor ceasing, no succession of stages, and no coming and going between the three realms;
all of these are but what is seen by one’s own mind. Yet ordinary, ignorant people cannot understand this.
Because they do not know it, I and the Buddhas speak in such a manner.”
Furthermore, Mahāmati, the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and those on the eighth stage of the bodhisattvas are intoxicated by the intoxication of the bliss of the cessation-samādhi (nirodha-samādhi).

They are unskilled in the manifestation of their own minds as mere appearances (svacittadṛśyamātra), being obstructed by the habitual tendencies of self-characteristics and common characteristics (svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa-vāsanā).

They fall into the view of grasping at the non-existence of persons and phenomena (pudgala-dharmanairātmya-grāhadṛṣṭi) and harbor the notion of nirvāṇa through false imagination; this is not the awakening of the wisdom of true quiescence.

[Wei Translation] Furthermore, Mahāmati, because Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are intoxicated by their attachment to the gate of the bliss of the samādhi of cessation within the eighth Bodhisattva stage,
they are unable to properly understand that [all things] are but the manifestation of one's own mind. Consequently,
they fall into the obstacle of the habitual tendencies of specific and general characteristics, and they fall into the erroneous views regarding the non-self of persons and the non-self of phenomena.
They take the mind of discrimination to be called nirvāṇa, yet they are unable to know the quiescence of all phenomena.
[Tang Translation] Mahāmati, when śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas reach the eighth stage, they become intoxicated by the bliss of samādhi;

they have not yet been able to thoroughly understand that what is seen is but the manifestation of the mind alone, and they remain entangled in the habitual tendencies of self-characteristics and common characteristics.
Their minds are obscured. Clinging to the two kinds of selflessness, they give rise to the notion of nirvāṇa rather than the wisdom of true cessation.

Mahāmati, a bodhisattva perceives the bliss of the gate of the samādhi of cessation; through the fulfillment of their original vows, compassion, and great pity, they understand the ten inexhaustible phrases of differentiation and do not falsely conceptualize the notion of nirvāṇa.
For such a one, who has already attained nirvāṇa, false conceptualization does not arise.
Therefore, having abandoned the delusions of grasping and the grasped, one realizes that all phenomena are merely the manifestations of one's own mind; thus, delusions do not arise.
One does not fall into the delusions of attachment to the characteristics of external natures and self-natures as conceived by the mind, intellect, and consciousness.
Not arising from causes other than the Buddha-dharma, one follows the birth of wisdom and attains the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-realization.

[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, because all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas perceive the gateway to the bliss of the samādhi of tranquility, they recollect their original vows and, with great compassion, deliver all sentient beings.
Knowing the wisdom of the ten inexhaustible practices of reality, they do not immediately enter nirvāṇa. Mahāmati, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas remain far removed from...
The mind of false discrimination, when it is far removed from the spheres of the grasper and the grasped, is called entry into nirvana.
By means of knowledge in accordance with reality, one knows that all phenomena are nothing but one's own mind; therefore, the mind of discrimination does not arise.
For this reason, the bodhisattva does not grasp at mind, thought, or consciousness, nor does he cling to the characteristic of external phenomena as being truly existent.

It is not that they do not practice the Buddha-dharma; rather, relying on fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), they practice progressively in order to seek within their own bodies the wisdom of the stage of realization of a Buddha-Tathāgata.

[The Tang Translation: Mahāmati, when the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas behold the gate of the bliss of the samādhi of cessation, they immediately recollect their original vows and great compassion, and fully cultivate the ten inexhaustible phrases.
For this reason, they do not immediately enter nirvāṇa; because entering nirvāṇa would result in no further fruit, and because they have transcended the grasped and the grasper. They realize...
Because they have realized that all is mind-only; because they are free from conceptual discrimination regarding all phenomena;

and because they do not fall into the attachment to the intrinsic nature and characteristics of external objects within the mind, mentation, and consciousness. Yet, it is not that the true cause of the Buddha-dharma does not arise, for it arises in accordance with the movement of wisdom.
Thus, they attain the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-realization.
It is like a person who, while dreaming, employs skillful means to cross water but awakens before having crossed it. Having awakened, they reflect upon whether [the dream] was real or false;

it is neither real nor false. Likewise, all other beginningless perceptions, sounds, cognitions, and consciousnesses—arising from conceptualization, various habitual tendencies, and various forms and locations—manifest as dreams within the mind, thought, and mental consciousness, falling under the categories of existence and non-existence.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, it is like a person who, while dreaming, crosses a great ocean;
employing great skillful means, he desires to carry himself across, but before he has finished crossing, he suddenly awakens.
He then reflects: "Was this real, or was it illusory? He further reflects: "Such a phenomenon is neither real nor illusory; it was merely my own [dream]."
Due to the causal conditioning of false discrimination regarding unreal objects, one perceives various forms;
these inverted appearances, which do not transcend existence and non-existence, are seen within dreams due to the conditioning of the mental consciousness.
[The Tang Translation: "Mahāmati, it is like a person who, while dreaming, employs skillful means to cross a river; before having crossed, he awakens.
Having awakened, he reflects upon what he saw previously: 'Was this real, or was it false? He further reflects to himself: 'It is neither real nor false.
It was merely a matter of seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing—an habitual tendency (*vāsanā*) arising from the discrimination of things previously experienced.'"
It is merely what appears within the dream-like consciousness of one who is free from the notions of existence and non-existence.
Mahāmati, in this way, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva reaches the eighth bodhisattva stage, they perceive the arising of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

From the first stage, they progressively advance through to the seventh stage, where they perceive all phenomena as being like illusions and so forth, through skillful means, and thereby transcend and gather [all beings].
Having gathered the mind from the practice of discursive thought, one employs the skillful means of the Buddha-dharma to cause those who have not yet attained it to attain it.

Mahāmati, this is the indestructible skillful means of the bodhisattva’s nirvāṇa; by departing from mind, thought, and consciousness, one attains the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas. Mahāmati!
In the ultimate sense, there is no sequential continuity; it is taught as the dharma of the cessation of all conceptual construction regarding non-existence.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, it is likewise for the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas:

within the eighth stage, they perceive the discriminating mind, wherein the dharmas of the first through seventh stages share the same characteristic—equal and without distinction, like a dream or a magical illusion.
Free from all functional efforts and the conceptual mind of grasped object and grasping subject, one perceives the mind and mental factors.
Because this causes practitioners who have not yet attained the supreme Buddha-dharma to attain it, the superior practice of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is called *nirvāṇa*.
It is not the extinction of all phenomena that is called *nirvāṇa*. This, O Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, is [the true meaning].

Because one is far removed from the conceptual characteristics of mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), one attains the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Mahāmati, within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there is neither succession nor successive practice; all phenomena are quiescent, just like space.
[Chinese Translation] Mahāmati, it is the same for the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
From the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the seventh stage, they progressively advance until they enter the eighth stage and attain non-conceptualization (*avikalpa*).

They perceive all phenomena as being like illusions and the like, free from the duality of subject and object (*grāhya-grāhaka*). They behold the vast and powerful functioning of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), and diligently cultivate the Buddha-...

It causes those who have not yet realized the Dharma to realize it; by abandoning the false conceptualizations of mind, intellect, and consciousness, one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
This is the nirvāṇa attained by Bodhisattvas, not a state of annihilation. Mahāmati, within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there is no sequence and no continuity;
it is far removed from all objective realms and conceptual discrimination. This is what is called "quiescence" (*śānti*).
The Dharma of Cessation.

[Wei Translation] Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the World-Honored One has spoken of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas entering the gate of the bliss of cessation in the eighth bodhisattva stage. Furthermore, the Tathāgata has spoken of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas..."
The Buddha does not realize that these are merely the conceptual constructions of one's own mind.
Furthermore, he says that while the śrāvakas have attained the selflessness of persons (pudgala-nairātmya), they do not attain the emptiness of the selflessness of phenomena (dharma-nairātmya).

If this is the case, then even śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are unable to realize the dharmas of the first bhūmi, let alone the gate of the bliss of cessation in the eighth bhūmi. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "I now, for..."
"Mahāmati, you should explain this through your discernment. There are three kinds of śrāvakas. Regarding those who are said to enter the gate of the bliss of cessation in the eighth stage:
these are those who previously practiced the bodhisattva path but fell into the level of the śrāvaka;

they return to rely upon their original mind to practice the bodhisattva path and thus likewise enter the gate of the bliss of cessation in the eighth stage. They are not śrāvakas of cessation characterized by overweening pride."
Because they are unable to enter the bodhisattva practice, have never realized that the three realms are mind-only,
have never cultivated the various dharmas of a bodhisattva, and have never cultivated the practices of the perfections and the ten stages,
these śrāvakas who are fixed in their tranquility cannot realize the gate of the bliss of tranquility practiced by those bodhisattvas.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The measure of mind is non-existent; This is the dwelling and the Buddha-ground. The Buddhas of the three periods—past, future, and present— Have all proclaimed this."
The seventh stage is the Ground of Mind-Measure; the eighth is the Ground of Non-Existence. These two stages are called "Abidings. The Ground of Buddhahood is the most supreme.
It is the self-realized wisdom and purity; this is my own ground. It is the place of sovereign supremacy, pure and wondrously adorned.
It shines like a blazing fire, its radiance reaching everywhere; its fierce flames do not dazzle the eyes.

It transforms the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*) through its universal wheel, manifesting within the present three realms, or manifesting them at an earlier time. Therein it expounds the vehicles (*yāna*); all these are the stages of the Tathāgata.
The tenth stage is the first; the first is the eighth. The ninth is the seventh; the seventh is likewise the eighth. The second is the third;
the fourth is the fifth. The third is the sixth. When there is nothing at all, what sequence can there be?
[Wei Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse: "Mind-only exists; there are no external things.

The various practices and the stages of Buddhahood, The Buddhas of the past, future, and present— Throughout the three times, they have taught thus. The seven stages are the ground of mind; The eighth stage is non-existence.
The two stages are called the ground of practice; The remaining stages are called the ground of self. Realized within one's own body and purified."
It is called my own ground, the sovereign and most excellent place, the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
Radiant like a blazing flame, it emits wondrous rays of light, various and beautiful, delightful to behold. It manifests as the triple world and displays the forms of the triple world.
Some appear first through transformation; therein the various vehicles are taught. This is my own ground of mastery, wherein the ten stages reside.
The first stage becomes the eighth stage; the ninth stage becomes the seventh stage; the seventh stage becomes the eighth stage;
the second stage becomes the third stage; the fourth stage becomes the fifth stage; and the third stage becomes the sixth stage. What sequential order can there be in such quiescence?
Those śrāvakas who have attained certainty do not practice the bodhisattva path; yet those who enter the eighth stage together are, in fact, practicing the original bodhisattva path.
[The Tang Translation: At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse: "The various stages of abiding and the Buddha-ground are mind-only, without images;
this is what has been taught by all Buddhas of the past, future, and present. The seven stages involve the mind; the eighth stage is without images.
These two stages are called 'abiding'; the remainder is what I have attained. It is self-realized and pure."
This is my realm, the supreme abode of Maheśvara, adorned by Akaniṣṭha.
Like a great mass of fire with blazing, radiant flames, it manifests within the three realms of existence, delightful and cooling.
Some manifest through transformation, while others manifest as prior transformations; therein all vehicles are taught—all these are the stage of the Tathāgata. As for the ten stages...
The first becomes the eighth; the ninth becomes the seventh; the seventh again becomes the eighth; the second becomes the third;
the fourth becomes the fifth; the third becomes the sixth. When there is no characteristic, what sequence can there be?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, are the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the Samyaksaṃbuddhas, permanent or impermanent?
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "The Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the Samyaksaṃbuddhas, are neither permanent nor impermanent."
This means that both positions entail faults. If [the Tathāgata] were eternal, there would be the fault of being an agent; for all non-Buddhists assert that an eternal creator performs no action.

Therefore, because the faults of being both eternal and non-eternal, as well as being an agent, would apply, the Tathāgata is neither eternal nor non-eternal. If the Tathāgata were impermanent, there would be the fault of impermanence as an agent;
for the characteristics marked by the aggregates would lack intrinsic nature, and upon the destruction of the aggregates, he would necessarily be annihilated. However, ...
The Tathāgata is not subject to cessation.
[Wei Translation] At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, permanent or is he impermanent? The Buddha told the noble Mahāmati:
The Bodhisattva Mahāmati said: "Mahāmati, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is neither eternal nor impermanent.
Why is this? Because both extremes involve faults, Mahāmati. Both the extremes of existence and non-existence must entail errors, Mahāmati.
If one were to say that the Tathāgata is an eternal phenomenon, he would be identical to an eternal cause, Mahāmati, as the various non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) assert."
"Mahāmati, because atoms and all causes are eternal, they are not conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).

Therefore, Mahāmati, one cannot say that the Tathāgata is eternal, for he is not a conditioned phenomenon yet is spoken of as eternal. Furthermore, Mahāmati, one cannot say that the Tathāgata is impermanent."

To speak of impermanence is to equate it with conditioned phenomena. The five aggregates are the objects of perception, yet the perceiving subject does not exist because the five aggregates have ceased.
If the five aggregates were to cease, then the Buddhas and Tathāgatas would likewise have to cease;
however, the Buddhas and Tathāgatas are not subject to annihilation.
[The Tang Translation: At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, are the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, permanent or impermanent? The Buddha said:
"Mahāmati, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is neither permanent nor impermanent. Why is this? Because both positions entail faults. What are these faults, Mahāmati?"
If the Tathāgata were permanent, there would be the fault of being a creator; for all non-Buddhists assert that the creator is permanent.

If he were impermanent, there would be the fault of being something created; like the aggregates, he would be characterized as both the characteristic and the characterized, and would ultimately not exist at all.
Yet, the Buddha, the Tathāgata, is truly not subject to annihilation.
Mahāmati, all that is produced is impermanent, such as jars, garments, and so forth; thus, everything would fall into the error of being impermanent.
Furthermore, all the requisites and skillful means for omniscience would be rendered meaningless because they are produced.
Moreover, all that is produced would have to be the Tathāgata, since there would be no distinct causal nature. Therefore, Mahāmati, the Tathāgata is neither permanent nor impermanent.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, all things that are produced are impermanent. For example, jars, clothing, carts, houses, and mats made of grass and hair—all these are produced things;

therefore, they are impermanent. Mahāmati, if one were to say that everything is impermanent, then omniscience, the Omniscient One, and all spiritual merits would likewise have to be impermanent, as they are the same [in being produced].

Because all conditioned phenomena possess characteristics. Furthermore, there is another fault: if one were to say that everything is impermanent, then the Buddhas and Tathāgatas would necessarily be conditioned phenomena;
yet the Buddhas and Tathāgatas are not conditioned phenomena, because there is no further superior cause to be taught.
Therefore, I say that the Tathāgata is neither permanent nor impermanent.
[The Tang Translation: "Mahāmati, all things that are produced—such as jars, garments, and the like—are impermanent.
If this were so, the Tathāgata would incur the fault of impermanence; furthermore, the cultivation of merit and wisdom would all be empty and useless.
Moreover, all conditioned phenomena would be the Tathāgata, because there would be no other cause. Therefore, the Tathāgata is neither permanent nor impermanent."

Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Tathāgata is not eternal in the same manner as space. If he were eternal like space, there would be the fault that the various requisites for the noble wisdom of self-realization would be rendered purposeless.
Mahāmati, for example, space is neither eternal nor non-eternal;

because it is free from the faults of being eternal or non-eternal, identical or different, both or neither, or eternal and non-eternal, it is inexpressible. Therefore, the Tathāgata is not eternal. Furthermore...
Furthermore, Mahāmati, if the Tathāgata were an unarisen permanence, he would be like the horns of a rabbit or a horse;
because of the fault of being an unarisen permanence, skillful means would be purposeless, and because of the fault of being an unarisen permanence, the Tathāgata would not be permanent.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there is another way by which one knows the Tathāgata is permanent. Why is this? It is because the wisdom attained through uninterrupted realization is permanent. Thus...
[The Tathāgata] is eternal. [Wei Translation: Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Tathāgata is not eternal. Why?
Because even the nature of space does not possess the cultivation of various meritorious virtues. Mahāmati, for example, space is neither eternal nor non-eternal. Why?
For this reason, because it is free from permanence and impermanence, and because it does not fall into the categories of identity, difference, both, or neither;
existence, non-existence, neither existence nor non-existence; or permanence, impermanence, neither permanent nor impermanent—it is therefore beyond all faults and cannot be described.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, one must not say that the Tathāgata is permanent. Why is that?
If one says that [the Tathāgata] is eternal, it would be the same as the horns of rabbits, horses, camels, donkeys, tortoises, snakes, flies, fish, and so forth.
Therefore, one cannot say that the Tathāgata is eternal. Furthermore, Mahāmati, one must not say that the Tathāgata is eternal, for fear of falling into the eternalism of the unarisen.
For this reason, one cannot say that the Tathāgata is eternal. Furthermore, Mahāmati, there is yet another [point].
Dharma. Because of that Dharma, it can be said that the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is eternal. Why is this?
Because he has realized the eternal Dharma through his own internalized wisdom of realization. Therefore, it can be said that the Tathāgata is eternal.
Mahāmati, the Dharma of the internally realized wisdom of all Buddha-Tathāgatas is eternal, constant, cool, and unchanging.
[Chinese Translation] Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Tathāgata is not eternal.
If he were eternal, he would be like space, established without depending on causes. Mahāmati, for example, space is neither eternal nor non-eternal. Why?
Because it is free from all faults such as being eternal or non-eternal, being identical or different, or being both or neither, and so forth. Furthermore, Mahāmati...
Mahāmati, the Tathāgata is not permanent. If he were permanent, he would be unarisen, identical to the horns of a rabbit, a horse, a fish, or a snake.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, for another reason, he may also be said to be permanent. Why is this?
Because he realizes the permanent dharma through direct gnosis; since that realized gnosis is permanent, the Tathāgata is also permanent.
Mahāmati, whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, phenomena remain fixed. Śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all Tathāgatas dwell in the unconditioned;
they do not dwell in empty space, nor is this realized by foolish commoners, Mahāmati.

The wisdom attained by the Tathāgata is permeated by *prajñā*; it is not permeated by mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), or consciousness (*vijñāna*), nor by those aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*).
Mahāmati, all that exists within the three realms of existence is produced by unreal conceptualization;
the Tathāgata is not born from unreal, false conceptualization. Mahāmati, because of duality there is permanence and impermanence, not non-duality.
Non-duality is quiescence, because all phenomena lack the characteristic of dualistic arising.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, whether the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the Samyaksaṃbuddhas appear in the world or do not appear in the world, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is always thus;
the essence of phenomena is always thus; the norm of phenomena is always thus. Because...
That dharmatā has never been heard of nor ever seen by any śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and the like.
Such a nature of phenomena does not exist within empty space; yet, foolish ordinary beings (bāla-pṛthagjana) do not perceive or know it.
Mahāmati, the Buddhas and Tathāgatas receive their name based on that which is the wisdom of internal realization. Mahāmati, it is because they rely upon suchness-realizing wisdom (yathābhūta-jñāna).
One is named a Buddha by virtue of cultivation; it is not named through the perfuming of mind, thought, consciousness, ignorance, or the five aggregates.
Mahāmati, all that exists within the three realms is named through unreal conceptualization, discrimination, and frivolous discourse.
Mahāmati, as for the two kinds of unreal discrimination regarding phenomena, they are named "permanent" and "impermanent"; yet the Buddha-Tathāgata...
They do not fall into dualistic dharmas; they do not fall into the two extremes of the grasper and the grasped, because for the Tathāgata, who is quiescent, these two dharmas do not arise.
[Tang Translation] Mahāmati, the dharma-nature, the abiding of dharmas, and the fixed position of dharmas realized by all Buddha-Tathāgatas—[the Tathāgata...]
Whether the Tathāgatas appear in the world or do not appear, it remains eternally constant and unchanging.

It exists within all that is attained by the followers of the two vehicles and the non-Buddhists; it is not a mere emptiness or nothingness. Yet, it is not something that can be known by the ordinary and the ignorant.

Mahāmati, the Tathāgata receives his name because he has internally realized the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) through pure wisdom; it is not by means of the mind, the intellect, or mental objects.
The aggregates, elements, and sense-bases are designated based on the false habitual tendencies of consciousness. All three realms arise from false conceptual discrimination;

the Tathāgata does not arise from false conceptual discrimination. Mahāmati, if there were duality regarding permanence and impermanence, the Tathāgata would not be non-dual, for he has realized that all phenomena possess the characteristic of non-arising.

Therefore, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is neither eternal nor non-eternal. Mahāmati, as long as verbal conceptualization arises, there will be the fault of [clinging to] eternity or non-eternity.

For one whose conceptualizing awareness has ceased, who is free from the views of eternity and non-eternity held by the foolish, and whose wisdom is not unpeaceful, there is forever an absence of the perfuming of eternity, non-eternity, or that which is neither eternal nor non-eternal.
[Wei Translation] Therefore, Mahāmati, the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas cannot be said to be either permanent or impermanent.

Mahāmati, regarding all that can be spoken of as permanent or impermanent, those who have transcended all conceptual discrimination and reached its exhaustion cannot be said to grasp at the dharmas of permanence or impermanence. For this reason, I prohibit it.

All ordinary beings cannot differentiate between the permanent and the impermanent; however, those who have attained the truly quiescent Dharma exhaust all discrimination and no longer give rise to discrimination.

[The Tang Translation: Therefore, it is neither eternal nor non-eternal. Mahāmati, as long as there arises even the slightest verbal conceptualization, there will be the fault of [clinging to] eternity or non-eternity.
For this reason, you should eliminate these two types of dualistic discrimination so that not even the slightest remains.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: Those who possess various conceptual constructs fall into the errors of permanence and impermanence.
If one is free from discriminative cognition, one is forever detached from permanence and impermanence. From the positions they establish, there arise manifold meanings;
yet when one equally contemplates the measure of one's own mind, verbal expression is found to be unattainable.
[Wei Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:

"Free from permanence and impermanence, Neither permanent nor impermanent— Whoever perceives the Buddha in this way Shall not fall into the evil realms. To speak of permanence or impermanence Is to render all virtues false;
It is the discrimination of the ignorant. To refute the teaching of permanence and impermanence, All those who establish such doctrines..."
There are various faults; if one can perceive that there is only mind, one does not fall into those faults.
[Tang Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:

"Far removed from permanence and impermanence, yet manifesting as permanent and impermanent—constantly observing the Buddha in this way, one does not give rise to wrong views. As for those who hold to permanence or impermanence, they accumulate [faults]."
All of these are without benefit. To eliminate discursive conceptualization, I do not speak of permanence or impermanence; indeed, whatever is established is entirely erroneous.
If one perceives that there is only one’s own mind, then there will be no contradiction or dispute.
The Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra: A Combined Translation, Volume Four, Part Two (of the first half).
Translated by the Śramaṇa Yuánkē of Zhōudū during the Zhōng Period of the True Lineage of Línjì in the Ming Dynasty.
The Fourth Chapter on the Heart of All Buddha-Speech, Part Two.

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I pray that the World-Honored One will further explain for me the arising and ceasing of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*).
Since there is no self therein, who is it that arises and who is it that ceases? It is only the deluded who rely upon arising and ceasing."
They do not perceive the exhaustion of suffering, nor do they recognize nirvana. The Buddha said, "Excellent! Listen attentively; I shall explain it for you.
Mahamati replied to the Buddha, "Yes, we shall receive your instruction."
[Wei Translation] At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again requested of the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, I pray that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha will explain for me; Sugata, please explain for me the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas).
World-Honored One, if there is no self, who is it that arises and who is it that ceases? World-Honored One, all..."
Ordinary beings dwell in accordance with arising and ceasing and do not perceive the exhaustion of suffering; therefore, they do not know the characteristics of nirvāṇa.
The Buddha said to the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva: "Excellent, excellent! Excellent, Mahāmati! Listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you.
Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying: "Excellent, World-Honored One! We shall indeed receive your instruction."
[The Tang Translation: At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for me the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and bases (āyatanas). If there is no self, who arises and who ceases? Yet all ordinary beings rely upon arising and ceasing;

they do not seek the exhaustion of suffering nor realize nirvāṇa. The Buddha said: "Mahāmati," *Note: This translation reflects the structure and content of the provided Chinese text, which corresponds to the opening section of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*. The Sanskrit terms are provided in their standard IAST transliteration.*
"Listen attentively, listen attentively; I shall explain it for you.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "The Tathāgata-garbha is the cause of both the wholesome and the unwholesome.

It is capable of universally producing all realms of existence, just as an actor manifests various roles. Yet, being devoid of 'I' and 'mine,' because they do not realize this, [the three conditions] come together."
It arises through the conjunction of conditions and expedient means. Externalists, failing to realize this, falsely calculate it to be a creator.

Perfumed by beginningless, false, and evil habits, it is called the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness). It gives rise to the ground where ignorance dwells and coexists with the seven consciousnesses. Like the body of ocean waves, it constantly arises without interruption.
It is free from the fault of impermanence and free from the doctrine of self; its intrinsic nature is stainless and ultimately pure.
[Wei Translation] The Buddha told Mahāmati: "The Tathāgata-garbha is the cause of both the wholesome and the unwholesome;
therefore, it does not act as the causal condition for birth and death within the six realms of existence. It is like a skilled performer who displays various feats.
Because sentient beings rely upon the Tathāgata-garbha, there is birth and death within the five destinies. Mahāmati, the Tathāgata-garbha is free from 'I' and 'mine'."
The non-Buddhists and others do not know or perceive this; therefore, the causes and conditions for birth and death within the three realms are not severed.
Mahāmati, because the various non-Buddhists falsely conceptualize a self, they are unable to see the Tathāgatagarbha as it truly is.
This is because, since beginningless time, those non-Buddhists have been habituated by the false attachments to various forms of frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*). Mahāmati!

The ālayavijñāna is called the tathāgatagarbha; it coexists with ignorance and the seven consciousnesses, like the waves of the great ocean that are never interrupted, arising simultaneously with the body.
It is free from the fault of impermanence and free from the fault of a self, being pure by nature.
[The Tang Translation: Mahāmati, the Tathāgatagarbha is the cause of both the wholesome and the unwholesome; it is capable of universally producing and manifesting all realms of existence.
It is like an actor who transforms and appears in various states of existence, yet remains free from the notions of "I" and "mine.
Because of non-awakening, when the three conditions harmonize, the fruit arises. The heterodox teachers do not understand this and cling to it as a creator. It is beginningless and illusory.
Perfumed by evil habits, it is called the *ālayavijñāna*. It gives rise to the seven consciousnesses upon the ground of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*).

Just as there are waves upon the great ocean, its substance continues in a constant, uninterrupted flow. Its fundamental nature is pure, free from the fault of impermanence, and devoid of the doctrine of a self.
The remaining consciousnesses arise and perish. Within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and its associates, there are seven [consciousnesses] at every moment.

Due to unreal conceptualization (*abhūta-parikalpa*), they grasp at various objects and their diverse forms and locations, calculating and clinging to names and characteristics (*nāma-rūpa*). Failing to realize that these are manifestations of one’s own mind, they perceive external forms;

failing to realize the nature of suffering and pleasure, they do not attain liberation. Bound by the entanglements of names and characteristics, they give rise to craving and continue to produce craving, whether through causes or...

As they focus their attention, those various faculties of sensation cease and do not arise in succession; no longer perceiving pleasure or pain through the false imaginings of their own minds, they enter the fourth dhyāna, the meditative attainment of the cessation of sensation and perception (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

[Wei Translation] As for the remaining seven consciousnesses—namely, the mind (*manas*), the intellect (*manas*), and the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*)—they do not abide from moment to moment and are dharmas subject to arising and ceasing.

These seven consciousnesses arise from those false causes; they are unable to discern all phenomena as they truly are because they contemplate characteristics such as high and low, long and short, and because they cling to names and appearances.
Consequently, they cause one's own mind to perceive the marks of form.

Therefore, because one is able to experience pleasure and pain; because it is the cause for abandoning and attaining liberation; because the name and form arising from causes lead to the falling into afflictions and craving;
because the various faculties are extinguished based on those causal recollections; because they do not arise in succession;

and because other mental discriminations do not give rise to the sensations of pleasure and pain—one enters the *saṃjñāvedayitanirodhasamāpatti* (the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling) after having entered the *asaṃjñisamāpatti* (the attainment of non-perception). Thus, one enters the three [attainments].
Māvatī’s fourth dhyāna. [Tang Translation:
The remaining seven consciousnesses—the mental faculty (*manas*) and the cognitive faculty (*vijñāna*)—arise and perish from moment to moment.

With false conceptualization as the cause and objective appearances as the condition, they arise through conjunction. Failing to realize that form and other phenomena are manifestations of one's own mind, they cling to and name them.
The arising of signs gives rise to feelings of pleasure and pain; this is called the entanglement of signs.

Since it arises from craving and in turn gives rise to craving, if the causes and the objects of perception—the roots of all grasping—are extinguished and do not continue to arise, one who discriminates feelings of pleasure and pain through their own wisdom [is liberated].
Some attain the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), and some attain the four dhyānas;

they possess a skillful understanding of the truths and liberation, and practitioners conceive the notion of liberation. Yet, that which is neither separated from nor transformed is called the *tathāgatagarbha* or the *ālayavijñāna*.
The seven consciousnesses continue to flow and do not cease. Why is this? Because those [seven] arise by taking the various consciousnesses as their objective conditions (*ālambana*).

This is not the sphere of practice for śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; they do not realize selflessness. The aggregates, elements, and sense-bases arise through the grasping of both specific and general characteristics.
When one perceives the tathāgatagarbha, the five dharmas, the three natures, and the selflessness of persons and phenomena, these are extinguished.
[Wei Translation] True Reality is liberation. If a practitioner gives rise to the mark of liberation, it is because they do not transform or extinguish false marks.
Mahāmati, the Tathāgatagarbha-ālayavijñāna does not reside within the ālayavijñāna;
therefore, the seven kinds of consciousness have arising and ceasing, whereas the Tathāgatagarbha-ālayavijñāna is neither born nor extinguished. Why is this? Because that...
The seven kinds of consciousness arise based on various objects through recollection and observation.

These objects of the seven consciousnesses cannot be realized by any śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or practitioners of external paths, because they do not know the selflessness of persons as it truly is;
because they grasp at phenomena characterized by commonality and particularity; and because they perceive the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and other such dharmas. Great...

Wisdom. One sees the essential characteristics of the five dharmas within the Tathāgatagarbha as they truly are; because of the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya), one knows with reality that [the self] does not arise.
[Tang Translation: Or again, having skillfully entered the various truths and liberations, one falsely gives rise to the notion that one has attained liberation.

In reality, however, the name "ālayavijñāna" within the Tathāgatagarbha has not yet been relinquished or transformed. If the ālayavijñāna did not exist, the seven consciousnesses would cease to function.
Why is this? Because they arise dependent upon it as their cause and object-condition (*ālambana*).
Nevertheless, this is not an objective realm known by any non-Buddhists, followers of the two vehicles, or practitioners, for they understand only the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*).

Nature (*dhātu*). Because one grasps the specific and general characteristics within the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, if one perceives the Tathāgatagarbha, the five dharmas, the self-nature, and the selflessness of all phenomena, one proceeds through the stages in successive order and cannot be shaken by the views of other outsiders; this is called abiding as a bodhisattva.
On the Immovable Ground (Acalā-bhūmi), one attains the bliss of the thirteen gates of the path of samādhi, sustained by the awakening of samādhi.
One contemplates the inconceivable Buddha-dharma and one’s own vows; yet, one does not grasp the bliss of the gates of samādhi nor the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).

One proceeds toward the noble realization of self-awakening, a path practiced exclusively by oneself and not shared with any śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or non-Buddhists, thereby attaining the ten natures of the noble ones.
The Way, as well as the body, wisdom, and mind-born [bodies], are free from the practice of samādhi.
Therefore, Mahāmati, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who desires to seek supreme progress should purify the names "Tathāgatagarbha" and "Ālayavijñāna."
[Wei Translation] Because the various stages (bhūmis) are progressively and harmoniously integrated, other heterodox outsiders with incorrect views are unable to discern them.

Mahāmati, when a bodhisattva dwells in the Immovable Stage (Acalā-bhūmi), at that time they attain ten kinds of samādhi-gates as their primary focus, and they attain immeasurable and boundless samādhis.
Relying on the empowerment of the Buddha through these samādhis, they perform observation.

By virtue of the inconceivable qualities of all Buddha-dharmas and the power of their own original vows, they shield and protect the gateway of samādhi and the realm of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

Having so shielded it, they enter the true realm of the dharma realized through noble wisdom within their own internal bodies—a realm unlike that observed through the practices of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or non-Buddhists. At that time, they transcend those ten kinds [of dharmas].
The Noble Path enters into the Tathāgata’s mind-born body and wisdom-body because it is free from the mental states of effortful meditative concentration.
Therefore, Mahāmati, those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who wish to realize the supreme Dharma—
the Tathāgatagarbha and the Ālayavijñāna— should practice so as to bring them to purity.
[The Tang Translation: They gradually turn and cease according to the sequence of the stages (*bhūmi*). They are not moved by the evil views of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Abiding in the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*), they attain ten kinds of gates to the bliss of samādhi.

Sustained by all Buddhas through the power of samādhi, they contemplate the inconceivable Buddha-dharmas and the power of their original vows. They do not dwell in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) nor in [mere] samādhi.
One delights in attaining the wisdom of self-realization, which is not shared with those of the two vehicles or the various non-Buddhists.
One attains the path of the ten noble lineages and the wisdom-body of mental transformation, which is free from all conditioned formations.
Therefore, Mahāmati, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who desires to attain the supreme Dharma should purify the designations "Tathāgatagarbha" and "Ālayavijñāna."

Mahāmati, if there were no storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) called the Tathāgatagarbha, there would be neither arising nor ceasing. Mahāmati, yet all ordinary beings and noble ones alike possess arising and ceasing;
therefore, practitioners, through the noble wisdom of self-realization, abide in the bliss of the present dharma and do not abandon skillful means.
Mahāmati, this Tathāgata-garbha, the storehouse-consciousness (ālayavijñāna), is what is perceived by the mental conceptions of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Although it is pure by nature, because it is shrouded by adventitious defilements, they still perceive it as impure; this is not the case for the Tathāgatas, Mahāmati.
For the Tathāgatas, it is a manifest object, like looking at an āmalaka fruit held in the palm of one's hand.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, if the Tathāgatagarbha and the ālayavijñāna were called "non-existent," then apart from the ālayavijñāna there would be neither arising nor ceasing.
It is because all ordinary beings and noble ones rely upon that ālayavijñāna that there is arising and ceasing.
Because they rely upon the ālayavijñāna, practitioners enter [into realization].
This is realized through the noble practice within one's own body; it is the practice of bliss in the present life, pursued without ceasing.

Mahāmati, this realm of the Tathāgata’s mind—the *ālayavijñāna*, the *tathāgatagarbha*—cannot be discerned by any śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or followers of external paths. Why is this? Because the *tathāgatagarbha* is characterized by purity.
It is defiled and impure by the stains of adventitious afflictions.
[Tang Translation: Mahāmati, if there were no such thing as the Tathāgatagarbha, namely the ālayavijñāna, then there would be no arising and ceasing.
Yet, both ordinary worldlings and noble ones alike experience arising and ceasing. Therefore, all practitioners...
Although they perceive internal objects and abide in the bliss of the present life, they do not relinquish their courageous diligence.
Mahāmati, this Tathāgatagarbha, the ālayavijñāna, is pure by nature; it becomes impure when defiled by adventitious stains.

All followers of the two vehicles and the various non-Buddhists speculate and give rise to views regarding it, yet they cannot realize it through direct manifestation. Regarding this, the Tathāgata [has distinguished...]
It is clearly manifest, as if observing an *āmalaka* fruit in the palm of one's hand.

Mahāmati, by means of my supernormal power (*ṛddhibala*), I have established this principle so that Queen Śrīmālā and those bodhisattvas who are endowed with sharp and perfected wisdom may proclaim and expound upon the Tathāgatagarbha and the Ālayavijñāna, which arises simultaneously with the seven consciousnesses.
The Śrāvakas are attached to their views; they perceive the selflessness of persons and phenomena.
Therefore, Lady Śrīmālā, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, spoke of the realm of the Tathāgata, which is not the realm of Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or outsiders.

The Tathāgatagarbha and Ālayavijñāna are the realm of wisdom belonging only to the Buddhas and to other Bodhisattvas of sharp intelligence who rely upon the meaning. For this reason, you and the other Bodhisattvas...
O Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, you should diligently cultivate and study the Tathāgatagarbha, which is the Ālayavijñāna; do not merely take satisfaction in hearing and understanding it.

[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, based on this meaning, and relying upon Queen Śrīmālā and upon Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas of profound wisdom, I have taught the Tathāgatagarbha-Ālayavijñāna, which arises together with the seven kinds of consciousness.
This is called the characteristic of transformation and cessation. For the sake of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others, it demonstrates the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).
Addressing Śrīmālā, he said: "The tathāgatagarbha is the domain of the Tathāgatas. Mahāmati, the tathāgatagarbha-consciousness, the ālayavijñāna, is the domain [of the Tathāgatas].
I shall now, for you and for the bodhisattvas who possess profound wisdom, clearly analyze and distinguish it."
These two kinds of dharmas cannot be fully understood by other śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas,
or followers of external paths who are attached to names. Therefore, Mahāmati,
you and the other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should study this dharma.

[The Tang Translation: "Mahāmati, for the sake of Queen Śrīmālā and other Bodhisattvas of profound, subtle, and pure wisdom, I have taught that the Tathāgatagarbha is called the Ālayavijñāna, which arises together with the seven consciousnesses, so as to enable all Śrāvakas to perceive the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya).
Mahāmati, this realm of the Buddha taught to Queen Śrīmālā is not the domain of non-Buddhists or those of the two vehicles."
“Mahāmati, this Tathāgata-garbha ālayavijñāna is the realm of the Buddhas;
it is the sphere of activity for you and other Bodhisattvas of pure wisdom who accord with the true meaning.
It is not the sphere of activity for any non-Buddhists who cling to words or for those of the two vehicles. Therefore, you and all the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, regarding the Tathāgata...”
One should diligently observe the ālayavijñāna, the storehouse consciousness; do not merely hear of it and then give rise to the thought that you have attained enough.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "The profound Tathāgatagarbha Coexists with the seven consciousnesses.
Arising from two kinds of grasping, The wise one remains far removed from them. Like images appearing in a mirror, The mind is beginningless."
Habitual tendencies are what is perfumed. One who observes according to reality sees that all phenomena are ultimately without substance. It is like a fool looking at the finger pointing at the moon;
he gazes at the finger but does not see the moon. Those who are attached to names and words do not perceive my true reality.
The mind acts as the stage manager, the intellect is like the director, the five consciousnesses are the assistants, and false conceptualization is the audience watching the performance.
[Wei Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse: The profound *tathāgatagarbha* arises together with the seven consciousnesses.
When one grasps at two dharmas, birth occurs; when one knows them as they truly are, there is no birth. Like images appearing in a mirror, the mind is perfumed by beginningless habitual tendencies.
For one who observes according to reality, all objects are entirely empty and non-existent. It is like a fool looking at the finger pointing at the moon. Thus one should contemplate.
One who points does not see the moon; one who clings to names does not see my true reality.

The mind is like a skilled acrobat, and the intellect is like a cunning rogue. The mental consciousness and the five sensory consciousnesses falsely grasp at objects, like an ensemble of performers deceiving the common person.
[The Tang Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse: "The profound Tathāgatagarbha coexists with the seven consciousnesses;

Through attachment to the two kinds [of self], birth occurs. If one understands this, one is far removed from them. Perfumed by habitual tendencies since beginningless time, It appears in the mind like a reflected image.
If one can contemplate according to reality, The characteristics of objects will all cease to exist. It is like a fool looking at the finger pointing at the moon. Observing...
One who points at the moon does not see the moon itself; likewise, those who are attached to words do not perceive my true reality.
The mind is like a stage performer, the intellect is like the assistant director, the five consciousnesses are its companions, and conceptualization is the audience watching the performance.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for me the ultimate characteristics of the five dharmas, the self-natures, consciousness, and the two kinds of selflessness through detailed analysis.

By means of this, I and the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas may, throughout all stages in their successive continuity, analyze these dharmas and enter into all Buddha-dharmas. To enter into all Buddha-dharmas—”
"Up to the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-awakening," the Buddha told Mahāmati, "listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon this well.

Mahāmati replied to the Buddha, "Yes, I shall receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati, "The five dharmas, the three natures (*svabhāva*), the consciousnesses, the two kinds of selflessness, and the characteristics of the stages of discrimination are:
namely, name, appearance, conceptualization, right knowledge, and suchness (*tathatā*). If a practitioner cultivates..."

They enter the Tathāgata’s own realization of the noble path, which is free from views of annihilationism, eternalism, existence, non-existence, and so forth. They dwell in the presence of the meditative attainment of happiness in the present life.

Mahāmati, it is the deluded imagination of ordinary people—not that of the noble ones—that fails to realize that the five dharmas, the three natures, the two forms of selflessness, and the external objects that appear as manifestations of one's own mind are merely the projections of one's own mind. It is not the case for the noble ones.
[Wei Translation] At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again requested the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, I pray that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, will explain for me;
Sugata, please explain for me the essential characteristics of the five dharmas and the distinct modes of the two kinds of selflessness. If I and all other bodhisattvas..."

Having attained excellent knowledge of the essential characteristics of the five dharmas and the distinct characteristics of the two kinds of selflessness, one practices these dharmas and enters sequentially into all the stages (*bhūmi*).
By practicing these dharmas, one is able to enter into all the Buddha-dharmas.
To enter the Buddha-dharmas means, ultimately, to be able to enter the stage of the Tathāgata’s own internally realized wisdom (*pratyātma-adhigama-jñāna-bhūmi*). Thus said the Buddha.
He addressed the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva, saying: "Excellent, excellent! Well done, Mahāmati! Listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you.
Mahāmati Bodhisattva said: "Excellent, World-Honored One! We shall indeed receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"I shall explain for you the five dharmas, the characteristics of reality, the two kinds of selflessness, and the various modes of their differentiation."
Mahāmati, what are these five dharmas? First, name; second, appearance; third, discrimination; fourth, correct gnosis; and fifth, suchness.
By means of internal cultivation and practice, one realizes the wisdom of the noble ones, which is free from the views of annihilationism and eternalism.
Because those who practice according to reality as it is enter the gate of practice consisting of the bliss of samādhi and samāpatti, Mahāmati, all...
Ordinary beings do not awaken to or understand the essential nature and characteristics of the five dharmas or the two kinds of selflessness;
they perceive external objects solely through their own minds. Consequently, they give rise to a mind of discrimination, which is not the way of the sages.
[The Tang Translation] At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for me the characteristics of the distinctions between the five dharmas, the self-natures, the various consciousnesses, and non-self.
Having thoroughly understood these, I and the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas shall gradually cultivate the stages, be endowed with all the Buddha-dharmas, and reach the state of a Tathāgata."
Regarding the stage of self-realization, the Buddha said: "Listen attentively, and I shall explain it for you.
Mahāmati, there are five dharmas, the three natures, the various consciousnesses, and non-self—namely, name, appearance, discrimination, right knowledge, and suchness.

If a practitioner contemplates these dharmas, they will enter the realm of the Tathāgata’s self-realization, remain far removed from views of permanence and annihilation, existence and non-existence, and so forth, and attain [liberation]."
“Mahāmati, this is the samādhi of profound bliss in the present life. Fools and ordinary people do not understand the five dharmas, the self-natures, the various consciousnesses, and selflessness;
they perceive external objects within what is manifested by the mind and give rise to discrimination, whereas the noble ones do not.”
Mahāmati said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, how is it that the deluded imaginings of fools arise, while those of the noble ones do not?
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Fools are attached to conventional numbers, names, and signs; their minds flow and disperse accordingly.

Having dispersed, they fall into various forms and appearances, descending into the views of 'self' and 'what belongs to self. They long for and become attached to exquisite forms. Once attached, they are shrouded by ignorance."
Thus, stained attachment arises. Once stained attachment has arisen, karma produced by greed, hatred, and delusion is accumulated.

Having been accumulated, one entangles oneself with false imaginings like a silkworm spinning its cocoon, falling into the ocean of birth and death and the vast wilderness of the various realms of existence, like a waterwheel drawing from a well.

Because of ignorance, one cannot know that [all things] are like illusions, mirages, or the moon reflected in water, and that their intrinsic nature is devoid of self and what belongs to a self; thus, one gives rise to [the notion of] oneness.
All unreal conceptualizations are devoid of both the characteristic and that which is characterized, as well as arising, abiding, and ceasing; they arise from the conceptualization of one's own mind.
They do not arise from Īśvara, time, atoms, or primordial matter (*pradhāna*). Foolish worldlings follow after names and characteristics.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, why is it that ordinary people give rise to discriminative thoughts, whereas noble ones do not?
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "All ordinary people cling to names and appearances, and accordingly give rise to dharmas."
Having followed the nature of arising and perceived various signs, one falls into a mind of false views regarding "self" and "what belongs to self.
One becomes attached to the complete characteristics of all phenomena; having become attached, one enters the realm of the darkness of ignorance.

Having entered that realm of obstruction, one gives rise to a mind of craving; having given rise to a mind of craving, one is able to create the karma of greed, hatred, and delusion. Having created [this karma]...
Karmic actions cannot be stopped of their own accord; like a silkworm making a cocoon, they entangle themselves with a discriminating mind.
They fall into the perilous ocean of the six realms of existence, revolving like a waterwheel on a pulley without self-awareness.
Because they lack wisdom, they do not know that all phenomena are like illusions, nor do they know that there is no self or what belongs to a self, and that all phenomena are [empty].

In truth, these arise from false conceptualization and discrimination; yet they do not know that they are separate from the seen and the seer, nor do they know that they are free from the characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing.
Failing to understand that they arise from the delusions of one's own mind, they claim that they are produced by following after Īśvara, time, atoms, or a self.
[The Tang Translation: Mahāmati said: "How is it that one gives rise to conceptual discrimination without understanding? The Buddha said:

"Mahāmati, ordinary fools do not know that names are merely provisional designations. Their minds follow along with the flow [of phenomena] and perceive various marks. They reckon in terms of 'self' and 'what belongs to self,' becoming stained and attached to form.
They obstruct noble wisdom and give rise to greed, hatred, and delusion, thereby creating all manner of karma, just like a silkworm."

They form cocoons, binding themselves with their own deluded thoughts and falling into the great ocean of birth and death within the various realms of existence. Like a water-lifting wheel, they revolve without ceasing.
They do not know that all phenomena are like illusions, like mirages, or like the moon reflected in water; they are merely what is seen by one's own mind, arising from false conceptualization.
These phenomena are free from the grasped and the grasper, as well as from arising, abiding, and ceasing. [They falsely claim they arise] from a creator god (Īśvara), time, or atoms...
Arising from the supreme nature of the dust (*rajas*), they flow according to names and signs (*nāma-nimitta*).
Mahāmati, as for those signs: that which is illuminated by the visual consciousness is called "form" (*rūpa*);

that which is illuminated by the auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental consciousnesses is called "sound, odor, taste, touch, and phenomena" (*śabda-gandha-rasa-spraṣṭavya-dharma*). These are called signs. Mahāmati, as for that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), it is an establishment [of designations].

The various names manifest all characteristics; in this way, they are not different. Names such as "elephant," "horse," "chariot," "infantry," "man," and "woman"—these are called false conceptualization (*parikalpita*).
Mahāmati, true wisdom (*samyagjñāna*) is that in which those names and characteristics cannot be apprehended, being like passing guests.
The various consciousnesses do not arise, and they are neither annihilated nor eternal; they do not fall into the stages of any externalists, *śrāvakas*, or *pratyekabuddhas*.

[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, what is "name"? It refers to the perception of the characteristics of phenomena such as visible forms by the eye-consciousness, as well as the characteristics of sound, the ear, the nose, the tongue, and the body. Mahāmati, such characteristics as these, I call "name-characteristics" (nāma-nimitta).
Mahāmati, what is "discrimination" (vikalpa)? It is the apprehension of characteristics based on whatever phenomena are designated by names. It is the act of discerning.

This dharma is distinct in this way; it is thus ultimately non-different. That is to say, the various conceptualized marks such as elephants, horses, chariots, infantry, and people—this is called "discrimination" (*vikalpa*).
Mahāmati, what is "correct knowledge" (*samyagjñāna*)? It is the observation of names and marks.
Having observed them, one does not perceive any real phenomena, because they are seen to arise through mutual causality and to be produced through mutual co-arising.

When these various consciousnesses no longer arise, and the characteristics of discerning consciousness are neither interrupted nor eternal, one therefore does not fall into the stages of any heterodox teachers, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas. Mahāmati, this is called right knowledge.
[The Tang Translation: "Mahāmati, herein, 'characteristic' (lakṣaṇa) refers to that which is seen by the visual consciousness, called 'form' (rūpa).

That which is apprehended by the auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental consciousnesses is called 'sound,' 'odor,' 'taste,' 'touch,' and 'phenomena' (dharma). Such things as these, I say, are characteristics.
'Discrimination' (vikalpa) refers to the establishment of various names to manifest these characteristics; that is to say, [the designation] of elephants, horses, chariots, and so forth."
The names of "male" and "female," and so forth, are used to manifest their characteristics. This matter is thus determined and not otherwise;

this is called discrimination (*vikalpa*). Correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) means observing that names and characteristics are mutually adventitious, such that the consciousness-mind neither arises nor ceases, and is neither eternal nor annihilated.
Not falling into the stages of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) or the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), this is called correct wisdom.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, by means of this correct wisdom, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva neither establishes names and characteristics nor fails to establish them;
he abandons the two views of establishment and denial, and knowing that names and characteristics do not arise, this is called suchness (*tathatā*).
Mahāmati, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva abides in suchness (tathatā), because they attain the realm of non-existence, they attain the Bodhisattva’s Stage of Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi).
Having attained the Bodhisattva’s Stage of Joy, they are forever separated from all external paths and evil destinies.

They correctly abide in the supramundane path and bring the characteristics of dharmas to maturity. They discern all dharmas as being like illusions and so forth, and personally realize the course of the Dharma.

Characteristics. Having departed from all false conceptualizations and seeing the distinct characteristics of the nature of reality, one proceeds through the stages up to the Dharma-cloud stage (*dharmameghā bhūmi*).

Within this interval, the power of samādhi, mastery, and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) blossom forth. Once the stage of the Tathāgata has been attained, various transformations are perfectly illuminated and manifested to mature sentient beings like the moon reflected in water.
One thus skillfully brings the ten inexhaustible phrases (*akṣaya-pada*) to ultimate fulfillment. For...

Sentient beings explain the Dharma through various conceptual understandings and discriminations; the Dharmakāya is free from mental activity. This is called the Bodhisattva’s entry into that which is attained through suchness (*tathatā*).
[Wei Translation] Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva relies on correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) and does not grasp at names or signs (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*).
One regards phenomena as existent; yet one does not grasp at or perceive their characteristics as non-existent. Why is this? Because it is free from the false views of existence and non-existence.
Since not perceiving names and characteristics is the meaning of right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*), I therefore call this "Suchness" (*tathatā*).
Mahāmati, the bodhisattva who dwells in the dharma of Suchness attains entry into the signless and tranquil realm. Having entered...
Having already attained entry into the first stage, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), of the bodhisattva mahāsattva, when a bodhisattva attains the first Stage of Joy,
they realize one hundred gateways of the luminosity of vajra-samādhi and relinquish all karmic results of the twenty-five states of existence.
Having transcended the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, they abide in the realm of *tathatā* within the family of the Tathāgatas.
Cultivating practice according to reality, they know that the characteristics of the five dharmas are like illusions and dreams.

Observing all phenomena as they truly are, they give rise to the cultivation of noble wisdom realized within their own bodies. Thus, through this progressive process, they become increasingly distant from the false conceptualizations of the mundane world.
In the ground of his choice, he proceeds sequentially through to the Dharma-cloud Ground (*dharmameghā bhūmi*).
Having entered the Dharma-cloud Ground, he next enters the Tathāgata-ground, which is adorned with various flowers through the mastery of samādhis, powers, and supernormal knowledges.

Having entered the Tathāgata-ground, for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings, he manifests various radiances and a body adorned according to need, like the moon reflected in water. Relying upon—

The inexhaustible phrase is that which skillfully binds those who are bound; it teaches the Dharma according to the faith of sentient beings because it is free from the body of mind, intellect, and consciousness.
Mahāmati, once a bodhisattva has entered into suchness, they attain within the stage of Buddhahood such and such immeasurable and boundless dharmas.
[The Tang Translation: Mahāmati, by means of their correct wisdom, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas observe that names and characteristics are neither existent nor non-existent.
