They remain far removed from the two extremes of harmful and beneficial false views; for names, characteristics, and consciousness have never arisen from the very beginning.
I call this dharma "Suchness" (*tathatā*). Mahāmati, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in Suchness, they attain the non-manifestation of objective realms.

Ascending to the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), they leave behind the evil destinies of the non-Buddhists and enter the supramundane dharma, wherein the characteristics of dharmas become fully matured.
They know that all dharmas are like illusions and the like, and they realize the dharma traversed by their own noble wisdom.
Free from conceptualization and views, proceeding in this sequence up to the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*);
having reached the Cloud of Dharma, through the powers of samādhi, mastery, and supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), one blossoms and becomes fully perfected as a Tathāgata.
Having become a Tathāgata, for the sake of sentient beings, one manifests the body everywhere like the moon in water, preaching the Dharma according to their inclinations and desires. Its...
With a body purified and free from mind, intellect, and consciousness, donning the armor of the great vows, and fully accomplishing the ten inexhaustible aspirations—
this is called the attainment gained by a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva upon entering suchness (*tathatā*).
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how is it that the World-Honored One includes the three natures within the five dharmas?
Or do they each have their own distinct characteristics and systems? The Buddha told Mahāmati:

"The three natures, as well as the eight consciousnesses and the two kinds of selflessness, are all included within the five dharmas. Mahāmati, those names and appearances constitute the nature of false discrimination."
Mahāmati, if the mind and mental factors arise based on that conceptualization, they are said to arise simultaneously, like the sun and its rays.

They maintain various distinct characteristics through individual discrimination; this is called the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). Mahāmati, as for right knowledge and suchness (*tathatā*):
Because it is indestructible, it is called the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, does the World-Honored One subsume the five dharmas within the three natures?"
Regarding how the three dharmas are included within the five dharmas, and how their own essential natures are each distinct, the Buddha told Mahāmati:
"Mahāmati, the three dharmas are included within the five dharmas. Mahāmati, it is not only that the three dharmas are included within the five dharmas;
the eight consciousnesses and the two kinds of selflessness are also included within the five dharmas. Mahāmati, how are the three dharmas included within the five dharmas?"

"Mahāmati, what is called 'discrimination' (vikalpa) is the conceptualization of the characteristics of phenomena (dharma-lakṣaṇa). Mahāmati, based on those two factors, the mind and its mental concomitants (citta-caitasika-dharma) arise through discrimination;
they occur simultaneously, not sequentially, just as the sun and its radiance exist simultaneously, yet there is a discrimination of various characteristics.
Mahāmati, these are called the three characteristics, because they arise by the power of causes and conditions. Mahāmati, [this is] true knowledge (samyag-jñāna) and reality..."
This is called the characteristic of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), because it is a non-extinguishing dharma.
[Tang Translation] At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, do the three natures enter into the five dharmas, or do they each have their own specific characteristics? The Buddha said: "Mahāmati, there are the three natures and the eight consciousnesses."
Furthermore, the two kinds of selflessness are both subsumed within the five dharmas. Among these, name and appearance constitute the nature of parikalpita (imagined nature).
Because the mind and mental factors arise simultaneously based upon them, they are like the sun and its light; this is the nature of paratantra (dependent origination).
Because true wisdom and suchness are indestructible, this is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

Furthermore, Mahāmati, the eightfold discrimination of the false imagination manifested from one's own mind—namely, the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), the manas, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and the five groups of sensory consciousnesses—is characterized by unreal marks of false imagination;
thus, the two-fold grasping of "self" and "what belongs to self" is extinguished, resulting in the non-duality of the two [graspings].

I have taught it. Therefore, Mahāmati, these five dharmas encompass the stages of the self-realized noble wisdom of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas, as well as their continuous succession; all Buddha-dharmas are entirely contained within them.

[Wei Translation] Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are eight kinds of distinctions regarding the attachment to the phenomena discriminated by one's own mind, because one regards these various signs as real.
When one is free from the dharmas of self and what belongs to self, as well as arising and ceasing, at that time one realizes the two kinds of selflessness.
Mahāmati, through the five dharma-gates, one enters the stages of the Buddhas; such are the dharmas of the stages.
The marks (*lakṣaṇa*) also enter into the five dharma-gates. All the dharmas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas likewise enter into the five dharma-gates.
Even the dharmas of the Tathāgata’s internal realization of noble wisdom (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*) also enter into the five dharma-gates.
[Chinese Translation] Mahāmati, when one clings to what is manifested by one's own mind as being truly arisen, eight kinds of discrimination arise.
These various characteristics are all unreal and are merely of the nature of false conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

If one can abandon the two kinds of self-clinging, the wisdom of the two kinds of selflessness (*dvi-nairātmya*) will then grow and flourish. Mahāmati, [this applies to] Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas...
Come! Within the stages and sequences of the noble self-realized wisdom, all Buddha-dharmas are entirely subsumed within these five dharmas.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, the five dharmas are: appearance, name, conceptualization, suchness, and correct wisdom. Mahāmati, as for "appearance," if...
The manifestation of locations, shapes, colors, and forms is called "characteristic" (*nimitta*). If something possesses such characteristics, it is designated as a "vase" or the like;

this very thing, and nothing else, is called a "name" (*nāman*). The application of various names to manifest these characteristics regarding vases and other things—both the mind and mental factors—is called "conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*).
Ultimately, neither that name nor that characteristic can be found; from beginning to end, they are without any cognitive apprehension.
In all phenomena there is no mutual succession; being free from unreal conceptualization, this is called *tathatā* (suchness).
It is the true, definitive, ultimate self-nature which cannot be apprehended; that is the characteristic of suchness.

It is the point of entry into which I and all Buddhas have accordingly entered, which we universally expound to sentient beings according to reality, and which we establish and demonstrate therein, entering into perfect awakening as neither interrupted nor eternal.
When false conceptualization does not arise, one accords with the noble path of self-realization—a state that cannot be attained by any outsiders, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas.
This is called right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*). Mahāmati, these are what are known as the five dharmas, the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds of selflessness.
All the Buddha-dharmas are entirely contained within them. Therefore, Mahāmati, you should study them through your own skillful means. Furthermore...
Instruct others not to follow after others.
[Wei Translation] Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are five things: characteristics, names, conceptualization, suchness, and right knowledge. Mahāmati!
What is called "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*)? Characteristic refers to seeing the forms, shapes, and appearances of matter as superior or inferior; this is what is called "characteristic.
Mahāmati, based on those dharmic characteristics, one gives rise to conceptual characteristics, such as:
"This is a jar," "These are oxen, cows, horses, and so forth," or "This dharma is thus, it is not otherwise. Mahāmati, this is what is called "name" (*nāman*). Mahāmati, based upon...
Those dharmas are established by names; they are distinguished and manifested through their characteristics. Therefore, various names such as "ox," "cow," and "horse" are established.
This is called the discrimination of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*).

Mahāmati, when one examines names and characteristics down to even the finest atom, one never perceives the characteristic of a single dharma; all dharmas are unreal, for discrimination arises from the illusory mind.
Therefore, Mahāmati, that which is called *tathatā* (suchness) is named the non-false. It is the definitive, ultimate, and exhaustive nature of its own essence.

To perceive correctly the characteristic of *tathatā*, I, as well as all bodhisattvas and all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, declare that while the meanings are distinct, the substance is one.
Mahāmati, such [teachings] accord with right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) and are neither annihilated nor eternal.
Mahāmati, it is a state where non-conceptualization and conceptualization do not function;

it accords with the noble wisdom realized within one’s own body, and it stands apart from all the heterodox views, factions, and incorrect cognitions of outsiders, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas. Mahāmati!
Regarding the five dharmas, the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds of selflessness—all Buddha-dharmas are subsumed within the gateway of the five dharmas.
Mahāmati, you and all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice and study them in order to seek supreme wisdom.
Mahāmati, you should understand the five dharmas so that you do not follow the teachings of others.

[The Tang Translation: Furthermore, Mahāmati, the five dharmas are as follows: namely, characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), names (*nāman*), discrimination (*vikalpa*), suchness (*tathatā*), and correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).
Among these, "characteristics" refers to the distinct shapes and forms of perceived objects such as color and so forth; this is called "characteristic.
Based upon those various characteristics, one establishes names such as "vase"; that it is "thus" and "not otherwise" is called "name. This is the designation (*prajñapti*).
The various names that manifest all characteristics of the mind and mental factors are called "discrimination. Those names and those characteristics ultimately do not exist;
they are merely the successive discriminations of a deluded mind. One should observe in this manner until even the awakening [of insight] ceases.
This is called suchness (*tathatā*). Mahāmati, the true, definitive, ultimate, and fundamental self-nature is attainable; it is the characteristic of suchness.
I and all the Buddhas have entered into realization in accordance with it, and we reveal and expound it according to its true nature.

If one can accord with and awaken to this, remaining free from both annihilationism and eternalism, not giving rise to conceptual discrimination, and entering the sphere of self-realization—thereby transcending the realms of the non-Buddhists and the two vehicles—this is called right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*).
Mahāmati, these five dharmas, the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds of selflessness encompass all Buddha-dharma without exception. Mahāmati, regarding...
Within this Dharma, you should skillfully penetrate it through your own wisdom, and you should also encourage others to penetrate it.
Once you have penetrated it, your mind will become resolute and will no longer follow after others.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

"The five dharmas, the three natures, And the eight kinds of consciousness, The two kinds of selflessness— These fully encompass the Mahāyāna. Names, marks, and false conceptualization Are the two aspects of the nature of self-existence (*svabhāva*).
Correct wisdom and suchness Constitute the aspect of fulfillment."
[Wei Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:

"The five dharmas, the self-natures, and the eight kinds of consciousness, The two kinds of selflessness—these encompass all of the Mahāyāna. Name, appearance, and conceptualization—these three are the self-natures;
Correct knowledge and suchness—this is the characteristic of the ultimate truth."
[The Tang Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"The five dharmas, the three natures, And the eight kinds of consciousness, Along with the two kinds of selflessness— These universally encompass the Mahāyāna.
Names, signs, and conceptualization Are subsumed within the two natures. Correct wisdom and suchness Constitute the perfected nature."

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, regarding the statement spoken by the World-Honored One—that the Buddhas of the past are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and those of the future and present are likewise so—how should this be understood, World-Honored One?
Is it to be accepted exactly as stated, or is there further meaning beyond it? We pray that the Tathāgata will compassionately explain this for us."
[Wei Translation] At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One,
as the World-Honored One has taught according to conventional designations that the Buddhas of the past, future, and present are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River—
World-Honored One, when the Buddha speaks thus, do I accept it in accordance with what is spoken from the mouth of the Tathāgata?"
"If there is further meaning, I pray that you will explain it to me.
[Tang Translation: At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, as it is stated in the sūtras that the Buddhas of the past, future, and present are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River—how is this to be understood?"
"Is it to be accepted exactly as it is stated, or is there a different meaning?
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Do not accept it exactly as it is said. The measure of the Buddhas of the three periods of time is not like that of the sands of the Ganges. Why is this?

Because it transcends worldly perspective and cannot be illustrated by any analogy; for it is merely a conceptual construction born of the delusions of ordinary, ignorant people and non-Buddhist outsiders who cling to permanence."

Nurturing wrong views leads to an endless cycle of birth and death. Desiring to cause them to become weary of and detached from the wheel of saṃsāra so that they may apply themselves with diligence and excel, [the Buddha] says to them:
"The Buddhas are easy to encounter; they are not as difficult to see as the udumbara flower. Thus he causes them to cease their expedient seeking.
At other times, again observing those who are to be transformed, he makes this statement: "A Buddha is difficult to encounter, like the udumbara flower."
The *udumbara* flower. The *udumbara* flower has never been seen, is not being seen now, and will not be seen; yet the Tathāgata is seen by all in the world.
It is not because he establishes his own realization that it is said, "The appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is like the *udumbara* flower," Mahāmati.
That which is established by itself and validated by itself transcends worldly expectations; it cannot be believed in by those ordinary, ignorant people.

It is the realm of the noble wisdom of self-awakening, for which no analogy can be found. Great Wisdom, the true Tathāgata transcends the characteristics perceived by mind, thought, and consciousness, and thus cannot be illustrated by analogy.
However, Great Wisdom, when I speak of the Buddha being like the sands of the Ganges, there is no fault in this.
[Wei Translation] The Buddha addressed the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva, saying: "Mahāmati, do not grasp at the names, phrases, and sentences as I have spoken in such a manner.
Mahāmati, the Buddhas of the three periods of time are not merely equal in number to the sands of the Ganges River."
Why is this? The metaphors spoken that transcend the world are not like ordinary metaphors.

Why? Because they possess both similarities and dissimilarities. Mahāmati, the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, do not invariably employ metaphors that transcend the world which are either similar or dissimilar. Why? Mahāmati, I speak of metaphors...
"Mahāmati, metaphors are merely partial. The metaphors spoken by me and all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, express only a limited meaning.
Why is this? Because foolish ordinary people and various non-Buddhists are attached to the permanence of phenomena, thereby increasing their false views;
they follow along with worldly saṃsāra and birth-and-death. For their sake, I bring about a sense of weary detachment."

Upon hearing this, they were struck with fear and alarm. Furthermore, hearing that there are Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they conceived the notion that the unsurpassed holy path of the Tathāgatas is easily attained, and thus sought the supramundane Dharma.

Mahāmati, for this reason I say that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are like the sands of the river Ganges. Why is this? Because in other sūtras I have said that the appearance of a Buddha in the world is as rare as the udumbara flower.
"Flower. Having heard this, sentient beings say, "The path of the Buddha is difficult to attain; one must cultivate diligence.
For this reason, I say that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.

Mahāmati, when I say that the appearance of the Buddhas in the world is like the *udumbara* flower, it is for the sake of those sentient beings who are capable of being transformed; thus, I say that the Buddhas are like the *udumbara* flower. Mahāmati, [this is my intention]."
Furthermore, Mahāmati, the udumbara flower has never been seen by anyone in the world; it shall likewise not be seen.

Mahāmati, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones have been seen in the world, are being seen now, and will be seen in the future. Mahāmati, when I speak in this manner, I do not speak based on a dharma attained by my own self.
Therefore, I say that the Tathāgatas are like the udumbara flower. The Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones are also...
It is likewise so, Mahāmati. I teach the Dharma based on the realization of my own internal body. Therefore, I speak of metaphors that transcend the world.
This is because ordinary people and beings lacking faith cannot believe in the metaphors I have spoken. Why is this?
Because the realm of noble wisdom realized within one's own internal body cannot be expressed through metaphors; it is utterly free from mind and intellect (*citta-mano*).
The mental consciousness transcends all grounds of views, for the *tathatā*-dharma of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, is ineffable.
Therefore, Mahāmati, I employ various metaphors. When I say that the Buddhas are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, it is for this reason.
This is a partial analogy. Mahāmati, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are equal and not unequal, because they do not engage in conceptualization through conceptualization.
[Tang Translation] The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Do not accept things according to their literal expression. Mahāmati, the Buddhas of the three periods of time are not like..."
As numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Why is this? The Tathāgata is most supreme, transcending all worlds;
there is none equal to him, and he cannot be reached by analogy, yet I employ only a small portion as a metaphor.

Because ordinary, ignorant people and the various non-Buddhists constantly cling to the notions of permanence and impermanence, their evil views increase, causing them to revolve in the cycle of birth and death. I do so to lead them to feel weary of and detached from it.
To inspire superior aspiration, I say that a Buddha is easy to achieve and easy to encounter.

If I were to say that he is difficult to meet, as rare as the udumbara flower, they would become discouraged and fail to apply themselves with diligent vigor. Therefore, I say that Buddhas are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are times when I observe those to be converted and speak of how difficult it is to encounter a Buddha, like the udumbara flower. Mahāmati, the udumbara...
A flower has never been seen, is not being seen, and will not be seen; however, for the Tathāgata, there is that which has already been seen and that which will be seen.
Mahāmati, such a metaphor does not describe my own teaching. My own teaching is the realm of activity of the noble wisdom realized within.
It is peerless in the world and transcends all metaphors; all ordinary and ignorant people are unable to believe or accept it.
Mahāmati, the true Tathāgata transcends the characteristics perceived by mind, thought, and consciousness, and thus no metaphor can be established for him.
Nevertheless, there are times when one does establish such [metaphors], speaking of things being "equal to the sands of the Ganges," which involves no contradiction.
Mahāmati, it is like the sands of the Ganges, which are trampled by all kinds of fish, turtles, crocodiles, lions, elephants, horses, humans, and beasts;
yet those sands do not think, "They are disturbing me," nor do they give rise to delusive thoughts. Their intrinsic nature is pure and free from all defilement.
In the same way, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha’s river of self-realized noble wisdom possesses great power and supernormal faculties.
Regarding the sands of the Ganges: all non-Buddhists, humans, animals, and others may cause every kind of disturbance;
yet the Tathāgata does not give rise to deluded thoughts regarding them. The Tathāgata is tranquil and free from conceptualization.

Because the Tathāgata’s original vow was to establish sentient beings in the bliss of samādhi, there is no disturbance whatsoever—remaining as undifferentiated as the sands of the Ganges. Furthermore, this is because he has severed both greed and anger.

[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, it is as if, for example, all the sands within the Ganges River were trampled by fish, turtles, crocodiles, dragons, cattle, sheep, elephants, horses, and various other beasts;
yet those river sands do not give rise to discrimination, nor do they feel aversion or resentment.
Nor do they give rise to the thought, "They are disturbing me. Because they are without discrimination, they are pure and free from all defilements. Mahāmati.

The Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, are likewise thus. Having internally realized noble wisdom, they are fully endowed with powers, supernormal knowledges, and sovereign merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
When the foolish fish and turtles of all non-Buddhist teachers and proponents of false doctrines revile the Tathāgata with hearts of malice, the Tathāgata remains unmoved and unshaken.

They give rise to discrimination. By the power of their original vows, they grant sentient beings samādhi and samāpatti, and because they cause all forms of happiness to be fulfilled, they do not discriminate while discriminating.
Mahāmati, for this reason I say that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.
"Equal" means they are equal and without differing characteristics; they have already abandoned craving.
Because of the body.
[Tang Translation: Mahāmati, it is like the sands of the Ganges, which, though trampled by turtles, fish, elephants, and horses, do not give rise to discrimination;
they are eternally pure and stainless. The noble wisdom of the Tathāgata is like that Ganges River, possessing power, supernormal faculties, and mastery.
It became sand. Heretics, turtles, and fish vied with one another to disturb it, yet the Buddha did not give rise to a single thought of discrimination.
Why was this? Because the Tathāgata’s original vow was to universally pacify all sentient beings with the bliss of samādhi;
like the sands of the Ganges, he is without love or hatred and free from discrimination.
It is like the sands of the Ganges, which are the intrinsic nature of the earth element. When the world is consumed at the end of the kalpa, all the earth is burned;

yet that earth element does not abandon its own nature because it arises simultaneously with the fire element. Other foolish people conceive the notion that the earth is burning, but the earth is not actually burned because of the presence of the fire cause.
In this same way, Mahāmati, the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is indestructible, like the sands of the Ganges.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, it is like the sands of the Ganges River, which do not depart from the characteristic of earth.

Mahāmati, when the great earth is burned by fire, the fire does not burn the earth because the fire is not different from the earth; for the great element of earth possesses the essence of a continuous succession with the characteristic of fire.
Mahāmati, foolish ordinary people fall into inverted cognition; they conceptually discriminate that the earth is being burned by their own minds and say, "The earth is burning.
Yet the earth is not burned, because it does not depart from the earth, and because there exists another body of the four great elements and fire.
Mahāmati, the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, are also like this. The essence of the Dharma-body of the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, is like the river Gaṅgā.
[...sand and so forth... because they are neither extinguished nor lost.

[Tang Translation: Mahāmati, it is like the sands of the Ganges. When the earth-element is consumed by fire at the end of the kalpa, burning all the earth, that great element of earth does not abandon its own nature, for it arises simultaneously with the great element of fire. All...
Ordinary fools say that the earth is burned, yet in reality it is not burned, because it is the cause of fire.
The *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata is likewise; like the sands of the Ganges, it is ultimately indestructible.
“Mahāmati, just as the sands of the Ganges are without limit, so too is the radiance of the Tathāgata without limit;
it universally illumines all the great assemblies of Buddhas for the sake of bringing sentient beings to maturity.
Mahāmati, just as one cannot ever find different sand by seeking it apart from the sands of the Ganges, even so, Mahāmati, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—”
Awakening is without birth-and-death or arising-and-ceasing, because the causes and conditions [for them] have been severed.
[Wei Translation: Mahāmati, it is like the sands of the Ganges River, which are immeasurable and boundless.
Mahāmati, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are also like this; appearing in the world, they emit immeasurable light that pervades all things.

The Buddha’s Great Assembly is for the purpose of transforming sentient beings so that they may attain awakening and knowledge. Mahāmati, it is like the sands of the Ganges River, which do not give rise to further characteristics;
just as those atoms abide with their atomic essence and characteristics, so it is, Mahāmati, with the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
Within the world, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, neither arise nor cease. The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have severed...
Because there is a cause.
[Tang Translation] Mahāmati, for example, just as the sands of the Ganges are without limit, so too is the radiance of the Tathāgata.
It is for the sake of bringing immeasurable sentient beings to fulfillment that it universally illuminates all the great assemblies of the Buddhas.
Wisdom. For example, just as the sands of the Ganges abide in their own nature without changing or transforming into anything else, so too is the Tathāgata:
he neither arises nor ceases within the world, for all causes of birth have been completely severed.
Mahāmati, it is like the sands of the Ganges, whose increase or decrease cannot be perceived.

In the same way, Mahāmati, the Tathāgata’s wisdom matures sentient beings without increasing or decreasing, because it is not a physical phenomenon (*kāyadharma*). Physical phenomena are subject to destruction;
however, the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) of the Tathāgata is not a physical phenomenon.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, it is like the sands of the Ganges River: when they emerge from the river, they cannot be seen;
when they enter into the river, they also cannot be seen. Nor do they give rise to the thought, "I am entering or emerging from the river.
Mahāmati, the power of the wisdom of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas is likewise so: though they deliver all sentient beings, there is neither exhaustion nor diminution.
It does not increase. Why? Because all dharmas are bodiless (*an-ātmaka*). Mahāmati, everything that possesses a body is a dharma subject to impermanence and destruction;
it is not a bodiless dharma. This is because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, possess only the Dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*).
[The Tang Translation: "Mahāmati, it is like the sands of the Ganges: they do not decrease when taken away, nor do they increase when added. The Buddhas are likewise;
through the wisdom of skillful means, they bring sentient beings to maturity without decrease or increase.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body has no physical body. Mahāmati, it is because there is a physical body that there is destruction; the Dharma-body has none."
Therefore, his body is subject to no destruction or decay.
Just as one cannot obtain oil by pressing the sands of the Ganges, so it is with all these beings of extreme suffering who oppress the Tathāgata;
yet, until all beings have attained *nirvāṇa*, he does not relinquish his own *samādhi*, vows, and aspirations within the *dharmadhātu*, out of great compassion.
Therefore, [Wei Translation] states: "Mahāmati, it is like a person who wishes to obtain ghee or oil by pressing the sands of the Ganges;
they would never obtain it because there is no ghee or oil therein. Mahāmati, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, for the sake of all sentient beings afflicted by suffering..."
One cannot suppress anger. One does not abandon the characteristic of one's own dharma-realm; one does not abandon the characteristic of the flavor of one's own dharma;
one does not abandon the original vow to bestow happiness upon sentient beings. Having attained the fulfillment of great loving-kindness and great compassion, [one thinks]:
"If I do not cause all sentient beings to enter nirvana, my own body shall likewise not enter nirvana."
[The Tang Translation: "Mahāmati, it is like the sands of the Ganges: though one might press them with oil-seeds in an attempt to extract ghee or oil, it can never be obtained.

The Tathāgata is likewise; although he is oppressed by the manifold sufferings of sentient beings until even the most minute creatures have attained nirvāṇa, his deep-seated aspiration and delight within the dharmadhātu cannot be made to abandon [his resolve]."
Why is this? Because they have fully accomplished the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
Mahāmati, it is like the sands of the Ganges, which flow along with the water and are not without water.
In the same way, Mahāmati, all dharmas spoken by the Tathāgata flow toward *nirvāṇa*; therefore, it is said that they are like the sands of the Ganges. Thus spoke the Tathāgata.
One does not follow the flow of various goings, for "going" has the meaning of destruction. Mahāmati, the original limit of birth and death is unknowable;
because it is unknowable, how can one speak of "going"? Mahāmati, "going" has the meaning of annihilation, yet the foolish do not understand this.

[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, just as the sands of the Ganges River flow with the current and never flow against it, so too, Mahāmati, do the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, teach the Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings; they accord with *nirvāṇa* and do not flow against it.
Mahāmati, for this reason I say that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are like the sands of the Ganges River. Mahāmati.
To say that the sands of the Ganges flow along with the current does not imply the sense of "going.
Mahāmati, if the Buddha-Tathāgata possessed the sense of "going," then all Buddha-Tathāgatas would be subject to impermanence and cessation.

Mahāmati, since the primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) of the world cannot even be known, how could I rely upon that which is unknowable to speak of the sense of "going"? Therefore, the Tathāgata is not [subject to going].
The meaning of "departure" (*gati*). Mahāmati, the meaning of departure is the meaning of cessation (*uccheda*). Foolish ordinary beings do not perceive or understand this. [Tang Translation:
Mahāmati, for example, it is like the sands of the Ganges which flow along with the water and are not without water.
The Tathāgata is also like this; all his teachings of the Dharma follow the current of *nirvāṇa*. For this reason, it is said that all...
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Mahāmati, the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata does not follow after the realms of existence (*gati*).
"Realm" has the meaning of destruction. Since the original limit of birth and death cannot be known, how can one speak of "realms"?
Mahāmati, the meaning of "realm" is the severance [of continuity], which the foolish and ignorant do not understand.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, if the original limit of birth and death for sentient beings cannot be known, how can liberation be known?
The Buddha told Mahāmati, “It is through the cessation of the causes—the beginningless habit-energies of false delusions, faults, and conceptual constructions—that [liberation] is known.”
Knowing that external objects are manifestations of one’s own mind, the false conceptualization of the body ceases; yet liberation is not annihilation, and for this reason it is boundless.

It is not that nothing exists at all, but rather that "boundlessness" and other such terms are merely alternative names for that which is falsely conceptualized. By observing both the internal and external as being free from false conceptualization, one sees that there is no separate sentient being.
Wisdom (*jñāna*) and the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), along with all phenomena, are entirely quiescent. One does not perceive a self...
Because the mind manifests as false conceptualization, false conceptualization arises; if consciousness ceases, [it] is extinguished.

[Wei Translation: Mahāmati said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, if sentient beings revolve in the cycle of existence within the world, and their past and future limits are unknowable, how does the Tathāgata attain liberation? Furthermore..."
"May sentient beings attain liberation. The Buddha said to Mahāmati:
"Mahāmati, what is called 'liberation' is because one is free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), afflictions, and the discriminative mind habituated since beginningless time.

It is because one can know reality as it is—that what is perceived externally is but the manifestation of one's own mind—and because the turning of the mind that discriminates external objects has ceased. For this reason, I call it 'liberation.'"

“Mahāmati, that which is called liberation is not the extinction of dharmas. Therefore, your question—‘If one does not know the primal limit (pūrvakoṭi), how can one attain liberation?’—is not a valid question.
Mahāmati, what is called the ‘primal limit’ is merely a different name for the single essence of the discriminating mind.
Mahāmati, apart from the discriminating mind, there are no sentient beings; it is precisely this [mind]...”
Discrimination is what is called "sentient beings. Mahāmati, true wisdom contemplates internal and external phenomena because there is neither an object to be known nor a subject that knows.

Mahāmati, because all phenomena are originally quiescent, those who do not know them as they truly are—seeing only the false discriminations of their own minds—therefore give rise to a mind of discrimination. As it truly is...
The Knower does not give rise to conceptual discrimination.
[Tang Translation] Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If the original limit of birth and death cannot be known, how do sentient beings attain liberation while within birth and death? The Buddha said: "Mahāmati, it is beginningless..."
When the habit-energies of falsehood are extinguished through their causes, one realizes that external objects are manifestations of one’s own mind;
this transformation of the basis of discrimination is called liberation, not annihilation. Therefore, it cannot be said that there is no limit.
Mahāmati, "limitlessness" is merely another name for discrimination. Mahāmati, apart from the discriminating mind, there are no separate sentient beings.
With wisdom one observes all internal and external phenomena; knowing that both the knower and the known are entirely quiescent is Great Intelligence (*mahāmati*).
All phenomena are merely what is seen through the discrimination of one's own mind. Because of a lack of understanding, the discriminating mind arises;
when the mind is understood, it ceases.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "Observe all the Guides, who are like the sands of the Ganges:
they are neither destroyed nor do they depart, and yet they are not ultimately [static]. This is what constitutes equality. Observe all the Tathāgatas, who are equal to the sands of the Ganges:
they are entirely free from all faults; though they follow the flow, their nature is eternal. This is..."
The Buddha’s Perfect Enlightenment.
[Wei Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"One who contemplates all Buddhas as being like the sands of the Ganges—neither extinguished nor born—that person can see the Buddha, far removed from all dust and defilements. As the Ganges...
As the sands of every river flow along in accordance with the current without changing, so too is the Dharma-body.
[Translated by Xuanzang: At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse: "Observing all the Teachers, they are like the sands of the Ganges;
neither destroyed nor moving toward anywhere—such a person can see the Buddha. Like the sands of the Ganges, they are entirely free from..."
[It is] free from all faults, yet it constantly flows in accordance [with conditions]. The essence of the Buddha is also like this.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for me the characteristic of the momentary destruction of all dharmas.
World-Honored One, in what way are all dharmas momentary? The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Listen attentively, listen attentively..."
"Listen attentively and reflect well upon it; I shall explain it for you. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "All dharmas refer to those that are wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate;
conditioned or unconditioned; mundane or supramundane; faulty or faultless; and with outflows or without outflows."
Regarding "acceptance" and "non-acceptance":
at that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, I pray that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha will explain for me; Sugata, please explain for me all things."
[Regarding] the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of dharmas: Why does the Tathāgata say that all dharmas do not abide for even a single moment?
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Mahāmati: "Excellent, excellent, excellent, Mahāmati! Listen attentively now, and I shall explain it to you.
Mahāmati said: "Excellent, World-Honored One! We shall indeed receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "All..."
Dharma. All dharmas refer to what are called wholesome dharmas and unwholesome dharmas; conditioned dharmas and unconditioned dharmas;
mundane dharmas and supramundane dharmas; outflowing dharmas and non-outflowing dharmas; internal dharmas and external dharmas.
[The Tang Translation: At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for me the characteristic of the momentary destruction of all dharmas. Which dharmas are designated as 'momentary'?"
The Buddha said, "Listen attentively; I shall explain it for you. Mahāmati, 'all phenomena' refers to wholesome phenomena and unwholesome phenomena;
conditioned phenomena and unconditioned phenomena; mundane phenomena and supramundane phenomena; tainted phenomena and untainted phenomena;
and phenomena subject to grasping and phenomena not subject to grasping."

Mahāmati, in brief, the mind (citta), the intellect (manas), the consciousness (vijñāna), and their habitual tendencies (vāsanā) are the causes of the five aggregates of clinging (pañca-upādāna-skandha).
These habitual tendencies of the mind, intellect, and consciousness nourish the false conceptualizations (parikalpa) of ordinary, ignorant people regarding what is wholesome and unwholesome.

[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, to speak briefly of the dharmas of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*): they grow through the perfuming (*vāsanā*) of mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Because ordinary people rely on the perfuming of mind, thought, and consciousness, they discriminate between wholesome and unwholesome dharmas.

[The Tang Translation: "Mahāmati, to state the essentials: the phenomena of the five aggregates of clinging grow by taking the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of mind, thought, and consciousness as their cause.
Fools and ordinary people give rise to conceptual discrimination regarding these, labeling them as 'wholesome' or 'unwholesome.'"

"Mahāmati, the cultivation of the bliss of samādhi, the meditative absorption of samādhi-samāpatti, and dwelling in the happiness of the present dharma is called the noble, virtuous, and untainted (anāsrava).
[Wei Translation: Mahāmati, the noble ones directly realize the untainted, virtuous dharmas of samādhi and samāpatti."
"Mahāmati, the practice of delight is called wholesome dharmas.
[Tang Translation: "The noble ones' dwelling in the bliss of the samādhi of direct realization is what is called wholesome, untainted dharmas."
“Mahāmati, as for the wholesome and the unwholesome, they refer to the eight consciousnesses. What are these eight? They are the *tathāgatagarbha*, which is called the *ālayavijñāna*;
the *manas*, the *manovijñāna*, and the five bodies of sensory consciousness (*pañca-vijñānakāya*). These are not as described by the non-Buddhists.

Mahāmati, the five bodies of sensory consciousness, together with the *manas*, the *manovijñāna*, and the *ālaya*, possess both wholesome and unwholesome characteristics; they undergo successive transformation and decay, yet they continue in a flowing stream, giving rise to an indestructible body.”

They arise and they cease. Failing to realize that these are manifestations of one's own mind, the subsequent consciousnesses cease in succession as others arise, grasping at the distinctions of forms and characteristics.
The mental consciousness arises in conjunction with the five sensory consciousnesses; because it does not abide for even a single moment, it is called "momentary" (*kṣaṇika*).
[Wei Translation] Furthermore, Mahāmati, what are called wholesome and unwholesome dharmas refer to the eight consciousnesses.
What are these eight? First is the ālayavijñāna; second is the manas; third is the manovijñāna; fourth is the cakṣurvijñāna.
Fifth is ear-consciousness; sixth is nose-consciousness; seventh is tongue-consciousness; eighth is body-consciousness.

Mahāmati, the five groups of consciousness together with the group of mental consciousness mutually differentiate between wholesome and unwholesome dharmas through their continuity. Their essence is a non-differentiated body that follows the arising of phenomena;
once arisen, they cease. They do not know that what they perceive as external objects are merely false appearances of their own minds.
At the very moment of cessation, it can grasp the characteristics of objects, such as their shape, size, and superior or subtle qualities.

Mahāmati, the mental consciousness arises in conjunction with the five bodies of sensory consciousness; it does not abide for even a single thought-moment. Therefore, I say that those dharmas do not abide for a thought-moment.

[Chinese Translation] Furthermore, Mahāmati, as for the wholesome and the unwholesome, they refer to the eight consciousnesses. What are these eight? They are the Tathāgatagarbha, which is called the Ālayavijñāna;
the Manas, the Manovijñāna, and the five groups of sensory consciousnesses. Mahāmati, those five groups of sensory consciousnesses operate together with the Manovijñāna;
their characteristics of being wholesome or unwholesome mutually differentiate one another in a continuous, uninterrupted succession. There is no... [end of fragment].
When a distinct entity arises, it ceases immediately. Failing to understand that objects are manifestations of one's own mind, as each preceding moment ceases, a different consciousness arises.
The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) functions in conjunction with those five sensory consciousnesses, grasping various differentiated forms and characteristics.
These do not abide for even a single moment; I call such things "momentary phenomena" (*kṣaṇadharma*).

Mahāmati, "moment" (kṣaṇa) refers to the storehouse-consciousness (ālayavijñāna). It is the momentary habit-energy of the evolving consciousnesses that arise together with the Tathāgatagarbha and the manas.
The habit-energy of the untainted (anāsrava) is not momentary; it is not perceived by ordinary, foolish people because they are attached to the doctrine of momentariness.
Failing to realize whether all phenomena are momentary or non-momentary, they destroy unconditioned dharmas through their nihilistic views.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, that which is called *kṣaṇika* (momentary) is termed "empty. The *ālayavijñāna* is named the Tathāgatagarbha;

because it is not perfumed by the common evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), it is termed "empty," yet because it is fully endowed with the perfuming of untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*), it is termed "not empty.
Mahāmati, foolish ordinary beings do not perceive or understand this, and thus they cling [to it].
Adhering to the view that all phenomena do not abide for even a single moment, they fall into false views and declare:
"Even untainted dharmas do not abide for even a single moment. This is because they thereby destroy true suchness and the Tathāgatagarbha.

[The Tang Translation: "Mahāmati, the Tathāgatagarbha is called the ālayavijñāna. It is accompanied by the various habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the manas and other [consciousnesses], and these are momentary phenomena (*kṣaṇika-dharma*).
The untainted habitual tendencies (*anāsrava-vāsanā*) are not momentary phenomena.

This is not something that can be known by the ignorant and foolish who propound the theory of momentariness; they are unable to discern that among all phenomena, some are momentary and others are not."
For that reason, those who reckon the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) in such a way fall into the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*), just as all phenomena perish.
Mahāmati, the seven consciousnesses do not transmigrate; they do not experience suffering or pleasure, nor are they the cause of nirvāṇa.

Mahāmati, the Tathāgatagarbha experiences suffering and pleasure together with their causes; it arises and ceases, being intoxicated by the four stages of abiding and the stage of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*).
Ordinary fools do not realize that what they perceive is momentary; their deluded thoughts permeate their minds.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, the five bodies of consciousness do not produce the six destinies, do not experience suffering or pleasure, and do not act as the cause for nirvāṇa.
Mahāmati, the Tathāgatagarbha does not experience suffering or pleasure and is not the cause of saṃsāra. As for other dharmas...
They arise and perish together. Because they are intoxicated by the four kinds of perfuming, ordinary beings fail to perceive and fail to know the perfuming of false views;
thus they claim that all phenomena do not abide for even a single moment.
[The Tang Translation: "Mahāmati, the five bodies of consciousness do not undergo transmigration; they do not experience suffering or pleasure, nor are they the cause of nirvāṇa.
It is the tathāgatagarbha that experiences suffering and pleasure, which arises and ceases together with their causes, and is obscured by the four kinds of habitual tendencies (vāsanā).
Yet, the deluded minds of ordinary fools, being permeated by conceptualization, fail to understand this and give rise to the view of momentariness."
Furthermore, Mahāmati, just as gold, vajra, and the relics of the Buddha possess extraordinary qualities that are never subject to deterioration, so it is with the state of being a Sage.
Mahāmati, if there were moments (kṣaṇa) within the attainment of the Uninterrupted [Samādhi], then the Sage would be non-Sage; yet the Sage has never been anything other than a Sage.
Just as gold and vajra do not diminish even when weighed after passing through kalpas, how is it that the foolish and ignorant are not skilled regarding my hidden [teachings]?
The discourse on concealment: one should conceive of all internal and external phenomena as being momentary.
[Wei Translation] Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Vajra Tathāgatagarbha, the Dharma realized by the Tathāgata, is not non-momentary and unstable.
Mahāmati, if the Dharma realized by the Tathāgata were non-momentary and unstable, then all noble ones would not...
They become sages, Mahāmati; they are not non-sages, because they are indeed sages.
Mahāmati, gold and vajra remain for an eon; their measure remains constant, neither increasing nor decreasing.
Mahāmati, how is it that foolish ordinary people discriminate among phenomena, claiming they do not abide for even a moment? Thus, these ordinary people fail to grasp my intention and do not awaken.
[They] do not know that all internal and external phenomena do not abide for even a single moment.

[Tang Translation: Mahāmati, just as gold, vajra, and the relics of the Buddha possess extraordinary characteristics that are ultimately indestructible, if the realized Dharma were subject to moments (*kṣaṇa*), then the noble ones would cease to be noble; yet those noble ones have not...

It has never been anything other than the sacred. Just as gold and vajra remain unchanged in weight even after enduring for kalpas, why do the foolish and ignorant fail to understand my secret teaching, conceiving of all phenomena as being merely momentary?

The Bodhisattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has taught that one attains perfect enlightenment by fulfilling the six pāramitās, what are these six?"
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, the Tathāgata has often spoken of attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by fulfilling the dharma of the six *pāramitās*.
World-Honored One, what are these six *pāramitās*, and how are they fulfilled?"
[The Tang Translation] Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, you have often said that if one fulfills the six pāramitās, one will attain perfect enlightenment. What are these six? How does one fulfill them?"
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "There are three kinds of distinctions regarding the pāramitās: namely, the worldly, the world-transcending, and the world-transcending supreme.
Mahāmati, as for the worldly pāramitās: they involve attachment to the grasping of 'self' and 'mine,' and the grasping of the two extremes;
they are for the sake of the pleasures of various places of birth, such as forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles, and thus fulfill the dāna-pāramitā."
Honey. The same applies to ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom. [Ordinary beings attain] supernatural powers and rebirth in the Brahma heavens.
[Wei Translation] The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāmati, saying: "Mahāmati, there are three distinctions among the *pāramitās*:
namely, worldly *pāramitās*, world-transcending *pāramitās*, and the supreme world-transcending *pāramitās*."
Pāramitā. Mahāmati, what is called worldly pāramitā refers to foolish ordinary beings who, clinging to the dharmas of "self" and "what belongs to self," fall into the two extremes.
For the sake of various excellent and sublime objects, they practice pāramitā, seeking the karmic retribution of objects such as form.
Mahāmati, foolish ordinary beings practice the pāramitā of śīla, kṣānti, [vīrya, dhyāna, and prajñā...]
The perfection of giving, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom—
even up to being born in the Brahma heavens and seeking the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), which are worldly dharmas— O Mahāmati,
these are called the worldly perfections (*laukika-pāramitā*).
[The Tang Translation: The Buddha said, “Mahāmati, there are three distinctions regarding the pāramitās: namely, the worldly, the world-transcending, and the world-transcending supreme.

Mahāmati, as for the worldly pāramitās, they refer to those ordinary, ignorant people who are attached to ‘self’ and ‘what belongs to the self,’ who grasp at the two extremes, and who seek various forms of existence while craving objects such as form and so forth. It is thus.”
They practice the pāramitās of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration; they achieve supernormal powers and are reborn in the Brahma world.
Mahāmati, as for the supramundane pāramitās, because śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas fall into the grasping of nirvāṇa, they practice them [in that manner].
The six pāramitās. [The Wei translation states:
"Mahāmati, that which is called supramundane pāramitā refers to the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who delight in their own personal nirvāṇa."
They take up the mind of the nirvāṇa of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and practice the pāramitās.
Mahāmati, just as those foolish worldlings practice worldly pāramitās for the sake of seeking the bliss of nirvāṇa for themselves, so too do the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
for their own sake, they seek the bliss of nirvāṇa and practice [the path].
Regarding the supramundane *pāramitā* practices, they nevertheless seek that which is not ultimate bliss.

[Tang Translation: Mahāmati, as for the supramundane *pāramitās*, this refers to the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas who, being attached to *nirvāṇa*, long for their own personal happiness and thus cultivate these various *pāramitās*.

Regarding the supramundane, supreme *pāramitā*: because one realizes that the objects of grasping are merely the measure of the false imagination manifested by one's own mind, and because one understands the duality of one's own mind, false imagination does not arise.

Not partaking in the grasping of the various realms of existence, and being free from attachment to the forms and appearances of one's own mind, one gives rise to the *dāna-pāramitā* for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings, and initiates the most supreme skillful means. Thus...
The precept in which conceptualization does not arise regarding those objects is the *śīla-pāramitā*. That very non-arising of conceptualization is patience;
knowing the grasped and the grasper is the *kṣānti-pāramitā*.

Diligent application during the first, middle, and last watches of the night, practicing in accordance with skillful means so that conceptualization does not arise, is the *vīrya-pāramitā*. When all conceptualizations are completely extinguished...
To be embraced by the nirvana of the śrāvakas is the dhyāna-pāramitā. To observe with wisdom that the false imaginings of one's own mind lack intrinsic nature,
thereby not falling into the two extremes, and to attain the noble realization of self-awakening such that the previous body is transformed into something superior and indestructible—
this is the prajñā-pāramitā.

[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, as for the supramundane, unsurpassed *pāramitā*, it is the ability to know, in accordance with reality, that external objects are merely seen through the false discrimination of one's own mind.
At that time, one truly knows that only one's own mind manifests as internal and external phenomena;
one does not engage in false discrimination, nor does one grasp at the forms and characteristics of internal and external things within one's own mind.

Therefore, because the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is able to know all dharmas as they truly are, he practices the dānapāramitā in order to cause all sentient beings to attain fearlessness and peace and happiness. This is called the dānapāramitā.

Mahāmati, when a bodhisattva contemplates all those dharmas and does not give rise to discrimination, but remains in accordance with that which is cool and refreshing, this is the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā).

Mahāmati, when a bodhisattva, free from the discriminating mind, endures that practice and knows as it truly is that the realms of the grasper and the grasped are not real, this is called the bodhisattva’s perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā). Mahāmati...

Mahāmati, how does a bodhisattva cultivate the practice of vigor? By constantly and diligently practicing during the first, middle, and last watches of the night, following the Dharma as it truly is to sever all conceptual discrimination—this is called vīryapāramitā.

Mahāmati, when a bodhisattva is free from the discriminating mind and does not fall into the marks of the objective realm of the grasper and the grasped characteristic of the non-Buddhists, this is called...
The Dhyāna-pāramitā. Mahāmati, what is the Prajñā-pāramitā of a bodhisattva? It is when a bodhisattva observes the characteristics of the conceptualization of his own mind as they truly are;
seeing no conceptualization, he does not fall into the two extremes. Relying on practice according to reality, he transforms his basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti).
He sees not a single dharma arising, nor does he see a single dharma ceasing. This is the noble internal realization within one's own body.
Practicing this cultivation is called the Bodhisattva’s prajñāpāramitā.
Mahāmati, when the meaning of pāramitā is thus fulfilled, one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

[The Tang Translation: Mahāmati, that which is called the supramundane, supreme *pāramitā* refers to the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas’ thorough understanding that the two dharmas within their own minds are merely manifestations of discrimination;

they do not give rise to conceptual construction, do not produce attachment, and do not grasp at the marks of form. Desiring to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings, they constantly engage in cultivation.

The perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) consists in not giving rise to conceptual discrimination regarding any objective sphere; this is the practice of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).
At the very moment that no such discrimination arises, to patiently realize the intrinsic nature of both the grasper and the grasped is called the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
Diligently practicing without slackening during the first, middle, and last watches of the night, one accords with true understanding.
The non-arising of conceptual discrimination is called the *vīrya-pāramitā*.
The non-arising of conceptual discrimination and the failure to give rise to the views of non-Buddhist nirvana is called the *dhyāna-pāramitā*.
By observing with wisdom that the mind is without discrimination and does not fall into the two extremes, one transforms the basis of reliance without destroying it, thereby attaining...
The realm realized through the internal realization of noble wisdom is what is called Prajñāpāramitā.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "Empty, impermanent, and momentary—these are the conceptual constructions of the ignorant.
Like a river, a lamp, or a seed, they give rise to the notion of momentariness. Through the cessation of moments, there is tranquility and stillness."
Detached from all that is produced, all phenomena are non-arising; this is what I call the meaning of *kṣaṇa* (moment).
[Wei Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse: "Empty, impermanent, and momentary—thus do the foolish discriminate conditioned things.
Like a river, a lamp, or a seed, they are empty, impermanent, and momentary. By discriminating the meaning of *kṣaṇa*, they perceive them as moment by moment."
It is also thus: momentary things do not arise; they are quiescent and free from activity. All phenomena are non-arising;
this is what I call the meaning of "moment. [Tang Translation: At that time, the World-Honored One further spoke in verse: "The deluded discriminate conditioned things as empty and impermanent."
The moment (kṣaṇa). To analyze the meaning of the moment: like a river, a lamp, or a seed, all phenomena are unarisen;
they are quiescent and without activity; they are devoid of the nature of all things—this is my definition of the moment.
When things arise, they are subject to cessation; this is not taught for the sake of the foolish. This nature of uninterrupted continuity is perfumed by false conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is its cause, and from it the mind arises. Until form (*rūpa*) has yet to arise, what interval could there be in between?
[Wei Translation] That which arises at first is subject to cessation; this is not taught for the sake of ordinary beings.

Through the analysis of the dharma of continuity, one perceives the six realms through deluded imagination. If ignorance serves as the cause that can give rise to all states of mind, then [this remains so] until form has yet to arise.
Upon what does the intermediate state depend?

[Tang Translation: It arises and immediately perishes; this is not taught for the sake of the ignorant. These dharmas of uninterrupted continuity arise through the differentiation of the various realms of existence.
Ignorance is their cause, and from that, the mind arises. Being unable yet to discern the coming of form, [it exists].
What does it abide in the interim?
As the preceding moment ceases in succession, another mind arises following it. When it does not abide in form, what object does it take as its condition to arise?
Because it arises from that [cause], it does not arise from a cause that is not as it truly is. How can there be no establishment [of the effect], yet one knows the destruction of the moment?
[Wei Translation: As soon as it arises, it has cessation; another mind arises following it. Matter does not abide for even a single thought-moment.
Upon observing what dharma arises, and depending upon what cause the dharma arises—if the mind were to arise without a cause, then arising would not be established.
How is it known that mindfulness perishes?
[Tang Translation: It is because there is an uninterrupted succession of cessation, yet another mind arises. When it does not abide in form, what object of perception gives rise to it?
If it arises by taking that [preceding] mind as its object, then its cause is false. Since the cause is false, its substance is not established.
What is momentary destruction?
It is the meditative absorption of the practitioner, the diamond-like relics of the Buddha, the palaces of the Ābhāsvara Heaven, and those things in the world that are indestructible.
Abiding in the True Dharma, one attains it; the Tathāgata is fully endowed with wisdom. The bhikṣu attains equanimity. How can one perceive moments?
Like a gandharva-city or a magical illusion, form has no momentary existence. Regarding unreal forms and the like, one views them as if they were real.
The practitioner realizes meditative concentration. The vajra-like relics of the Buddha. The palaces of the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
The indestructible phenomena of the world. The reality of the Dharma as realized through suchness. The accomplishment of the Tathāgata’s wisdom. The bhikṣu realizes equality.
How is it that mindfulness does not abide? It is like the illusory forms of a gandharva. Why does mindfulness not abide? Because one perceives form without the four great elements.
What, then, would the four great elements be for?
The practitioner’s right concentration, the vajra-like relics of the Buddha, the palaces of the Ābhāsvara heaven,
the indestructible phenomena of the world, the Tathāgata’s perfected wisdom, and the realization attained by bhikṣus— the nature of all dharmas is eternally abiding.
How is it that the forms of a city in the sky, illusions, and the like are seen as momentary? Why are the great elements (*mahābhūta*) not momentary?
Since they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), how can they be said to be the creators [of derived matter]?

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the World-Honored One has prophesied that Arhats shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, being no different from all Bodhisattvas.
Since the dharmas of all sentient beings do not enter parinirvāṇa, who is it that reaches the Buddha-way? From the initial attainment of Buddhahood until parinirvāṇa, throughout this interval..."
In the interim, not a single word was spoken, nor was there any response. Because the Tathāgata is eternally in meditative concentration, he has neither thought nor deliberation;
it is the emanated Buddha who performs the Buddha-works. For what reason do you speak of the mark of consciousness as perishing moment by moment?

The Vajrapāṇi always follows and guards [the Buddha]; why do you not establish the primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*)? You manifest Māra, the works of Māra, the retribution of evil karma, and the [destruction by] Ciñcā.
"O Māṇava, the woman Sundarī departed with an empty bowl; thus, the obstruction of her evil karma has manifested.
How can it be said that the Tathāgata has attained all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) yet is not free from faults?"
[Wei Translation] At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again addressed the Buddha,
saying: "World-Honored One, just as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has bestowed upon the various Arhats the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,
the Tathāgata has further stated that all Buddhas and Tathāgatas do not enter nirvāṇa, and has further stated that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyak-saṃbuddha..."
Omniscient One! At what night did you realize Great Bodhi? At what night did you enter Parinirvāṇa?

During that interval, you did not speak a single word. Furthermore, the Tathāgata has said that all Buddhas and Tathāgatas constantly abide in the samādhi that is without vitarka, without vicāra, and without conceptual discrimination;
yet he has also said that they perform various manifestations and transformations to deliver all sentient beings. World-Honored One, furthermore...
It is taught that all consciousnesses arise and cease in every moment, never remaining still, and that Vajrapāṇi constantly follows and guards them.

Furthermore, it is taught that the original limit of the world is difficult to know; yet it is also said that sentient beings enter parinirvāṇa, which would imply the existence of an original limit if they were to enter nirvāṇa.
Moreover, it is taught that while the Buddhas have no enemies, they nevertheless perceive the various Māras; and it is further taught concerning the Tathāgata—
Having severed all obstacles, [the Buddha] was slandered by Ciñcā Mānavikā, Subhaddarī, and others.
When the World-Honored One entered the village of Śālavana, he departed with an empty bowl, having failed to obtain any food.
World-Honored One, if this were so, the Tathāgata would possess immeasurable sinful karma. How then could the Tathāgata be free from all faults and evils? And yet—
[They] attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
[Tang Translation: At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, for what reason does the Tathāgata bestow upon Arhats the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*? For what reason..."
Furthermore, it is taught that sentient beings who lack the nature for parinirvāṇa can attain the path of Buddhahood.
Again, for what reason is it said that from the initial attainment of Buddhahood until parinirvāṇa, not a single word was spoken in the interim?

Moreover, it is said that the Tathāgata is always in meditative absorption, without applied thought or sustained thought. Furthermore, it is said that all Buddha-activities are merely transformations. And it is said regarding the various consciousnesses...
It undergoes momentary transformation and decay. Furthermore, it is said that the Vajra-gods constantly follow and protect it;
it is also said that while its prior limit is unknowable, there is parinirvāṇa; moreover, Māras and the deeds of Māra are presently manifest, and there are also remaining karmic retributions.
That is to say, there were such matters as the Brahmin woman Ciñcā, the heretical woman Sundarī, and returning with an empty bowl.
Since the World-Honored One possessed such karmic obstructions, how could he have attained all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*)?
And since he had already attained all-encompassing wisdom, why did he not remain free from such faults?
The Buddha said to Mahāmati, “Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall speak for your sake.

Mahāmati replied to the Buddha, “Excellent, World-Honored One! We shall indeed receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati, “It is for the sake of *nirvāṇa* without remainder, and to encourage and advance those who practice the bodhisattva path, that I speak thus.
This and other bodhisattva practitioners in other worlds delight in sound.”
Hearing of the vehicle of nirvāṇa, they are led away from the Śrāvaka vehicle and directed toward the Mahāyāna.

It is the *nirmāṇabuddha* (transformation buddha), not the *dharmabuddha* (dharma-body buddha), that bestows predictions upon the śrāvakas. Mahāmati, for this reason, the predictions given to the śrāvakas are no different from those given to the bodhisattvas. Mahāmati!

Regarding "not different": for śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all buddha-tathāgatas, there is a single flavor of liberation through the abandonment of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*), but not through the abandonment of the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

Mahāmati, the cognitive hindrance consists in seeing the excellence and purity of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*); the afflictive hindrance consists in... [the hindrance to the selflessness of persons].

First, one practices to realize the non-self of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and eliminates the obstacles to liberation consisting of the cessation of the seven consciousnesses. When the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) are extinguished, there is ultimate purity.
[Wei Translation] The Buddha addressed the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva, saying: "Excellent, excellent! Well done, Mahāmati!"
“Mahāmati, listen attentively now; I shall explain this for you. Mahāmati said to the Buddha, “Excellent, World-Honored One!

We shall indeed receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati, “For those bodhisattvas who have practiced the bodhisattva path in the past, I grant predictions of enlightenment based upon *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana without remainder).
Mahāmati, when I grant predictions to śrāvakas, it is because they are timid...”

To inspire courageous minds in weak sentient beings, Mahāmati, there are sentient beings in this world and in other Buddha-lands who practice the bodhisattva path yet take pleasure in the practices of the śrāvaka-dharma.
In order to turn them toward the attainment of great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), the *nirmāṇa-buddha* bestows predictions of enlightenment upon those *nirmāṇa-śrāvakas*;
it is not the *vipāka-buddha* or the *dharmakāya-buddha* that does so.

The Distinction of Prophecy. Mahāmati, there is no difference between the nirvāṇa of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Why is this? Because there is no distinction in their severing of the afflictions (*kleśa*).

They have severed the obstacle of afflictions, but not the obstacle to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Furthermore, Mahāmati, by seeing the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), one severs the obstacle to knowledge;
by seeing the selflessness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*), one severs the obstacle of afflictions. Mahāmati, [this occurs through] the transformation of the mind (*manas*).

Because of consciousness, one severs the obstacles of dharmas and the obstacles of karma. By means of the transformation of the mental consciousness (*manas*) and the perfuming of the *ālayavijñāna*, one attains ultimate purity.
[Tang Translation] The Buddha said: "Listen attentively; I shall explain it for you. Mahāmati, for the sake of *nirvāṇa* without remainder..."
Because of the realm, he secretly exhorted them to cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva.

Since there were bodhisattvas in this realm and other lands whose minds delighted in seeking the nirvana of a śrāvaka, he spoke these words to cause them to abandon such a mind and advance in the cultivation of the Great Practice.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, it is the *nirmāṇa-buddha* (transformation buddha) who bestows predictions upon transformed śrāvakas, not the *dharmatā-buddha* (buddha of the nature of reality).

Mahāmati, the bestowing of predictions upon śrāvakas is a teaching of intentional secrecy (*saṃdhyābhāṣya*). Mahāmati, the statement that there is no difference between the Buddha and the two vehicles is based on the single flavor of liberation through the severance of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*), and does not refer to the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
As for the cognitive hindrance, one must realize the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) [to overcome it].

Because it is pure. As for the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*), when one abandons the consciousness that perceives a self in persons (*pudgalanairātmya*), at that time the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) are first severed and extinguished;
only through liberation from the hindrance to phenomena (*dharmāvaraṇa*) does one attain eternal purity.
Because of the principle of primordial abiding (*pūrvasthita-dharma*), there is no nature of before or after.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, I always abide by the essence of the fundamental dharma and do not further give rise to dharmas.
[The Tang Translation: "Mahāmati, I have uttered this esoteric teaching based on the primordially abiding Dharma;
it is not that there is something further to be said after the previous Buddhas, for they were already fully endowed with such syllables."
Because his fundamental vows are inexhaustible, the Tathāgata expounds the Dharma without deliberation or investigation. Because he is transformed by right knowledge, his mindfulness is not deluded;

thus, he is without deliberation or investigation. Because he has severed the habitual tendencies of the four stages of dwelling and the stage of the dwelling of ignorance, he has abandoned the two afflictions and is free from the two kinds of death.
He has awakened to the selflessness of persons and phenomena and has severed the two obstacles.
[Wei Translation] Relying on the original names, phrases, and sentences, the Tathāgata speaks of all dharmas without conscious effort or deliberation.
Mahāmati, the Tathāgata’s knowledge is always as he intends, and he never loses mindfulness; therefore, the Tathāgata is without vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought).
Having transcended the four stages, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are far removed from the two kinds of death, the two kinds of obstacles, and the two kinds of karma.
Therefore, [the Tang translation states]: "Mahāmati, the Tathāgata possesses correct knowledge and is free from delusive thoughts; he does not require deliberation before preaching the Dharma.
The Tathāgata has long since severed the four kinds of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), is liberated from the two kinds of death, and has eliminated the two kinds of obstructions."
Mahāmati, the seven—mind, intellect, mentation, and the visual consciousnesses and so forth—are momentary and have habit-energies as their cause;

they are excluded from the category of the wholesome and the outflow-free, and thus do not undergo cyclic existence. Mahāmati, the Tathāgatagarbha is the cause of both cyclic existence and nirvāṇa, and of suffering and happiness;
it cannot be realized by foolish ordinary people whose wisdom is confused by emptiness.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, the seven consciousnesses—the mental consciousness, the manas, and those of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body—do not abide for even a single moment.
This is because they are conditioned by false habitual tendencies and are devoid of all untainted wholesome dharmas.
Mahāmati, the Tathāgatagarbha is neither born nor dies in the world; it neither comes nor goes; it is eternal, constant, cool, and unchanging. Furthermore, Mahāmati...
Wisdom: It is because of the Tathāgatagarbha that there exist the causes of worldly existence and nirvāṇa, as well as suffering and pleasure;
yet ordinary beings do not perceive or know this, and thus fall into emptiness, falsehood, and perversion.

[The Tang Translation: "Mahāmati, the manas, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and the seven [consciousnesses] beginning with the visual consciousness have habitual tendencies as their cause and are momentary in nature.
They are apart from the untainted wholesome [states] and are not dharmas of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
Mahāmati, the Tathāgatagarbha is the cause of the flow of birth and death, as well as of nirvāṇa, suffering, and pleasure. Ordinary fools do not know this and falsely cling to emptiness."
Mahāmati, he who is followed and protected by the Vajrapāṇi is merely a transformation Buddha (nirmāṇa-buddha), not the true Tathāgata.
