Mahāmati, the true Tathāgata is free from all faculties and measures (pramāṇa). Because all the faculties and measures of ordinary people, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and outsiders have been extinguished, and because he has attained the patience of the knowledge of the uninterrupted dharma (anantara-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti) and dwells in the bliss of the present dharma, he is not [protected] by the Vajrapāṇi.
That which is protected: all emanation-buddhas (*nirmāṇa-buddha*) are not born of karma. An emanation-buddha is neither a buddha nor separate from a buddha.
He preaches the Dharma by means of signs produced by sentient beings, such as a potter’s wheel; he does not preach from his own direct realization regarding the realm of self-awakened wisdom.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, Vajramitra constantly attends and protects him. He is surrounded by the front and back by the Nirmāṇakāya Tathāgatas.
It is not the Dharmakāya Buddha or the Saṃbhogakāya Buddha, but the Mūlatathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Mahāmati, the Mūlatathāgata is far removed from all sense faculties and from the measurements of the great and the small; he is far removed from all ordinary beings, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas.

Pratyekabuddhas and others, Mahāmati, who practice according to reality and attain the realm of the blissful practice of that *tathatā* (suchness), know the fundamental Buddha because they have attained the *dharma-kṣānti* (patience regarding the dharma) of equality.
Therefore, Vajramitra is the transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇa-buddha*) who appears in accordance with needs.
Mahāmati, as for the transformation Buddha, there is no karma and no slander; yet the transformation Buddha is not different from the Dharma-Buddha (*dharma-buddha*).

The *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) of the Buddha Tathāgata is likewise not one [with the other bodies]. Just as a potter or salt performs various functions, the *nirmāṇakāya* performs the work of transforming sentient beings.
It teaches the Dharma through diverse manifestations, but it does not teach the internal realized Dharma, which is the realm of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*).
[The Tang Translation: Mahāmati, the transformation Tathāgatas are constantly guarded by Vajrapāṇi; they are not the true Buddha.
The true Tathāgata is beyond the measure of the sensory faculties and is unknowable to those of the two vehicles or the non-Buddhists.
Abiding in the bliss of the present dharma, he has accomplished the patience of wisdom (*jñāna-kṣānti*) and does not rely on the protection of Vajrapāṇi. This applies to all transformation Buddhas.
It does not arise from karma; it is neither the Buddha himself nor is it not the Buddha.
Just as a potter produces his wares through the combination of various factors, so too is the emanation-buddha (nirmāṇa-buddha):
endowed with all the marks, he expounds the Dharma, yet he cannot speak of the realm experienced by the noble wisdom of self-realization.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, fools give rise to the view of annihilation based on the cessation of the seven collections of consciousness. Because they do not realize the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), they give rise to the view of permanence.
Due to their own false conceptualization, they do not know the original limit (pūrvakoṭi). Through the cessation of the wisdom of their own false conceptualization, there is liberation;
through the severance of the habitual tendencies of the four stages of dwelling and the stage of ignorance-dwelling, all faults are severed.
[Wei Translation] Furthermore, Mahāmati, all ordinary beings, outsiders, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others, seeing the cessation of the six consciousnesses, fall into the view of annihilationism;
not seeing the ālayavijñāna, they fall into the view of eternalism.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, because they do not perceive that the differentiation of their own minds has no original limit (*pūrvakoṭi*), the world is said to have no original limit.
Mahāmati, for one who is far removed from the views of their own mind’s discrimination, this is called liberation and the realization of nirvāṇa.
Mahāmati, because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are far removed from the four kinds of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), they are therefore free from fault.
[The Tang Translation: Furthermore, Mahāmati, foolish ordinary people perceive the cessation of the six consciousnesses and give rise to the view of annihilationism;

failing to understand the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), they give rise to the view of eternalism. Mahāmati, because the conceptualization of one's own mind is its fundamental limit, it cannot be apprehended.
By departing from this conceptualization, one attains liberation. When the four types of habitual tendencies are severed, one is free from all faults.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "The three vehicles are also not vehicles; the Tathāgata is not subject to extinction.

That which is prophesied by all Buddhas is said to be free from all faults and evils. For the sake of those with uninterrupted wisdom and for the sake of nirvana without remainder, he employs expedient means to entice and advance those of inferior capacity;
therefore, he speaks with intentional concealment. The wisdom arising from all Buddhas is precisely [this]..."

To speak otherwise: those who claim that the various vehicles are not vehicles, and that there is no nirvana, are deluded. Desire, form, existence, and views—these are said to be the four grounds of abiding.
They arise from the mental consciousness; consciousness is the dwelling place and the mind is what resides therein.
When the mind and the visual consciousness and so forth are extinguished, they proclaim this as impermanence, yet they hold a view of nirvana and thus preach it to be eternal.

[Wei Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse: "The three vehicles and the non-vehicle, the immeasurable vehicles of all Buddhas, the prediction of all to the stage of Buddhahood, and the teaching on the severance of all afflictions;

the realization of noble wisdom within one's own body, as well as *nirvāṇa* without remainder—these were taught as hidden and concealed in order to encourage and lead those of timid disposition. Thus, even though the Tathāgata has attained realized wisdom..."

I have taught that path; sentient beings rely upon it to enter the Way. For the two vehicles, there is no nirvāṇa. One perceives desire, form, and existence, as well as the four kinds of perfumed stages (*bhūmi*).
Consciousness arises from these [objects]. One perceives the co-abiding of the mental consciousness, and perceives the mental consciousness along with the visual consciousness and so forth.
Based on permanence, impermanence, and annihilationism, one relies on the mind and its associates to give rise to the view of nirvāṇa.
[The Tang Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse: "The three vehicles and non-vehicles, There is no nirvāṇa for a Buddha;
All are granted the prophecy of the Tathāgata. It is taught as being free from all faults and evils, Accomplishing ultimate wisdom And nirvāṇa without remainder.
To entice and encourage those of timid and inferior capacity, This was spoken with such intentional meaning (saṃdhi). The wisdom attained by all Buddhas..."

I have taught this path; it is only this and nothing else. Therefore, for them there is no nirvāṇa. Desire, form, existence, and various views—these four kinds of habitual tendencies arise from the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
The store-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is also present therein. Seeing that the mental consciousness, the eyes, and so forth are impermanent, one speaks of annihilationism.
Being deluded about the mind and the store-consciousness, one gives rise to the notion of permanence; through false wisdom, one claims this to be nirvāṇa.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva asked in verse: “Regarding those bodhisattvas who are resolved to seek the Buddha-way:
how should they consume alcohol, meat, and onions? I pray that the Unsurpassed Honored One will compassionately explain this for us.
How can these things—objects of attachment for the foolish, foul-smelling, ill-reputed, and the very delicacies favored by tigers and wolves—be eaten?”
"Eating gives rise to all manner of faults; not eating is a source of merit and goodness. I pray that you will explain for me the transgressions and blessings of eating and abstaining from food.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati Bodhisattva asked: "Regarding wine, meat, onions, leeks, and garlic—the Buddha has declared these to be impure and forbidden all from being eaten.
They are the food consumed by rākṣasas and the like, not the flavors enjoyed by the noble ones. Those who eat them are censured by the sages."
And that an evil reputation may spread—may the Buddha explain this in detail: the merits and faults of eating and not eating meat.
[Tang Translation] At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāmati spoke again in verse:
"The Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, who aspire to seek supreme enlightenment, should consider whether wine, meat, and onions are fit to be eaten or not. Fools greedily crave meat."
Foul-smelling, impure, and without renown, it is like those wicked beasts. How could it be fit for consumption?
What fault is there in eating it, and what virtue is there in not eating it? I pray that the Most Victorious Honored One will fully explain this for me.
After the Bodhisattva Mahāmati had spoken these verses in inquiry, he again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We pray that the World-Honored One will explain for us the merits and faults of eating and not eating meat.

Thus, both I and the other Bodhisattvas, in the present and the future, shall expound the Dharma in various ways for those beings who desire to eat meat, so as to cause all such beings to direct their hearts toward one another with compassion."
Having attained the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta*), each shall, within their respective stages (*bhūmi*), become pure and clear, swiftly attaining ultimate, unsurpassed *bodhi*.
Even the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*, having brought rest to their own stages, shall also swiftly achieve unsurpassed *bodhi*.

As for the various non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) of evil and heterodox doctrines, who hold inverted attachments to the false views of annihilationism and eternalism, they still maintain prohibitions that forbid the consumption of [certain] foods.
How much less, then, would the Tathāgata—the protector of the world who has perfected the True Dharma—consume meat?
[Wei Translation] At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One..."
I observe the cycle of birth and death in this world, where beings are bound together by the knots of enmity and fall into the evil realms;
all this arises from eating meat and killing one another, which increases greed and hatred, preventing liberation and resulting in great suffering. World-Honored One!
"One who eats meat cuts off the seed of great compassion; those who cultivate the Noble Path should not eat it.

World-Honored One, even the various non-Buddhists who propound false views—such as the Lokāyata, which is a worldly discourse falling into the views of nihilism and eternalism, or existence and non-existence—all prohibit the eating of meat.
They themselves do not eat it and do not permit others to eat it. How much more so [should this be true for] one such as [the Buddha]?"
For those who come to practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*) within this pure Dharma, there should be no prohibition whatsoever regarding eating one's own food or the food of others.
Since the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, regards all sentient beings with equal compassion, why does he permit the eating of meat?
How excellent, World-Honored One! Out of pity for the world, we pray that you will explain to us the faults of eating meat and the merits of not eating it.
Having heard this, I and all the bodhisattvas shall attain reliance upon it to practice according to reality and propagate it widely,
so that all sentient beings of the present and future may fully understand it.
[The Tang Translation: At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for me the merits and faults of eating and not eating meat.

Having understood their meaning, I and the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas shall expound them for the sake of those sentient beings who eat meat, being perfumed by the habits of retribution in the present and future."
Speak thus, so that they may renounce the flavor of meat and seek the flavor of the Dharma;
so that they may give rise to great compassion for all sentient beings and cherish one another as if they were an only child;

so that they may abide on the bodhisattva stages and attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, or at least find temporary rest on the stages of the two vehicles, ultimately achieving unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

“World-Honored One, even the various non-Buddhist practitioners such as the Lokāyatas—who give rise to views of existence and non-existence and cling to the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism—still prohibit and forbid the eating of meat.
How much more so for the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, who nurtures all beings with great compassion and is the refuge of the world;
how could he permit both oneself and others to eat meat? Excellent, World-Honored One, you who possess great kindness!”
Filled with sorrow and compassion for the world, viewing all sentient beings as if they were an only child,

I pray that you will explain the faults and evils of eating meat and the merits of abstaining from it, so that I and the other bodhisattvas, having heard this, may practice it and extensively teach it to others.
The Buddha said to Mahāmati, "Excellent, excellent! Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall speak for you.
Mahāmati replied to the Buddha, "Yes, I shall receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati, "There are immeasurable causes and conditions for which one should not eat meat.
However, I shall now briefly explain them for you: all sentient beings, from the very beginning, have [been our kin]..."
Because all beings have at some point been one's own kin through the turning of causes and conditions, and because they are regarded as kin, one should not eat meat.
[Wei Translation] The Buddha addressed the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva, saying: "Excellent, excellent! Well done, Mahāmati!
Because you possess great compassion and pity for sentient beings, you are able to inquire about this matter. Listen attentively now; I shall explain it for you."
"You have spoken. Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying, "Excellent, World-Honored One! We shall indeed receive your instruction.
The Buddha told Mahāmati, "There are immeasurable faults in those who eat meat. All Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who cultivate great compassion must not eat meat.
I shall now briefly explain for you the merits of abstaining from it and the transgressions of eating it. You should now [listen].
"Listen attentively, Mahāmati. I observe that sentient beings, due to the habit of eating meat since beginningless time, become greedily attached to its flavor and kill one another.
They remain far removed from the noble ones and undergo the suffering of birth and death. Those who renounce the taste of meat will hear the taste of the True Dharma;
they will practice according to reality on the bodhisattva stages and swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Enlightenment. Furthermore, they cause sentient beings to enter the resting place of the stages of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas;
once they have rested there, they cause them to enter the stage of the Tathāgata. Mahāmati, such benefits as these have compassion as their root.
Those who eat meat sever the seed of great compassion; how then could they ever attain such great benefits? Therefore, Mahāmati, I...

I observe sentient beings cycling through the six realms of existence, all dwelling together in birth and death, mutually giving birth to one another and serving as parents, brothers, sisters, sons, daughters, paternal or maternal relatives, and inner or outer kin.

Whether male or female, whether distant or close, they are constant companions throughout the various good and evil paths. For these reasons, I observe that sentient beings are constantly related to one another.
"There is no one whose flesh may be eaten who has not been one's own kin. Driven by greed for the taste of flesh, beings devour one another;

they constantly harbor harmful intent, increase their karma of suffering, and transmigrate through birth and death without finding liberation. When the Buddha spoke these words, all the malevolent rākṣasas heard what the Buddha had said.
They completely abandoned their evil intentions and ceased eating meat, exhorting one another to give rise to compassion.
With a mind that protects the lives of all sentient beings more than one’s own body, he renounced and ceased eating all kinds of meat.

Weeping and shedding tears, he addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, having heard the Buddha’s teaching on the careful observation of the six realms of existence, I realize that the meat I have eaten was all from my own kin.
I now know that those who eat meat are great enemies to sentient beings and sever the seeds of great compassion; they shall forever remain [estranged from it]."
“Venerable One, wholesome karma is the root of great suffering. From this day forward, I shall abstain from eating meat, and I shall not permit my retinue to eat it either.
For those disciples of the Tathāgata who do not eat meat, I shall personally attend to and protect them day and night.
As for those who eat meat, I shall bring them great harm. Mahāmati, the rākṣasas are evil...”
Even those ghosts who constantly eat flesh, upon hearing what I have said, will give rise to a mind of compassion and renounce meat, refusing to eat it;

how much more so should my disciples who practice the wholesome Dharma refrain from eating meat? If one eats meat, know that such a person is a great enemy to sentient beings and severs my noble lineage.
Mahāmati, if my disciples hear what I have said but do not examine it with discernment...
One who observes and eats meat should be known as being of the *caṇḍāla* caste;
they are not my disciple, nor am I their teacher. Therefore, Mahāmati, if you wish to be my follower, you must not eat any kind of meat whatsoever.
[The Tang Translation: At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, saying:
"Mahāmati, listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect well upon this. I shall now analyze and explain it for you.
Mahāmati, there are immeasurable causes and conditions regarding all meats; therein, a Bodhisattva should give rise to compassion and must not consume them. I shall now..."
I shall explain a small portion of this for you, Mahāmati. Since beginningless time, all sentient beings have been revolving incessantly in the cycle of birth and death.
There has never been a time when they have not acted as parents, brothers, sons, daughters, or kinsmen, nor even as friends, loved ones, or servants;
they have repeatedly taken birth in the forms of birds, beasts, and other such bodies. How could one, in the midst of this, harbor [grasping]?
and eat it. Mahāmati, a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva regards all sentient beings as identical to his own self.
Considering that meat comes from the life-force of living beings, how could he eat it? Mahāmati, even when Rākṣasas and others hear this teaching of mine, they should still abstain from meat;
how much more so those who delight in the Dharma? Mahāmati, wherever a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva...
One should contemplate all sentient beings in their various states of birth as being one's own kin, even regarding them with loving-kindness as if they were an only child.

For this reason, one should not eat any kind of meat—neither that of donkeys, mules, camels, foxes, dogs, oxen, horses, humans, wild beasts, or others. Since butchers sell these meats mixed together, one should not consume them.
Flesh: Because it grows from impure elements and vapors, one should not eat meat.
When sentient beings smell its odor, they all give rise to terror, just as the Caṇḍālas and Taṃbas do; because dogs see it with loathing and bark in packs out of fear, one should not eat meat.

[Wei Translation] Furthermore, Mahāmati, a bodhisattva should contemplate that all meat arises from the impurity of the union of the father’s semen and the mother’s blood, resulting in an impure body. For this reason, a bodhisattva, contemplating the impurity of meat, should not eat meat.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, when sentient beings smell the odor of one who eats meat, they all [become terrified].
They flee in terror and keep their distance. Therefore, a bodhisattva should practice the conduct of reality.
To transform sentient beings, one should not eat meat. Mahāmati, it is like this:
wherever a caṇḍāla, a hunter, a butcher, a fisherman, or a fowler goes, sentient beings see them from afar and think to themselves, "I shall certainly die now that this person is coming."
This is a great evildoer. Ignorant of sin and merit, he takes the lives of sentient beings, seeking immediate profit;
having come here now to seek us out, we shall certainly die, for our bodies are all still possessed of flesh.
Mahāmati, because people eat meat, it causes all sentient beings who see them to give rise to such terror.
"Mahāmati, all sentient beings throughout the void of space are terrified upon seeing those who eat meat;
they give rise to doubts, thinking, 'Am I now to die or shall I live? Such evil persons do not cultivate a mind of loving-kindness;
they wander through the world seeking meat like jackals and wolves, just as oxen graze on grass or dung beetles [seek their food]."
Chasing after excrement, they know no satiety. My body is flesh; it is precisely their food, and they should not encounter me.
They immediately abandon [me] and flee, distancing themselves far away, no different from people who fear rākṣasas.
Mahāmati, those who eat meat cause all sentient beings who see them to give rise to such terror. You should know that for those who eat meat...
It gives rise to great enmity. Therefore, the Bodhisattva practices loving-kindness and compassion;
for the sake of gathering in sentient beings, he should not eat that which is the flavor consumed by non-noble and evil persons. Its ill repute spreads abroad and it is censured by the noble ones.
For this reason, Mahāmati, for the sake of gathering in all sentient beings, the Bodhisattva should not eat meat.

[The Tang Translation: "Mahāmati, in the streets and marketplaces, there are meat-sellers who, for the sake of profit, hawk the flesh of dogs, horses, humans, oxen, and so forth. How could such impure things be eaten?
Mahāmati, all meats are produced from the filth of semen and blood. How can one who seeks purity [consume them]?"
"Eat [this], Mahāmati. When sentient beings see those who eat meat, they are all struck with fear. How can one who cultivates a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) eat meat?
Mahāmati, it is like hunters, *caṇḍālas*, fishermen, bird-catchers, and other such evil people;
when dogs see them, they bark in alarm, and when wild animals see them, they flee. So it is for all beings—whether flying in the air, on water, or on land."
When they are born, if anyone sees them, everyone will think: "This person's breath is like that of a rākṣasa;
having come here now, he will surely kill me. For the sake of protecting their lives, they all flee and avoid him.
It is the same for those who eat meat. Therefore, a bodhisattva practicing the cultivation of loving-kindness should not eat meat.
Furthermore, one should not eat meat because it prevents the arising of a compassionate mind in practitioners.

One should not eat meat because it is a foul, impure thing relished only by the ignorant and lacks a good reputation. One should not eat meat because it causes various mantras and incantations to fail.
One should not eat meat because those who kill living beings perceive their forms and give rise to consciousness, becoming deeply attached to its flavor. He...
Because those who eat meat are abandoned by the devas, one should not eat meat. Because it causes the breath to stink, one should not eat meat.
Because it results in many evil dreams, one should not eat meat. Because tigers and wolves in the open forests will scent its odor, one should not eat meat.

Because it leads to a lack of moderation in eating and drinking, one should not eat meat. Because it prevents practitioners from developing a sense of weary detachment (*saṃvega*), one should not eat meat.
Therefore, one should not eat meat. I have previously said: "In all that you consume as food and drink, you should conceive of it as the flesh of your own child and as medicine;
therefore, you should not eat meat. There is no basis for permitting the eating of meat.
[Wei Translation] Furthermore, Mahāmati, a bodhisattva should not eat meat in order to protect the faith of sentient beings. Why is this?
Mahāmati, those called "bodhisattvas" are known by all sentient beings as the seeds of the compassionate heart of the Buddha-Tathāgata;
they are able to serve as a place of refuge for sentient beings, so that upon hearing [of them], people naturally do not give rise to doubt or fear. To give rise to...

One should conceive of them as kinsmen, as spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), and as those who inspire fearlessness; one should say that they have found a place of refuge, a place of security, and a virtuous guide.
Mahāmati, it is by abstaining from meat that one can generate such faith in sentient beings.
If those who eat meat cause sentient beings to lose all faith, they will say that there is no one in the world to be trusted, thereby severing the faculty of faith.
For this reason, Mahāmati, a bodhisattva, in order to protect the faith of sentient beings, must not eat any kind of meat whatsoever.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, my disciples [must refrain from eating meat] in order to prevent the world from slandering [the Dharma].
For the sake of the Triple Gem, one should not eat meat. Why is this? Because there are people in the world who, seeing one eat meat, slander and disparage the Triple Gem, saying:
"In the Buddha's Dharma, where could there truly be śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas practicing the holy life who abandon what is the natural food of sages and instead eat the flesh of living beings?"
Just as a rākṣasa, having filled his belly with flesh, sleeps soundly and unmoving, yet seeks out and devours meat by relying on the powerful influence of worldly, ordinary people;
and just as a rākṣasa king terrifies sentient beings, crying out everywhere:
"Where is there a true śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa who practices pure conduct? There is no Dharma, there is no śramaṇa!"

Where there is no Vinaya, there are no practitioners of purity; such immeasurable and boundless evil and unwholesome thoughts as these arise, severing my Wheel of Dharma and extinguishing the lineage of the noble ones—all of this is due to the fault of those who eat meat.
Therefore, Mahāmati, my disciples, in order to protect against evil people who slander the Triple Gem, should not even give rise to [such thoughts], let alone act upon them.

One should even maintain the perception of meat as such; how much more so should one refrain from eating it? Furthermore, Mahāmati, a bodhisattva seeking to purify a buddha-field and to transform sentient beings should not eat meat.

One should regard all meats as human corpses—such that one does not wish to see them with the eyes nor wish to smell their odor—let alone inhale them or place them in the mouth. All meats are likewise [to be regarded].

It is so, Mahāmati. Just as the foul odor of a burning corpse is no different from the stench of burning other meats, how could there be any distinction therein between what is edible and what is inedible?
Therefore, a bodhisattva seeking a pure buddha-field and intending to transform sentient beings should not eat meat. Furthermore, Mahāmati, a bodhisattva seeks to transcend birth...

Upon death, one should single-mindedly contemplate the practice of loving-kindness and compassion. With few desires and contentment, weary of the sufferings of the world, one should swiftly seek liberation.
One should abandon clamor and bustle to resort to open spaces, dwelling in charnel grounds, forest hermitages, among graves, or beneath trees, sitting alone in contemplation.
One should observe that there is not a single thing in all the worlds worth delighting in—not even wife, children, or kinsmen.
One should regard [the body] as shackles and fetters; one should regard palaces, towers, and pavilions as prisons;

one should view all precious jewels as heaps of excrement; one should see all food and drink as pus and blood; and when receiving food and drink, one should regard it as applying ointment to a festering ulcer.

One should seek only to sustain life while binding the mind to the Noble Path, not for the sake of craving flavors. All odors such as those of wine, meat, onions, leeks, garlic, and scallions [should be avoided].
They renounce and do not eat. Mahāmati, if one acts in this way, that is true cultivation; such a person is worthy of receiving the offerings of all devas and humans.

If, however, one does not give rise to weary detachment toward the world, but instead greedily clings to various flavors—wine, meat, and pungent vegetables—and eats them whenever the opportunity arises, one should not accept the faithful offerings of the world. Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are sentient beings...

In the past, they cultivated immeasurable causes and conditions; possessing subtle roots of goodness, they were able to hear my Dharma, left the household life with faith, and entered into my teaching.
Although in the past they were members of a rākṣasa retinue and were born among tigers, wolves, lions, cats, and wildcats, they still possess the residual habit of eating meat within my teaching;
thus, upon seeing those who eat meat, they feel joy and draw near to them. They enter...
In various cities, towns, villages, stupas, and monasteries, they take pleasure in drinking alcohol and eating meat.

When the devas look down upon them, they see that these people are no different from rākṣasas vying to devour corpses; yet they do not realize that they have already lost their status as my followers and have become part of the rākṣasa retinue.
Although they wear the kāṣāya robes and have shaved their hair and beards, when living beings see them, their hearts [are filled with fear].
They give rise to terror as if fearing a rākṣasa. For this reason, Mahāmati, those who take me as their teacher must not eat any meat whatsoever.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, even the worldly practitioners of false views and sorcery do not eat meat if they find that their incantations fail;
since they refrain from eating meat even for the sake of accomplishing their own perverted arts, how much more so should my disciples?
In seeking the unsurpassed, holy path of the Tathāgata and supramundane liberation, one cultivates great compassion and diligently practices asceticism, yet still fears that it may not be attained.
How could such liberation ever be obtained by those deluded people who eat meat?
Therefore, Mahāmati, my disciples, for the sake of seeking the bliss of supramundane liberation, do not...
"One should eat meat. Furthermore, Mahāmati, eating meat can increase physical strength. People who indulge in flavors become greedily attached to them;
therefore, one should carefully observe that all beings in the world who possess a body and life each cherish themselves as precious and fear the suffering of death.

There is no difference between humans and animals in their protection and attachment to their own bodies and lives. Would one rather take pleasure in the existence of a body like that of a mange-ridden jackal, or not?
One is able to sacrifice one's life to receive the pleasures of the devas. Why is this? Because one fears the suffering of birth and death.
Mahāmati, observing thus that death is a great suffering and a terrifying phenomenon, how could one who fears death for oneself eat the flesh of others?
Therefore, Mahāmati, those who wish to eat meat should first reflect upon their own bodies, and then contemplate all sentient beings.
One should not eat meat. Furthermore, Mahāmati, those who eat meat are shunned by the devas, let alone by the noble ones (ārya).
Therefore, a bodhisattva, desiring to see the noble ones, should cultivate compassion and must not eat meat. Mahāmati!
For one who eats meat, sleep is painful and waking is also painful.

If they see various evils in their dreams, they will be terrified with hair standing on end and their minds will remain constantly unsettled. Because they lack a heart of compassion, they are deficient in all wholesome powers.
If they are alone in a secluded place, non-human beings will frequently watch for an opportunity to harm them; even tigers, wolves, and lions [will do so].
They come to watch for and seek to eat their flesh; their minds are constantly filled with fear and alarm, finding no peace or security.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, those who eat meat find it difficult to satisfy their greedy desires. They do not know moderation in eating, and thus cannot digest what they consume.

This increases the impurities of the four great elements, causing their breath to smell of raw meat and their bellies to harbor immeasurable evil worms. Their bodies become riddled with sores, scabs, and malignant leprosy.
The various impurities of disease are currently unpleasant for ordinary people to hear or see;
how much more so is it that a future human body—free from illness and pure with fragrance—can be obtained?

Furthermore, Mahāmati, I say that even when ordinary people eat pure food for the sake of a pure livelihood, they should still give rise to the thought that it is like the flesh of their own son; how much more so regarding the eating of what is not fit for noble ones?
Regarding food: the Noble Ones abstain from it because meat can give rise to immeasurable faults and cause one to lose all supramundane merits.
How could I say that I permit my disciples to eat various impure flavors such as flesh and blood? To say that I permit this is to slander me.
Mahāmati, I permit my disciples to eat only those things which are appropriate for the Noble Ones to consume.
Regarding food: this does not refer to the food that the Noble Ones distance themselves from. The food of the Noble Ones can produce immeasurable merit and distance one from all faults.

Mahāmati, the food consumed by Noble Ones of the past and present consists of such things as non-glutinous rice, large and small wheat, various beans, various oils and honey, sugarcane, sugarcane juice, khaṇḍa, madhu, and so forth, according to [the circumstances].
"Mahāmati, at that time, those who obtain [meat] will be permitted to eat it as pure.

However, in future ages there will be foolish people who, because of their past habituation to eating meat and their attachment to its flavor, will claim that various forms of discipline (vinaya) permit the eating of meat."
They speak thus according to what they perceive with their own minds; it is not that the Buddhas and noble ones declare meat to be good food.
Mahāmati, those who do not eat meat must have, in the past, made offerings to the Buddhas and planted various roots of goodness.

They are able to believe the Buddha’s words, firmly abide by the Vinaya, and trust in cause and effect. Consequently, they are able to exercise self-restraint in body and speech, and do not act for the sake of the world.
[They] become attached to various flavors. Upon seeing those who eat meat, they are able to give rise to a mind of compassion.
[Tang Translation: Mahāmati, as for those who eat meat, their bodies are foul-smelling and impure, and an evil reputation spreads abroad;
the wise and holy, as well as virtuous people, do not associate with them. For this reason, a Bodhisattva should not eat meat. Mahāmati, as for blood and flesh...
It is that which has been discarded by the various seers and is not eaten by the multitude of sages; for this reason, a bodhisattva should not eat meat.
Mahāmati, a bodhisattva, in order to protect the faith of sentient beings and to prevent them from giving rise to slander toward the Buddha-dharma, should not eat meat out of compassion.
Mahāmati, if my disciples were to consume meat, it would cause all people in the world—

They all harbored derision and slander, saying: "How can these śramaṇas, who claim to be practitioners of pure conduct, abandon the flavors enjoyed by celestial beings and roam the world like savage beasts, their bellies full of flesh?
They cause all sentient beings to be filled with terror; they destroy pure conduct and lose the way of the śramaṇa. Therefore, one should know that the Buddha..."
Within the Dharma, there is no practice of disciplining others. Out of compassion for sentient beings, a bodhisattva protects them and does not allow such thoughts to arise;

one should not eat meat. Mahāmati, just as the stench and filth of burning human flesh are no different from burning other kinds of meat, how could there be a distinction between eating and not eating among them? Therefore, all...
Those who delight in purity should not eat meat, Mahāmati.

Sons of good family who practice in solitude among burial mounds, under trees, or in forest hermitages—whether they abide in a mind of loving-kindness, maintain incantations, seek liberation, or aspire to the Great Vehicle—will encounter all manner of obstacles and fail to achieve success because of eating meat. Therefore, a Bodhisattva...
Mahāmati, one who desires to benefit both oneself and others should not eat meat.
Mahāmati, as for those who eat meat, the mere sight of its form and color gives rise to a mind that craves its flavor.

Since a Bodhisattva regards all sentient beings with compassion as if they were his own body, how could he look upon them and conceive the thought of eating them? For this reason, Mahāmati, a Bodhisattva should not eat meat. Mahāmati.
Now, those who eat meat are shunned by the devas; their breath is perpetually foul. Their dreams are restless, and upon waking, they are filled with anxiety and dread.
Yakṣas and malevolent spirits steal away their vital essence. Their minds are frequently seized by terror. They know no satiety in eating.
Their illnesses increase, and it is easy for sores and scabs to arise. They are constantly being nibbled and eaten by various insects. They are unable to attain deep [insight] regarding food.
They develop revulsion and detachment. Mahāmati, I have always said that one should regard whatever is eaten as being like the flesh of one's own son;
this applies even more so to other foods. How, then, could I permit my disciples to eat meat? Mahāmati, meat is not excellent; it is impure.
It gives rise to all manner of evils and destroys all meritorious virtues. It is something abandoned by all the seers and holy sages. How [could I allow its consumption]?
"And yet you permit your disciples to eat it? If one says that eating is permitted, such a person slanders me.
Mahāmati, you should know that pure, excellent food consists of non-glutinous rice, millet, large and small wheat, beans, ghee, oil, and rock honey.
Such items as these were permitted by the Buddhas of the past and are what I have proclaimed; they are [the food] within my own lineage."
Virtuous sons and daughters, those who harbor pure faith, have long planted roots of goodness, and do not give rise to craving for body, life, or wealth;
who regard all beings with compassion as they would themselves—such are the ones for whom this food is intended.
It is not something cherished by those of evil habits or those with the nature of tigers and wolves.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, in the past there was a king named Siṃhasaudāsa who ate various kinds of meat until he eventually came to eat human flesh.
When his ministers and subjects could no longer endure this, they plotted a rebellion and cut off his stipend.
Because those who eat meat have such faults as these, one should not eat meat.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, I recall that in the past there was a king named Siṃhadāsa.

He ate various kinds of meat and became addicted to their flavors, until in due course he even came to eat human flesh. Because of eating human flesh, his parents, brothers, wife, children, and kinsmen all abandoned him;
likewise, all his ministers, the kingdom, and the villages immediately [deserted him].
They conspired together to take his life. Since those who eat meat have such faults as these, one should not eat any meat at all.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Lord of the Heaven of Sovereignty (Īśvara) manifested himself as a pigeon, and Śakra Devendra, the Lord of the Gods, because of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) from eating meat in the past, manifested himself as a hawk to startle and pursue him.

A pigeon. The pigeon came to seek refuge with me. At that time, I was King Śibi. Out of compassion for sentient beings who prey upon one another, I weighed my own flesh against a hawk to ransom the pigeon.
When the flesh I cut was insufficient, I placed it upon the scale; as my body was being weighed, I underwent great suffering.
Mahāmati, such is the habitual conditioning of eating meat from immeasurable past ages, affecting both one's own body and the bodies of others.
Such faults exist; how much more so for those who, lacking a sense of shame, constantly eat meat? Mahāmati, there was another king who did not eat meat.
While riding a horse for recreation, he was startled by waves and led deep into the mountains, where he lost his attendants and could not find the way back.
Because he did not eat meat, lions, tigers, and wolves harbored no harmful intent toward him, and [he encountered] a female lion...

Together they engaged in sexual acts until children were born. King Pādapāṇi and others, due to the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) from eating meat in past lives, continued to eat meat even while serving as human kings.
In the village of the seven families, they took great pleasure in eating meat;
through the great transgression of eating meat, they eventually began to eat human flesh. All the sons and daughters born to them became rākṣasas. Mahāmati, [this is the result of] eating meat.

Because sentient beings rely on the past habit of eating meat, they are mostly reborn among rākṣasas, lions, tigers, wolves, jackals, leopards, cats, ferrets, owls, hawks, eagles, vultures, and falcons.
Among these classes of living beings, each protects its own body and does not allow others to find an opportunity against it;
yet, suffering from hunger, they constantly give rise to evil thoughts of eating the flesh of others. When their lives end, they [again...]
One falls into the evil destinies and undergoes rebirth there; a human body is difficult to obtain, let alone attaining the path to nirvāṇa.
Mahāmati, you should know that those who eat meat have such immeasurable faults as these.
Those who do not eat meat are a mass of immeasurable merit. Mahāmati, yet ordinary people do not understand that eating meat is thus [faulty].
Such faults cause one to lose the merit of not eating [forbidden food]. I shall now briefly explain why it is forbidden to eat meat.
[Tang Translation] Mahāmati, in the past there was a king named Siṃhaja (Born of Lions). He was addicted to the taste of meat and ate various kinds of flesh.
Because he did not cease this practice, he eventually came to eat human beings. His ministers and subjects could no longer endure it, and they all deserted and rebelled against him. He perished.
He lost his kingdom and underwent great suffering and distress.
Mahāmati, Śakra-devānām-indra, while occupying the position of the Heavenly King, because of the residual habit of eating meat in the past, transformed himself into a hawk to pursue a dove.
At that time, I was a king named Śibi; out of compassion for the dove, I cut the flesh from my own body to substitute for its life. Mahāmati, Śakra...
If even those with residual habits still afflict sentient beings, how much more so those others who lack shame and constantly eat meat?
You should know that eating meat afflicts both oneself and others; therefore, a bodhisattva should not eat meat. Mahāmati, in the past there was a king who went hunting on horseback.
His horse became startled and bolted, fleeing into a perilous mountain pass where there was no way back and no human habitation. There was...
A female lion lived together with him in the same place, and they eventually engaged in unwholesome conduct and begot children.

The eldest was named Pādapāṇi (Spotted-foot). Later, he became king and ruled over seven hundred million households. Due to the residual habit of eating meat, he would not eat anything that was not meat;
first he ate birds and beasts, and later even humans. All the sons and daughters born to him were rākṣasas. This [lineage] continued...
Having already been born as such, they are further reborn among lions, jackals, wolves, tigers, leopards, eagles, vultures, and the like;
though they seek a human body, it can never be obtained, let alone the path to nirvana that transcends birth and death. Mahāmati, for those who eat meat, there are such immeasurable faults as these.
By renouncing and abstaining from it, one attains great merit. Yet the ignorant and foolish do not understand this.
This is [the matter of] harm and benefit. Therefore, I now expound it for you: no meat whatsoever should be eaten.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, those who kill for the sake of profit slaughter and trade in living beings;
those foolish beings who eat meat capture various meats by using money as a net. As for those who kill, if they use wealth or...
If one uses hooks and nets to capture those beings that move through the air, water, or on land, and slaughters, sells, or trades them for profit in various ways— O Mahāmati,
there is no such thing as fish or meat that does not involve instruction, seeking, or conceptualization. For this reason, one should not eat meat.
[Wei Translation] Mahāmati, if all people did not eat meat, there would likewise be no one who kills sentient beings.
Because people eat meat, if they cannot find it where it grows, they seek and purchase it elsewhere.
Those motivated by profit kill for the sake of sale, and those who buy cause killing. Therefore, the buyer is no different from the killer. For this reason, one should not eat meat.
It can obstruct the Noble Path. Mahāmati, those who eat meat become attached to its flavor;

eventually, they will come to eat even human flesh, let alone the meat of deer, roe deer, pheasants, rabbits, geese, wild ducks, pigs, sheep, chickens, dogs, camels, donkeys, elephants, horses, dragons, snakes, fish, turtles, or any living being on land or in water that they encounter and do not eat.
Because of their attachment to the taste of meat, they employ various means.
They then slaughter sentient beings, constructing various types of snares, nets, traps, and barriers; they obstruct mountains, set nets upon the ground, and dam rivers and seas.
They place fishing gear everywhere across water and land; with mechanical devices, pits, traps, bows, swords, and poisoned arrows, there is no space left unoccupied.
Whether in the void, on land, or in the waters, all kinds of sentient beings are slaughtered for the sake of eating their flesh.
Mahāmati, hunters, butchers, and those who eat meat possess a firm and evil intent that makes them incapable of practicing forbearance.
Upon seeing the bodies of sentient beings—fresh, plump, and full of flesh—they give rise to a craving for the taste of raw meat.
Pointing to one another, they say, "This is fit to be eaten," without conceiving even a single thought of forbearance. For this reason, I have said regarding the eating of meat:
"Such a person cuts off the seed of great compassion. Mahāmati, when I observe the world, there is no such thing as meat that does not come from a living being.
It is impossible for there to be meat that does not originate from a life taken—whether by oneself, by commanding another to kill, or by not refusing to kill when asked.
If there were such meat that did not issue from a life and yet was considered a fine delicacy, I would [accept it]."
Why do I not permit people to eat meat? Such meat cannot be found anywhere throughout the world. Therefore, I declare that eating meat is a transgression.
Because it cuts off the lineage of the Tathāgata, I do not permit its consumption.
Mahāmati, after my parinirvāṇa, in a future age when the Dharma is about to perish, there will be those who have gone forth from home within my teaching, having shaved off their hair and beards.
They claim, "I am a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas. Wearing my *kāṣāya* robe while remaining as deluded as a small child, they call themselves masters of the Vinaya yet fall into the two extremes.
With their minds distracted by various false conceptualizations (*vitarka-vicāra*), they are greedily attached to the taste of meat.
Following their own subjective views, they claim within the Vinaya that it is permissible to eat meat; they even slander me, saying that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, permitted people [to eat meat].

They eat meat. They also claim that meat was permitted because it was established by a specific regulation, and they slander me by saying that the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, also eats meat himself.

Mahāmati, in all my sūtras—such as the *Gajapramardana*, the *Aṅgulimālīya*, the *Nirvāṇa*, and the *Mahāmegha*—I have not permitted the eating of meat, nor have I said that meat constitutes a flavor of food. Mahāmati, I...
If I were to permit my śrāvaka disciples to eat meat, I would never be able to constantly praise with my own mouth those who practice compassion and act in accordance with reality;
nor would I praise those who practice the dhūta austerities in the śmaśānas;
nor would I praise those who practice the Mahāyāna and abide in the Mahāyāna; nor would I praise...
Regarding those who eat meat: I do not eat it myself, nor do I permit others to eat it. Therefore, I exhort the cultivation of the bodhisattva practice and praise abstaining from eating meat.
I urge one to regard all sentient beings as if they were one's only child. How could I proclaim that I permit the eating of meat?
For the sake of my disciples practicing the three vehicles, I have prohibited all meat in order that they may swiftly attain the fruit [of their practice].
It is not permitted to eat. Why then do you say that within my Vinaya, people are permitted to eat meat?
[Tang Translation] Mahāmati, those who kill living beings do so mostly for human consumption. If people did not eat them, there would be no act of killing.
Therefore, eating meat is a sin equal to that of killing. How strange it is that people in this world are so greedily attached to the taste of meat!
If they take even the flesh from their own bodies to eat it, how much more so would they not refrain from eating that of birds and beasts?
Out of greed for flavor, they employ various means, setting out snares, nets, and traps everywhere; thus, those that move on land, in water, or through the air are all slaughtered.
Even if they do not eat it themselves, they perform these deeds out of greed for profit. Mahāmati, there are also people in the world who...
Lacking compassion in their hearts, they act with exclusive cruelty like rākṣasas.
When they see sentient beings whose bodies are flourishing, they immediately conceive the thought of meat, saying, "This may be eaten.

Mahāmati, there is no meat in the world that has not been killed by oneself, nor killed by another, yet can be eaten without the mind suspecting it was killed [for one's sake]. For this reason, I permit the Śrāvakas...

"Mahāmati, having heard that such meat is permitted, there will be foolish people in future ages who, having gone forth within my Dharma, will falsely explain the Vinaya and corrupt the True Dharma. They will slander me, saying:
'He permitted the eating of meat and he himself once ate it. Mahāmati, if I had permitted the Śrāvakas to eat meat, I would not be [the Tathāgata]."
How should those who dwell in a mind of loving-kindness, those who practice contemplation, those who observe the dhūta ascetic practices,
and those who are intent upon the Mahāyāna exhort all sons and daughters of good family to conceive the thought of all sentient beings as their only child and to abstain from all meat?
"Mahāmati, at times I have spoken of prohibiting five kinds of meat, or restricted ten kinds.
Now, in this sutra, in every way and at all times—with the exception of those cases involving skillful means—I prohibit them entirely.

Mahāmati, even the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has nothing to eat, much less fish or meat; nor does he teach others to do so, because he is preceded by great compassion and regards [all beings] as his own children."
"All sentient beings are like one's only child; therefore, I do not permit them to eat the flesh of their children.

[Wei Translation] Furthermore, it is said: "If, in other sūtras of the Tathāgata, it is stated that three kinds of meat are permitted for people to eat, you should know that such a person does not cultivate the Vinaya.
Because they have gradually severed [the precepts], they proclaim that eating is permissible."
Why is this? Mahāmati, there are two kinds of meat: first, that killed by others; second, that which dies of itself.

Because worldly people say that some meats may be eaten while others may not—stating that the meat of elephants, horses, dragons, snakes, humans, ghosts, monkeys, pigs, dogs, and oxen may not be eaten, whereas other meats may be eaten—the butcher does not distinguish between what is permissible and what is impermissible.
They slaughter all [beings] and sell them everywhere; sentient beings, though innocent, are slain without cause.
For this reason, I have ordained that one must not eat meat from those killed by others or those who have died of natural causes. "Seen, heard, or suspected" refers to meat killed by others;
"not seen, heard, or suspected" refers to meat from those who have died naturally. Therefore, Mahāmati, in my Vinaya I proclaim these words: "In general..."
All meat is an impure food for all śramaṇas and sons of the Śākya; it defiles the pure life and obstructs the factors of the noble path.

There is no means by which it may be eaten. If anyone says that within the Buddha’s Vinaya three kinds of meat are mentioned as being permitted to eat, they do not mean it is permitted to eat them, but rather that they are not permitted to eat them. One should know that such a person is firmly established in the Vinaya.
The Bhikṣuṇī does not slander me. Mahāmati, in this Laṅkā Sūtra, at all times and in all circumstances, there is no expedient means by which meat may be eaten.
Therefore, Mahāmati, my prohibition against eating meat is not for the sake of one person alone;
it applies to all, both present and future. For this reason, Mahāmati, if those deluded people...
Claiming to be a *vinaya*-master, he says that within the *vinaya* it is permitted for people to eat meat; he also slanders me by saying that the Tathāgata himself ate meat.
That foolish person creates a great obstacle of sin. For a long night, he shall fall into places devoid of benefit, places where no noble ones dwell, and places where the Dharma is not heard.
He shall not even encounter the worthy and noble disciples of the present or the future, let alone others.

One shall come to behold the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas. Mahāmati, there are various grains, flours, oils, honeys, and legumes such as sesame and beans that are fit for the constant consumption of Śrāvakas to sustain a pure livelihood.
Yet, I have declared that even these are impure if they are stored improperly or acquired through improper means, and I do not permit their consumption;
how much less, then, would I permit the consumption of the impurity of blood and flesh? Mahāmati, my [disciples]...
Śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattva disciples subsist on the food of Dharma rather than on the food of physical sustenance; how much more so the Tathāgatas?
Mahāmati, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, subsist on the Dharma and abide in the Dharma; they do not have bodies sustained by physical food.
They are free from all craving for the necessities of life, the pursuit of existence, and the like, and are far removed from all afflictions.
Having transcended habitual tendencies, you possess the wisdom of the mind that skillfully discerns and knows all minds; you possess all-knowledge and all-seeing vision.
You behold all sentient beings with impartial compassion. Therefore, Mahāmati, I regard all sentient beings as equal to my only son.
How could I permit the eating of meat? I do not even rejoice in it, much less eat it myself. Great One! [End]
Mahāmati, all such things as onions, leeks, garlic, and scallions are foul-smelling, impure, and capable of obstructing the Noble Path;
they likewise obstruct the pure realms of worldly humans and devas, let alone the karmic rewards of the pure lands of the Buddhas. Alcohol is also like this:
it can obstruct the Noble Path, damage wholesome karma, and give rise to various faults. Therefore, Mahāmati, those who seek the Noble Path—
One must not consume any pungent flavors such as alcohol, meat, onions, leeks, garlic, or scallions.

[Tang Translation: Mahāmati, when I have spoken in various places of prohibiting ten kinds of meat while permitting three, this was for the purpose of gradual prohibition so that they might practice and train.
Now, in this sutra, regarding all meat—whether from animals that died naturally or were killed by others—[it is forbidden].
All [attachments] are completely severed. Mahāmati, I have never permitted my disciples to eat meat;
nor do I permit it now, nor shall I ever permit it in the future. Mahāmati, all meat-eating by those who have left the household life is entirely impure.
Mahāmati, if there should be deluded people who slanderously claim that the Tathāgata permits the eating of meat and even eats it himself, you should know that such persons...
Bound by evil karma, they will inevitably fall forever into states that are not beneficial.
Mahāmati, even my noble disciples do not consume the coarse food of ordinary people, much less the impure food of flesh and blood.
Mahāmati, even Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas subsist solely on the food of Dharma; how much more so the Tathāgata?
Mahāmati, the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata is not a body that consumes mixed food. Mahāmati, I have already eradicated all afflictions.
"I have already cleansed all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). I have well-discriminated the wisdom of all minds.
With great compassion and equanimity, I regard all sentient beings as if they were my only child.
How could I permit my śrāvaka disciples to eat the flesh of their own children, let alone eat it myself? To speak in such a manner is impossible."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses: "In former times, [flesh] was our own kin;
it is base, filthy, and mixed with impurities. Born from the unclean, its mere scent strikes terror into all.

All meats, along with onions, leeks, garlic, and the like, as well as various intoxicating liquors—those who practice the path should always keep far away from these. They should also always avoid sesame oil and..."
The perforated bed. Within it, those various tiny insects are utterly terrified.
[Wei Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse: "Mahāmati, listen attentively! I shall explain the faults of eating food:
wine, meat, onions, leeks, and garlic—these obstruct the factors conducive to the Noble Path. As I contemplate the three realms, and having attained..."
O assembly of the Noble Path: throughout the beginningless cycle of worlds, there has been no one who has not been our kin through successive rebirths.
How can it be that among them some are eaten while others are not? Contemplate the origin of meat: its source is utterly impure, produced from a mixture of pus and blood.
Feces, urine, pus, and mucus are all combined therein; therefore, one who practices the pure conduct should contemplate this and not eat various kinds of meat or onions.
One must also not drink alcohol, and one practicing the path should always keep far away from various types of leeks and garlic.

One should always stay away from sesame oil and not sleep on beds with holes, for the sake of not harming the lives of the myriad tiny insects that fly and dwell there. One must sever the taking of life.
[The Tang Translation] At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse: "All [beings] have once been our kinsmen;
they grow from manifold impurities and cause terror among all sentient beings. Therefore, one should not eat any meat, nor shall one consume onions, leeks, garlic, or various intoxicants.
A practitioner should avoid such impure things, and should also always abstain from sesame oil."
Regarding beds with many holes: because of those tiny insects within them, one becomes greatly terrified;
from food and drink arises negligence (*pramāda*); from negligence arise various discursive thoughts (*vitarka*); and from discursive thoughts arises craving (*rāga*). Therefore, one should not eat.
From food arises sensual desire; desire causes the mind to become deluded and intoxicated. This intoxication increases craving, and one is not liberated from birth and death.
To kill sentient beings for profit, or to obtain various meats through the net of wealth—both are evil karmas; after death, one falls into the Raurava Hell.
If there is no perception of [the animal] being killed for one’s sake, then the three kinds of pure meat do not exist; they do not arise without cause, and therefore they should not be eaten.
For this reason, all practitioners should completely abstain from them, as all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones of the ten directions, unanimously condemn them.

Passing from one state to another, they devour one another; upon death, they fall among the species of tigers and wolves. Foul-smelling and loathsome, those born there are perpetually ignorant and dull-witted.
They are mostly born as Caṇḍālas, hunters, or Tāṃbas; or they are born as Dāyinīs, or among those whose nature is to eat flesh.

Rākṣasas, cats, and wildcats are born everywhere within this world. For the sake of the Bound Elephant, Mahāmegha, Aṅgulimāla, and this Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, I have prohibited the eating of meat in all cases.
[Wei Translation] Consuming meat increases physical strength; from strength arises perverse thought; from perverse thought arises craving.
Therefore, I do not permit the eating of meat. From eating meat, craving is born; a greedy mind leads to delusion and intoxication; delusion and intoxication increase lustful desire.
They do not attain liberation from birth and death. For profit they kill sentient beings; for meat they pursue wealth.

Through the evil karma of these two types of people, they fall after death into the Raurava Hell. The three kinds of "pure meat"—that which is not seen, heard, or suspected—do not exist in this world.
Those who eat meat fall into rebirth among carnivorous creatures; they are foul-smelling, loathsome, and wretched, and they are constantly born among the insane. They are born many times over.
In the homes of *caṇḍālas*, hunters, and butchers; or among rākṣasīs and those places where meat-eaters dwell—such as among rākṣasas, cats, and wildcats—one is born there due to eating meat.
This is taught in the *Gaja-pārśva*, the *Mahāmegha*, the *Nirvāṇa*, and the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*.
And in the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, I have declared that one should not eat meat:
"Food and drink give rise to negligence; negligence gives rise to false thoughts; from these thoughts arises craving. Therefore, one should not eat [meat].
Because false thoughts give rise to craving, the mind becomes intoxicated by craving; when the mind is intoxicated, it increases desire."
They are not liberated from birth and death. To kill sentient beings for profit, or to take various meats for the sake of wealth—both are evil karmas;
after death, they fall into the Raurava Hell. That which is not sought, not commanded, and not requested—these three types are called "pure.
Yet such meat does not exist in this world; those who eat it I condemn. They will prey upon one another and, after death, fall among the fierce beasts in a foul and stinking place.
And they become insane; for this reason, one should not eat [meat]. Those born from the wombs of hunters, caṇḍālas, butchers, and rākṣasas—all these are the retribution for eating meat.
As stated in the *Elephant’s Flank*, the *Great Cloud*, the *Nirvāṇa*, and the *Aṅgulimālīya*.
And in this Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, I have prohibited the eating of meat.
It is censured by all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Śrāvakas; those who eat it without shame or remorse will remain perpetually ignorant and deluded in every birth.

It has already been stated that by abandoning meat seen, heard, or suspected, one has severed all [attachment to] flesh. Yet, through deluded thoughts and lack of awareness, one is born into places where meat is consumed;
this is like the fault of lustful desire, obstructing noble liberation. Alcohol, meat, scallions, leeks, and garlic are all obstacles to the Noble Path.
Sentient beings in future ages will speak out of ignorance regarding meat, saying: "This is pure and without fault; the Buddha permitted us to eat it.
One should regard eating it as taking medicine, or like eating the flesh of one's own son; being content and generating revulsion for the world, one should practice the mendicant’s way of life.

For one who dwells securely in a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), I say they are always free from aversion; even tigers, wolves, and all manner of evil beasts may constantly dwell and roam together with them.
Yet, when [beings] eat various kinds of flesh and blood, all sentient beings become terrified. Therefore, the practitioner, out of a mind of loving-kindness, does not eat meat.
Those who eat meat lack compassion and wisdom; they turn their backs forever on true liberation and contravene the outward signs of the noble ones. Therefore, one should not eat meat.
By not eating meat, one will be born into the lineage of brahmins, in various places of spiritual cultivation, and into families of wisdom and prosperity. This results from abstaining from meat.
[Wei Translation] The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, as well as the Śrāvakas, all censure those who eat meat without shame or remorse;

such people shall always be deranged throughout their successive lives. Previously, when I spoke of meat seen, heard, or suspected, I had already forbidden all meat; yet through deluded thoughts they fail to realize this.

Therefore, one should conceive the thought that eating meat is like [eating] raw flesh. Just as the fault of sensual desire obstructs noble liberation, so too do alcohol, meat, onions, leeks, and garlic all serve as obstacles to the Noble Path.
Sentient beings in future ages will speak out of delusion regarding meat, saying: "This is pure and without fault;
the Buddha permitted us to eat it. One should regard pure food as being like medicine, or like eating the flesh of one's own son, and remain content.
One who has developed revulsion and practices by begging for alms, dwelling securely in a mind of loving-kindness—I say that such a person is always free from revulsion [toward the world].
Even lions, jackals, tigers, and wolves may constantly dwell and roam together with them. Since those who eat flesh cause terror in those who see them, how could one possibly consume it?

Therefore, the practitioner maintains a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and does not eat meat. Eating meat severs the heart of loving-kindness, distances one from *nirvāṇa* and liberation, and contravenes the teachings of the Sages;

thus, the eating of meat is not permitted. By not eating meat, one preserves the pure lineage of the Brahmās, as well as all paths of cultivation, wisdom, and prosperity. All these arise from abstaining from meat.
[The Tang Translation: Having eaten [meat], they lack shame and remorse; in every birth they shall always be insane. They are loathed by all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Śrāvakas.
Having first declared that meat is forbidden on account of what has been seen, heard, or suspected, I have already prohibited all meat; yet because of their evil habits, [they persist].
The foolish engage in false conceptualization; just as craving obstructs liberation, so it is with meat and the like.
If there are those who eat it, they cannot enter the Noble Path. Sentient beings of future ages will speak out of delusion regarding meat, saying:
"This is pure and without fault; the Buddha has permitted us to eat it. Even pure meat is like medicine; one should regard it as the flesh of one's own child. Therefore—
The practitioner who knows the proper measure when begging for alms and dwells securely in a mind of loving-kindness—I say that such a one is always weary of and detached from [sensual life].
Such a person may dwell and travel together with lions, tigers, and wolves; yet those who eat meat turn their backs on liberation and violate the perception of being a noble one.
This causes sentient beings to give rise to fear; therefore, one should not eat it.
If one abstains from all things such as alcohol and meat, one will surely be born among the noble and holy ones, possessing abundant wealth and wisdom.
The Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, Compiled Translation, Volume Four, Part Two, Complete.
